title: The Theology of Covenant Marriage
body:
The most dangerous thing that has happened to marriage in the modern West is not the sexual revolution. It is not no-fault divorce. It is not the redefinition of the institution in law or culture. The most dangerous thing is that we stopped understanding what kind of thing marriage is. We turned a covenant into a contract, and then we wondered why it kept breaking.

A contract is an exchange of goods and services between two parties who retain their autonomy. If one party fails to deliver, the other is released. A covenant is something else entirely. A covenant is an exchange of selves. It does not say, "I will give you this as long as you give me that." It says, "I am yours. Period. The terms do not change when the feelings do." The entire biblical narrative — from Eden to Sinai to Calvary — runs on covenant. And marriage, in Scripture, is not merely an illustration of that narrative. It is one of its primary theaters.

I have performed more than a hundred weddings in fifteen years of ministry. I have watched couples stand at the altar in the full blaze of romantic certainty, voices steady, eyes locked, utterly convinced that their love is the kind that will not falter. I have sat with some of those same couples five years later in my office, the certainty gone, the voices unsteady, asking whether God would really hold them to promises they made when they did not know what the promises would cost. The answer to that question requires a theology of covenant, and the church has largely failed to provide one.

We live in a culture that treats every relationship as provisional. Dating apps have encoded optionality into the mechanics of romance — there is always another profile, another possibility, another person who might be a better fit. This consumer logic does not evaporate at the altar. It follows people into their marriages, whispering that commitment is conditional, that satisfaction is the metric, and that a better option might be one swipe away. The covenant cuts against this logic with the full force of the biblical tradition, and the cut is meant to draw blood.

The Ancient Near Eastern Background

To understand biblical covenant, you must understand what covenants meant in the ancient world before Israel adapted the form for its own purposes. In the ancient Near East, a covenant — Hebrew berith — was the most solemn form of agreement two parties could enter. The Hittite suzerainty treaties of the second millennium BCE established a pattern: a powerful king would bind himself to a vassal, not because the vassal had earned the relationship, but because the king chose to extend it. The treaty included a historical prologue recounting what the king had done, stipulations for the vassal's conduct, blessings for faithfulness, curses for unfaithfulness, and a ceremony involving the cutting of animals.

That last detail matters more than it might seem. The Hebrew phrase for making a covenant is karat berith — literally, "to cut a covenant." In Genesis 15, when God makes His covenant with Abraham, the patriarch cuts animals in half and arranges the pieces in two rows with a path between them. In the ancient world, both parties walked between the pieces, symbolically saying, "May I be torn apart like these animals if I break this covenant." But in Genesis 15, something extraordinary happens. God alone — represented as a smoking fire pot and a blazing torch — passes between the pieces. Abraham does not walk. God walks alone. The covenant is unilateral. God binds Himself, absorbs the risk, and stakes His own integrity on the promise.

This is the theological DNA that enters every biblical covenant, including marriage. And the church has largely forgotten it.

The covenant at Sinai deepened the pattern. In Exodus 24, Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice and throws half on the altar (representing God) and half on the people. The blood binds both parties. It is visceral, physical, unforgettable. The people who stood in that blood never forgot what they had entered. The modern wedding, with its flowers and photographers and reception playlists, has sanitized the ceremony to the point where the gravity of what is happening — two people binding their lives together in a bond that God Himself witnesses — is almost entirely obscured. We have made the covenant pretty. It was never meant to be pretty. It was meant to be permanent.

Marriage as Divine Pedagogy

The prophet Hosea received the strangest ministry assignment in all of Scripture: marry a woman who will be unfaithful to you. Gomer's infidelity was not incidental to Hosea's prophetic work. It was the prophetic work. God used a broken marriage to teach Israel something about divine love that no sermon could have communicated — that the covenant partner does not leave when the other partner wanders. That faithfulness is not contingent on reciprocity. That love, in the biblical sense, is not an emotion that arises in response to the beloved's worthiness but a decision that persists in the face of the beloved's unworthiness.

Jeremiah extended this imagery. Ezekiel made it graphic — startlingly, uncomfortably graphic, in ways that most preachers skip over. By the time Paul writes Ephesians 5, he is working with a metaphorical tradition that has been building for a thousand years: marriage is an icon of the relationship between God and God's people. "This mystery is profound," Paul writes, "and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." The profundity is not merely spiritual. It is structural. Marriage, in the biblical imagination, is designed to function as a living parable — a daily, embodied demonstration of what it looks like when two parties bind themselves together in a bond that neither party can unilaterally dissolve.

This is why the stakes are so high. Not because God is a rule-maker who enjoys holding people to uncomfortable commitments. But because marriage is the primary institution through which human beings learn what covenant love feels like from the inside. Every other covenant in Scripture — the Abrahamic, the Mosaic, the Davidic, the New — uses marriage as its interpretive key. If you gut the institution of its covenantal content, you lose the analogy, and with it, the capacity to understand the God who made it.

Karl Barth understood this with characteristic precision. In Church Dogmatics III/4, he argued that the covenant relationship between God and humanity is not merely illustrated by marriage but is the archetype of which marriage is the ectype. Marriage does not give us a metaphor for understanding God. God's covenant gives us the reality that marriage reflects. The order is important. We do not project our experience of marriage onto God. God's covenantal faithfulness is the original; our marriages are the copies. And the copies are meant to teach us something about the original that we could not learn any other way.

What Covenant Is Not

Before going further, I need to say what covenant marriage is not, because the concept has been badly abused.

Covenant is not a weapon. I have watched men use the theology of covenant to trap their wives in abusive marriages, quoting Malachi 2:16 — "I hate divorce, says the Lord" — while their wives carried bruises that the congregation was not allowed to see. This is not covenant theology. This is coercion dressed in religious language, and it is blasphemous. The God who makes covenants is the God who delivered Israel from Egypt, the God who does not tolerate the oppression of the vulnerable. A theology of covenant that enables abuse has betrayed the very God it claims to honor.

Covenant is not mere endurance. Two people can remain legally married for fifty years while living in emotional exile from each other — two strangers sharing a roof and a tax return, performing the choreography of marriage without inhabiting its substance. This is not faithfulness. It is inertia. The covenant calls not merely for presence but for engagement, not merely for staying but for turning toward the other person again and again, even when every instinct says to turn away.

Covenant is not the absence of cost. The prosperity gospel has a marital counterpart — the assumption that if you do marriage God's way, it will be satisfying, fulfilling, and deeply pleasurable. Sometimes it will be. Sometimes it will be the hardest thing you have ever done, a daily crucifixion of your preferences and your autonomy, a relentless exposure of selfishness you did not know you carried. The covenant does not promise ease. It promises presence. And presence, in a fallen world, is costly.

And covenant is not a legal fiction. The state can dissolve a marriage with a signature and a filing fee. The covenant exists in a different jurisdiction entirely — the jurisdiction of the God who witnesses the vows and holds both parties accountable to them. This does not mean that divorce is impossible or that every divorce is sinful. It means that the dissolution of a covenant is a far more serious matter than the dissolution of a contract, and the church that treats it casually has misunderstood both the institution and the God who stands behind it.

The Reformation and the Loss of Sacrament

Something significant happened to the theology of marriage during the Protestant Reformation, and its effects are still with us. The medieval Catholic Church had classified marriage as one of seven sacraments — a visible sign of invisible grace, an institution that not only symbolized divine reality but participated in it. When Luther and Calvin challenged the sacramental system, they demoted marriage from sacrament to ordinance. They did not do this carelessly. Their concern was legitimate: the sacramental classification had given the church legal jurisdiction over marriage, creating a sprawling canon-law apparatus that was often more about institutional power than pastoral care.

But something was lost in the demotion. When marriage ceased to be a sacrament, it became easier to think of it as merely a social arrangement — a good and godly one, but an arrangement nonetheless. The Reformers themselves did not take this step. Luther called marriage a "worldly thing" but meant by this that it belonged to God's governance of creation, not that it was trivial. Calvin saw marriage as a covenant that mirrored God's covenant with Israel. But their theological heirs, over the centuries, gradually drained the institution of its theological density. By the time the Enlightenment arrived, the groundwork had been laid for marriage to become what it is now in the popular imagination: a contract between two individuals pursuing mutual happiness.

John Witte Jr., in his exhaustive study "From Sacrament to Contract," traced this trajectory with devastating precision. The movement from sacrament to contract was not a single event but a slow erosion, spanning five centuries, in which the theological content of marriage was progressively replaced by legal and therapeutic categories. We did not wake up one morning in a culture that treats marriage as disposable. We arrived here by a long road of theological withdrawal.

The road back requires the church to recover what was lost without repeating the errors that prompted the Reformation in the first place. Marriage need not be a sacrament in the technical, Catholic sense to carry sacramental weight. It can be — and should be — understood as a covenant that participates in the reality it reflects, a human institution that carries divine freight, a visible sign that points to an invisible God whose faithfulness is the ground on which every human promise stands.

What Covenant Marriage Demands

If marriage is a covenant rather than a contract, what does that demand of the people inside it? Three things, at minimum.

First, it demands that you stop keeping score. A contract lives by the ledger — I gave this, you owe that. A covenant burns the ledger. This does not mean that imbalances do not matter. It means that the response to imbalance is not withdrawal but confrontation and grace — speaking the truth in love, as Paul instructs in Ephesians 4, and then refusing to hold the debt. The moment you begin tracking what your spouse owes you, you have exited the covenant and entered the marketplace.

Second, it demands that you tell the truth. Covenant relationships cannot survive on pretense. The entire prophetic tradition is God telling Israel the truth about itself — not to destroy but to heal. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend," Proverbs 27:6 says. In marriage, this means that real love will sometimes require you to say the thing your spouse does not want to hear, and it will require you to hear the thing you do not want said. Both are acts of covenant faithfulness. Silence, in a covenant, is not peace. It is abandonment.

Third, it demands that you die. This is the part no one puts on the wedding invitation. The cruciform shape of marriage — the pattern Paul describes in Ephesians 5 when he tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her — is not a metaphor for mild self-sacrifice. It is a description of death. The death of your right to be right. The death of your expectation that marriage exists to make you happy. The death of the self that entered the covenant imagining it could be kept at manageable cost.

I have died these deaths. Imperfectly, incompletely, with more resistance than I want to admit. I have stood in my own kitchen at eleven o'clock at night, exhausted, arguing about something that will not matter in a week, and felt every fiber of my being resist the act of laying down my position. The covenant does not care about my fibers. It calls me to die. And in the dying — not always, not immediately, but eventually — something comes to life that could not have existed any other way.

The Promise and Its Cost

The deepest paradox of covenant marriage is that its constraints produce the very freedom they appear to deny. The commitment that forecloses other options is the same commitment that creates the safety necessary for genuine intimacy. You cannot be fully known by someone who might leave. You cannot be fully vulnerable with someone whose presence is contingent on your performance. The covenant — the unconditional, irrevocable, until-death commitment — is the only container strong enough to hold the full weight of two human lives pressing against each other.

Stanley Hauerwas, the Methodist ethicist at Duke, put it with his characteristic bluntness: "We always marry the wrong person." His point was not cynicism. It was that the person you marry will inevitably turn out to be different from the person you thought you were marrying, and the person you are will inevitably turn out to be different from the person your spouse thought they were marrying. The question is not whether you married the right person. The question is whether you will keep your covenant with the actual person who shows up — the one with the real flaws, the real struggles, the real capacity to wound you in ways you did not know you could be wounded.

The covenant says yes. Not because the feelings persist. Not because the cost is manageable. Not because the alternative is worse. The covenant says yes because the God who made the covenant is a God who says yes — who walked between the pieces alone, who absorbed the curse, who kept the promise when every rational calculation said to walk away.

I have watched couples arrive at this yes after years of wandering in the no. I have watched marriages that should have ended — by every measure of human wisdom, by every calculus of cost and benefit — survive because two people decided that the covenant was more real than the pain. Their marriages are not fairy tales. They are scarred, limping, hard-won things. But they carry a weight that the easy marriages do not. They have been tested. They know what they are made of. And what they are made of is not their own strength. It is the faithfulness of a God who does not break His promises, even when the people inside those promises break everything else.

We do not stay married because marriage is easy. We do not stay married because we are strong. We stay married because we made a promise in the presence of a God who keeps His promises, and we have staked our lives on the wager that His pattern — not ours — is the one worth following.

That wager will cost you everything. It is also the only path to the kind of love that the contract cannot produce — the love that has been through the fire and came out not unburned but refined. The love that knows what it has survived. The love that, precisely because it was never contingent on feeling, outlasts every feeling and becomes something the world cannot explain.

The culture offers you a contract. The gospel offers you a covenant. The contract is safer. The covenant is better. And the distance between the two is the distance between a transaction and a life.
excerpt: Marriage is not a contract between two consumers shopping for satisfaction — it is a covenant between two sinners binding themselves to a promise that will outlast every feeling they brought to the altar.

title: What 'One Flesh' Actually Means in Hebrew
body:
Every Christian who has attended a wedding has heard the phrase. Most who have heard it think they know what it means. "And the two shall become one flesh." It appears in Genesis 2:24, gets quoted by Jesus in Matthew 19 and Mark 10, and shows up again in Paul's argument in Ephesians 5. It is one of the most frequently cited phrases in all of Scripture on the subject of marriage. It is also one of the most poorly understood.

The popular readings fall into two camps, both of them reductive. The sentimental reading treats "one flesh" as a poetic description of emotional closeness — two hearts becoming one, two souls merging, the romantic ideal of complete union. The sexual reading treats "one flesh" as a reference to physical intercourse — the bodily act that consummates the marriage and creates the bond. Both readings contain a fragment of truth. Neither comes close to what the Hebrew text is actually saying.

To understand "one flesh," you have to go back to the language, back to the garden, and back to a worldview in which human identity was not what we think it is. You have to set aside twenty-first-century assumptions about the body, about the self, and about what it means to be a human being. The text will not meet you on your terms. You must go to it on its own.

The Hebrew Word: Basar

The Hebrew word translated "flesh" is basar. And basar does not mean what the English word "flesh" means. In English, "flesh" typically refers to the physical body — skin, muscle, tissue. It carries connotations of the material as opposed to the spiritual, the body as opposed to the soul. This dualism — body versus soul, material versus spiritual — is deeply embedded in Western thought. It comes not from the Bible but from Plato, filtered through Descartes, and it distorts nearly everything the Bible says about human beings.

In Hebrew anthropology, basar does not refer to the body as opposed to the soul. It refers to the whole person in their creaturely vulnerability. When the psalmist writes, "All basar is like grass" (echoed in Isaiah 40:6), he is not saying that human bodies are temporary while human souls are permanent. He is saying that human beings — the whole of them, body and soul together — are fragile, mortal, dependent creatures. Basar is the word for the human being as finite. As needy. As the kind of creature that bleeds when cut and dies when abandoned.

Hans Walter Wolff, in his landmark study "Anthropology of the Old Testament," demonstrated that biblical Hebrew has no word that corresponds to the Greek soma (body) in the dualistic sense. The Hebrew person is not a soul trapped in a body. The Hebrew person is a nephesh — a living being, an animated body, a bodily soul. There is no division. When Genesis says that God formed the man from dust and breathed into him the breath of life and the man became a nephesh chayyah — a living being — it is not describing the insertion of a soul into a body. It is describing the creation of a unified creature who is irreducibly both.

This matters because the Western church has been reading Genesis through Platonic lenses for so long that it has forgotten what the text looked like without them. When a first-century rabbi heard "one flesh," he did not think of two bodies joining while two souls remained separate. He thought of two entire persons — their fears, their hopes, their histories, their bodies, their breath — becoming a single entity. The scope of basar is wider than anything the English word "flesh" can contain.

This is the anthropological background you need before you can understand "one flesh." The phrase is not operating inside a body-soul dualism. It is operating inside a worldview in which the human person is an indivisible unity, and "flesh" means the totality of that person in their vulnerability.

The Genesis 2 Context

The phrase appears in Genesis 2:24: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (ESV). Three things happen in this sentence, and all three are radical.

First, the man leaves. In the ancient Near East, this was socially disruptive. The patrilocal family system meant that sons stayed in their father's household, brought their wives into that household, and lived under the authority of the patriarch. For the man to "leave" his father and mother was not merely a change of address. It was a rupture in the social fabric, a declaration that the new union takes precedence over the family of origin. The rabbinical tradition recognized the force of this: the Talmud (Kiddushin 30b) notes that a man's obligation to his wife supersedes his obligation to his parents. In a culture where parental authority was nearly absolute, this was an extraordinary claim.

Second, the man "holds fast" — Hebrew davaq — to his wife. This is not a gentle word. It is the word used in Deuteronomy 10:20 for clinging to God: "You shall fear the Lord your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him." It is the word Ruth uses when she refuses to leave Naomi: "Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge" (Ruth 1:16). Davaq means to cling with the entirety of your being, to refuse separation, to bind yourself so completely to the other that your identity becomes inseparable from theirs. It is a word of total commitment, not of romantic feeling.

Third, they become "one flesh." And here is where the text does something that no amount of sentimentality or reductionism can contain.

What "One" Means

The Hebrew word for "one" in this passage is echad. It is the same word used in the Shema, the foundational confession of Israelite faith: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is echad" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Theologians have debated for centuries whether echad in the Shema means "one" in the sense of absolute singularity or "one" in the sense of composite unity — a unity that contains diversity within itself. The Trinitarian implications are well-known and contested. But the linguistic point stands: echad can denote a unity that is not simple but complex.

When Genesis says that two people become echad basar — one flesh — it is describing the creation of a new entity that did not exist before. Not a merger that eliminates the two individuals. Not a fusion that dissolves difference. A unity that holds two distinct persons together in a bond so deep that they become, in some real sense, a single organism. The metaphor is not mathematical (1 + 1 = 1). It is organic. Two vines grafted together, sharing one root system, drawing from the same source, growing in the same direction while remaining two distinct plants.

This is why Jesus, when asked about divorce in Matthew 19, quotes Genesis 2:24 and then adds: "So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate." The logic is not contractual — you made a deal, so keep it. The logic is ontological — something has happened to you. You are no longer what you were. A new reality has come into existence, and to tear it apart is to do violence to what God has made.

The rabbinical commentators understood this. Rashi, the great medieval Jewish commentator, noted that the phrase "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" in Genesis 2:23 established a kinship between the man and the woman that was deeper than any other human kinship. Parents and children are related by blood. Husband and wife are related by creation itself — by the divine act that made them for each other. The one-flesh union is not an addition to the natural order. It is part of the natural order, woven into the fabric of creation before the first sin was committed.

The Sexual Dimension

Sex is part of this — but not in the way the popular reading assumes. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 6:16, quotes the "one flesh" passage in the context of warning against prostitution: "Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, 'The two will become one flesh.'" Paul's argument is not that sex creates a marriage. It is that sex creates a bond — that the physical act of sexual union enacts something real, something that cannot be undone by walking away. This is why casual sex is, in the biblical framework, an oxymoron. There is no such thing as casual union. Every sexual encounter creates a one-flesh reality, whether the participants intend it or not.

But the "one flesh" of Genesis 2 is not reducible to sex. It includes sexual union, but it also includes shared meals, shared grief, shared laughter, shared silence, shared failure. It includes the daily interweaving of two lives at every level — economic, emotional, spiritual, physical. The one-flesh union is not a mystical event that happens at the altar and then floats above the mundane. It is an earthy, bodily, daily reality that is built and deepened through the thousand small acts of shared life.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in a wedding sermon he wrote from his prison cell for his niece and her fiance (a sermon he never got to deliver), put it with startling clarity: "It is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love." The one-flesh union is not the product of love. It is the container in which love grows. And the container must be stronger than the feelings it holds, because the feelings will fluctuate wildly across the decades while the container must remain.

The Vulnerability of Basar

Return to basar — flesh as vulnerability. When two people become one flesh, they become one vulnerability. The wounds of one become the wounds of the other. The shame of one becomes the exposure of the other. This is terrifying. It is meant to be.

Notice what happens immediately before and immediately after the "one flesh" statement in Genesis 2. Before it, in verse 23, the man sees the woman for the first time and speaks the first poetry in Scripture: "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." After it, in verse 25: "And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed." The sequence is intentional. Recognition. Union. Vulnerability without shame.

In the garden, before the fall, nakedness carried no shame because there was nothing to hide. The one-flesh union existed in a context of total transparency — no secrets, no pretense, no self-protection. And then Genesis 3 happened, and the first thing the man and the woman did after disobeying God was make coverings for themselves. They hid their basar. They hid their vulnerability. They hid from each other and from God.

Every marriage since Genesis 3 has been an attempt to recover what was lost in the garden — the capacity to be fully naked, fully known, fully exposed, and fully safe. We manage it in moments. We lose it for months. We spend decades trying to unlearn the instinct to cover ourselves, to hide our basar, to protect ourselves from the very person with whom we are supposed to be one.

The covering takes a thousand forms. The husband who will not admit he is afraid. The wife who will not say she is angry. The spouse who performs competence in public and collapses in private, alone, because the one-flesh union was supposed to mean that you could collapse with someone, not away from them. Every cover is a small betrayal of the text — a refusal to be one flesh, a retreat into the separated self that Genesis 3 inaugurated and that Christ's death was designed to heal.

What This Means for Us

If "one flesh" means what the Hebrew says it means — the union of two whole persons in their total creaturely vulnerability — then marriage is both more terrifying and more beautiful than any popular reading has allowed. It is more terrifying because it demands an exposure that every instinct in our fallen nature resists. It is more beautiful because it offers a participation in the very life of the God who is Himself a unity-in-diversity, a communion of persons bound together in self-giving love.

I have been married long enough to know that the one-flesh reality is not a state you achieve once and maintain automatically. It is a daily choice — the choice to remain exposed, to resist the urge to cover, to keep turning toward the person you married even when everything in you wants to hide. Some days, the unity is palpable. Some days, you feel like two strangers who happen to share a mortgage. Both days are part of the same marriage. Both are within the scope of the same flesh.

The text does not promise that the one-flesh union will always feel like unity. It promises that it is unity — that something real has been created, something that exists whether you feel it or not, something that sustains the marriage on the days when the marriage does not seem to sustain itself.

The implications extend beyond the individual marriage. If the one-flesh union is as profound as the text claims, then the church's treatment of marriage — its premarital counseling, its pastoral care, its theology of divorce and remarriage — must carry the same weight. We cannot treat as casual what God treats as ontological. We cannot reduce to a lifestyle choice what Scripture presents as a new creation. The one-flesh union is not a metaphor for closeness. It is a statement about reality — about what happens when God takes two people and makes them one.

The Hebrew does not offer you a romance. It offers you an identity. You are no longer merely yourself. You are bone of another's bone, flesh of another's flesh, and the God who made you one is the same God who holds you together when you cannot hold yourselves.

I think of the couples I know who have been married thirty, forty, fifty years. The ones who have done the work of remaining one flesh — not perfectly, not without seasons of distance and covering, but persistently — carry something in their presence that the young couples do not yet have. It is not happiness, exactly. It is more like gravity. A weight. The accumulated density of two lives so intertwined that you can no longer tell where one ends and the other begins. Their sentences finish each other's thoughts, not because they have rehearsed it but because their thinking has become shared. Their bodies lean toward each other unconsciously. Their grief is shared grief. Their joy is shared joy. They are basar — flesh, whole persons, vulnerable and mortal — and they have become, through decades of daily choice, echad. One.

That is what the Hebrew text is pointing toward. Not a destination you arrive at on the wedding day. A reality you grow into across a lifetime — slowly, unevenly, with more failure than success, and with the steadying hand of a God who holds what you cannot hold yourselves.

That is what "one flesh" actually means. Not a feeling. Not a metaphor. Not a theological abstraction. A reality — earthy, bodily, vulnerable, permanent — enacted in the daily stuff of shared life and sustained by the God who invented it before we had any idea what it would cost.
excerpt: The phrase 'one flesh' has been sentimentalized into a Hallmark card and weaponized into a demand for sex — but the Hebrew text is doing something far stranger and more radical than either reading allows.

title: Communication in Marriage: What the Research Says
body:
The advice you have been given about communication in marriage is almost certainly wrong. Not because the people who gave it were malicious, but because they were drawing on intuition rather than evidence, on slogans rather than research. "Just talk to each other." "Use I-statements." "Never go to bed angry." These are the communication commandments of popular marriage advice, and they are, at best, partially true. At worst, they are actively misleading.

Meanwhile, the actual research — four decades of clinical observation, longitudinal studies, and physiological measurement — tells a story that is both more complex and more hopeful than the slogans suggest. It tells us that communication in marriage is not primarily about technique. It is about physiology, about the patterns that form in the first three minutes of a conversation, about the ratio of positive to negative interactions, and about something the researchers call "repair attempts" that most couples have never heard of. The data does not confirm what we assumed. It rarely does.

I am a pastor, not a clinician. But I have spent fifteen years sitting with couples in crisis, and I have learned that good theology without good data produces counsel that sounds wise and does harm. The research matters. The God who made us embodied creatures is not threatened by empirical investigation into how those bodies work. He is the architect of the nervous system. Understanding how He built it is not a departure from faith. It is a form of worship.

The Gottman Revolution

No researcher has contributed more to our understanding of marital communication than John Gottman. Beginning in the late 1970s at the University of Washington, Gottman and his colleagues brought couples into a laboratory setting they called the "Love Lab" — an apartment-like space wired with cameras and physiological monitors — and watched them talk. For hours. About dishes, about money, about the thing that happened at Thanksgiving in 1997. They measured heart rate, skin conductance, blood pressure, and facial expressions while couples discussed areas of conflict.

What Gottman found overturned decades of conventional wisdom. The difference between couples who stayed together and couples who divorced was not whether they fought. All couples fight. The difference was how they fought — specifically, the presence or absence of four patterns that Gottman called "The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse": criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling.

Criticism is distinct from complaint. A complaint targets a specific behavior: "You said you would pick up the groceries and you forgot." Criticism targets the person: "You always forget everything. You are so irresponsible." The difference is the difference between "you did something I did not like" and "you are defective." Couples who habitually frame their complaints as criticisms are building a narrative in which their spouse is the problem, and that narrative becomes self-fulfilling. The criticized spouse begins to internalize the story — I am the problem, I am defective, nothing I do will ever be enough — and the internalization produces either withdrawal or counter-attack, both of which accelerate the cycle.

Contempt is the most corrosive of the four. It includes mockery, eye-rolling, name-calling, and hostile humor — any communication that conveys disgust or superiority. Gottman's research found that contempt is the single greatest predictor of divorce. Not conflict. Not incompatibility. Not financial stress. Contempt. When one spouse communicates to the other, through words or body language, that the other is beneath them, the marriage is in mortal danger. The physiological data bears this out: contempt elevates the heart rate of the receiving partner, flooding the body with cortisol, activating the fight-or-flight response. The body of the person being treated with contempt responds as though it is under physical attack. Because, in a very real sense, it is.

Gottman's data was so robust that he could predict, with 93.6 percent accuracy, which couples would divorce within six years based on observing fifteen minutes of conversation. Ninety-three percent. The numbers are staggering, and they should humble every pastor who has ever counseled a couple based on nothing more than theological intuition and good intentions.

Defensiveness and Stonewalling

Defensiveness is the natural human response to perceived attack, and it feels entirely justified in the moment. When your spouse says, "You forgot to call the plumber," and you respond, "Well, you did not remind me, and besides, I have been dealing with everything else around here," you are defending yourself. And you are also escalating the conflict, because defensiveness communicates, "The problem is not me. The problem is you." It is a form of counter-attack disguised as self-protection.

Stonewalling is withdrawal. It happens when one partner — overwhelmingly, research shows, the male partner — disengages from the conversation entirely. The eyes go blank. The responses stop. The person is physically present and emotionally absent. Gottman's physiological data showed that stonewalling is not a conscious choice to be cruel. It is a physiological response to what Gottman called "diffuse physiological arousal" — the state in which the heart rate exceeds 100 beats per minute, the adrenal system floods the body with stress hormones, and the prefrontal cortex goes offline. The person who stonewalls is not choosing to shut down. Their body is shutting down for them. The system is overwhelmed, and the only option the nervous system offers is retreat.

This physiological reality has profound implications for the advice "never go to bed angry." Sometimes you should go to bed angry. Sometimes the most productive thing a couple can do in a heated conflict is stop, separate, allow the nervous system to return to baseline, and return to the conversation twenty minutes later — or the next morning — when the body is no longer in survival mode. The Gottman Institute's research suggests that effective self-soothing requires at least twenty minutes of separation before re-engagement. The body needs time. Good communication requires honoring that.

I have preached "never go to bed angry" from the pulpit, quoting Ephesians 4:26 with the confidence of a man who had never read a single study on autonomic arousal. I was wrong. Paul's instruction not to let the sun go down on your anger is a principle about the urgency of reconciliation, not a clinical protocol. And the best way to honor that principle — the way that actually produces reconciliation rather than escalation — sometimes involves putting the conversation to rest until both bodies are capable of conducting it well.

The First Three Minutes

One of Gottman's most striking findings concerned what he called "startup." His research demonstrated that the trajectory of a conflict conversation is determined, with remarkable reliability, by its first three minutes. Conversations that begin with what he called a "harsh startup" — criticism, blame, contempt — almost never recover, regardless of what happens in the middle or at the end. Conversations that begin with a "soft startup" — specific complaint rather than global criticism, expressed need rather than accusation — have a dramatically higher chance of reaching resolution.

This finding has a theological parallel that I cannot ignore. The Proverbs are filled with observations about the power of first words: "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Proverbs 18:21). The ancient wisdom tradition knew what the laboratory confirmed: how you begin determines where you end. And the responsibility for how a conversation begins belongs to the person who starts it.

I say this knowing that I have started conversations badly more times than I can count. I have walked into the kitchen with a grievance pre-loaded, tone already set, verdict already rendered before my wife had a chance to speak. The research tells me that in those moments, I was not just being unfair. I was making resolution physiologically impossible. The harsh startup activates the same stress response in the listener that stonewalling reflects in the listener's partner. The body goes to war before the mind has a chance to engage.

The Magic Ratio

Perhaps Gottman's most famous finding is the 5:1 ratio. In stable marriages, the ratio of positive interactions to negative interactions during conflict is at least five to one. Five moments of connection, affirmation, humor, affection, or agreement for every one moment of criticism, disagreement, or frustration. In marriages headed for divorce, the ratio drops to 0.8:1 or lower — nearly equal negative and positive, or more negative than positive.

This ratio operates not only during conflict but throughout the daily life of the marriage. Gottman's research on what he called "bids for connection" — the small moments when one partner reaches out to the other for attention, affirmation, or engagement — found that couples who stayed together responded to each other's bids approximately 86 percent of the time. Couples who divorced responded approximately 33 percent of the time. The difference between a lasting marriage and a failing one was not the grand gestures. It was the accumulated weight of ten thousand tiny responses to ten thousand tiny invitations.

"Did you see that bird in the yard?" is a bid. It is not really about the bird. It is about connection — the desire to share a moment of attention with the person you live with. The spouse who looks up from the phone and says, "Which one?" has turned toward the bid. The spouse who says nothing, or grunts, or says, "I am busy," has turned away. One instance means little. A pattern means everything.

The theological implications of the bid research are striking. The God of Scripture is, by any measure, a God who makes bids for connection — who speaks to humanity in garden and wilderness and temple and incarnation, who reaches out again and again to a people who turn away again and again. The entire prophetic tradition is a record of divine bids and human rejection. And the love of God is not destroyed by the rejection. It persists. It bids again. The marriage that mirrors this pattern — the marriage in which both spouses keep bidding, keep turning toward each other, keep reaching out even after being turned away — is the marriage that survives.

Repair Attempts

The least discussed and most important of Gottman's findings concerns what he called "repair attempts." A repair attempt is any statement or action that prevents negativity from escalating during a conflict. It can be humor ("Okay, we are doing that thing again"), an expression of appreciation ("I know you are trying"), a request for a break ("Can we pause for a minute?"), or even a physical gesture — a hand on the arm, a softening of the voice.

The critical finding is this: the success of a repair attempt depends not on the skill of the person making it but on the receptivity of the person receiving it. In healthy marriages, repair attempts are received — the partner recognizes the bid for de-escalation and responds to it. In unhealthy marriages, repair attempts are rejected — the partner either does not notice or actively dismisses the attempt to lower the temperature. When a marriage has reached the point where repair attempts consistently fail, the couple is in serious trouble, regardless of how well they articulate their feelings.

This is where the communication skills industry gets it wrong. The problem in struggling marriages is rarely a deficit of technique. Couples do not fail because they cannot construct proper I-statements. They fail because the emotional climate of the marriage has deteriorated to the point where no technique can gain traction. The soil has gone bad. You can plant the most carefully selected seeds, and nothing will grow.

Sue Johnson and the Attachment Lens

While Gottman focused on observable behavior and physiology, Sue Johnson, the developer of Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT), approached marital communication through the lens of attachment theory. Drawing on the work of John Bowlby, Johnson argued that the conflicts couples have are rarely about the surface issue. They are about attachment — the deep, primal need to know that your partner is emotionally accessible, responsive, and engaged.

Johnson identified what she called "the demon dialogues" — three patterns of interaction that arise when attachment needs go unmet. "Find the Bad Guy" is the pattern of mutual blame. "The Protest Polka" is the pursuer-withdrawer pattern, in which one partner escalates demands for connection while the other retreats. "Freeze and Flee" is the pattern of mutual withdrawal, where both partners have given up trying.

The Protest Polka is the most common and the most illuminating. The pursuing partner — more often, though not always, the woman — appears angry. She criticizes, demands, pursues. But beneath the anger, Johnson argues, is a desperate attachment cry: "Are you there? Do you care? Will you respond to me?" The withdrawing partner — more often, though not always, the man — appears cold. He shuts down, retreats, stonewalls. But beneath the withdrawal is his own attachment fear: "I cannot meet your needs. I am failing. The safest thing I can do is disappear."

Both partners are terrified. Both are acting out of self-protection. And the tragedy is that their self-protective strategies are perfectly designed to trigger the other partner's deepest fear. Her pursuit triggers his sense of failure. His withdrawal triggers her fear of abandonment. The cycle accelerates until both are exhausted and neither can see the other's pain beneath the pattern.

What the Research Demands of the Church

The church has a choice. It can continue to offer communication advice based on proof texts and platitudes — "be slow to speak and quick to listen" quoted without any understanding of the physiological realities that make listening impossible when the heart rate exceeds 100 beats per minute. Or it can integrate what four decades of research have revealed about how human beings actually function in intimate relationships and build its pastoral practice on both theological conviction and empirical reality.

The two are not in conflict. The God who said "it is not good for the man to be alone" is the same God who designed the nervous system that floods with cortisol when we feel attacked. The God who commanded us to speak the truth in love is the same God who wired us with attachment needs that, when unmet, produce the very behaviors that destroy the relationships we need. Theology without research is sentimentality. Research without theology is technique. The couples in our congregations need both.

The research does not replace the gospel. But it does reveal the terrain on which the gospel must walk. And a church that refuses to learn that terrain will keep offering maps to a country it has never visited, while the couples who need real guidance wander without direction.

The good news buried in the data is this: the patterns are not destiny. The Four Horsemen can be confronted. The negative cycles can be interrupted. Repair attempts can be learned and received. The ratio can shift. The research is clear that couples who understand their patterns and practice different responses can change — not overnight, not without cost, but genuinely and durably. The brain is plastic. The heart is redeemable. And the God who makes all things new has not exempted marriage from the scope of that promise.
excerpt: The marriage advice industry sells communication tips like party favors — but four decades of clinical research reveal that how couples talk during conflict predicts divorce with over 90 percent accuracy, and the patterns are not what you think.

title: Fighting Well: Conflict as a Spiritual Discipline
body:
There is a lie circulating in the church about marriage, and it has done more damage than most heresies. The lie is this: good marriages do not fight. Godly couples resolve their differences calmly, with mutual submission and soft voices, and if you find yourself shouting in the kitchen at ten o'clock at night, something has gone wrong with your sanctification.

This is not wisdom. It is denial dressed in theological clothing. And the couples who believe it either suppress their conflict until it metastasizes into something far worse, or they conclude that their marriage must be uniquely broken because the calm resolution never seems to arrive. Both outcomes are destructive. Both are unnecessary. And both result from a misreading of Scripture so widespread that it has become an article of faith in most evangelical churches.

The biblical witness tells a different story. The God of Scripture is not conflict-averse. He argues with Abraham over Sodom. He wrestles Jacob at the Jabbok until the man's hip is dislocated. He spends the entire book of Job in a confrontation that leaves both parties — God and the human being — more fully revealed. The prophets are, by definition, agents of conflict, sent to say the things no one wants to hear because the things no one wants to hear are the things everyone needs to hear. Conflict, in the biblical imagination, is not a sign of failure. It is one of the primary instruments through which truth is surfaced and transformation becomes possible.

Marriage is no exception. If anything, marriage is the crucible where this principle is most fiercely tested, because nowhere else are two human beings pressed so closely together for so long with so little room to hide.

I have five sons, and I have been married long enough to know that the fights that mattered — the ones that actually moved us forward — were not the fights we avoided. They were the fights we entered with our full selves, our real grievances, our genuine fear that the other person might not hear us. Those fights were terrible while they were happening. They were also the moments when the marriage became most real, most honest, most alive. The absence of conflict is not peace. It is numbness. And a numb marriage is a marriage that has stopped growing, because growth requires friction, and friction requires the willingness to collide.

Why We Fight

The surface reasons for marital conflict are nearly universal and boringly predictable. Money. Sex. Parenting. In-laws. Housework. The distribution of labor, both visible and invisible. These are the topics that fill the minutes of every marital argument, and they matter — but they are almost never the real issue.

Beneath the surface content of every fight lies a deeper question, and the deeper question is almost always about identity, value, or security. "You spent how much?" is rarely about the dollar amount. It is about control, about trust, about the fear that the other person's judgment cannot be relied upon. "You never initiate" is rarely about sex. It is about desirability, about whether you are wanted, about whether the person who promised to choose you is still choosing you. "You always side with your mother" is rarely about the mother. It is about loyalty, about whether the covenant has actually rearranged the hierarchy of allegiances.

James 4:1-2 asks the question with characteristic bluntness: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder." James is not speaking of literal murder. He is speaking of the violence that erupts when desire goes unmet — the violence of the tongue, the violence of withdrawal, the violence of contempt. The war in the marriage is a reflection of the war within the self. And the self at war with itself will make war with anyone who gets close enough to trigger the conflict.

This is why mere communication technique is insufficient. You can teach a couple to use I-statements and active listening, and they will deploy those techniques with precision while their eyes communicate contempt. The problem is not the vocabulary. The problem is the heart. And the heart, as Jeremiah observed, is deceitful above all things and desperately sick. Who can understand it? This is not a rhetorical question. It is a clinical one. And the answer, in marriage, is that your spouse understands your heart better than anyone — and that is precisely what makes marital conflict so volatile. Your spouse sees what you are hiding. They have a front-row seat to your self-deception. And their observations, when delivered in a moment of conflict, feel less like feedback and more like annihilation.

The Spiritual Discipline of Listening

The first discipline of fighting well is the discipline of listening — not the performative listening of the communication seminar, where you repeat back what your spouse said to prove you were paying attention, but the genuine listening that requires you to temporarily suspend your own narrative and inhabit your spouse's.

This is extraordinarily difficult, and the difficulty is spiritual, not merely psychological. To genuinely listen to another person's grievance against you is to accept that you might be wrong. Not partially wrong, in the way that allows you to maintain your essential rightness while conceding a minor point. Actually wrong. Wrong in a way that requires repentance, not adjustment. Wrong in a way that reveals something about yourself you did not want to see.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in "Life Together" that the first service one owes to others in community is the service of listening. "Many people are looking for an ear that will listen," he wrote. "They do not find it among Christians, because these Christians are talking where they should be listening." That observation, made in the context of Christian community, applies with doubled force in marriage. The spouse who listens — who puts down the defense, who stops formulating the rebuttal, who actually receives what the other person is saying — is performing an act of radical self-denial. It is a small death. And, like every death in the Christian life, it is the doorway to something that cannot be reached any other way.

I fail at this constantly. In the middle of a disagreement, my mind is not listening. My mind is lawyering — building the case, cataloging the precedents, preparing the closing argument. I am so busy being right that I cannot hear the person I love telling me that she is in pain. And the rightness, even when it is factually accurate, becomes a kind of cruelty, because it prioritizes being correct over being present. The cross has something to say about that priority, and what it says is not comfortable.

The Discipline of Honest Speech

The second discipline is the discipline of honest speech — saying what is true rather than what is safe. This cuts against the grain of most conflict-avoidant marriages, where peace is maintained by the mutual agreement never to name the thing that both parties know is there.

Ephesians 4:15 instructs believers to speak the truth in love. Both halves of that phrase are essential and both are difficult. Truth without love is brutality — the spouse who uses honesty as a weapon, who says, "I am just being honest" while delivering a wound that will take years to heal. Love without truth is sentimentality — the spouse who says everything is fine when everything is collapsing, who mistakes niceness for kindness and avoidance for peace.

Honest speech in a marriage means naming the pattern that both of you have been dancing around for months. It means saying, "When you dismiss my opinion in front of our friends, I feel humiliated," instead of withdrawing into a cold silence that your spouse must somehow decode. It means saying, "I am afraid that we are growing apart" instead of burying the fear under busyness and hoping it resolves itself. It means, sometimes, saying, "I am angry with you, and the anger is legitimate, and I need you to hear it before I can let it go."

This kind of speech requires courage, and the courage is spiritual. The reason most people avoid honest speech in marriage is not that they lack the vocabulary. It is that honest speech creates vulnerability, and vulnerability creates the possibility of rejection. To say "this hurt me" is to reveal that you can be hurt, and to reveal that you can be hurt is to hand the other person a power you cannot control. The entire fallen human project is a project of self-protection — covering ourselves, hiding our nakedness, building walls between our vulnerability and the world. Honest speech in marriage dismantles those walls, and the dismantling feels like dying because, in a very real sense, it is.

The Discipline of Repair

The third discipline is the discipline of repair — the willingness to return to the breach after the fight, to acknowledge what was said and done, and to rebuild what was damaged. This is where most couples fail, not because they lack the will but because they lack the model.

The cultural models for post-conflict behavior are uniformly inadequate. The "move on" model says: the fight is over, let it go, stop bringing it up. This model produces couples who accumulate unprocessed wounds like geological strata, each layer hardening over time until the marriage is built on a foundation of unresolved pain. The "process everything" model says: we must talk about every conflict until both parties feel fully heard and completely resolved. This model produces couples who spend so much time processing their marriage that they have no energy left to live it.

The biblical model is different. It involves confession, forgiveness, and what I would call covenantal re-commitment — the explicit reaffirmation, after the damage, that the covenant still holds. "I was wrong. I am sorry. I am still here." Those three sentences, spoken honestly after a genuine conflict, contain more theological content than most sermons. They enact, in miniature, the entire gospel: the acknowledgment of sin, the appeal for grace, the persistence of covenant love in the face of human failure.

The discipline of repair also requires the willingness to forgive — genuinely, not performatively. I will write about forgiveness at length elsewhere, but here I will say this: forgiveness in marriage is not a feeling. It is a decision to cancel the debt, to refuse to use the offense as ammunition in future conflicts, to treat the person who wounded you as though the wound has been healed even when it still hurts. This is unjust by every human standard of fairness. It is also the only thing that works, because the alternative — keeping the ledger, hoarding the grievances, building the case — turns the marriage into a courtroom, and no one has ever been loved in a courtroom.

What Conflict Reveals

If you will let it, conflict in marriage will teach you things about yourself that no other experience can reveal. It will show you how quickly you retreat to self-protection. It will show you the particular words and tones that trigger your oldest wounds. It will show you the gap between who you believe yourself to be and who you actually are at eleven o'clock at night when you are tired and your defenses are down.

This is sanctification. Not the clean, upward-trending sanctification of the systematic theology textbook, where the believer progresses steadily from glory to glory. The actual sanctification of the New Testament, which involves being conformed to the image of Christ through suffering, through failure, through the repeated death of the self that refuses to die. Marriage is the most relentless instrument of this sanctification, because marriage does not let you hide. You can perform competence at work. You can perform godliness at church. You cannot perform anything at home, because the person who shares your bed knows exactly who you are when the performance ends.

Gary Thomas asked the question that reframed the entire conversation: "What if God designed marriage to make us holy more than to make us happy?" The question is not a denial of happiness. It is a reordering of priorities. Happiness is the byproduct, not the goal. Holiness — the slow, painful, beautiful process of becoming the person God made you to be — is the goal. And conflict is one of the primary means by which that goal is pursued.

I have five sons. I have watched them wrestle — literally, physically, on the living room floor — and I have noticed something. The wrestling makes them stronger. Not in spite of the conflict but through it. The resistance is the training. The push-back is the exercise. Take away the conflict and you take away the growth. Marriage works the same way. The spouse who pushes back against your selfishness, who refuses to accept your excuses, who holds a mirror up to your behavior when you would rather look away — that spouse is not your adversary. That spouse is your sanctifier. And the conflict, rightly understood, is not the enemy of the marriage. It is one of its most powerful means of grace.

The couples who fight well are not the couples who fight less. They are the couples who have learned to stay in the room when every instinct says to leave, to keep their hands open when every instinct says to make a fist, to return to each other after the damage and say the three hardest sentences in any language: I was wrong. I am sorry. I am still here.

The fight is not the enemy of the marriage. The refusal to fight honestly — or the refusal to repair after the fight — is the enemy. And the church that teaches its couples to avoid conflict is teaching them to avoid the very furnace in which their love might be refined into something that lasts.

I think of a couple I counseled years ago — married twenty-three years, came to me because the wife was ready to leave. Not because of any specific offense. Because of the accumulation of a thousand unresolved conflicts, each one avoided, each one buried, each one adding another layer to the sediment that was slowly choking the life out of the marriage. When I asked them when the last time they had a real fight was, they looked at each other and could not answer. They had not fought. They had survived. And survival, in a marriage, is not the same as living.

We spent six months learning to fight. Learning to name the thing. Learning to stay in the room. Learning to say, "That hurt me," and mean it, and hear it, and not run from it. It was the hardest thing either of them had done. It was also the thing that saved the marriage. Not the avoidance. Not the peace-keeping. The fighting. The honest, painful, redemptive fighting that the church had told them was a sign of failure.

The furnace is hot. It is supposed to be. The gold does not come out any other way.
excerpt: The goal of a Christian marriage is not the absence of conflict — it is the transformation of conflict into the furnace where two people learn to die to themselves and, in the dying, discover what love actually costs.

title: When One Spouse Grows and the Other Doesn't
body:
It does not happen all at once. It happens over months, sometimes years. One spouse picks up a book and something shifts. One spouse starts therapy and begins to see patterns that were invisible before. One spouse has a crisis — a death, a diagnosis, a moment of clarity in the shower — and the world rearranges itself around a new center of gravity. The growth is genuine. It is good. And it creates a problem that no one warned them about.

Because growth in a marriage is not symmetrical. It does not happen at the same pace, in the same direction, or in response to the same catalysts. One person wakes up. The other is still sleeping. And the distance between them, which was always there in some form, becomes visible in a way that can no longer be ignored.

I have watched this happen in my congregation more times than I can count. I have watched it happen in my own marriage. And I have learned that the church's typical responses — "be patient," "pray harder," "submit to one another" — are not wrong, exactly, but they are insufficient. They do not address the specific loneliness of being married to someone who does not seem to want what you now want, does not see what you now see, and cannot understand why you are no longer content with what used to be enough.

The experience is particularly acute among ministry couples, where one spouse has been trained in theology and spiritual formation and the other has absorbed the faith secondhand, through osmosis rather than study. The pastor whose spiritual life has deepened through years of sermon preparation and theological education may find themselves married to a person whose faith remains at the level it was when they married — sincere but shallow, adequate for Sunday but insufficient for Tuesday. The gap is not about intelligence or desire. It is about exposure. One person has been marinated in the text for decades. The other has been swimming in the demands of daily life. Both are faithful. But their faithfulness has different depths, and the difference is felt most acutely in the marriage.

The loneliness is compounded by the impossibility of explaining it to anyone who has not experienced it. Your friends who are single do not understand, because they think the problem is solvable by leaving. Your friends who are happily married do not understand, because they assume their spouse is growing alongside them. Your pastor does not understand, because the sermon on marriage assumes two people moving in the same direction at roughly the same speed. You are alone with a grief that does not fit any of the available categories, and the lack of a category makes the grief harder to bear.

The Grief of Asymmetric Growth

The first thing that needs to be named is the grief. When one spouse grows and the other does not, the growing spouse grieves — not for something lost, but for something never arrived. They grieve the conversations they want to have but cannot. They grieve the emotional depth they have discovered but cannot share. They grieve the version of the marriage they can now imagine but cannot build alone.

This grief is compounded by guilt, because the growing spouse usually knows, at some level, that their growth has made things harder. They have changed the terms of the relationship without the other person's consent. The marriage that was working — or at least functioning — under the old terms no longer works under the new ones. And the growing spouse feels responsible for the disruption, even as they know they could not stop the growth if they tried.

The non-growing spouse has their own grief, though they may not name it as such. They experience the other's growth as a kind of abandonment — a departure from the shared world they thought they inhabited together. "You have changed," they say, and what they mean is, "You have left me." The accusation is not entirely unfair. Growth, when it is genuine, does create distance. The person who has seen something new cannot pretend they have not seen it, and the person who has not seen it cannot understand why the pretending has stopped.

I have been on both sides of this dynamic. I have been the spouse who was growing, frustrated by what felt like resistance and stagnation. And I have been the spouse who was not growing — or not growing in that particular direction — and experienced my partner's growth as an implicit criticism of who I was. Both positions are painful. Neither is simple. And the worst thing the church can do is flatten the complexity into a formula.

The Theology of Uneven Sanctification

The Reformed tradition speaks of sanctification as a process — the gradual work of the Holy Spirit conforming the believer to the image of Christ. What the tradition does not adequately address is the fact that this process is wildly uneven, not only between individuals but within individuals. You may grow rapidly in patience and not at all in honesty. You may develop a rich prayer life while your capacity for emotional presence remains stunted. Sanctification is not a uniform upgrade. It is a jagged, selective, unpredictable renovation.

In marriage, this unevenness becomes impossible to ignore. You are living with someone whose renovation is on a different schedule than yours, targeting different rooms, using different blueprints. And because you share the same house, every change one person makes affects the other, whether the other is ready for the change or not.

Paul addresses this obliquely in 1 Corinthians 7, when he speaks about the believing spouse married to the unbelieving spouse. His counsel is striking in its restraint: stay married, because "how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" The theology underneath that counsel is a theology of patience that does not promise results. Paul does not say, "Stay, and your spouse will eventually come around." He says, "Stay, and you do not know what will happen." The uncertainty is the point. Faith, by definition, operates in the absence of guarantees.

But Paul's situation — a believer married to an unbeliever — is actually simpler than the situation I am describing. What happens when both spouses are believers, both claim to follow Christ, both attend church and read Scripture, but one is being transformed and the other is merely performing? What happens when the gap is not between faith and unbelief but between depth and surface, between a faith that costs and a faith that comforts?

The New Testament does not address this situation directly, which is why the church has struggled to address it pastorally. But the New Testament does offer a principle that applies: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). The burden of asymmetric growth is a real burden, carried by both spouses, and the church's refusal to name it does not make it lighter. It makes it lonelier.

The Temptation of Contempt

Here is the danger that the growing spouse must face: the temptation to feel superior. Growth, when it is genuine, produces humility — a deeper awareness of one's own brokenness, a greater capacity for compassion, a reduced need to be right. But growth, when it is incomplete, can produce the opposite — a spiritual arrogance that looks down on the spouse who has not yet arrived where you have arrived.

This arrogance is devastating to a marriage. It communicates, in every tone and glance and sigh, that the other person is not enough. That they are behind. That you have outgrown them. And the cruelest form of this arrogance is the one that wraps itself in spiritual language — "I just wish you were more intentional," "I need someone who can meet me at this level," "I am growing and you are staying the same." These sentences, spoken from a position of spiritual superiority, are not expressions of love. They are expressions of contempt, and contempt — as I have written elsewhere — is the most corrosive force in any relationship.

Jesus told a parable about two men who went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, the other a tax collector. The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other people. The tax collector beat his breast and said, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." Jesus said the tax collector went home justified. The parable is a warning to everyone who has ever stood in the temple of their own growth and looked down at the person who has not grown as fast.

If your growth has made you kind, patient, and more capable of loving the person you married, it is genuine growth. If your growth has made you critical, impatient, and convinced that you deserve a more evolved partner, it is not growth at all. It is pride with a new vocabulary.

What the Non-Growing Spouse Might Be Carrying

Before I go further, I need to say something in defense of the spouse who appears to be standing still. Because the appearance of non-growth is not always what it seems.

Some people do not grow because they are resistant — because growth threatens the identity they have constructed, because change is terrifying, because the familiar dysfunction is preferable to the unfamiliar health. This is real, and it needs to be named.

But some people do not grow because they are exhausted. They are carrying burdens the growing spouse cannot see — depression that has not been diagnosed, anxiety that manifests as rigidity, trauma that has been buried so deep it does not register as trauma but as personality. The spouse who seems unwilling to grow may be unable to grow — not because they lack the desire but because their internal resources are fully committed to survival. You cannot renovate a house while the house is on fire. And some people's internal houses are on fire in ways that are completely invisible from the outside.

Others are growing in ways that are invisible to their partner. The spouse who cannot articulate emotional insight may be growing in faithfulness, in consistency, in the quiet discipline of arriving every day and laboring without fanfare. Growth does not always look like self-awareness. Sometimes it looks like endurance. And the marriage that dismisses endurance as stagnation has confused depth with articulateness.

I have watched husbands sit in my office, unable to name a single emotion, dismissed by their wives as emotionally unavailable, while those same husbands worked seventy-hour weeks without complaint to provide for families who never thanked them. That is not nothing. That is a form of love that does not translate well into the language of emotional intelligence, but it is love nonetheless. The growing spouse who cannot see this love is not as perceptive as they think.

The Path Forward

There is no formula for navigating asymmetric growth in a marriage. But there are disciplines that can keep the asymmetry from becoming a permanent division.

The first discipline is honesty without superiority. The growing spouse must be honest about what they need and what they see, but the honesty must be delivered from a position of solidarity, not from a height. "I am struggling with where we are" is different from "You are not enough for me." The first is an invitation. The second is a verdict.

The second discipline is curiosity without agenda. Before assuming that your spouse is not growing, ask them what is happening inside them. Ask what they are struggling with. Ask what they are afraid of. And listen — not to fix, not to diagnose, not to assess whether their answer meets your standard of growth, but to understand. You may discover that the person you thought was standing still has been running a marathon you could not see.

The third discipline is patience without passivity. Patience does not mean accepting a permanent status quo without comment. It means accepting that transformation takes time and that you do not control the timeline. You can invite. You can model. You can create conditions that make growth possible. You cannot make another person grow. That is the work of the Spirit, and the Spirit does not operate on your schedule.

The fourth discipline is the hardest: the willingness to grieve what is and to love what is at the same time. To grieve the marriage you imagined while investing fully in the marriage you have. To hold the tension between what you want and what exists, without resolving it prematurely in either direction — neither pretending that the gap does not matter nor concluding that the gap cannot be crossed.

The marriage where one spouse grows and the other does not is not a failed marriage. It is a marriage in the middle of its story — a story whose ending has not been written, whose next chapter may surprise both of them, whose Author has a longer patience than either of them can imagine.

Stay in the story. Not because staying is easy. Not because staying guarantees the outcome you want. Stay because the covenant you made was not contingent on synchronized growth, and the God who holds you both is doing work in both of you that neither of you can fully see. The view from inside the process is always incomplete. The view from the end — the end you have not yet reached — may reveal a coherence that the middle obscured.

I know a couple — I will not use their names — who lived inside this asymmetry for nearly a decade. The wife had gone through a transformation so profound that she described it as being born a second time into the same life. The husband had not. He was the same man she had married: decent, faithful, steady, and completely uninterested in the inner work that had remade his wife from the inside out. She spent years grieving the conversations she could not have, the depth she could not share, the partnership she could see but not reach.

And then, in the ninth year, something shifted. Not because she pushed. Not because he capitulated. Something broke open in him — a health scare, a loss, a moment of reckoning that was entirely his own — and the man who had been standing still began to move. He did not move in the direction she expected. He moved in his own direction, at his own pace, toward a version of growth she had not imagined. And the marriage that resulted was not the marriage she had pictured during all those years of grieving. It was something else — something stranger, messier, and more genuinely theirs than anything she could have designed.

That is not a promise. It is a hope. And hope, in the Christian life, is not wishful thinking. It is the substance of things not yet seen, held together by a God who finishes what He starts.
excerpt: One of the loneliest experiences in a marriage is the slow realization that you are becoming a different person and the person you married is not coming with you — and the church has almost nothing to say about it.

title: Sexual Intimacy as Theology
body:
The church has a sex problem, and the problem is not what most people think. It is not that the church talks about sex too much or too little. It is that the church talks about sex badly — vacillating between two equally distorted positions. The first position treats sex as danger, something to be fenced off, warned against, and guarded from with purity pledges and metaphors about chewed gum and used tape. The second position, the evangelical reaction to the first, treats sex as reward — God's gift to married people, the prize for doing it right, the holy pleasure that makes all the waiting worthwhile. Both positions reduce sex to something it is not. Neither arrives at what it is.

What sex is, in the biblical framework, is theology. Not a metaphor for theology. Not an illustration of theological principles. An actual theological act — a bodily enactment of the covenant, a physical participation in the mystery that Paul says is "profound," a revelation of something about God and humanity that cannot be accessed any other way.
