The church that cannot say this clearly — that cannot hold together the goodness, the gravity, and the vulnerability of sexual intimacy without collapsing into either prudishness or banality — has failed at one of its most fundamental pastoral tasks.

I write this as a pastor who has sat with hundreds of couples whose sexual lives are sources of pain, shame, confusion, and grief. I write this as a man who grew up in a culture that saturated him with sexual imagery and a church that gave him almost nothing to counter it except rules. I write this knowing that the subject requires more honesty than the church typically permits and more reverence than the culture typically offers. Both are necessary. Neither alone is sufficient.

The Body Is Not the Problem

The deepest distortion in the church's theology of sex is the assumption, rarely stated but pervasively felt, that the body is the problem. That the sexual urge is a concession to fallen nature rather than a feature of created goodness. That the spiritual life is the real life and the bodily life is the obstacle to it.

This assumption does not come from the Bible. It comes from Plato, filtered through Gnosticism, absorbed by certain strands of early Christianity, and embedded so deeply in Western religious consciousness that most Christians do not realize they hold it. The Gnostic heresy taught that the material world was created by a lesser deity, that the body was a prison for the soul, and that salvation consisted in escaping the body's demands. The early church condemned Gnosticism formally. It absorbed Gnosticism practically. And the practical absorption shows up most clearly in the church's treatment of sex.

The biblical witness is unambiguous. "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Everything. The bodies. The hormones. The desire. The capacity for physical pleasure. All of it preceded the fall. All of it was pronounced good before sin entered the picture. The Song of Solomon — an entire book of erotic poetry that the church has spent centuries trying to allegorize into something safer — celebrates the beauty of the human body and the pleasure of sexual desire with an explicitness that would make most church small groups deeply uncomfortable.

"Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue" (Song 4:11). "Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits" (Song 4:16). "I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey" (Song 5:1). The language is sensual. It is deliberate. And it is Scripture. The God who inspired these words is not embarrassed by the body. The question is why we are.

Origen of Alexandria, one of the early church's greatest minds, castrated himself in response to Matthew 19:12 — a literalism so extreme that even the church of his day condemned it. But the impulse behind Origen's act — the conviction that the body's desires are the enemy of the soul's purity — survived his censure and infected Christian theology for centuries. Augustine, whose own sexual history shaped his theology in ways he did not fully acknowledge, treated concupiscence as the mechanism through which original sin was transmitted. The implication was devastating: the sexual act, even within marriage, was tainted by the fall. It was permitted, but it was not clean. The stain of that theology is still on the church's hands.

The One-Flesh Union Revisited

I have written elsewhere about the meaning of "one flesh" in Hebrew, and I will not repeat that analysis in full here. But the sexual dimension of the one-flesh union requires specific attention, because it is the dimension the church most consistently mishandles.

When two bodies come together in sexual union, something happens that is not merely biological. The act of sexual intercourse is the most complete physical vulnerability two human beings can share — the removal of every barrier, the exposure of every surface, the mutual surrender of bodily autonomy. It is the bodily enactment of what the covenant promises verbally: I am yours. All of me. Without reservation. Without defense.

This is why sexual intimacy outside of covenant — outside the binding, permanent, public commitment — is, in the biblical framework, not merely rule-breaking but self-contradictory. The body is saying what the will has not said. The act of total physical surrender is being performed without the context of total personal commitment. The flesh is becoming one while the lives remain separate. And the resulting dissonance — the gap between what the body says and what the life says — is what the biblical writers call porneia, sexual immorality. Not because the body is bad. Because the body is saying something that is not true.

Within the covenant, sexual intimacy becomes something else entirely. It becomes a sacramental act — a visible, physical sign of an invisible, spiritual reality. The mutual self-giving of two bodies mirrors the mutual self-giving of two lives. The pleasure is not the point, though it is genuinely good. The vulnerability is the point. The willingness to be fully exposed, fully received, fully held by another person who has promised not to leave — this is what makes marital sex a theological act rather than merely a physical one.

The Damage Done by Purity Culture

I cannot write about sexual intimacy in marriage without addressing the wreckage left by the purity culture movement of the 1990s and 2000s. The movement — epitomized by Joshua Harris's "I Kissed Dating Goodbye" (1997), the True Love Waits campaign, and a thousand youth group talks featuring crumpled roses and unwrapped candy bars — was built on a legitimate concern: young people were being harmed by the sexual chaos of the culture, and the church wanted to protect them.

But the protection was purchased at a catastrophic price. Purity culture taught, implicitly and often explicitly, that sexual desire was the enemy — that the body's longing for intimacy was something to be suppressed, controlled, and feared. It taught women that their bodies were dangerous — sources of temptation that must be hidden, covered, and guarded lest they cause a brother to stumble. It taught men that their desire was predatory — an animal impulse that, if not caged by accountability partners and internet filters, would destroy everything it touched.

The result was a generation of Christians who arrived at their wedding nights carrying not anticipation but terror. Sheila Wray Gregoire's research, published in "The Great Sex Rescue," documented what many pastors had observed anecdotally: women who had absorbed purity culture messaging reported significantly higher rates of sexual pain, difficulty with arousal, and inability to experience pleasure in marriage. The message that sex was dangerous before the wedding did not magically transform into the message that sex was beautiful after it. The body does not work that way. The shame that was learned in adolescence did not evaporate with the exchange of rings. It followed them into the marriage bed and took up permanent residence.

Harris himself eventually renounced both the book and his faith — a trajectory that should give the church pause. When the architect of a movement walks away from the building, it is worth asking whether the foundation was sound. The foundation was not sound. It was built on fear, not theology. On shame, not Scripture. On the premise that the body is the problem, which is the oldest heresy in the Christian tradition, repackaged for the youth group.

The church owes these women — and these men — a profound apology. Not merely for the excesses of the movement but for the underlying theology that made the excesses possible: the theology that treats the body as the enemy of the soul, that confuses purity with repression, that cannot distinguish between sexual discipline and sexual fear.

What Healthy Sexual Theology Requires

A theology of sexual intimacy adequate to the biblical witness must hold together at least four things that the church has historically separated.

First, it must hold together goodness and gravity. Sex is good — genuinely, bodily, pleasurably good. It is also weighty — a covenantal act with the power to bond, to heal, to wound, and to reveal. A theology that has only goodness produces triviality. A theology that has only gravity produces fear. The biblical witness holds both: the Song of Solomon's delight and Paul's warning that the body is a temple. The pleasure and the weight belong together. Separating them distorts both.

Second, it must hold together desire and discipline. Sexual desire is not the enemy. It is a created capacity, a gift of the God who made bodies and pronounced them good. But desire, like every created capacity, requires direction. The discipline is not the suppression of desire but the training of desire — learning to want what is good, in the way that is good, at the time that is good. This is true of every appetite. The solution to gluttony is not the elimination of hunger. It is the ordering of hunger toward its proper end. The same is true of sexual desire.

Third, it must hold together mutuality and difference. Paul's instructions in 1 Corinthians 7 are striking in their symmetry: "The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does." The symmetry is deliberate and radical. In a first-century context where a wife's body was legally the property of her husband, Paul insists that the authority is mutual. Both bodies belong to the other. Both partners have the right to give and the obligation to receive. Neither can claim ownership without reciprocating it.

This mutuality has been badly abused. The passage has been used to coerce unwilling spouses into sex — "your body is not your own" deployed as a weapon rather than an invitation. This is a perversion of Paul's meaning so profound that it constitutes its own form of sexual sin. The mutuality Paul describes is not about obligation. It is about generosity — the willingness of two people to give themselves to each other freely, without coercion, without manipulation, and without the withholding of the self as punishment.

Fourth, and most difficult, it must hold together the sexual and the sacred without making them identical. Sex is not worship. It is not a substitute for prayer. It does not earn spiritual credit. But it participates in something sacred — the covenant between two people that mirrors the covenant between God and humanity. The church that cannot make this distinction will either sacralize sex into something oppressively holy or desacralize it into something casually biological. Both errors miss the point.

The Practical Realities

Theology that does not touch the ground is not theology. It is abstraction. And the ground where sexual intimacy lives in most marriages is more complicated than any theological framework can fully address.

There are couples in every congregation dealing with mismatched desire — one partner who wants sex frequently and another who does not. There are couples dealing with sexual dysfunction — pain, inability to achieve arousal or orgasm, erectile difficulty — that makes the physical act of union difficult or impossible. There are couples carrying wounds from sexual abuse — one in four women and one in six men, according to the CDC — whose bodies respond to sexual touch with fear rather than pleasure. There are couples who have never had an honest conversation about what they enjoy, what they need, and what they do not want, because the church gave them a theology of sex that was too embarrassed to get specific.

These realities require more than theology. They require clinical competence, professional counseling, medical intervention, and the kind of pastoral care that is willing to sit in uncomfortable specificity rather than retreating to comfortable abstraction. The pastor who cannot refer a couple to a sex therapist without embarrassment is not protecting the sanctity of the subject. That pastor is failing the people who need help.

The body is not the enemy of the soul. It is the place where the soul lives. And the sexual union of two people within the covenant of marriage is not a concession to human weakness. It is a participation in divine self-giving — the bodily enactment of a love that holds nothing back, that refuses to hide, and that trusts the other with the whole unguarded self.

The church that can say this — can say it without blushing, without hedging, without retreating into either prudishness or crudeness — will be a church that finally gives its people what they need: not rules about sex, but a theology of sex. A theology that honors the body, respects the covenant, takes pleasure seriously, and refuses to let shame have the last word about something God called very good.

I have watched couples in my congregation discover, sometimes after decades of marriage, that they had never talked honestly about sex. Not once. They had done it. They had avoided it. They had fought about it. They had endured it. But they had never talked about it — about what they wanted, what they feared, what they enjoyed, what they needed. The silence was not because they were private people. It was because the church had given them no language for the conversation. The only language available was the language of rules — what is permitted, what is prohibited — and rules do not cover the terrain that matters most. The terrain that matters most is the terrain of two embodied souls trying to be fully present to each other in the most vulnerable act available to human beings. That terrain requires a language of reverence, curiosity, honesty, and grace. The church has barely begun to develop it.

That theology is overdue. The people in our pews have been waiting for it. Some of them have stopped waiting. The church that speaks last speaks to an empty room.
excerpt: The church has managed to make sex both an idol and a taboo simultaneously — but Scripture treats sexual intimacy as a theological act, a bodily enactment of the covenant that reveals something about God that nothing else can.

title: The Marriage That Survives Ministry
body:
I need to say something that most pastors will not say publicly, because saying it publicly feels like a confession of weakness, and weakness in ministry is the one thing you are never allowed to show. Here it is: there have been seasons in my ministry when my marriage survived not because of my faithfulness but in spite of my unfaithfulness — not unfaithfulness in the sexual sense, but in the vocational sense. I gave the church my best energy, my best attention, my best emotional presence, and I gave my wife what was left. What was left was not enough. It was never enough.

This is not a unique confession. It is a nearly universal one among pastors, and the fact that it is rarely spoken does not mean it is rarely felt. The Barna Group's 2017 study on pastoral health found that 52 percent of pastors reported that the demands of ministry had a negative effect on their family. The Hartford Institute's research found that 80 percent of pastors believed pastoral ministry negatively affected their families. Francis Schaeffer, reflecting on his own ministry failures, wrote with painful honesty about the gap between the community he preached and the marriage he practiced.

The question is not whether ministry is hard on marriages. The question is why. And the answer is more structural than personal, more systemic than spiritual, more about the way we have designed the pastoral role than about the character of the people who fill it.

The Structural Problem

The modern pastoral role is structurally designed to destroy marriages. This is not an exaggeration. Consider what the role demands: the pastor is expected to be available at all hours for emergencies — hospital visits, suicidal parishioners, marital crises, deaths. The pastor is expected to prepare and deliver multiple sermons per week, each one representing hours of study, writing, and emotional labor. The pastor is expected to attend committee meetings, lead staff, manage budgets, cast vision, respond to criticism, mediate conflict, visit the elderly, counsel the struggling, and show up at every church event with a smile that communicates both warmth and pastoral authority.

The pastor is also expected to have a thriving marriage and well-adjusted children, because these are understood to be qualifications for the role. First Timothy 3:4-5 says that an overseer must "manage his own household well." The congregation reads this as a requirement and then builds a system that makes compliance nearly impossible. We demand the fruit while poisoning the soil.

The structural problem is compounded by the absence of boundaries that would be considered non-negotiable in any other profession. A surgeon does not take calls during surgery. A trial lawyer does not step out of the courtroom to handle a church member's anxiety attack. But the pastor is expected to leave the dinner table when the phone rings, to cancel the anniversary date when a deacon has a crisis, to prioritize the congregation's needs over the family's needs as a demonstration of ministerial faithfulness.

And the spouse — the pastor's spouse — is expected to accept this arrangement without complaint, because the work is "the Lord's work," and who would compete with the Lord? The theological framing of ministry makes it nearly impossible for the spouse to name the deprivation without feeling guilty. How do you say, "I need you to be home tonight" when the alternative is a teenager in the ER? How do you say, "I need your attention" when the alternative is a grieving widow? The pastor's spouse learns, over time, that their needs will always lose the triage, because the congregation's needs are always more urgent, more visible, and more spiritually weighted.

The system is reinforced by a pastoral culture that rewards self-sacrifice and punishes self-care. The pastor who takes a full day off is suspected of laziness. The pastor who goes on vacation without checking email is suspected of disengagement. The pastor who says, "I cannot take that meeting because I have a date with my wife" is suspected of misplaced priorities. The culture of pastoral ministry has confused martyrdom with faithfulness, and the confusion is destroying families.

The Emotional Depletion

The structural demands would be manageable if the emotional toll were acknowledged and addressed. It is not. Ministry is one of the most emotionally intensive professions in existence, and it operates with almost no emotional infrastructure.

Consider what a typical week contains. Monday: debriefing from Sunday, responding to the person offended by the sermon, processing the conversation in the lobby with the couple whose marriage is ending. Tuesday: hospital visit with a dying church member, followed by a staff meeting about budget shortfalls, followed by a counseling session with a man struggling with pornography. Wednesday: midweek teaching, youth group crisis, email from a board member questioning a decision. Thursday: sermon preparation — which is not merely intellectual work but emotional and spiritual labor, the work of wrestling with a text until it yields something true enough to say out loud. Friday: wedding rehearsal, phone call from a church member whose child was just diagnosed with cancer. Saturday: the wedding, followed by a few hours of exhausted presence at home before the cycle begins again on Sunday.

By the time the pastor arrives at the dinner table — if they arrive at the dinner table — they have given away the best of themselves to people who are not their family. The empathy has been spent. The emotional availability has been drained. The capacity to be present, to listen, to engage, to care — the very capacities that the marriage needs most — have been distributed across thirty or forty pastoral interactions, and there is nothing left.

The spouse sees the exhaustion. The spouse understands the demands. The spouse tries to be gracious, patient, supportive. But grace has limits, patience has a shelf life, and support without reciprocity eventually becomes resentment. And the resentment, when it arrives, carries an additional burden of guilt, because the spouse knows they are resenting "God's work," and what kind of person resents God's work?

The kind of person who has been neglected by their spouse for fifteen years while the congregation got the best of them. That kind of person.

The Fishbowl Effect

Ministry marriages carry an additional burden that few other marriages face: they are lived in public. The pastor's marriage is the congregation's property — not legally, but functionally. The congregation watches how the pastor and spouse interact on Sunday mornings. They form opinions about the health of the marriage. They gossip when the spouse seems withdrawn. They expect the marriage to model what the pastor preaches, and when it does not — when the strain shows, when the facade slips, when the marriage looks ordinary rather than exemplary — the judgment arrives.

This public scrutiny makes vulnerability impossible. The pastor cannot stand before the congregation and say, "My marriage is struggling this month." The spouse cannot ask for prayer in the small group without it becoming a talking point in the parking lot. The couple lives inside a performance that they cannot exit, and the performance itself becomes one of the primary sources of marital stress. They are performing intimacy for an audience while the actual intimacy erodes behind the curtain.

The loneliest couple in most churches is the couple in the parsonage. They have access to everyone and intimacy with no one. They know the congregation's secrets but cannot share their own. They carry the weight of the church's dysfunction while pretending their own household is functional. And the pretense, sustained over years, becomes a kind of spiritual sickness — a disease of the soul that masquerades as ministerial faithfulness.

The Theological Distortion

Underneath the structural and emotional problems lies a theological distortion that the church has rarely examined: the idolatry of ministry. The belief — absorbed, not articulated — that pastoral work is the highest calling, that the church's needs are God's needs, and that the family must be sacrificed on the altar of vocational faithfulness.

This is not what Scripture teaches. Scripture teaches that the first institution God created was not the church but the family. Before there was a tabernacle, before there was a temple, before there was a congregation, there was a man and a woman in a garden, called to be one flesh. The family precedes the church in the order of creation, and while I do not want to build an entire theology on chronological priority, the ordering is not accidental. The God who made marriage before He made Israel is a God who does not regard the family as a resource to be consumed by institutional religion.

Jesus Himself modeled something the church has largely ignored: the discipline of withdrawal. He withdrew from the crowds to pray. He withdrew from the demands of ministry to be alone with His Father. He told His disciples, after a period of intense ministry, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Jesus did not treat every need as a claim on His time. He did not respond to every urgency with immediate availability. He withdrew. He rested. He said no.

The pastor who cannot say no to the congregation for the sake of the marriage has made the congregation an idol. This is an uncomfortable sentence, and I am aware of it. But it is true. The God who called you to ministry is the same God who gave you a spouse, and He did not give you the second to sacrifice for the first.

Eugene Peterson understood this. In "The Pastor," he wrote about his deliberate decision to be home for dinner, to keep Mondays free, to refuse the tyranny of the urgent in favor of the discipline of the important. Peterson was not a lazy pastor. He was a pastor who understood that the rhythms of the pastoral life must include rhythms of absence from the congregation — absence that is not abandonment but stewardship. The pastor who is always available is not being faithful. That pastor is being consumed. And the family that watches the consumption has learned a lesson about the church that will take years to unlearn.

What Must Change

The marriage that survives ministry does not survive by accident. It survives by deliberate, sustained, counter-cultural choices that will cost the pastor something — and the something it costs may be the approval of the congregation that has come to expect unlimited access to their pastor's life.

First, the pastor must establish and enforce boundaries that protect the marriage. This means designated times that are non-negotiable — date nights that do not get cancelled for committee meetings, vacations that do not include a laptop and a sermon outline, evenings that are given to the family without the phone on the table. The congregation will not like this. Some will interpret it as a lack of dedication. The pastor must be willing to pay that price, because the alternative — the slow erosion of the marriage in the name of ministerial availability — is a price that is too high.

Second, the pastor must find safe spaces for their own vulnerability. This means a counselor, a spiritual director, a small circle of trusted friends outside the congregation who can hold what the pastor cannot hold alone. The pastor who tries to be the sole emotional caregiver for a congregation while receiving no care themselves is a pastor who will either burn out, blow up, or both. And when the pastor burns out or blows up, the marriage is usually the first casualty.

Third, the congregation must change its expectations. This is the hardest shift, because it requires the congregation to see the pastor as a human being rather than a spiritual utility. The pastor is not a vending machine that dispenses pastoral care on demand. The pastor is a person with a body that gets tired, a heart that gets wounded, and a marriage that needs the same investment that every marriage needs. Congregations that demand unlimited access to their pastor are not being faithful. They are being consumptive. And the consumption will eventually destroy the person they claim to need.

Fourth, and this is the thing I have learned most slowly: the pastor must bring the same pastoral skill to their own marriage that they bring to everyone else's. The irony of pastoral ministry is that the pastor is often the most skilled relational person in the congregation and the least skilled relational person in their own home. They listen to parishioners with full attention and scroll through their phone while their spouse is talking. They counsel couples with empathy and patience and argue with their own spouse with impatience and defensiveness. They know, theoretically, what a healthy marriage requires. They fail, practically, to practice it where it matters most.

The marriage that survives ministry is not the marriage that sacrifices everything for the church. It is the marriage that recognizes that the church does not own the pastor, that the family is not an obstacle to ministry but the first ministry, and that the God who called the pastor to serve is the same God who commanded the pastor to love — and the love starts at home.

I have learned this slowly, imperfectly, with more failure than I want to admit. My marriage has survived ministry not because I got this right but because grace covered the years when I got it wrong. That grace does not excuse the wrong. It redeems it. And the redemption calls me not to repeat the pattern but to break it — to be the pastor who goes home, who puts the phone down, who looks his wife in the eye and says, "You are not second. You were never supposed to be second. And I am sorry for every season when I made you feel like you were."

I think of the pastors I know who lost their marriages. Not one of them lost it because they were lazy. They lost it because they were faithful — faithful to the wrong thing, or faithful to the right thing in the wrong proportion. They gave everything to the church and assumed the family would understand. The family understood for a while. Then the family stopped understanding. Then the family left.

The tragedy is not that these men were bad pastors. Many of them were extraordinary pastors — gifted preachers, compassionate counselors, visionary leaders. The tragedy is that the very gifts that made them effective in ministry were the gifts they withheld from their marriages. The empathy they showed the grieving widow, they did not show their wives. The patience they extended to the difficult deacon, they did not extend to their children. The presence they brought to the hospital bedside, they did not bring to the dinner table. The ministry received their best. The family received what remained.

The ministry will survive your absence for an evening. Your marriage may not survive your absence for a decade. Choose accordingly.
excerpt: Ministry marriages do not fail because pastors are bad spouses — they fail because the church has built a system that demands the pastor give everything to the congregation and expects the family to survive on the leftovers.

title: Forgiveness in Marriage: What It Is and What It Isn't
body:
Forgiveness is the word Christians reach for most quickly and understand least deeply. In marriage, this misunderstanding is not merely academic. It is corrosive. Couples are told to forgive — by their pastors, by their small group leaders, by the books on the nightstand — without ever being told what forgiveness actually is. And so they perform a version of forgiveness that is not forgiveness at all but its counterfeit: they suppress the anger, pretend the wound does not still bleed, and call the suppression obedience. The wound goes underground. The marriage continues on top of it. And years later, when the wound surfaces — as it always does, because buried things do not stay buried — everyone is shocked by the scale of the damage. They should not be. The damage was always there. They just agreed not to look at it.

I have watched this pattern destroy marriages from the inside. I have participated in it in my own marriage. I have stood in pulpits and preached forgiveness without fully understanding what I was asking people to do. The subject requires more care than the church has typically given it, and the couples in our congregations deserve a theology of forgiveness that is rigorous enough to be practiced and honest enough to be trusted.

What Forgiveness Is Not

Forgiveness is not amnesia. It is not the erasure of memory, the pretense that the offense did not occur, the deliberate forgetting of what was said or done. The popular Christian phrase "forgive and forget" has no basis in Scripture and no basis in neuroscience. The brain does not forget significant emotional events. To demand that it do so is to demand the impossible, and demanding the impossible from wounded people is cruelty dressed as piety.

God Himself does not forget. When Scripture says that God "remembers our sins no more" (Jeremiah 31:34), the Hebrew word zakar does not mean cognitive erasure. It means that God chooses not to hold the sin against us — not to bring it up as evidence, not to use it as a weapon, not to let it determine the terms of the relationship going forward. God remembers what we did. He chooses not to count it. These are profoundly different things.

Forgiveness is not tolerance. It does not mean accepting bad behavior as though it were acceptable. It does not mean saying, "It is okay" when it is not okay. It does not mean absorbing repeated injury without naming it. Tolerance says, "What you did does not matter." Forgiveness says, "What you did matters enormously, and I am choosing not to hold it against you." The difference is not semantic. It is structural. Tolerance minimizes the offense. Forgiveness takes the full weight of the offense and carries it voluntarily.

Forgiveness is not the suppression of anger. This may be the most pastorally destructive confusion of all. The church, by and large, treats anger as a sin — or at least as a spiritual failure, a sign that you have not fully surrendered the situation to God. But anger, in the biblical framework, is not inherently sinful. "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26) is not a contradiction. It is a command that assumes the legitimacy of anger while insisting on its proper expression. Anger is the appropriate emotional response to injustice, to betrayal, to the violation of something precious. A person who is not angry when they have been wronged is not spiritually mature. They are dissociated.

The anger must be felt before it can be released. The wound must be acknowledged before it can be forgiven. The church that rushes past the anger to arrive at the forgiveness has not arrived at forgiveness at all. It has arrived at suppression, and suppression is not a Christian virtue. It is a psychological defense mechanism that the gospel did not prescribe and does not endorse.

I have seen the damage of suppressed anger in marriages that appeared, from the outside, to be paragons of Christian grace. The couple who "forgave" an affair in three weeks. The wife who "let go" of her husband's deception without ever naming how deeply it cut. The husband who swallowed his wife's contempt year after year because the Bible says to bear all things. In each case, the suppression produced not peace but pathology — depression, anxiety, physical illness, the slow deadening of the soul that comes from telling yourself, repeatedly, that the thing that is killing you does not matter. It matters. The anger is proof that it matters. And the God who made you capable of righteous anger did not make you capable of it so that you could pretend it does not exist.

Forgiveness is not reconciliation — and this distinction may be the most important of all. Forgiveness is a unilateral act of the will. Reconciliation is a bilateral restoration of the relationship. You can forgive someone who has not repented. You cannot reconcile with them. Forgiveness frees the wounded person from the burden of carrying the debt. Reconciliation restores the relationship to a place of trust and intimacy. The first requires only one person's decision. The second requires two people's participation. Confusing the two produces marriages in which wounded spouses are pressured to trust people who have not earned their trust, because the church has told them that forgiveness demands it. It does not.

What Forgiveness Is

Forgiveness is a decision — not a feeling — to cancel a debt. It is the deliberate choice to relinquish the right to collect what is owed. When someone wrongs you in marriage — lies to you, betrays your trust, speaks to you with contempt, fails to show up when you needed them most — they incur a debt. Justice says the debt must be paid. Forgiveness says the debt is cancelled. Not because the debt was not real. Not because the debtor does not owe it. But because the creditor has chosen, at enormous personal cost, to absorb the loss rather than extract the payment.

This is the logic of the cross. The cross is not God pretending that sin does not matter. It is God acknowledging that sin matters so much that someone has to bear its weight — and then choosing to bear it Himself rather than impose it on the debtor. The cost of forgiveness is not eliminated. It is transferred. Someone pays. In the case of divine forgiveness, God pays. In the case of marital forgiveness, the wounded spouse pays — absorbing the pain, releasing the claim, and choosing to move forward with the person who inflicted the wound.

This is why forgiveness is the most costly thing a human being can do. It is not passive. It is not easy. It is not the path of least resistance. It is the path of greatest resistance — the path that runs directly against every instinct for self-protection, every demand for justice, every impulse to make the other person pay. Forgiveness is a crucifixion. The person who forgives takes the cross voluntarily. And the church that demands forgiveness without acknowledging the cross at its center has trivialized both.

The Process of Forgiveness

Forgiveness in marriage is rarely a single event. It is a process — sometimes a long one — that involves multiple decisions, multiple returns to the same wound, multiple acts of release that must be renewed as the pain resurfaces.

Lewis Smedes, in his essential work "Forgive and Forget" (a title that, ironically, contains the very confusion he works to dismantle), described forgiveness as a movement through four stages: hurt, hate, healing, and coming together. The movement is not linear. You do not pass through the stages once and arrive at resolution. You cycle through them — sometimes moving forward, sometimes falling back, sometimes stuck in a stage you thought you had left behind.

The first stage is the honest acknowledgment of the hurt. This sounds simple. It is not. Many couples skip this stage entirely, moving straight from the offense to the expected resolution. The husband says, "I am sorry." The wife says, "I forgive you." And nothing has actually happened, because the wife has not yet allowed herself to feel the full weight of the wound. She has performed forgiveness without processing the injury, and the performance will not hold.

The second stage — what Smedes called "hate" — is the phase of anger, resentment, and the desire for retribution. This is the stage the church most wants to skip, because it is ugly and uncomfortable and does not photograph well. But it is essential. The anger is the evidence that something real was violated. To skip the anger is to deny the reality of the violation, and you cannot forgive what you have not fully acknowledged.

The third stage is the gradual release — the slow, often non-linear movement from "you owe me" to "I release you." This is where the decision of forgiveness lives. Not in the initial declaration but in the repeated choice, day after day, not to pick up the debt again. Not to use the offense as ammunition in the next argument. Not to bring it up when you are tired and your defenses are down and the old wound throbs with a familiar pain. This is the hardest stage, because the temptation to reclaim the debt is strongest when you are most depleted. The discipline of release is precisely that — a discipline, practiced daily, sustained by grace, and tested by every disagreement that follows the original wound.

The fourth stage — coming together — is not guaranteed. Smedes was honest about this, and the church should be too. Forgiveness does not always lead to reconciliation. It does not always restore the relationship to what it was before. Sometimes the relationship is permanently altered — still intact, still covenantal, but carrying a scar that will not fully disappear. The scar is not a sign of failed forgiveness. It is a sign that something real happened, and the body — the body of the marriage — bears the mark.

Forgiveness and Repentance

Here is a question the church handles badly: does forgiveness require the offender's repentance?

The answer is yes and no, and the distinction matters.

Unilateral forgiveness — the decision to release the debt regardless of whether the debtor acknowledges it — is a spiritual practice that frees the wounded person from the prison of their own resentment. You can forgive someone who has not apologized, who does not see the wrong, who would do the same thing again if given the opportunity. This forgiveness is for your own soul. It releases you from the corrosive effects of carrying a grudge. And it is possible — necessary, even — without the other person's participation.

But relational forgiveness — the restoration of trust, the rebuilding of intimacy, the re-entry into full partnership — requires repentance. It requires the offending spouse to acknowledge the offense, to take responsibility without deflecting or minimizing, and to demonstrate, through sustained behavior over time, that the pattern has changed. Forgiveness without repentance frees the wounded spouse's heart. It does not obligate the wounded spouse to trust an unrepentant partner.

This distinction is critical in cases of serious betrayal — infidelity, deception, abuse. The church's demand that the wounded spouse "just forgive" without requiring the offending spouse to do the hard work of repentance is not grace. It is complicity. It enables the continuation of the very behavior that caused the wound. Grace does not mean the absence of consequences. It means the presence of love in the midst of consequences. And sometimes love requires the wounded spouse to say, "I forgive you, and I need to see change before I can trust you again." Both halves of that sentence are faithful. Both are necessary.

The Ongoing Practice

In a long marriage, forgiveness is not an occasional event. It is a daily practice — the continuous releasing of the small debts that accumulate in shared life. The forgotten errand. The dismissive tone. The attention given to the phone instead of the person sitting across the table. The failure to say thank you for the thousandth load of laundry or the thousandth meal prepared. These are not major offenses. They are the silt that, left uncleared, gradually blocks the channel through which love flows.

The daily practice of forgiveness is less dramatic than the forgiveness required after a major betrayal, but it is no less important. The couples who thrive over decades are not the couples who never offend each other. They are the couples who have developed the habit of quick release — naming the offense, feeling the sting, and letting it go before it hardens into resentment. This is a skill, and like every skill, it can be learned, practiced, and refined.

It can also be abused. The daily practice of forgiveness is not a license for the offending spouse to be carelessly hurtful because they know they will be forgiven. Paul anticipated this objection in Romans 6:1 — "Shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase?" — and his answer was emphatic: "By no means." The grace of forgiveness creates not permission but obligation — the obligation to become the kind of person who wounds less, who pays attention more, who honors the gift of forgiveness by working to need less of it.

Forgiveness in marriage is not the absence of pain. It is the refusal to let pain have the final word. It is the decision — made once in the crisis and remade every morning after — that the covenant is stronger than the wound, that the love is deeper than the betrayal, and that the God who forgave you at infinite cost has given you the capacity to forgive at yours.

This capacity is not natural. It is not produced by willpower or good intentions. It is a gift of the Spirit, cultivated by practice, sustained by grace, and tested by every day of a marriage that is longer and harder and more beautiful than anything you imagined when you said "I do."

I will tell you what I have seen in the marriages that practice real forgiveness. They are not the easiest marriages. They are not the happiest marriages, if happiness is measured by the absence of difficulty. But they are the deepest marriages — marriages with a solidity that the untested marriages do not have, a resilience that was forged in the very fires that threatened to destroy them. These couples know something that couples who have never been seriously tested do not know: they know that their love can survive the worst thing. And that knowledge — hard-won, painfully earned, never taken for granted — is a kind of freedom that nothing else can provide.

The freedom is not the freedom from pain. It is the freedom from the fear that pain will end the marriage. And that freedom — the deep, settled confidence that the covenant is stronger than the wound — is the fruit of a forgiveness that is practiced daily, tested regularly, and sustained by a grace that is not their own.

The testing does not end. Neither does the grace. And the marriage that learns to practice forgiveness — real forgiveness, not the counterfeit — will carry scars. But it will also carry something the counterfeit can never produce: the deep, hard-won trust of two people who have seen each other's worst and chosen, at great cost, to stay.
excerpt: Forgiveness is the most demanded and least understood practice in Christian marriage — because the church has confused forgiveness with amnesia, with tolerance, with the suppression of legitimate anger, and the confusion is killing marriages.

title: When Trust Has Been Broken
body:
There is a moment in the life of a marriage when something breaks that cannot be unbroken. It might be an affair — sexual or emotional, discovered or confessed. It might be a financial betrayal — hidden debt, secret accounts, money spent or gambled or given away without the other's knowledge. It might be a revelation — a lie sustained over years, a double life exposed, a secret that, once out, rearranges everything the other person thought they knew about their spouse and their marriage.

The moment of discovery is a kind of death. The marriage that existed before the revelation no longer exists. It died in the instant the truth emerged. What remains is not the old marriage wounded. It is the wreckage of the old marriage and the question of whether a new one can be built in its place. The answer to that question is not guaranteed. It depends on factors that no formula can predict and no timeline can control. And the church, which has a powerful theology of resurrection but a weak theology of death, often rushes past the death to get to the resurrection, doing damage to both.

I have sat with couples in the immediate aftermath of discovered betrayal. The room has a particular quality — a charged silence, a flatness, as though the air has been sucked out by the force of the revelation. The betrayed spouse is often calm in a way that is more frightening than anger. The calm is shock. The nervous system has absorbed more than it can process, and it has shut down the emotional response to protect the organism from overload. The anger will come later. It always does. And when it comes, it will be as fierce and as justified as anything the human heart can produce.

I have also sat with the betraying spouse in those same rooms. Their pain is different but real — the pain of exposure, the pain of seeing what their choices have done to the person they love, the pain of watching a world they built crumble because of something they did. The church that has no compassion for the betrayer has forgotten that its own theology is built on the premise that all of us are betrayers. The cross was erected by human betrayal, and the God who hung on it forgave the hands that drove the nails. Compassion for the betrayer does not minimize the betrayal. It places the betrayal inside a gospel that holds both justice and mercy without collapsing either.

What Betrayal Does to the Brain

Before addressing the theology of trust, it is necessary to address the neuroscience, because the body's response to betrayal is not a spiritual failure. It is a biological reality that must be respected before it can be transcended.

When a person discovers that their spouse has betrayed them, the brain responds as though it has encountered a physical threat. The amygdala — the brain's threat detection center — activates. Cortisol and adrenaline flood the system. The prefrontal cortex, which governs rational thought, executive function, and emotional regulation, goes partially offline. The betrayed person is, in a very real neurological sense, not fully capable of rational processing in the days and weeks following the discovery.

This is why the immediate aftermath of betrayal is not the time for decisions about the future of the marriage. The betrayed spouse cannot think clearly. The betraying spouse, overwhelmed by guilt and fear, cannot think clearly either. Both are operating in survival mode, and survival mode does not produce wisdom. The best thing a pastor or counselor can do in the first days after discovery is to slow everything down — to resist the pressure (usually from the betraying spouse, who wants the crisis to end) to rush toward resolution, and to create space for the shock to be absorbed.

Bessel van der Kolk's research on trauma, published in "The Body Keeps the Score," demonstrates that traumatic events are stored not only in cognitive memory but in the body itself. The betrayed spouse may experience flashbacks, hypervigilance, sleep disruption, and intrusive thoughts — the same symptoms associated with post-traumatic stress. This is not weakness. This is the body doing what bodies do in response to the destruction of safety. And safety — the sense that the person closest to you is trustworthy — is the most fundamental need in any intimate relationship.

The Architecture of Trust

To understand what it takes to rebuild trust, you must first understand what trust is. Trust is not a feeling. It is a structure — a load-bearing structure that holds the weight of everything else in the marriage. Intimacy, vulnerability, shared decision-making, co-parenting, financial partnership, sexual openness — all of these rest on the foundation of trust. When the foundation collapses, everything it supported collapses with it.

The structure of trust is built over time through the accumulation of consistent, reliable, honest behavior. Every kept promise adds a beam. Every moment of transparency adds a brick. Every time one spouse says, "Here is who I am, here is what I did, here is what I am thinking," and the other spouse receives it without punishing the honesty — that exchange is a structural element in the architecture of trust.

Betrayal does not remove a beam. It demolishes the building. And the demolition is so complete that the rebuilding cannot begin where the old building stood. The rubble must be cleared first. The ground must be examined. The soil that allowed the collapse must be understood before new construction begins. Otherwise, the new building will be erected on the same faults that brought down the old one, and it will fall again.

The clearing of the rubble is the hardest phase, because both parties want to skip it. The betrayer wants to move past the destruction as quickly as possible — partly out of genuine remorse, partly out of the selfish desire to stop feeling the consequences. The betrayed spouse may also want to skip the rubble, because sitting in the wreckage means feeling the full weight of what has happened, and the full weight is almost unbearable. But the rubble must be examined. Every lie must be named. Every deception must be surfaced. Every hidden thing must be brought into the light. Only then can the ground be cleared for new construction.

What Rebuilding Requires of the Betrayer

The burden of rebuilding falls primarily — though not exclusively — on the spouse who broke the trust. This is not a popular position in a culture that prefers to distribute blame equally, but it is the only honest position. The person who demolished the building is the person who must do the heaviest lifting in the reconstruction. And the reconstruction requires at least four things.

First, full disclosure. Not the partial truth that minimizes the damage. Not the trickle of revelations that emerge over weeks and months, each one reopening the wound just as it begins to close. Full disclosure means telling the whole truth at once, in the presence of a counselor or pastor who can support the betrayed spouse through the impact. The temptation to withhold details — "I am protecting them from pain" — is almost always self-serving. The betrayer is protecting themselves from the betrayed spouse's response to the full truth. And the withholding, when it is eventually discovered (and it almost always is), does more damage than the original betrayal, because it proves that the pattern of deception has not changed.

Second, sustained transparency. The betrayer must be willing to live, for an extended period, with a level of accountability that feels invasive. Open phones. Open email. Open schedules. Voluntary check-ins. The willingness to answer questions — the same questions, asked repeatedly — without defensiveness, without impatience, without the complaint that "you said you forgave me." Forgiveness and trust are not the same thing. The betrayed spouse may have forgiven the betrayal and still not trust the betrayer. Both responses are legitimate. Both can coexist.

Third, genuine remorse. Not guilt — guilt is self-focused, consumed with the betrayer's own shame and fear of consequences. Remorse is other-focused — consumed with the pain inflicted on the other person. The betrayer who says, "I cannot believe I did this to myself, my career, my reputation" is expressing guilt. The betrayer who says, "I cannot believe I did this to you" is expressing remorse. The difference is the direction of the gaze, and the betrayed spouse can tell the difference with absolute precision.

Fourth, the willingness to understand and address the underlying issues that led to the betrayal. Affairs do not happen in a vacuum. Financial deceptions do not emerge from nowhere. The betrayal was the visible symptom of an invisible illness — unmet needs, unresolved resentment, untreated addiction, undeveloped emotional capacity. Addressing the symptom without diagnosing the illness is malpractice. The betrayer who says, "It will never happen again" without doing the deep work of understanding why it happened in the first place is making a promise they cannot keep.

What Rebuilding Requires of the Betrayed

The betrayed spouse's work is different but no less difficult. It requires the willingness to remain in the process long enough for the rebuilding to happen — and the process will be longer, messier, and more painful than anyone wants it to be.

The betrayed spouse must be willing to feel the full weight of the anger without being consumed by it. The anger is legitimate. It is necessary. But if it becomes the permanent posture of the relationship — if every interaction is filtered through the lens of the betrayal, if every lapse in the betrayer's behavior is interpreted as evidence of continued deception, if the anger becomes a weapon rather than a signal — then the anger has crossed from healthy processing into destructive vengeance, and the marriage will not survive it.

The betrayed spouse must also be willing to make a decision — and the decision must be genuine. Either you are in the process of rebuilding, or you are not. Either you are willing to give the betrayer the opportunity to demonstrate change, or you are not. There is no shame in deciding that the betrayal is too great, that the damage is too deep, that the marriage cannot be rebuilt. That is an honest and sometimes necessary conclusion. But staying in the marriage while refusing to participate in the rebuilding — punishing the betrayer indefinitely, using the betrayal as a permanent weapon, withholding engagement as a form of retaliation — is not faithfulness. It is imprisonment for both parties, and it serves no one.

The Timeline Nobody Wants to Hear

The rebuilding of trust after major betrayal takes, on average, two to five years. Not months. Years. The research on post-affair recovery — from clinicians like Shirley Glass, whose work "Not Just Friends" is the most clinically grounded treatment of the subject — consistently shows that the recovery process involves setbacks, regressions, and periods of apparent hopelessness that are normal and expected.

The first year is typically the hardest. The betrayed spouse cycles through waves of grief, anger, hypervigilance, and despair. Triggers are everywhere — a song, a restaurant, a time of day, a phrase that recalls the betrayal. The emotional roller coaster is exhausting for both parties. The betrayer wants the crisis to be over. The betrayed spouse wants the pain to stop. Neither gets what they want for a very long time.

The second year is often characterized by what therapists call "the long slog" — the period when the acute crisis has passed but the underlying damage remains. The dramatic emotions subside, replaced by a flat, persistent sadness and a deep uncertainty about whether the investment in rebuilding is worth the cost. Many couples give up during this phase, not because the marriage is beyond repair but because the repair is taking longer than they had the endurance to sustain.

The couples who make it through the second year and into the third often report something unexpected: a marriage that is, in significant ways, better than what preceded the betrayal. Not because the betrayal was good. It was not. But because the rebuilding process forced a level of honesty, vulnerability, and intentionality that the pre-betrayal marriage never achieved. The old marriage was functional but shallow. The rebuilt marriage is scarred but deep. This is not a justification for betrayal. It is a testimony to the human capacity for reconstruction when the work is done honestly and the grace is given time to take root.

What the Gospel Offers

The gospel does not guarantee that every broken marriage can be rebuilt. But it does offer the only framework adequate to the task: a God who specializes in resurrection, who makes new things out of dead things, who looked at the wreckage of human sin and did not walk away but walked into it, absorbed its cost, and built something new on the other side.

The cross is the definitive statement about trust broken and love sustained. God trusted humanity with the garden. Humanity broke the trust. God did not abandon the project. He entered it — entered the mess, the betrayal, the wreckage — and paid the price of restoration with His own body. The cross is not a fairy tale about easy reconciliation. It is the most honest account of what reconciliation actually costs: everything. And the God who paid everything is the God who stands with every couple trying to rebuild what was demolished, offering not a formula but a presence, not a guarantee but a hope.

Trust, once broken, is never the same. It is either rebuilt into something different — something that has been tested by fire and survived — or it is not rebuilt at all. Both outcomes are possible. Both are real. And the choice between them is made not in a single moment of decision but in a thousand small moments of honesty, transparency, and the willingness to stay in the room when everything in you says to leave.

The room is painful. The rebuilding is slow. The scars are permanent. But the God who raises the dead has not exempted marriages from the scope of His resurrection power. And the couples who have walked through this valley — who have done the work, paid the cost, and emerged on the other side — carry a testimony that the world needs to hear: that love, real love, is not the love that was never tested. It is the love that was tested to the point of destruction and chose, at unimaginable cost, to begin again.

I have witnessed this love. I have seen it in a couple who sat in my office for two years — every week, without fail, through the worst season of their lives. I have seen it in the husband who answered the same question about his whereabouts for the hundredth time without defensiveness, because he understood that the question was not about tonight. It was about every night he had lied. I have seen it in the wife who chose, one morning, to stop looking at his phone — not because she trusted him but because she decided to practice trust as an act of faith, knowing that faith is always practiced in the absence of certainty. Their marriage is not the marriage they started with. It is better. Not because the betrayal made it better. Because the rebuilding, done honestly, produced a depth that the original construction never achieved.

That is the promise hidden in the wreckage: not that the old building can be restored, but that a new one — stronger, deeper, built on a foundation that has been tested — can rise in its place. The promise is not guaranteed. But it is possible. And for the couple willing to pay the cost, possible is enough.
excerpt: Trust is not a light switch you flip back on after a betrayal — it is a structure that was demolished and must be rebuilt beam by beam, and the rebuilding requires more honesty than most couples have ever practiced.

title: The Emotionally Absent Spouse
body:
The complaint arrives in my office in different words, but it is always the same complaint. "He is there but he is not there." "She has shut down and I cannot reach her." "We live in the same house and I have never been lonelier." The presenting issue varies — sometimes it is framed as a communication problem, sometimes as a conflict about parenting or money or sex. But underneath the presenting issue, the wound is the same: one spouse has become emotionally absent, and the other is starving.

Emotional absence is not dramatic. It does not announce itself with a crisis or a revelation. It is quiet, gradual, almost invisible. The absent spouse still comes home. They still eat dinner at the table. They still sleep in the same bed. They may even be pleasant, competent, responsible. They pay the bills, mow the lawn, drive the kids to practice. From the outside, nothing is wrong. From the inside, everything is wrong, because the one thing that makes a marriage a marriage — the emotional connection between two people — has been withdrawn.

This is the most common and least discussed form of marital suffering. It does not make the headlines like infidelity. It does not trigger the alarm bells like addiction. It is a slow starvation — a death by inches — and the person experiencing it often cannot explain what is wrong because nothing identifiable has happened. The spouse has not done anything wrong. That is precisely the problem. They have not done anything at all.

What Emotional Absence Looks Like

Emotional absence manifests in patterns that are recognizable once you know what to look for. The absent spouse does not initiate conversation about anything beyond logistics. They do not ask how your day was and mean it. They do not notice when you are upset. They do not respond when you try to share something that matters to you — a worry about the children, a frustration at work, a moment of beauty that you wanted to share. They are not hostile. They are not cold, exactly. They are simply elsewhere — their attention directed inward or outward, anywhere but at you.

The absent spouse often does not realize they are absent. This is not an excuse. It is a diagnostic observation. Many emotionally absent people are not withholding intentionally. They are living inside a pattern they did not choose and cannot see — a pattern formed in childhood, reinforced by culture, and sustained by the sheer momentum of adult life. They learned early that the safest place to be was inside themselves, that emotional exposure was dangerous, that the best way to survive was to become a fortress. The fortress kept them safe as children. It is killing their marriage as adults.

The absent spouse may also be absent because they are overwhelmed. The demands of work, parenting, financial pressure, and the constant low-grade anxiety of modern life can consume the emotional resources that the marriage needs. The spouse who comes home after a twelve-hour workday, having managed people and problems and crises for someone else's profit, may simply have nothing left. The tank is empty. And the marriage, which requires fuel to run, stalls. This form of absence is not a character flaw. It is a structural problem — a problem of a culture that extracts more from its workers than human beings were designed to give.

The attachment literature is helpful here. John Bowlby, the British psychiatrist who developed attachment theory in the mid-twentieth century, identified a pattern he called "avoidant attachment" — a relational style formed in early childhood when the primary caregiver was consistently unavailable or unresponsive. The child learns that emotional needs will not be met, and rather than continuing to reach out into empty space, the child adapts. The child learns to suppress the need, to self-soothe rather than seek comfort, to build an internal world that does not depend on anyone else.

This adaptation is brilliant in childhood. It is a survival strategy of remarkable sophistication. And it is catastrophic in adulthood, because the strategy that was designed to protect the child from the pain of unmet attachment needs now prevents the adult from meeting their spouse's attachment needs. The avoidant partner is not choosing to be distant. They are running software written thirty years ago, in a context that no longer exists, for a purpose that no longer applies.

The Pursuing Spouse's Dilemma

The spouse on the other side of emotional absence faces a dilemma that has no easy resolution. They need connection. They are married to someone who does not provide it. And every strategy they employ to get it tends to make the problem worse.

The most common strategy is pursuit — escalating attempts to draw the absent spouse out. More questions. More requests for conversation. More expressions of need. More complaints about the distance. The pursuit is logical: if the problem is distance, the solution should be closeness. But in the attachment dynamic, pursuit triggers withdrawal. The absent spouse, already overwhelmed by the demand for emotional engagement they do not know how to provide, retreats further. The pursuing spouse, interpreting the retreat as rejection, pursues harder. The cycle accelerates until both are exhausted — the pursuer angry and depleted, the withdrawer cornered and shut down.

Sue Johnson, the developer of Emotionally Focused Therapy, calls this the "pursue-withdraw cycle" and identifies it as the single most common pattern in distressed couples. The pattern is not a character flaw in either partner. It is a system — an interlocking set of behaviors that each partner triggers in the other, sustained by the attachment fears that both carry. The pursuer fears abandonment. The withdrawer fears engulfment. Both fears are real. Both are driving the behavior that makes the other's fear come true.

The cruelest dimension of this cycle is that both partners are in pain. The pursuing spouse's pain is visible — the tears, the anger, the desperate attempts to connect. The absent spouse's pain is invisible — the shame, the paralysis, the terrible awareness that they are failing at the one relationship that matters most and have no idea how to stop failing. The pursuing spouse sees a partner who does not care. The absent spouse sees a partner who can never be satisfied. Both are wrong. Both are suffering.

The Gendered Dimension

I need to say something about gender here, because the research consistently shows a gendered pattern in emotional absence, and ignoring the pattern does not serve the couples who live inside it.

Men are disproportionately the emotionally absent partner. Not exclusively — women can be emotionally absent, and the experience is equally painful when they are. But the pattern skews male, and the reasons are not mysterious. Boys in Western culture are systematically trained out of emotional expression from an early age. "Boys don't cry." "Man up." "Don't be so sensitive." The socialization is relentless, and by adulthood, many men have lost access to their own emotional interior — not because the emotions are not there, but because the capacity to identify, name, and express them has atrophied from disuse.

Niobe Way's longitudinal research, published in "Deep Secrets," documented that adolescent boys in the United States have rich, emotionally intimate friendships in early adolescence that they systematically abandon by late adolescence, under the pressure of masculine norms that equate emotional closeness between males with weakness or homosexuality. By adulthood, the average American man has zero intimate friendships — zero people to whom he can say what he actually feels. His wife is often the only person in his life with whom emotional intimacy is even theoretically possible. And he has been trained, for his entire life, to be incapable of it.

This is not an excuse for emotional absence. It is a context. And the church, which has largely reinforced the masculine norms that produce emotional absence — the strong, silent leader, the provider who does not need, the man who leads his family with quiet authority rather than emotional vulnerability — bears a particular responsibility for addressing it.

What the Absent Spouse Must Learn

The emotionally absent spouse must learn something they were never taught: that emotional presence is a skill, not a personality trait, and that skills can be acquired. This learning is painful, because it requires the absent spouse to re-enter the emotional terrain they spent their childhood learning to avoid. It requires them to feel things they have been suppressing for decades. It requires them to be bad at something in front of the person whose opinion matters most.

The learning begins with awareness — the recognition that the absence is real, that it has consequences, and that the spouse's complaints about it are not nagging but a legitimate cry of pain. This recognition is often the hardest step, because the absent spouse's defensive system is designed to minimize the significance of emotional connection. "I am here, aren't I?" "I work hard to provide for this family." "What more do you want?" These responses are not malicious. They are the sound of a defensive system protecting itself from a demand it does not know how to meet.

The learning continues with practice — small, deliberate acts of emotional engagement that, over time, begin to rewire the patterns. Asking a question and waiting for the answer. Noticing when your spouse is upset and saying so. Sharing something you feel — not something you think, but something you feel — without being prompted. Putting the phone down during conversation. Making eye contact. These are elementary things. For the emotionally absent spouse, they feel like crossing a minefield.

The learning is sustained by therapeutic support. I cannot say this strongly enough: the pattern of emotional absence is rarely broken without professional help. The defensive system that produces the absence is deeply embedded, often rooted in childhood experiences that the absent spouse has never processed. A competent therapist — particularly one trained in emotionally focused therapy or attachment-based approaches — can guide the absent spouse into the emotional territory they have been avoiding, with the safety and structure that makes the re-entry survivable.

What the Pursuing Spouse Must Learn

The pursuing spouse's learning is equally difficult, though it takes a different form. The pursuer must learn to regulate their own anxiety without depending on the absent spouse's response. This does not mean suppressing the need for connection. It means finding ways to soothe the attachment fear that drives the pursuit — developing the internal resources that allow them to tolerate the gap between what they need and what their spouse can currently provide.

The pursuer must also learn to translate their anger into vulnerability. The absent spouse does not respond to anger. Anger triggers their defensive system and drives them further into withdrawal. But vulnerability — the soft, exposed expression of the need beneath the anger — can sometimes reach the absent spouse in a way that anger cannot. "I miss you" lands differently than "You never talk to me." "I am scared we are losing each other" lands differently than "You do not care about this marriage." The message is the same. The delivery determines whether it is received.

This is not fair. I know it is not fair. The pursuing spouse should not have to translate their legitimate pain into a form the absent spouse can receive. But fairness and effectiveness are not the same thing, and the goal is not to win the argument but to reach the person. And reaching the person sometimes requires speaking their language rather than demanding that they learn yours.

What the Church Must Do

The church must stop celebrating emotional absence as spiritual maturity. The quiet, steady, unemotional man is not the model of Christian masculinity. He may be the victim of a socialization process that has cut him off from half of his own humanity. The church that holds up stoicism as a virtue is holding up a wound as a trophy, and the marriages in its pews are paying the price.

The church must create spaces where emotional honesty is possible — where men can say what they actually feel without being judged, where vulnerability is treated as strength rather than weakness, where the pastoral leadership models emotional presence rather than emotional performance. This requires pastors who are themselves willing to be emotionally present — not performed vulnerability for a sermon illustration, but genuine, risky, unscripted honesty about their own inner lives.

The emotionally absent spouse is not a villain. They are a person who learned, long before they learned to love, that the safest place in the world was inside themselves. The work of marriage — and the work of the Spirit — is to show them that there is a safer place: the space between two people who have chosen to stay, to feel, and to be fully present to each other, not because it is natural but because it is necessary, and not because it is easy but because it is love.

That work is long. It is humbling. It does not produce the dramatic breakthroughs that make for good testimonies. It produces small, incremental changes — a question asked, an emotion named, a hand held in silence — that accumulate over years into something that begins to resemble the intimacy both partners have been craving.

I have watched this happen in my own marriage. I have been the emotionally absent spouse — present in body, absent in soul, giving the church everything and giving home the remnants. I have sat across from my wife and realized, with a shame I cannot adequately describe, that she was telling me something important and I had not heard a word. Not because I was not listening. Because I had nothing left to listen with. The empathy had been spent on parishioners. The attentiveness had been deployed in counseling sessions. The capacity for emotional presence had been distributed across forty hours of pastoral work, and the well was dry.

The recovery was not dramatic. It was not a single conversation or a breakthrough moment. It was a slow, humbling relearning of skills I should never have let atrophy — the skill of asking a question and caring about the answer, the skill of putting the phone down without being asked, the skill of noticing the look on my wife's face and saying, "Something is wrong. Tell me." These are elementary skills. I had to learn them like a child learning to walk. And the relearning required a willingness to be bad at something in front of the person whose judgment I feared most. That willingness, more than any technique or insight, was the beginning of the return.

The intimacy will not look like the movies. It will look like two imperfect people, fumbling toward each other in the dark, learning to say the things they were never taught to say. It will be awkward and halting and sometimes painful. It will also be real. And real, in a marriage, is worth more than any performance could ever be.
excerpt: The most common complaint in my office is not about affairs or addiction — it is about the spouse who is physically present and emotionally gone, and the loneliness of lying next to someone who is not really there.

title: Money and Marriage: Why It's Always About More Than Money
body:
In fifteen years of pastoral ministry, I have never seen a couple fight about money. I have seen them fight about what money represents — security, freedom, control, identity, the fear of becoming their parents, the fear of failing their children — but never about money itself. Money is the surface. It is always the surface. And the couples who spend their energy arguing about the surface never get to the substance underneath, which is why the arguments recur with such depressing regularity. You cannot resolve a conflict you have not correctly diagnosed.

The research confirms what pastoral experience suggests. A study published in "Family Relations" by Sonya Britt-Lutter and colleagues found that arguments about money are the top predictor of divorce — more than arguments about sex, parenting, or in-laws. But the same research found that the predictive power was not about the amount of money. Couples with high incomes fought about money with the same intensity and frequency as couples with low incomes. The variable was not the balance in the account. It was the meaning assigned to the balance. And meaning, as every theologian knows, is where the real battles are fought.

I have five sons. I grew up without a father. The intersection of those two facts means that my relationship with money is shaped by scarcity and responsibility in ways I did not understand for most of my adult life. I provided fiercely because I had not been provided for. I worried obsessively because worry felt like vigilance, and vigilance felt like love. It took years — and a wife who refused to accept my anxiety as virtue — to see that the money story I was living was not a financial plan. It was a wound wearing a suit.

The Money Stories You Inherited

Before you ever opened a joint checking account, you had a money story. It was written for you in childhood, by parents and circumstances you did not choose, and it was inscribed so deeply into your operating system that by the time you married, you did not even know it was there. You thought you were just being "responsible" or "generous" or "careful." You were actually enacting a script that was written decades ago, in a household you no longer live in, by people whose financial anxieties became your own.

The child who grew up in poverty carries a particular relationship with money into adulthood. Money is scarce. Money can disappear. Money must be hoarded, protected, worried over. Every purchase is a risk. Every expenditure is a potential catastrophe. The adult who carries this story may have a six-figure income and a full savings account and still feel the anxiety of the child who watched the power get shut off. The rational brain knows the bills are paid. The child brain does not trust it.

The child who grew up in affluence carries a different relationship. Money is available. Money is a tool. Money solves problems. The adult who carries this story may spend freely, give generously, and feel genuinely confused when their spouse panics about the credit card statement. They are not being irresponsible. They are living inside a story in which money is not a source of fear.
