When these two stories marry each other — and they frequently do, because opposites attract precisely because they compensate for each other's anxiety — the result is a conflict that neither party can resolve by argument, because the conflict is not about the current expenditure. It is about the childhood wound that the expenditure has activated. He sees a dining room table she wants to buy and feels the panic of a child whose family could not afford furniture. She sees a savings account he obsesses over and feels the suffocation of a child whose family's frugality was actually control. Both are responding to the present through the lens of the past, and neither knows it.

The first step in resolving money conflicts in marriage is not a better budget. It is a better autobiography. Each spouse must tell the story of money as they experienced it growing up — not the financial details, but the emotional reality. What did money feel like in your home? Was it discussed openly or hidden? Was it a source of anxiety or a source of freedom? What was the worst money moment of your childhood? What did you swear you would never repeat? These questions do not appear in any financial planning software. They are more important than any spreadsheet.

The Four Money Personalities

Financial counselors and researchers have identified broad patterns in how individuals relate to money. The specific taxonomies vary, but the general categories are consistent across the literature. Savers hoard. Spenders deploy. Avoiders refuse to engage. Risk-takers gamble on future returns. Every person carries a primary orientation, and every marriage involves the collision of two orientations that are almost never the same.

The saver-spender marriage is the most common combination and the most volatile. The saver sees the spender as reckless, irresponsible, a threat to the family's stability. The spender sees the saver as controlling, fearful, unwilling to enjoy the resources they have worked to earn. Both are partially right. Both are projecting their own money story onto their spouse's behavior. And the argument about whether to take the vacation or add to the emergency fund is never, ever about the vacation or the emergency fund. It is about two competing visions of what money is for, rooted in two different childhoods, expressing two different fears.

The avoider-engaged marriage is less volatile but equally damaging. One spouse handles the finances. The other checks out — does not look at the statements, does not participate in the budgeting, does not want to know. The engaged spouse carries the burden and the anxiety alone. The avoiding spouse enjoys the comfort of ignorance. And the power imbalance — because financial control is power, whether or not the controlling spouse intends it to be — grows wider with every year of avoidance.

The Theology of Money in Marriage

The Bible treats money as a diagnostic tool. It does not tell you how much to save or how much to spend. It tells you that your relationship with money reveals your relationship with God. "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). The verse is not a prohibition against having treasure. It is a warning that your treasure — whatever you value most, whatever you protect most fiercely, whatever you worry about losing — will reveal the location of your heart. And in a marriage, the way each spouse relates to money reveals the location of their heart with uncomfortable precision.

The spouse who cannot stop saving is placing their security in the account balance rather than in God. I say this not as judgment but as diagnosis, because I recognize the pattern in myself. The anxiety that drives compulsive saving is the anxiety of a heart that does not trust God to provide. It is the functional atheism of the Israelites who gathered more manna than they needed, despite God's explicit instruction that each day's portion would be sufficient. The extra manna rotted. It always does. Because the security we manufacture for ourselves is not the security God offers. It is the illusion of security, sustained by vigilance and anxiety, and it consumes the very life it was meant to protect.

The spouse who cannot stop spending is placing their identity in acquisition rather than in God. The purchase provides a momentary relief from the emptiness, a brief injection of significance, a temporary sense that life is abundant. But the relief fades, the significance evaporates, and the emptiness returns, demanding another purchase. Ecclesiastes 5:10: "Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income." The wisdom is three thousand years old. The pattern has not changed.

Neither saving nor spending is inherently sinful. Both are necessary. The question is what drives them — whether the saving is prudence or fear, whether the spending is generosity or compulsion, whether the money is a tool in service of the marriage or an idol in competition with it.

The Power Dynamics

Money is power in a marriage, and the refusal to acknowledge this truth does not make it less true. It makes it more dangerous, because unacknowledged power operates without accountability.

In marriages where one spouse earns significantly more than the other — or where one spouse earns and the other does not — the earning spouse holds a structural power advantage that shapes every financial decision. The non-earning spouse may technically have equal access to the accounts. They do not have equal standing in the negotiation. The unspoken reality — "I earned this money" — hangs over every conversation about how the money is spent, even when it is never said aloud. Especially when it is never said aloud, because the unspoken has a power that the spoken cannot match.

The stay-at-home parent is particularly vulnerable to this dynamic. Their contribution to the household — the cooking, the cleaning, the child-rearing, the emotional labor that keeps the family functioning — is invisible in the economy's accounting. It does not generate a paycheck. It does not appear on a balance sheet. And in a culture that equates value with earning power, the stay-at-home parent absorbs a subtle but persistent message: your work does not count. This message, absorbed over years, erodes the parent's sense of agency in financial decisions and can produce a dependency that feels less like partnership and more like permission.

The covenant of marriage demands the dismantling of this power dynamic. Not because power differences are inherently sinful but because the covenant transforms two individuals into one economic unit, and the resources of that unit belong to the unit, not to the individual who generated them. Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7 about the body applies to the finances: "The husband's income does not belong to the husband alone, and the wife's income does not belong to the wife alone." I am paraphrasing, but the principle holds. The one-flesh union does not permit the financial sovereignty of either partner.

The Practice of Financial Unity

What does financial unity look like in practice? It looks like two people sitting at the same table, looking at the same numbers, with equal voice and equal information, making decisions together. This is simple to describe and agonizing to practice, because it requires both spouses to expose their money stories, their fears, their desires, and their shame — and money shame is among the deepest and least discussed shames a person can carry.

The practice begins with full transparency. Both spouses must know the complete financial picture — all income, all debt, all assets, all obligations. The spouse who hides a credit card balance or a savings account or a financial obligation is not protecting the marriage. They are lying to it. And financial deception, while it lacks the dramatic force of sexual infidelity, is a betrayal of the covenant that erodes trust with the same corrosive effect.

The practice continues with regular financial conversations — not the crisis conversation that happens when the credit card bill arrives, but the proactive, scheduled, calm conversation about where the money is going, where it should go, and what each spouse values. These conversations will be uncomfortable. They will expose differences that feel irreconcilable. They will surface the childhood wounds that neither spouse has fully processed. And they are absolutely necessary, because the alternative — financial silence, financial avoidance, financial unilateralism — produces the very outcomes that both spouses fear.

The practice is sustained by a shared vision. What are we building together? What do we want our money to make possible? What would our finances look like if they reflected our actual values rather than our unexamined habits? These questions are not merely financial. They are theological. They ask what the marriage is for, what the family serves, and whether the life being built reflects the kingdom or merely the culture.

Generosity as Marital Practice

I will say one more thing, because it is true even though it sounds counterintuitive: one of the most powerful things a couple can do for their marriage is give money away. Generosity — regular, sacrificial, deliberate giving — does something to a marriage that no budget software can replicate. It breaks the grip of scarcity. It dismantles the idol of security. It forces both spouses to confront the question that every money fight is ultimately about: do we trust God to provide, or do we trust ourselves?

The couples in my congregation who tithe — who give ten percent or more of their income to the church and to the poor — are not wealthier than the couples who do not. But they fight about money less. Not because they have solved the financial puzzle but because generosity has loosened money's hold on their hearts. The money has been put in its place. It is a tool, not a god. And a tool does not generate the anxiety that a god demands.

Every money fight is an invitation — an invitation to go deeper, to name the fear, to excavate the story, to ask what the money actually represents and whether the thing it represents can be found in a balance sheet or only in the God who owns everything and gives freely to those who ask.

The invitation is uncomfortable. It always is. But the couples who accept it — who sit down together and do the hard, humbling work of understanding not just what they earn and spend but why they earn and spend the way they do — those couples discover something that the money itself could never buy: the freedom of two people who are no longer controlled by the thing they thought they were controlling.

I learned this in my own marriage. I grew up without a father, and the absence left me with a money story written in fear — the fear that provision could disappear without warning, the fear that I would not be enough, the fear that the people I loved would go without. I saved compulsively. I budgeted rigidly. I said no to things that would have brought my family joy because the joy cost money and money, in my internal economy, was the only barrier between my family and catastrophe. My wife did not share this fear. She grew up in a household where money was present and shared freely, where generosity was practiced without anxiety, where the future was trusted. She saw my saving as control. I saw her spending as recklessness. We were both wrong. We were both right. And the resolution did not come through compromise — split the difference, save half, spend half. It came through the slow, painful, deeply personal work of telling each other our stories and listening to what the stories revealed.

That freedom is available. It is costly. And it begins not with a better budget but with a braver conversation.
excerpt: Every fight about money is a fight about something else — about security, about control, about the stories you absorbed before you were old enough to question them — and until you name the something else, the money fights will never end.

title: In-Laws, Boundaries, and Leaving and Cleaving
body:
Genesis 2:24 contains a command so socially disruptive that nearly every culture in human history has found a way to soften it. "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife." In the ancient Near East, where the family of origin was the primary unit of economic survival, social identity, and religious practice, this command was not sentimental. It was revolutionary. It declared that the marriage bond supersedes the parental bond — that the new family takes precedence over the old one — and that any arrangement that does not honor this priority is structurally disordered.

The church has largely failed to preach this text with the force it demands. We have softened "leave" into "adjust." We have interpreted "hold fast" as "balance." We have produced a generation of marriages in which the parents of one or both spouses exercise an authority over the marriage that the text explicitly forbids. And then we wonder why the marriage is struggling, as though the cause were obscure.

I write this as a pastor who has counseled dozens of couples whose primary source of marital conflict is not each other but the family of origin that one or both spouses has never left. I write this as a man who has had to learn, through failure, what leaving actually requires. It requires more than a change of address. It requires a restructuring of loyalty so fundamental that it will cost you something in the relationship with the people who raised you. That cost is not optional. It is the price of the marriage.

What "Leaving" Actually Means

The Hebrew word translated "leave" in Genesis 2:24 is azav. It is a strong word. It is the same word used in Psalm 22:1 — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — the cry Jesus quoted from the cross. Azav does not mean "gradually reduce contact." It does not mean "establish a polite distance." It means to relinquish, to abandon a previous position, to cut a tie that was binding. The word carries a force that the English "leave" does not.

This does not mean cutting off your parents. It does not mean dishonoring them. The fifth commandment — "Honor your father and your mother" — stands alongside the creation mandate. Both are true. Both must be honored. But the honoring changes shape when you marry. Before marriage, your primary loyalty belongs to your family of origin. After marriage, your primary loyalty belongs to your spouse. The parents do not disappear. They are repositioned. They move from the center of the relational universe to the orbit. And many parents — particularly parents whose identity is deeply invested in their children — experience this repositioning as a loss. Because it is a loss.

The grief of the parent whose child has truly left is real and should be acknowledged. The mother who spent twenty years as the most important woman in her son's life must now accept that another woman holds that position. The father who was his daughter's protector must now trust another man with that role. This is painful. It is also necessary. And the parent who cannot grieve the loss and release the child is a parent who will, intentionally or not, undermine the marriage.

The church has a role to play in helping parents grieve this transition — in normalizing the grief, honoring the loss, and helping parents find their identity in something more durable than their children's dependence. But the church has largely abdicated this role, either because it does not recognize the grief or because it does not want to confront the parental behaviors that the unprocessed grief produces. The result is a generation of parents who have not been helped to let go and a generation of marriages that are paying the price for the holding on.

The Ways Parents Undermine Marriages

The undermining is rarely malicious. It is almost always unconscious, driven by the parent's own attachment needs, control patterns, or unresolved grief about the child's departure. But unconscious harm is still harm, and the patterns need to be named.

The intrusive parent inserts themselves into the marriage's decisions — where to live, how to raise the children, how to spend money, how to manage the household. They offer "advice" that is actually directive. They express "concern" that is actually control. They frame their interference as love, and because it is love — distorted, boundary-violating love, but love nonetheless — the adult child feels guilty about resisting it.

The enmeshed parent maintains an emotional bond with the adult child that competes with the marriage bond. The mother who calls her son every day and expects an hour of conversation. The father who expects his daughter to confide in him about the marriage's struggles. The parent who reacts to the adult child's appropriate emotional transfer to the spouse as a personal abandonment. Enmeshment feels like closeness. It is actually a failure of differentiation — the failure of the parent and child to develop separate identities that can relate to each other from a position of autonomy rather than dependency.

The critical parent judges the spouse — sometimes openly, sometimes through subtle signals that the adult child learns to read with precision. The raised eyebrow when the spouse speaks. The comparison to how things were done in the family of origin. The pointed comment that lands exactly where it was aimed. The adult child who absorbs these signals without challenging them is siding with the parent against the spouse, whether they realize it or not.

The dependent parent reverses the relationship — making the adult child responsible for the parent's emotional well-being, financial security, or social life. The parent who guilt-trips the adult child for spending holidays with the spouse's family. The parent who manufactures crises to reclaim the adult child's attention. The parent who says, "After everything I've done for you," deploying sacrifice as a debt that can never be fully repaid.

The triangulating parent communicates through the adult child rather than directly with the spouse — creating alliances, sharing confidences that should not be shared, and positioning the adult child as the mediator in a conflict that the parent has with the son-in-law or daughter-in-law. Triangulation is one of the most destructive patterns in family systems because it prevents the two people who actually have the conflict from resolving it directly. The adult child, trapped in the middle, cannot be loyal to both without betraying one.

Why the Adult Child Cannot Leave

The adult child who has not left their parents is not weak. They are caught in a system that was designed, from their earliest days, to make leaving feel like betrayal. The mechanisms vary by family, but the logic is consistent: the family of origin has defined the child's identity, and any move toward independent identity is experienced — by the family and by the child — as a threat to the family's cohesion.

Murray Bowen, the founder of family systems theory, called this "undifferentiation" — the failure to develop a self that is separate from the family of origin. The undifferentiated adult makes decisions based on the family's emotional system rather than their own values. They cannot disagree with their parents without feeling overwhelmed by guilt. They cannot set a boundary without feeling that they are being cruel. They cannot prioritize their spouse without feeling that they are abandoning the people who raised them.

The guilt is the key. The guilt is what keeps the adult child tethered to the family of origin in a way that prevents the full transfer of loyalty to the spouse. And the guilt feels righteous — it feels like honor, like faithfulness, like the evidence of a good heart. But it is not honor. It is bondage. And the God who commands us to honor our parents is the same God who commands us to leave them, and He does not issue contradictory commands. The commands are compatible. The compatibility requires that honor take a new form — the form of adult-to-adult relationship rather than child-to-parent dependency.

What Boundaries Look Like

A boundary is not a wall. It is a property line. It defines where one entity ends and another begins. In the context of in-law relationships, a boundary is a clear, communicated, enforceable limit that protects the marriage from external interference while maintaining respectful relationships with the families of origin.

Boundaries look like this: "Mom, we appreciate your input, but we have decided how we are going to handle this, and we need you to respect our decision." Boundaries look like this: "Dad, when you criticize my wife in front of the family, it is not acceptable, and I need you to stop." Boundaries look like this: "We will be spending Christmas morning at our house this year. We would love to see you in the afternoon."

Every one of those sentences will produce a reaction. The reaction may include anger, hurt, guilt-tripping, accusations of ingratitude, or the silent treatment. The reaction is not evidence that the boundary was wrong. It is evidence that the boundary was necessary. Systems that are functioning well do not react to reasonable limits with outrage. Systems that are functioning poorly do.

The boundary must be set by the adult child, not by the spouse. This is essential. When the daughter-in-law sets the boundary with her mother-in-law, it is experienced as an outsider's attack on the family. When the son sets the boundary with his own mother, it is experienced as the son's decision — painful, perhaps, but legitimate. The adult child who outsources boundary-setting to their spouse is placing their spouse in an impossible position and is failing, at the most fundamental level, to fulfill what Genesis 2:24 demands.

The boundary must also be enforced, which is where most couples fail. Setting a boundary is one conversation. Enforcing a boundary is a thousand conversations — a thousand repetitions of the same limit, a thousand refusals to capitulate to the guilt, a thousand moments of discomfort that the adult child must be willing to endure. The parent who violated the boundary once will violate it again. The question is whether the adult child will hold the line or collapse under the pressure. And the answer to that question will determine whether the marriage survives the in-law conflict or is slowly consumed by it.

The Marriage That Has Left

The marriage that has genuinely left — where both spouses have transferred their primary loyalty to the new family — is a marriage that is free in a way that the unleft marriage is not. It makes decisions based on its own discernment rather than the family of origin's expectations. It develops its own traditions rather than replicating the ones it inherited. It parents according to its own convictions rather than the grandparents' preferences. It is a new thing — not a continuation of the old families but a genuinely new creation, formed by the merger of two histories but not enslaved to either one.

This does not mean the marriage cuts itself off from the families of origin. The healthiest marriages I have observed are marriages that maintain warm, respectful, boundaried relationships with both families — relationships in which the parents are honored, their wisdom is valued, their presence is welcomed, and their authority over the marriage is zero. The parents are guests in the new household, not governing board members. They are loved. They are not obeyed.

I have seen this freedom in couples who have done the work — who have weathered the parental reaction, endured the guilt, held the boundary through years of testing, and emerged on the other side with a marriage that belongs to them rather than to their families of origin. These couples are not estranged from their parents. Many of them have better relationships with their parents than they had before the boundaries were set, because the relationship is now based on mutual respect rather than mutual dependency. The parent who initially resisted the boundary — who experienced it as rejection — often comes, over time, to respect the adult child who had the courage to set it. Respect follows strength. And the strength to leave is, paradoxically, what makes the staying possible.

The distinction between being loved and being obeyed is the entire point. The child obeys the parent. The adult child loves the parent. The difference is not a demotion of the relationship. It is a maturation of it. And the parent who cannot accept the maturation — who insists on the child's obedience long past the point where obedience is appropriate — is the parent who will lose the child's affection along with the child's compliance, because adults who are treated as children eventually stop coming home.

Leaving your father and mother is not an act of cruelty. It is an act of obedience — obedience to the God who designed marriage to supersede the family of origin, who knew that the new thing could not flourish if the old thing maintained its grip, and who asked you to do something painful because the marriage He gave you is worth the cost.

The cost is real. Some parents will not understand. Some will be hurt. Some will retaliate with guilt or withdrawal. But the marriage — the covenant you made before God and witnesses — requires your first loyalty. Not your only loyalty. But your first. And the difference between first and only is the difference between a boundary and a wall. The boundary protects the marriage. The wall destroys the family. The task of the adult child is to build the first without constructing the second, and to trust that the God who commanded both leaving and honoring will provide the wisdom to hold them together.

I grew up without a father. The absence shaped everything — my understanding of manhood, my approach to relationships, my deep and often unconscious desire to be part of a family that functioned the way I believed families were supposed to function. When I married, I carried that desire into my wife's family of origin, and I carried my own history of fatherlessness into the new family we were creating. The leaving was complicated, because I had less to leave than most. The cleaving was complicated, because I was cleaving not only to my wife but to the family structure I had never had.

The complications are always particular. Your family of origin is not mine. Your patterns of enmeshment or distance or control or dependency are shaped by a history I cannot see from the outside. But the principle is universal: the marriage comes first. Not because the parents do not matter. Because the covenant demands it. And the God who gave you that covenant knew what He was asking. He asked it anyway.

He will. He always does. But the wisdom comes to those who ask for it, not to those who avoid the question.
excerpt: The Bible's most radical statement about marriage is not about love or sex — it is the command to leave your father and mother, and the church has spent centuries softening a directive that was meant to cut.

title: Marriage After Children: Rediscovering Each Other
body:
The arrival of the first child is the most celebrated and least understood crisis in the life of a marriage. It is celebrated because it should be — a new life, a new identity, the embodiment of the one-flesh union in a person who carries both of you in their face. It is a crisis because the research is unambiguous: marital satisfaction declines, on average, with the birth of the first child and does not recover until the last child leaves home. The decline is not universal, but it is the norm. And the church, which celebrates the gift without acknowledging the cost, leaves couples unprepared for the disorientation that follows.

I have five sons. I love them with a fierceness that frightens me. And I will tell you honestly that the early years of parenting nearly destroyed my marriage — not because my wife and I stopped loving each other, but because we stopped seeing each other. The children consumed everything. They consumed our time, our energy, our attention, our patience, our sleep, our capacity for adult conversation. They did not do this maliciously. They did it because they were children, because children need everything, and because the need of a child is more immediate and more visible than the need of a spouse. The spouse can wait. The infant cannot. And so the spouse waits. And waits. And the waiting, accumulated over years, becomes a distance that neither partner intended but both feel.

The Research on Marital Satisfaction

John Gottman's research on the transition to parenthood found that 67 percent of couples experienced a significant decline in marital satisfaction within three years of the birth of their first child. The decline was steeper for couples who had not developed strong friendship and conflict-resolution skills before the baby arrived. The 33 percent who did not experience the decline were not better parents. They were not wealthier or more rested or more temperamentally suited to the chaos of infant care. They were couples who had built a relational foundation strong enough to absorb the shock of parenthood without collapsing.

The decline in satisfaction is driven by multiple factors, all of which are exacerbated by the refusal to name them. Sleep deprivation is the most underestimated: chronic sleep disruption impairs emotional regulation, reduces empathy, increases irritability, and lowers the threshold for conflict. New parents are operating, for months or years, in a state of physiological impairment that would not be tolerated in any other context. A surgeon operating on two hours of sleep would be pulled from the operating room. A new parent is expected to manage a household, maintain a relationship, and endure the most demanding emotional labor of their lives on the same two hours. The body is not designed for this. The marriage is not designed for this. And the expectation that both should function normally under these conditions is a cruelty we have normalized.

The division of labor is the second driver. Even in egalitarian marriages, the arrival of a child tends to produce a regression toward traditional gender roles. The sociological research is consistent: mothers, even mothers who work full-time, perform significantly more household labor and childcare than fathers. Arlie Hochschild documented this pattern in "The Second Shift" in 1989, and the data has not substantially changed in the decades since. The disparity is a source of resentment, and the resentment is compounded by the cultural narrative that tells mothers they should be grateful for the privilege of doing it all. The father who "helps" — a word that implies the work belongs to the mother and he is doing her a favor — is not being generous. He is confirming a division of labor that was never agreed upon and is slowly poisoning the marriage.

The Identity Crisis

Children create an identity crisis in both parents, but the crisis takes different forms. The mother's identity is subsumed by motherhood. She is no longer primarily a wife, a professional, a friend, a person with interests and desires and an inner life. She is a mother. The culture reinforces this: the idealization of motherhood — "the hardest job in the world," "there's no love like a mother's love" — simultaneously elevates the role and erases the person. The woman who was a complex, layered human being before the baby arrived is now a function. And the function, while deeply meaningful, is not the same as a self.

The father's identity crisis is different but equally real. The cultural script for new fatherhood is thin. Be present. Be supportive. Change diapers without being asked. But the emotional recalibration — the shift from partner to parent, from two to three, from a marriage that centered on the couple to a family that centers on the child — is largely unaddressed. Many new fathers feel displaced, unnecessary, peripheralized. The baby needs the mother in a primal, biological way that the father cannot replicate. The mother, exhausted by the demands of nursing and infant care, has little energy left for the marriage. The father, unsure of his role and unable to articulate his own needs without feeling selfish, withdraws. The withdrawal is interpreted as disengagement. The distance grows.

I withdrew. I am not proud of it. I responded to the disorientation of new fatherhood by doing what I knew how to do — I worked. I threw myself into ministry, into productivity, into the performance of competence, because competence was something I understood and fatherhood was something I did not. My wife needed a partner. She got a provider. The distinction between the two is the distinction between a marriage and a business arrangement, and for a season, we were closer to the latter than the former.

The Children as Proxy for the Marriage

One of the most insidious patterns in marriages with children is the displacement of marital energy onto the children. The parents stop investing in each other and invest entirely in the children — their activities, their education, their emotional development, their social lives. The children become the project, and the marriage becomes the infrastructure that supports the project. The couple does not think of themselves as a couple. They think of themselves as co-managers of a small enterprise, and the enterprise's product is well-adjusted children.

This displacement is understandable. Children are responsive. You pour into a child, and you see results — the first word, the first step, the first goal scored, the first A on the report card. The feedback loop is immediate and rewarding. Marriage, by contrast, requires investment that often produces no visible return for years. You have a conversation that seems to go nowhere. You sit on the couch in exhausted silence. You go to bed without resolving the tension that has been building all week. The returns on marital investment are real, but they are slow, and in a culture addicted to immediate results, slow feels like failure.

But the displacement has consequences that no parent anticipates. Children who grow up in a home where the marriage is strong and visible have a fundamentally different experience of family than children who grow up in a home where the marriage has been sacrificed for the sake of the children. The first group learns that adult love is real, that commitment persists, that two people can choose each other in the midst of chaos. The second group learns that love is a function, that marriage is a means to an end, and that the end — the children — is more important than the means.

I have watched this displacement happen in real time in my own congregation. Couples who were vibrant and connected in their twenties become logistical partners in their thirties and forties, their entire relational energy consumed by the enterprise of raising children. They sit in the pew together on Sundays, but the togetherness is geographical, not relational. They are two people occupying the same space, oriented toward the same children, connected by the shared project but disconnected from each other. And the disconnection is so gradual, so normalized, so camouflaged by the busyness of family life, that neither of them notices until the busyness stops.

The greatest gift you can give your children is not another activity, another tutor, another enrichment program. It is a marriage that is alive — a marriage in which their parents visibly love each other, prioritize each other, and demonstrate that the covenant between a man and a woman is a thing of substance and beauty. Children are watching. They are always watching. And what they see in your marriage will shape what they expect in their own.

Fighting for the Marriage

The marriage does not sustain itself during the parenting years. It must be fought for, with the same intentionality that is given to the children's well-being. And the fight looks different than most couples expect.

It looks like a weekly date night that is protected with the same ferocity as a doctor's appointment. Not because date nights are romantic — often they are not; often they are two tired people eating mediocre food and struggling to remember how to talk about something other than the children — but because the act of setting aside time for the marriage communicates that the marriage matters. The time does not need to be magical. It needs to be protected.

It looks like physical affection that is not contingent on sex. Touch — a hand on the back, a kiss in the kitchen, an embrace that lasts three seconds longer than necessary — is the body's way of saying, "I see you. I choose you. You are not just a co-parent." The couples who stop touching stop connecting, because the body knows things that the mind forgets, and the body's memory of being loved is sustained by the body's experience of being touched.

It looks like conversations about something other than the children. This is harder than it sounds, because the children provide a safe, shared topic that requires no vulnerability. Talking about the kids is easy. Talking about your inner life, your fears, your desires, your disappointments — that is hard. And hard is exactly what the marriage needs, because the marriage was built on two people knowing each other, and you cannot know someone who only talks about logistics.

It looks like the decision — made deliberately and counter-culturally — to say no to the children's demands in order to say yes to the marriage. Not always. Not cruelly. But sometimes, the family does not attend the tournament because the parents need a weekend together. Sometimes the children go to bed early because the adults need an evening. Sometimes the answer to "Can I have" is "Not tonight, because Mom and Dad need time." The children will survive the disappointment. The marriage may not survive the neglect.

Rediscovery

The word "rediscovery" implies that something was lost. It was. In the chaos of parenting — the diapers, the feedings, the school runs, the homework battles, the adolescent crises — the couple who fell in love got buried under the weight of what they built together. The love did not die. It went underground, displaced by demands that were more urgent even if they were not more important.

Rediscovery begins with curiosity. When was the last time you asked your spouse what they are reading, thinking, struggling with, hoping for? When was the last time you looked at them and saw not the co-parent, not the co-manager, not the person who forgot to switch the laundry, but the person you chose — the specific, irreplaceable, fascinating person you chose?

The person is still there. They have changed, certainly — as you have changed, as everyone changes across the decades of adult life. But the core of them — the thing that drew you, the quality that made you think, "This one. This is the one I want" — that core has not disappeared. It has been covered over. And the work of the parenting years, alongside the work of raising the children, is the work of uncovering what was buried, of remembering who you married, and of choosing them again.

The choice must be daily and it must be specific. It is not enough to say, "I love you." You must say, "I noticed that you handled that situation with the kids beautifully." You must say, "I was thinking about you today, and I remembered the trip we took before the children came." You must say, "I want to know what you are dreaming about, because I realize I have not asked in months." Specificity is the language of attention, and attention is the currency of love. The spouse who receives specific attention knows they are seen. The spouse who receives only generic affirmation suspects they are being managed.

Your children do not need perfect parents. They need parents who love each other imperfectly but persistently — parents who model what it looks like to choose someone every day, not because the choosing is easy but because the choosing is the point.

The choosing is the point. Not the children. Not the house. Not the schedule or the savings account or the school district. The choosing. Two people, in the middle of the beautiful, exhausting chaos they have created together, turning toward each other and saying, with their time and their touch and their attention: You are not lost. I still see you. And I am still here.

I remember a night — five boys asleep, finally, after the last glass of water and the last negotiation about bedtime — when my wife and I sat on the couch in the sudden quiet and realized we had nothing to say to each other. Not nothing in the angry sense. Nothing in the empty sense. We had been so consumed by the logistics of the day — the school forms, the soccer practice, the sibling conflict that required mediation, the homework that required patience we did not have — that we had used up every word. The silence was not hostile. It was exhausted. And inside the exhaustion was a sadness neither of us named, because naming it would have required energy we did not possess.

That night was a turning point, though I did not recognize it as such at the time. It was the night I realized that the marriage was not going to survive on autopilot. That the children, for all the joy they brought, were consuming the very relationship that had created them. And that the only remedy was deliberate, counter-cultural, sometimes inconvenient attention to the person sitting next to me on the couch — not because the attention was easy, but because without it, there would be nothing left when the couch was finally ours.

That is the marriage after children. Not a fairy tale. Not a catastrophe. A daily, deliberate, deeply ordinary act of remembering — remembering who you were, who you are, and who you are becoming together, even when the noise of the house makes it hard to hear each other speak.
excerpt: Children do not ruin marriages — but they do expose every fault line that was already there, and the couple that does not fight for its identity apart from the children will one day discover that the children were the only thing holding them together.

title: The Empty Nest Marriage
body:
The house gets quiet. It does not get quiet gradually, the way the mornings lengthen in spring. It gets quiet all at once — a door closing, a car pulling out of the driveway, a bedroom that is suddenly just a room. The child who filled that room — who filled it with noise and mess and need and presence — is gone. Not gone permanently, not gone irretrievably, but gone in the way that matters for the daily life of the household. The dinner table has an empty chair. The bathroom counter has space. The schedule, which for two decades was organized around someone else's needs, is suddenly and disoriently organized around nothing.

And the two people who remain — the couple who built this life, who raised these children, who spent twenty or twenty-five or thirty years in the consuming project of parenthood — look at each other across the quiet house and realize that they are, in some essential sense, strangers. Not hostile strangers. Not indifferent strangers. But strangers in the way that two people become strangers when they have spent decades standing side by side, facing the same direction, attending to the same tasks, without ever turning to face each other.

The empty nest is not a vacation. It is a reckoning. And the marriage that has not prepared for it — that has used the children as the connective tissue between two people who stopped connecting with each other years ago — will find the reckoning devastating.

The Statistics and the Silence

The divorce rate among adults over fifty has doubled since 1990, according to research by Susan Brown and I-Fen Lin at Bowling Green State University. The phenomenon is significant enough to have earned its own label: "gray divorce." And while gray divorce has multiple causes — longer lifespans, reduced stigma, financial independence of women, the influence of the baby boom generation's cultural values — one of the most common precipitating factors is the departure of the last child.

The AARP survey on divorce after fifty found that 66 percent of divorces in this age group were initiated by women. The most commonly cited reason was not infidelity or abuse. It was emotional disconnection — the sense of having grown apart, of living with someone who no longer knew them, of enduring a marriage that was functional but dead. The women who left did not leave in anger. Many left in grief — grief for the marriage they had wanted, grief for the intimacy they had never received, grief for the years they had spent waiting for the relationship to become what it had never been.

The men, by and large, were blindsided. They thought the marriage was fine. They had been providing, protecting, working, doing the things they understood marriage to require. The fact that their wives were starving — emotionally, conversationally, romantically — did not register, because the language of emotional starvation was not in their vocabulary. They were not bad men. They were men who had mistaken presence for connection and provision for partnership, and the mistake, uncorrected across decades, proved fatal.

I pastor men in this exact situation. I have watched the bewilderment on their faces when they discover, in their fifties, that the wife they thought was content was actually enduring. The bewilderment is genuine. They did not know. They did not know because they did not ask, and they did not ask because the culture that shaped them did not teach them that asking was part of the job description. The failure is real. The responsibility is theirs. But the context matters, because understanding how we got here is the first step toward getting somewhere else.

What the Children Were Covering

The departure of the children does not create the distance between spouses. It reveals it. The distance was always there, hidden beneath the noise and activity of family life. The children provided a shared project, a common purpose, a daily structure that made the marriage feel active even when the marriage itself was dormant. You do not need to connect with your spouse when every evening is consumed by homework supervision, sports practice transportation, bedtime routines, and the logistics of managing multiple small lives. The children filled the space. The children generated the conversation. The children provided the excuse not to face each other.

I do not say this to blame the children. The children did not ask to be the marriage's connective tissue. They did not volunteer to be the buffer between two people who had stopped doing the work of intimacy. They simply filled the available space, because that is what children do. And when they left, the space they had filled revealed what had been there all along: two people who had forgotten how to be married to each other.

This is a particular grief — the grief of discovering, in your fifties or sixties, that the marriage you thought you had was actually a parenting partnership that has now concluded its primary project. The love is not gone. The history is not meaningless. But the relationship, stripped of its organizing principle, feels hollow. And the hollowness is terrifying, because it suggests that the best years of the marriage were not really about the marriage at all.

The Identity Crisis

The empty nest triggers an identity crisis in both spouses, and the crisis is sharper for the spouse whose identity was most fully invested in the parenting role. For many women — particularly those who stayed home during the parenting years or who organized their professional lives around the children's needs — the departure of the last child is an existential event. The role that gave shape to their days, purpose to their decisions, and meaning to their sacrifices has ended. They are still alive, still married, still capable. But they do not know who they are outside the identity of "Mom."

Men face a parallel crisis, though it typically manifests differently. The father who defined himself by his ability to provide and protect discovers that there is no one left who needs his provision or protection in the immediate, daily sense. The house is secure. The college fund is depleted. The work that once felt meaningful — providing for a family — now feels purposeless. What are you working for when the people you were working for have gone?

Both crises are real. Both require attention. And both can either drive the spouses apart — each retreating into their own existential reckoning — or draw them together, if the couple has the courage to face the reckoning as a shared experience rather than parallel solitudes.

The crisis is compounded by the culture's obsession with youth. A culture that worships the young implicitly devalues the old, and the empty-nest couple stands at the threshold of a stage of life that the culture has almost nothing positive to say about. The advertisements do not feature them. The churches do not program for them. The marriage books are written for the newly married or the struggling married, not for the long-married who are trying to figure out what comes next. The cultural silence communicates a message that the empty-nest couple absorbs without realizing it: your best years are behind you. The message is a lie, but it is a pervasive and persuasive one, and the couple that believes it will not invest in a future they do not think they have.

The Opportunity

Here is what no one tells you about the empty nest: it is not only a crisis. It is also an opportunity — the first genuine opportunity in decades for the marriage to become what it was always meant to be. The children are gone. The schedule is open. The energy that was consumed by parenting is available for other investments. The question is what you will invest it in.

The marriages that thrive in the empty nest are marriages that treat the transition not as a loss but as a second beginning. Not a return to the pre-children marriage — that marriage was inhabited by younger, less experienced, less scarred versions of both spouses. A new beginning. A marriage between the people you are now — people who have been shaped by decades of shared experience, who have survived crises together, who carry a depth of history that no new relationship can replicate.

The depth of history is an asset, though it may not feel like one. You know this person. You know their weaknesses and their fears. You know the sounds they make when they sleep. You know how they handle grief and what makes them laugh and what they look like when they are pretending to be fine. This knowledge is not the enemy of romance. It is the foundation of the deepest intimacy available to human beings — the intimacy of being fully known and choosing to stay.

I have watched couples in this stage discover things about each other that they somehow missed during the parenting years. The husband who discovers that his wife has been reading philosophy in the early mornings for years and has thoughts about human consciousness that he never knew about. The wife who discovers that her husband has been quietly grieving his own father's death for a decade and never said a word, because the children's needs always seemed more urgent than his own. These discoveries are both wonderful and devastating — wonderful because they reveal a depth in the other person that the busyness had obscured, devastating because they expose the years of disconnection that allowed the depth to remain hidden.

The empty nest invites you to redeploy this knowledge. To stop knowing each other as co-parents and start knowing each other as companions. To have the conversations you postponed because the children needed dinner. To take the trip you deferred because the schedule would not allow it. To sit on the porch in the evening and discover that the quiet, which felt so threatening at first, is actually the space in which the marriage can finally breathe.

The Work of Reconnection

Reconnection does not happen automatically. It requires the same kind of intentionality that built the marriage in the first place — the willingness to pursue, to be curious, to risk vulnerability, to say things that have gone unsaid for too long.

Start by asking questions you stopped asking years ago. What are you thinking about these days? What do you want the next ten years to look like? What have you always wanted to do that we never did? What are you afraid of? What do you need from me that you have not been getting? These are dangerous questions. They may produce answers you did not expect. They may surface grievances that have been buried for decades. They may reveal desires that feel impossible to reconcile with the life you have built. Ask them anyway. The alternative — the polite, surface-level coexistence of two people sharing a house and a tax return — is not a marriage. It is a roommate arrangement with legal standing.

Reconnection also requires physical reengagement. Many empty-nest couples have let the physical dimension of the marriage atrophy — not necessarily sex, though that may have declined as well, but the entire spectrum of physical connection. Touch. Proximity. The willingness to sit close on the couch rather than in separate recliners. The willingness to reach for each other in bed rather than turning away. The body remembers what the mind has forgotten, and the reintroduction of physical closeness can awaken emotional connections that words alone cannot reach.

Reconnection may require professional help. There is no shame in this. A marriage therapist is not a sign of failure. It is a sign of investment — the decision that this marriage is worth the same kind of professional attention that you would give to your health, your career, or your finances. The couples who seek help early in the empty-nest transition — before the distance calcifies into permanent disconnection — have the best outcomes. The couples who wait until the distance is total and the resentment is established face a much harder road.

The Theological Invitation

The empty nest is a theological moment. It is the moment when the marriage is stripped to its essence — two people, a covenant, and the God who made it. The accessories are gone. The distractions have departed. What remains is the question that every marriage must eventually answer: was this a covenant or a convenience?

If it was a covenant, then the empty nest is not the end of the marriage's purpose. It is the beginning of a new chapter — a chapter in which the purpose of the marriage is no longer the raising of children but the mutual sanctification of two people who have committed to walk together until death. The children were a stewardship, temporary and precious. The marriage is a covenant, permanent and foundational. The stewardship has ended. The covenant continues.

And the covenant, freed from the demands of the stewardship, has the space to become something it could not become while the children were present — something deeper, quieter, more honest, more tender. The love that survives the empty nest is not the love of the honeymoon. It is a love that has been tested by decades of shared life, refined by conflict and forgiveness and the accumulated weight of ten thousand ordinary days. It is a love that does not need to prove itself because it has already been proven — in the staying, in the choosing, in the daily decision to turn toward each other rather than away.

The church has a role to play here — a role it has largely neglected. Most churches invest heavily in premarital counseling and young-married ministry and parenting programs. Almost none invest in empty-nest ministry — in supporting couples through the transition, in creating community for people whose social lives were built around their children's activities, in addressing the specific spiritual and relational needs of people in the second half of life. This is a failure of pastoral imagination, and the gray divorce statistics are, in part, its consequence.

The empty nest is not a void. It is a clearing — a space where two people, freed from the beautiful burden of raising the next generation, can finally turn to face each other and discover whether the love they promised at the altar has survived the years it took to keep the promise.

For many couples, the discovery will be painful. The distance will be real. The work of reconnection will be difficult. But the discovery is also an invitation — an invitation to build something new on the foundation of something old, to let the marriage become what it was always meant to be, to choose each other one more time in the quiet house where the echoes of children's voices are fading and the sound of two people learning to be married again is just beginning.

The beginning is available. It does not require youth or energy or the absence of scars. It requires only the willingness to start — to look at the person across the table and say, not with the passion of the wedding day but with the gravity of someone who knows exactly what the words cost: I am still here. And I want to know you again.
excerpt: The day the last child leaves is the day the marriage discovers whether it was a partnership or a parenting arrangement — and for many couples, the silence that fills the house is the loudest thing they have ever heard.

title: When Your Spouse Doesn't Share Your Faith
body:
You drive to church alone. Or you sit in the pew with an empty seat beside you — the seat your spouse would occupy if they believed, or cared, or were willing to pretend. You sing the songs and hear the sermon and smile at the people who ask, "Where is your husband today?" or "Is your wife not feeling well?" You have a dozen answers rehearsed, all of them true enough to end the conversation without revealing the truth: your spouse does not share your faith. Your spouse may not believe in God at all. And the most important relationship in your life is divided at the deepest possible level — the level of ultimate commitment, ultimate meaning, the level where you answer the question of what the world is for and what happens when it ends.

I came to faith from atheism. I know what it looks like from the other side of the divide. I know the intellectual objections that are not merely intellectual but existential — the problem of suffering, the exclusivity claims, the institutional failures that make the whole enterprise look like a well-meaning fraud. I know that the believing spouse, however sincere, often does not understand what they are asking when they ask their spouse to believe. They are not asking them to add a Sunday activity. They are asking them to reorganize their entire understanding of reality around a set of claims that, to the unbelieving spouse, appear indistinguishable from wish fulfillment.

And I know, from the believing spouse's side, the particular grief of loving someone who cannot share the thing that matters most to you. The grief of praying beside a person who does not pray. The grief of raising children between two worldviews. The grief of knowing that the deepest part of your life — your relationship with God — is the one part your spouse cannot enter.

This is one of the loneliest experiences available to a married person. And the church, for all its talk about marriage, has almost nothing substantive to say about it.

What Paul Actually Said

The primary text is 1 Corinthians 7:12-16, and it deserves more careful attention than the church typically gives it. Paul writes: "To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband."

Several things stand out. First, Paul explicitly identifies this as his own pastoral counsel, not a direct dominical command — "I, not the Lord." This is not a demotion of the counsel's authority. It is a specification of its type. Paul is applying the principles of the gospel to a situation Jesus did not directly address, and he does so with the full weight of his apostolic authority while maintaining the intellectual honesty to distinguish between a direct quotation from Jesus and his own apostolic reasoning. The church would do well to practice the same honesty in its own counseling.

Second, Paul's counsel is to stay. Not to proselytize. Not to evangelize. Not to conduct a sustained campaign of spiritual persuasion within the marriage. To stay. The staying itself, Paul argues, has a sanctifying effect — the unbelieving spouse is "made holy" by the believing spouse's presence. The Greek word is hagiazo, and its precise meaning in this context has been debated for centuries. It does not mean that the unbelieving spouse is automatically saved. It means that the believing spouse's faithfulness creates a context in which holiness is possible — a proximity to grace that would not exist if the marriage were dissolved.

Third, Paul offers no guarantee: "For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" (v. 16). The uncertainty is the point. Paul does not promise conversion as the reward for faithfulness. He acknowledges that the outcome is unknown, and he counsels faithfulness anyway. This is the shape of Christian faith in nearly every domain: act faithfully without certainty of results, and trust the God whose timeline is not yours.

Fourth — and this is the element most often overlooked — Paul includes a provision for departure. "But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved" (v. 15). Paul does not demand that the believing spouse endure every possible situation without recourse. If the unbelieving spouse chooses to leave, the believing spouse is free. The principle is voluntariness. The believing spouse should not initiate departure. But neither should they be imprisoned by a partner who will not stay.

The Temptation to Evangelize Your Spouse

The most natural instinct of the believing spouse is to try to convert the unbelieving spouse. This instinct is understandable and almost always counterproductive. The marriage is not a mission field. The dining table is not a pulpit. The spouse who left a book on the nightstand, who forwards podcast episodes, who quotes Scripture during arguments, who prays conspicuously in the hope of provoking spiritual curiosity — that spouse is not doing evangelism. They are doing coercion, and the unbelieving spouse can feel the difference with absolute precision.

The coercion is damaging not only because it does not work but because it violates the integrity of the relationship. The unbelieving spouse begins to feel that they are not loved for who they are but targeted for who they might become. Every conversation becomes suspect — is this genuine interest in my day, or is this the setup for another spiritual redirect? Every kindness carries a potential agenda. The marriage, which should be the safest place in the unbelieving spouse's life, becomes the place where they feel most surveilled, most evaluated, most insufficient.

Peter's counsel in 1 Peter 3:1-2 is directed specifically to wives with unbelieving husbands, but its principle applies broadly: "Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct." The critical phrase is "without a word." Not without theology. Not without faith. Without a word. The witness is the life, not the lecture. The sermon is the conduct, not the conversation. And the believing spouse who cannot trust God to work through their life rather than their arguments has a faith problem of their own.

The Grief of Spiritual Loneliness

Even when the believing spouse accepts Paul's counsel — stays, does not pressure, trusts the process — there remains a grief that must be named, because naming it is the first step toward surviving it.

The grief is the grief of spiritual solitude within an intimate relationship. You cannot share your prayer life with someone who does not pray. You cannot process a sermon with someone who was not there. You cannot turn to your spouse in a moment of spiritual crisis — doubt, fear, the dark night of the soul — and find a partner who understands the terrain. The very thing that gives your life its deepest meaning is the thing you must carry alone.

This grief is compounded in the parenting years. How do you raise children in the faith when your spouse does not share it? How do you answer your child's theological questions when your spouse's answers will be different? How do you take the children to church on Sunday without it becoming a source of marital tension? How do you explain to a twelve-year-old why Daddy does not come to church without either condemning Daddy or minimizing the faith?

There are no clean answers to these questions. There are only honest negotiations — conversations between two people who love each other and disagree about the most fundamental questions of human existence, trying to find a way to raise children that honors both perspectives without pretending that the disagreement does not exist. The conversations are hard. They are necessary. And they require a level of mutual respect that is itself a form of sanctification, though it may not feel like it.

The grief also has a particular sharpness during the moments when faith is most needed. When a parent dies. When a child is in the hospital. When the world breaks in a way that drives the believing spouse to their knees, and they look to their left and their partner is standing, arms folded, unable or unwilling to kneel beside them. The isolation of those moments is a particular species of suffering that the church has not adequately addressed, perhaps because the church assumes that everyone sitting in its pews has a believing spouse at home. Many do not.

What the Unbelieving Spouse Needs

The unbelieving spouse needs to be loved without agenda. Fully. Unconditionally. Without the subtext of hoped-for conversion coloring every interaction. They need to know that their believing spouse married them — not the person they might become if God answers a certain prayer, but them. The actual person who does not believe, who has legitimate reasons for not believing, whose skepticism is not a spiritual pathology but an honest intellectual position that deserves respect even from those who disagree with it.

The unbelieving spouse needs to not be made to feel inferior. The implicit hierarchy that faith creates — the saved and the unsaved, the found and the lost, the redeemed and the unredeemed — is theologically real but relationally toxic when it enters the marriage. The believing spouse who treats their partner as a spiritual project rather than an equal partner has replaced the covenant with a rescue mission, and the unbelieving spouse can feel the condescension even when it is wrapped in love.

The unbelieving spouse needs to be free — free to attend or not attend, free to participate or not participate, free to ask questions without being cornered, free to be honest about their doubts without those doubts being treated as a problem to be solved. Freedom is the condition of genuine faith. The God who will not coerce belief has given us the model. The believing spouse who cannot extend the same freedom to their partner has not understood the God they claim to serve.

What the Believing Spouse Needs

The believing spouse needs community. Not as a substitute for the spouse but as a supplement — a circle of people who share the faith, who can pray together, who can discuss the sermon, who can hold the believing spouse's spiritual life when the spouse at home cannot. The church must be this community. And the church must be this community without treating the believing spouse as an object of pity or the unbelieving spouse as a project.

The believing spouse needs permission to grieve. The grief of spiritual loneliness in marriage is real, and it does not go away. It may lessen. It may become familiar enough that it no longer feels acute. But it remains — a low-grade ache, a persistent absence, the knowledge that the person you love most in the world cannot share the thing that matters most in your life. The church that acknowledges this grief — that says, "We see you, and we know this is hard, and you are not failing" — is doing more than most churches do.

The believing spouse needs theology that is honest about uncertainty. The verse that promises "train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6) is a proverb, not a guarantee. The prayer for the unbelieving spouse's conversion may be answered in a year, in a decade, or never in this lifetime. The God who is sovereign over all things has not promised to operate on your timeline, and the faith that demands a specific outcome on a specific schedule is not faith. It is a negotiation disguised as prayer.

The Marriage Itself as Witness

Here is what I have seen, over and over, in marriages where one spouse believes and the other does not: the most powerful witness is not the believing spouse's words. It is the marriage itself. The unbelieving spouse watches. They watch how their partner handles stress, how they respond to suffering, how they treat the people who cannot repay them. They watch whether the faith produces kindness or judgment, humility or arrogance, patience or frustration. They watch whether the believing spouse is becoming a better person — not a more religious person, but a genuinely better human being.

And sometimes — not always, not on schedule, not in the way anyone expected — the watching produces something. A question asked quietly, in the dark, in bed, when the defenses are down: "What do you actually believe?" A willingness to attend a service, not out of obligation but out of curiosity. A crack in the certainty that there is nothing beyond the material world. The crack may widen into a door. The door may open. Or it may not. Both outcomes are within the scope of God's sovereignty.

The believing spouse's job is not to open the door. It is to live in such a way that the door is visible — not through argument, not through pressure, not through the subtle coercion of spiritual superiority, but through the daily, embodied demonstration of what a life transformed by grace actually looks like. If the transformation is real, it will be evident. If it is not evident, the problem is not the unbelieving spouse's resistance. It is the believing spouse's inconsistency.

The marriage between a believer and an unbeliever is not a mistake to be corrected. It is a calling to be lived — a calling to love without condition, to witness without coercion, to grieve without bitterness, and to trust a God whose work in the human heart operates on a timeline that no human being controls.

The calling is hard. The loneliness is real. The temptation to force the issue is constant. But the God who called you to this marriage — the God who holds both of you, whether both of you know it or not — is at work. The work is slow. The work is often invisible. And the work may not produce the outcome you are praying for in the way you are praying for it.

But the God who raised the dead is not constrained by your expectations. And the love that sustains a marriage across the deepest divide two people can inhabit is itself a testimony — a testimony that some things are stronger than agreement, that some commitments outlast understanding, and that the covenant, held in the hands of a faithful God, can bear the weight of questions that have no easy answers.

Stay. Love. Pray. And leave the results to the One who started the work and has promised to finish it — in His time, in His way, and by means you cannot yet imagine.
excerpt: The loneliest seat in any church is occupied by the person who came alone — whose spouse is at home, indifferent or hostile to the faith that has become the center of their life — and the church has offered that person almost nothing but platitudes.

title: Blended Families: The Theology Nobody Prepared You For
body:
There is a moment in nearly every blended family when the illusion breaks. It might come at the dinner table, when a child looks at the new spouse and says, flatly, "You are not my dad." It might come at Christmas, when the logistics of who goes where and when reduce a holy day to a spreadsheet. It might come on an ordinary Tuesday, when a stepparent disciplines a child and the biological parent feels a surge of protectiveness so fierce it frightens them both.

The church has a theology of first marriages. It has wedding liturgies, premarital counseling curricula, and an entire sermonic tradition built around the assumption that two people who have never been married are standing at the altar. What it barely has — what it has mostly refused to develop — is a theology for the family that forms after the first one ended. Not because these families are rare. They are everywhere. In every congregation of any size, blended families sit in the pews carrying questions the sermon will not address. They came because they believed the church had something to say about family. They stay despite growing evidence that the church has almost nothing to say about theirs.

This silence is not neutral. It is a theological failure with pastoral consequences, and it is long past time to name it.

The Myth of the Clean Slate

The first thing the church gets wrong about blended families is the assumption that a new marriage creates a new start. The wedding happens, the vows are spoken, and the expectation — usually unspoken but always present — is that this family will now function like a first family. The stepparent will love the children as their own. The children will accept the stepparent with gratitude. The ex-spouse will fade into the background. The past will be, if not forgotten, at least overcome.

None of this happens. It cannot happen, because a blended family is not a first family with complications. It is a fundamentally different kind of family, one that operates by different rules, faces different challenges, and requires a different theology to understand.

In a first family, the couple relationship precedes the parent-child relationship. The adults chose each other, and the children arrived into a household that already had its shape. In a blended family, the parent-child relationship precedes the couple relationship. The children were there first. Their loyalties, their grief, their sense of home — all of it was established before the new spouse arrived. The new spouse enters a system that is already in motion, already has its rhythms, already has its unspoken rules about who sits where and what we eat on Friday nights.

This is not a problem to be solved. It is a reality to be honored. And the church's failure to honor it — its insistence on treating the blended family as a repaired version of the first family — has caused immeasurable harm.

What the Children Carry

The hardest truth about blended families is one the adults prefer not to face: the children did not choose this. They did not choose the divorce or the death that ended the first family. They did not choose the new person their parent fell in love with. They did not choose the new house, the new routines, the new siblings who eat differently and laugh at different jokes and take up space in rooms that used to be theirs.

Children in blended families carry a particular kind of grief that the church has almost no language for. It is not the grief of loss — the first parent is usually still alive, still present, still a parent. It is the grief of displacement. The world they knew has been rearranged without their consent, and the people who rearranged it keep telling them how wonderful it is going to be.

A child who resists the new family is not being difficult. A child who refuses to call the stepparent "Mom" or "Dad" is not being disrespectful. A child who acts out after a weekend at the other parent's house is not being manipulative. These are the behaviors of a human being trying to maintain their identity in a world that keeps shifting under their feet. And the church, if it has anything to offer at all, ought to begin by taking that grief seriously rather than rushing past it toward the happy ending.

The Psalms know something about this. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That is not a question that needs an answer. It is a cry that needs a witness. The children in blended families are crying out — sometimes loudly, sometimes in silence — and the first theological act is not to explain but to hear.

The Stepparent's Impossible Position

If the children carry grief, the stepparent carries ambiguity. They are asked to love children who may not want their love. They are expected to discipline without the authority that comes from having been there from the beginning. They are told to be patient, to earn trust, to not take it personally — and then they go to bed at night wondering whether they have married into a family that will never fully include them.

The church's counsel to stepparents is almost always some version of "love them like your own." This is well-meaning and catastrophically unhelpful. You cannot love a child like your own when the child already has their own parent, when that parent's photograph sits on the shelf, when the child goes to that parent's house every other weekend and comes back speaking a different emotional language. The love a stepparent offers must be a different kind of love — not lesser, but different. It is the love of someone who chose to be present without being chosen in return. It is closer to the love of God for Israel than the love of a parent for a newborn, and the church would do well to say so.

I have watched stepparents in my congregation pour themselves out for children who gave them nothing back. Year after year, showing up, making lunches, attending games, absorbing hostility without retaliating. Some of them eventually earned a relationship so deep it surprised everyone, including themselves. Some of them never did. Both outcomes are faithful. The church needs to stop promising the first and start honoring the second.

The Ex-Spouse in the Room

Here is a truth the church does not want to hear: in a blended family, the ex-spouse is a permanent member of the family system. Not a member of the household. Not a welcome presence. But a permanent influence whose decisions, moods, parenting choices, and remarriage prospects will shape the blended family for decades.

The church's instinct is to treat the ex-spouse as the past — the mistake that was made, the chapter that closed. But when children are involved, no chapter closes. The ex-spouse will be at graduations and weddings. They will have opinions about schools and bedtimes and whether the child can get a tattoo at seventeen. They will, by their very existence, remind everyone in the blended family that this family was built on the rubble of another one.
