A theology adequate to this reality would need to account for the ongoing presence of someone who is no longer a spouse but is still a co-parent. It would need to speak about forgiveness not as a one-time event but as a daily practice — forgiving the same person for the same things, week after week, in the school parking lot and the text message thread. It would need to acknowledge that the co-parenting relationship is, in its own way, a covenant: not a marriage covenant, but a covenant of shared responsibility for the lives of children who did not ask to be caught between two households.

Paul wrote to the Philippians about "working out your salvation with fear and trembling." That phrase has always struck me as the most honest description of the co-parenting relationship after divorce. It is a working out. It is fearful. And it trembles.

What Scripture Actually Offers

The Bible does not contain a theology of blended families, but it contains the raw materials for one. The story of Scripture is, from beginning to end, a story of God forming a family out of people who did not start together.

Abraham's household was a blended family in every meaningful sense — Isaac and Ishmael, Sarah and Hagar, competing loyalties and unresolved grief. Jacob's household was worse: two wives, two concubines, twelve sons, and a level of dysfunction that makes modern blended families look functional by comparison. The story of Ruth is the story of a woman who chose to enter a family she was not born into, who committed herself to a mother-in-law she could have abandoned, and who became, through that choice, an ancestor of the Messiah.

And then there is Joseph. Not the patriarch — the carpenter. The man who married a woman already pregnant with a child who was not his. The man who raised a son he did not conceive, who taught that son to work with wood, who fled with him to Egypt, who — the Gospels suggest — died before the boy became the man who changed the world. Joseph is the patron saint of stepparents, and the church has almost never said so.

What these stories share is not a formula. They share a pattern: God works through families that are messy, complicated, and formed by circumstances no one would have chosen. The blended family is not a deviation from God's plan. It is, in a fallen world, one of the shapes God's plan takes.

What the Church Owes

The church owes blended families three things it has mostly withheld.

First, honesty. Stop pretending that the blended family, if it just prays hard enough and loves well enough, will eventually feel like a first family. It will not. It will feel like what it is: a brave, complicated, sometimes beautiful, sometimes painful attempt to build something real out of materials that include both hope and wreckage. That is not a failure. That is the human condition.

Second, patience. Family researchers consistently say that blended families take five to seven years to develop their own identity and rhythms. Five to seven years. The church, which can barely sit through a three-minute silence in worship, needs to learn to sit with blended families through years of awkwardness, conflict, and incremental progress. Stop asking, "How is everyone adjusting?" Start saying, "We are here. However long it takes."

Third, theology. Real theology, not warmed-over first-marriage theology with a few adjustments. A theology that takes seriously the grief of children, the ambiguity of stepparents, the permanence of co-parenting relationships, and the strange grace that operates in families that were not anyone's first choice but might yet become the place where God does God's deepest work.

The blended family sitting in your pew next Sunday did not come because they wanted a lecture about God's ideal for marriage. They came because they are trying to build a life together, and it is harder than anyone told them it would be, and they are wondering whether God has anything to say to people whose family looks like theirs.

The answer to that question will determine whether they come back.
excerpt: The church has a theology of first marriages. It barely has a theology of second ones. And it has almost nothing to say to the family trying to become a family when half the people at the table did not choose each other.

title: Military Marriage: Distance, Deployment, and Covenant
body:
The phone call comes at 0200 and the line is bad. There is a three-second delay that makes conversation feel like speaking across a canyon. You say "I love you" and wait. The silence stretches. Then the voice comes back, thin and far away: "I love you too." And you both know that the words are true and that the words are not enough and that the words are all you have.

Military marriage exists in a category the church has never adequately addressed. It is not merely a marriage under stress — all marriages face stress. It is a marriage in which the state has a prior claim on one spouse's body, time, location, and availability. The service member did not simply take a job with long hours. They swore an oath that supersedes every other obligation except the oath they swore at the altar, and the two oaths exist in a tension that no amount of patriotic sentiment can resolve.

I have sat across from military couples in my office — young men and women who married at twenty-one because deployment was coming and they wanted to be married before they left, who came home to find that the person they married had become someone they did not recognize, or who discovered that they themselves had become someone their spouse could not reach. The divorce rate among military families tells part of the story. The rest of the story sits in the silences of couples who stayed together but lost something they cannot name.

The Covenant Under Competing Oaths

Every military spouse eventually confronts a question the church rarely helps them articulate: What does it mean to be in covenant with someone who has sworn a prior oath to a nation? The marriage vow says "forsaking all others." The military oath says "I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic." Both are sacred. Both demand everything. And when they conflict — when the deployment comes during the pregnancy, when the reassignment uproots the family for the fourth time, when the midnight call means leaving the dinner table mid-sentence — the military oath almost always wins.

This is not a betrayal. The spouse who serves did not break their marriage vow by honoring their military oath. But the marriage absorbs the cost of that honoring, and the cost is real. The cost is birthdays missed and anniversaries spent alone. The cost is single parenting for months at a stretch, making every decision about the house and the children and the bills without the partner who promised to share them. The cost is the slow erosion of shared experience — the inside jokes that fade, the daily rhythms that diverge, the growing awareness that you and your spouse are living in different worlds and calling it one marriage.

The church has mostly responded to military marriage with gratitude and admiration, which is appropriate but insufficient. Gratitude does not help at 0200 when the baby is screaming and the spouse is on the other side of the world. Admiration does not speak to the anger — the entirely legitimate anger — that surfaces when a service member comes home and expects the household to reorganize around their presence, as if the family had been on pause rather than in motion.

What Deployment Does to the One Who Stays

The spouse who stays home during deployment undergoes a transformation that is rarely acknowledged and almost never theologically engaged. They become, in effect, a single parent with a married person's obligations. They manage the household, raise the children, handle the finances, maintain the property, manage the military bureaucracy, and do it all while carrying an ambient dread that the next knock on the door might be the one that changes everything.

Over time, the staying spouse develops competence, independence, and decision-making authority that the deployed spouse did not see emerging. This is not a problem; it is a survival mechanism. But when the deployed spouse returns, the competence that kept the family afloat during their absence can feel like a threat. The spouse who stayed has learned to function without them. The spouse who returns has to find their place in a household that learned to run without them.

This reintegration — the return — is often harder than the deployment itself. The deployment has a narrative: separation, endurance, reunion. The reintegration has no narrative. It is the daily, undramatic, exhausting work of two people learning to share a life again after months of living separate ones. It is the fight about where the dishes go, because the staying spouse rearranged the kitchen. It is the tension at bedtime, because the children have a routine with one parent and the other parent does not know it. It is the sex that is supposed to be a reunion but feels like an audition.

The church can name this. The church should name this. Reintegration is not a homecoming party and a thank-you-for-your-service. It is a covenant being renegotiated in real time, and both spouses need the church to say: this is normal. This is hard. You are not failing.

What Deployment Does to the One Who Goes

The service member who deploys carries a burden the church is even less equipped to address. They live in an environment that demands hypervigilance, hierarchy, and emotional compression. They see things — or do things — that cannot be translated into the language of home. They develop relationships with fellow service members that are forged in a furnace of shared danger, and those relationships have an intensity that marriage, by its very domesticity, cannot replicate.

I do not mean that the deployed spouse loves their unit more than their family. I mean that the deployed spouse experiences a form of intimacy — the intimacy of shared risk — that their spouse at home cannot access. And when they come home, they carry the guilt of that intimacy along with everything else they carry. They wonder why the bond with their battle buddy feels more real than the bond with their spouse. They wonder what it says about them that they miss the deployment — not the danger, but the clarity, the purpose, the knowledge of exactly who they were and what they were supposed to do.

The church has a word for what the returning service member experiences, though it rarely uses it in this context. The word is exile. The service member returns to a home that is still their home but no longer feels like it. The furniture is the same. The family is the same. But something has shifted — in them, in the household, in the space between — and the shift cannot be undone by simply being present.

The Psalms of ascent — those songs the Israelites sang as they climbed toward Jerusalem after exile — know this feeling. "When the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream." The return from exile does not feel like arrival. It feels like dreaming. The military spouse who comes home and sits on their own couch and feels, inexplicably, like a stranger — that person needs to hear that they are not broken. They are in exile, and exile is a biblical category, and God meets people there.

The Children Between Two Worlds

Military children learn early that home is not a place. It is a relationship that moves. They change schools every two or three years. They make friends knowing they will leave them. They develop a resilience that adults admire and a rootlessness that adults underestimate. The phrase "military brat" carries a strange pride, but it also carries a grief that many military children do not have permission to express — the grief of never quite belonging anywhere, of always being the new kid, of loving a parent who keeps leaving.

The church that serves military families must take these children seriously. Not as props for patriotic Sundays. Not as illustrations of sacrifice. As people — young people who are carrying a weight they did not choose and who need a community that will still be there after the next reassignment. The most powerful thing a church near a military base can do is not hold a special service on Veterans Day. It is to know the names of the children, to remember them after they move, to be the stable presence in a life defined by instability.

Toward a Theology of Military Marriage

A theology adequate to military marriage would need to hold several tensions simultaneously. It would need to honor service without idolizing it. It would need to acknowledge sacrifice without romanticizing it. It would need to name the real costs — to marriages, to children, to mental health, to faith itself — without undermining the legitimacy of the call to serve.

It would also need to reckon with the moral complexity that military service introduces into a marriage. The spouse who serves may be ordered to do things that trouble their conscience. The spouse who stays may carry a moral weight — complicity by association, pride tangled with dread — that the church's categories of sin and righteousness cannot easily sort. These are not theoretical concerns. They are the concerns of real people in real marriages, and the church's silence on them is a pastoral failure.

What military marriage teaches — what it teaches all of us, if we are willing to learn — is that covenant is not sustained by proximity. It is sustained by fidelity in the absence of proximity. The military couple who stays married through three deployments has learned something about covenant that the couple who has never spent a night apart cannot know. They have learned that love is not a feeling sustained by presence. It is a decision renewed in absence. It is the letter written at midnight. It is the prayer offered across time zones. It is the choice, made again and again, to remain married to someone you cannot see, cannot touch, cannot hear except through a bad phone line with a three-second delay.

That is not a diminished form of marriage. It is marriage refined by fire. And the church should say so — not on Veterans Day, not in a special bulletin insert, but in its regular theology of marriage, in its sermons and its counseling and its understanding of what covenant looks like when it costs everything it promises.

The military family in your congregation does not need your admiration. They have plenty of that. They need your theology. They need to know that the God who sustains covenant is present in the distance and the deployment and the 0200 phone call. They need to know that the church sees them — not as heroes, not as victims, but as married people doing the hardest version of a hard thing.

They need to know they are not alone. Even when they are.
excerpt: The marriage that survives deployment does not merely endure distance. It learns to carry a weight that most civilian marriages never have to name.

title: Marriage After Affair Recovery
body:
The moment of discovery divides a marriage into before and after. There is the marriage that existed before the truth came out — the one built on assumptions of fidelity, on the belief that whatever else was wrong, at least this one thing was solid. And there is the marriage that exists after — the one in which every memory is retroactively contaminated, every business trip is suspect, every late night at the office carries a charge it did not carry before.

The betrayed spouse does not merely learn that their partner was unfaithful. They learn that the world they inhabited was not the world they thought they inhabited. The dinner they ate together while the affair was happening — that dinner was a lie. The vacation they took — the one with the photographs on the mantel — that vacation was a performance. The "I love you" spoken at bedtime, during the months when the other relationship was at its most intense — those words were either false or they were true in a way that makes truth itself feel unreliable.

This is why betrayal is not merely a moral failure. It is an epistemological catastrophe. It does not just break trust. It breaks the betrayed person's confidence in their own ability to perceive reality. And the recovery of a marriage after infidelity is not primarily a matter of forgiving the act. It is a matter of rebuilding a shared world — a world in which both people can agree on what is real.

What the Unfaithful Spouse Owes

The church has been better at forgiving infidelity than at naming what it costs. We are quick to invoke grace, quick to remind the betrayed spouse of their own sinfulness, quick to quote the passage about the one without sin casting the first stone. All of this is true and all of it is premature. Before grace can do its work, the cost must be named. And the first person who must name it is the one who incurred it.

The unfaithful spouse owes, before anything else, a full accounting. Not a confession extracted under pressure. Not a partial truth offered to manage consequences. A full, voluntary, detailed accounting of what happened, when it happened, how long it lasted, and what it meant. This is excruciating. It is also non-negotiable. The betrayed spouse's world has been revealed as a fiction, and they cannot begin to rebuild until they know the full scope of what was fictional.

Therapists who specialize in infidelity recovery — Shirley Glass, whose work remains definitive; Esther Perel, whose perspective is more complicated — consistently identify the trickle truth as the most destructive pattern in the aftermath of an affair. Trickle truth is the practice of revealing the truth in small, reluctant increments, each new revelation reopening the wound just as it was beginning to close. Every time the betrayed spouse discovers a new piece of the truth they were not told, the trauma resets to zero. The clock starts over. Whatever trust had been rebuilt is demolished.

The unfaithful spouse also owes transparency — not as a punishment, but as a rebuilding material. Open access to phones, to email, to schedules. Willingness to account for time. Patience with questions that feel repetitive but are not — because the betrayed spouse is not asking the same question again. They are checking, again, whether the answer holds. Whether this new world, the post-discovery world, is solid enough to stand on.

This transparency is costly. It feels infantilizing to the unfaithful spouse. It feels like surveillance. And it is, for a season, necessary — the way a cast is necessary for a broken bone. You do not remove the cast because the patient is tired of wearing it. You remove it when the bone has healed.

What the Betrayed Spouse Carries

The betrayed spouse carries a wound that is unlike any other wound in marriage. It is not the wound of a bad argument or a period of emotional distance or even a prolonged season of unhappiness. It is the wound of having lived, unknowingly, in a constructed reality — a Truman Show marriage in which the other person knew the truth and chose, every day, to maintain the fiction.

The emotional aftermath of betrayal follows a pattern that clinicians describe in terms remarkably similar to post-traumatic stress. Intrusive thoughts. Hypervigilance. Sleep disruption. Emotional flooding triggered by seemingly innocuous stimuli — a restaurant, a song, a particular shade of lipstick. The betrayed spouse is not choosing to be consumed by the affair. They are being consumed by it, the way a person who has been in a car accident is consumed by the sound of screeching tires. The nervous system does not distinguish between categories of trauma. It responds to the magnitude of the threat.

The church must take this seriously. The pastoral instinct to move quickly toward forgiveness — to remind the betrayed spouse that they, too, are sinners, that holding onto anger is its own form of unfaithfulness — is not just unhelpful. It is re-traumatizing. It tells the wounded person that their wound is less important than the comfort of the person who inflicted it. It prioritizes the peace of the community over the healing of the individual. And it misreads the biblical witness, which takes betrayal with a seriousness that the contemporary church rarely matches.

The prophets spoke of Israel's unfaithfulness to God in the language of adultery — not because they were being metaphorical, but because they understood that betrayal in the most intimate relationship is the closest human analogue to the violation of covenant with God. Hosea did not forgive Gomer quickly. The book does not allow it. The restoration of the covenant took time, took grief, took a reckoning with the full scope of what was broken.

The Myth of the Affair-Proof Marriage

The church loves to teach affair prevention. Guard your heart. Set boundaries. Never be alone with someone of the opposite sex. Install accountability software. The Billy Graham Rule. The Mike Pence Rule. All of these measures contain a kernel of wisdom and a dangerous assumption: that affairs happen to people who failed to take precautions.

The truth is harder than that. Affairs happen in good marriages. They happen in marriages where both people love each other, where the sex is adequate, where the friendship is real. They happen not because the marriage was deficient but because the human capacity for self-deception is bottomless. Shirley Glass called this "the surprise of the affair" — the discovery, by otherwise decent people, that they are capable of things they swore they would never do.

The affair-proof marriage does not exist. What exists is the marriage in which both spouses know they are capable of betrayal and choose, daily, not to betray. This is a darker and more honest foundation than the church usually offers, but it is the only foundation that holds. The moment you believe you are incapable of infidelity is the moment you become most vulnerable to it. Pride does not prevent affairs. Humility prevents affairs — the humility to know what you are capable of and to structure your life accordingly.

Whether to Stay

The question that haunts every marriage after an affair — the question that the church wants to answer immediately and definitively — is whether to stay. And the honest answer is that this question cannot be answered immediately or definitively. It must be lived into, over months, sometimes over years.

The church's instinct is to say: stay. Marriage is a covenant. God hates divorce. Forgiveness is commanded. And all of this is true. But it is also true that Jesus, in Matthew 19, names sexual immorality as a condition under which divorce is not a violation of covenant but a recognition that the covenant has already been violated. The betrayed spouse who chooses to leave is not breaking a vow. They are acknowledging that a vow was broken — by someone else.

The betrayed spouse who chooses to stay is not exhibiting weakness. They are making a decision that will cost them everything — the comfort of moral clarity, the clean break of a new beginning, the right to be unambiguously the wronged party. Staying means giving up the high ground. It means choosing to rebuild with the person who demolished what was built. It means waking up, every morning, next to the source of the worst pain you have ever experienced, and choosing that person again.

This is not for everyone. It should not be for everyone. And the church must stop making betrayed spouses feel that staying is the only faithful option. Sometimes leaving is faithful. Sometimes leaving is the only way to honor the self that God created and the dignity that the affair violated. The betrayed spouse does not owe the marriage their destruction.

What the Rebuilt Marriage Looks Like

The marriage that survives infidelity does not return to what it was. This is the hardest thing for couples in recovery to accept. They want the old marriage back — the one before the discovery, the one that felt safe and solid and real. But that marriage is gone. It died on the day the truth came out. What recovery offers is not resurrection of the old marriage but the creation of a new one — built on the ruins of the first, carrying the scars of the first, but fundamentally different in its foundation.

The old marriage was built on assumed trust. The new marriage is built on earned trust — which is a different and, in some ways, stronger material. Assumed trust has never been tested. Earned trust has been tested by the worst thing that could happen, and it held. The couple who rebuilds after an affair knows something that other couples do not: they know what their marriage can survive. They have seen the bottom, and they chose each other anyway.

This does not make the affair worthwhile. Nothing makes the affair worthwhile. But it does mean that the rebuilt marriage, if it is honestly rebuilt, carries a depth that the original marriage lacked. The rebuilt marriage has no illusions. It has looked at the worst of what both people are capable of, and it has chosen to proceed. That is not naivety. It is the most clear-eyed form of love there is.

The rebuilt marriage also carries scars. There will be moments — triggered by a date, a place, a scent — when the old pain surfaces and the betrayed spouse needs to grieve again. The unfaithful spouse who says "I thought we were past this" does not understand how trauma works. You do not get past it. You learn to carry it. And the spouse who caused the wound does not get to decide when it stops hurting.

What the Church Must Learn

The church that wants to serve marriages after infidelity must learn three things.

First, it must learn to sit with the betrayed spouse's rage without rushing to neutralize it. Anger after betrayal is not a sin. It is a sign of health — a sign that the betrayed person knows they deserved better. The Psalms are full of this anger. "Break the teeth in their mouths, O God." That is not a failure of faith. That is faith speaking honestly to God about what was done to it.

Second, it must learn to hold the unfaithful spouse accountable without crushing them. The person who had the affair is not a monster. They are a sinner — which is to say, a human being — who did something devastating and must now reckon with it fully. Accountability without compassion is cruelty. Compassion without accountability is enabling. The church must learn to offer both, simultaneously, without collapsing into either.

Third, it must learn to accept that some marriages after affairs will not survive, and that this is not a failure of faith. It is the recognition that some betrayals break what cannot be repaired. The God who hates divorce also hates the circumstances that make divorce the least destructive option. The church must stop treating the survival of the marriage as the only metric of success. Sometimes the metric of success is two people who treated each other with honesty, sought genuine healing, and concluded — with grief, with prayer, with the counsel of wise people — that the marriage could not be rebuilt.

That conclusion does not dishonor God. What dishonors God is a marriage maintained as a shell — two people performing commitment while living in mutual contempt. The form without the substance. The covenant as a prison rather than a home.

The marriage after an affair is the hardest thing two people can attempt. The church owes those people not its judgment but its presence — steady, patient, honest, and willing to sit in the wreckage for as long as it takes to see whether something new can grow.
excerpt: The marriage that survives infidelity does not return to what it was. It becomes something else entirely — something that required a death before it could begin.

title: The Sexless Marriage Nobody Talks About
body:
They sit in the pew on Sunday morning, close enough that their shoulders touch. They look, to anyone watching, like a couple. And they are a couple — legally, domestically, in every external measure. They share a mortgage and a minivan and a last name. But they have not touched each other in months. Some of them have not touched each other in years. And neither of them knows how to talk about it — not to each other, not to their friends, and certainly not to their pastor.

The sexless marriage is one of the most common and least discussed realities in the American church. Researchers define it clinically — fewer than ten sexual encounters per year — but the clinical definition misses the lived experience, which is not primarily about frequency but about rejection, longing, shame, and the slow death of something that was supposed to be a gift.

The church has two modes when it comes to sex in marriage: celebration and prohibition. Before marriage, sex is forbidden. After marriage, sex is a blessing, a gift, a sacred act of union. The wedding night is the great transition — from no to yes, from sin to sacrament. But the church has almost nothing to say about the marriage in which the yes never came, or came and then stopped, or came with so much complication that it barely felt like a gift at all.

This silence has consequences. The spouse who desires physical intimacy and does not receive it carries a shame that has no outlet. The spouse who cannot offer physical intimacy — for reasons that range from trauma to medication to simple loss of desire — carries a guilt that has no relief. And between them, the silence grows, filling the space where honesty should be.

What We Refuse to Name

The first thing the church must do is name the problem honestly. A sexless marriage is not a minor inconvenience. It is a significant deprivation — for both spouses, regardless of who desires more and who desires less. Paul wrote to the Corinthians that married couples should not deprive one another except by mutual consent for a limited time. The church has used this passage to guilt reluctant spouses into compliance, which is a grotesque misreading. But the passage contains a genuine insight: physical intimacy in marriage is not optional. It is constitutive. It is part of what makes a marriage a marriage rather than a partnership or a friendship or a cohabitation arrangement.

This does not mean that every spouse is entitled to sex on demand. It means that both spouses are entitled to a marriage in which physical intimacy is present, valued, and mutually sought — even if the seeking is difficult, even if the intimacy looks different from what either person imagined, even if the path to it requires more honesty than either person wants to offer.

The reluctant spouse is not the villain. The desiring spouse is not the victim. These are two people caught in a dynamic that neither of them chose and neither of them knows how to change. The church's job is not to assign blame. It is to provide a framework — theological, pastoral, practical — for two people to talk about the most intimate dimension of their life together without shame.

The Roots of Sexual Withdrawal

Sexual withdrawal in marriage has causes, and the causes matter. They are not excuses. They are explanations, and explanations are the beginning of change.

For some spouses, the withdrawal is rooted in trauma. Sexual abuse in childhood, assault in adolescence, a previous relationship in which sex was coerced or punishing — these experiences do not disappear at the altar. They follow the survivor into the marriage bed, and they surface in ways that are confusing to both spouses. The trauma survivor may want intimacy desperately and find themselves unable to receive it. Their body freezes. Their mind disconnects. The very act that is supposed to express love triggers a cascade of fear responses that have nothing to do with their spouse and everything to do with what happened before their spouse existed.

For others, the withdrawal is medical. Antidepressants suppress desire with a reliability that no one warns patients about until it is too late. Hormonal changes after childbirth, during perimenopause, or as a side effect of other treatments can reduce desire to near zero. Chronic pain makes the physical act of sex difficult or impossible. These are not choices. They are conditions, and the church that treats them as spiritual failures — as a lack of willingness to give one's body to one's spouse — adds cruelty to suffering.

For still others, the withdrawal is relational. It is the accumulated residue of years of unresolved conflict, emotional distance, criticism, contempt, or neglect. The spouse who has been belittled at the dinner table cannot be expected to open themselves in the bedroom. The body keeps score. It registers every dismissive comment, every eye roll, every evening spent in separate rooms staring at separate screens. And eventually it says no — not as a punishment, but as a protection.

And for some, the withdrawal is simply the mystery of desire — that desire has its own logic, its own seasons, its own stubborn refusal to be summoned on command. The church that insists desire is a choice — that you can decide to want your spouse — is speaking a language that does not correspond to how human beings actually work. Desire is not a faucet. You cannot turn it on by trying harder.

The Spouse Who Waits

The spouse who desires intimacy and does not receive it inhabits a particular kind of loneliness. It is not the loneliness of being alone. It is the loneliness of being with someone — sleeping next to someone, sharing a life with someone — and feeling untouched. Unwanted. Invisible.

This spouse often carries shame about their desire. The culture sends contradictory messages: men are supposed to want sex all the time, which means that the man in a sexless marriage feels like a failure; women are not supposed to want sex as much as men, which means that the woman in a sexless marriage feels like a deviant. Both of these scripts are false, and both cause real damage.

The desiring spouse may begin to question their attractiveness, their worth, their identity. If my spouse does not want me, what does that say about me? This question, asked in enough silent moments, becomes a conviction: I am not enough. I am not desirable. Something is wrong with me. And the longer the sexlessness continues, the deeper the conviction roots.

The church must speak to this spouse without patronizing them. You are not wrong to want physical intimacy with the person you married. Your desire is not excessive or sinful or needy. It is the desire that the covenant itself creates — the longing for the union that the vows promised. The absence of that union is a real loss, and you are allowed to grieve it.

The Spouse Who Cannot

The spouse who withholds intimacy — and I use that word carefully, because "withhold" implies agency, and many of these spouses do not experience themselves as withholding anything — carries their own burden. They know what their spouse wants. They know they are not providing it. And they feel, most days, like a failure — or worse, like a fraud. They stood at the altar and promised themselves to this person, body and soul, and their body is not keeping the promise their mouth made.

The guilt is corrosive. It manifests as defensiveness — "Why is sex the only thing that matters to you?" — or as avoidance — staying up late, going to bed early, engineering the schedule so that opportunities for intimacy never arise. These are not strategies of cruelty. They are strategies of shame. The spouse who avoids intimacy is often avoiding the reminder of their own inadequacy.

The church must speak to this spouse with equal honesty and equal compassion. You are not broken. You are not failing at marriage because your body or your desire does not cooperate with your intentions. But you owe your spouse the truth about what you are experiencing — not performance, not excuses, but the vulnerable, frightening truth. "I do not know why I cannot want this. I am sorry. I want to find out." That sentence, spoken honestly, is more intimate than any physical act.

The Path Forward

There is no formula for restoring sexual intimacy to a marriage that has lost it. Anyone who offers you five steps is selling something. But there are practices — honest, difficult, slow practices — that create the conditions in which intimacy can grow.

The first is naming. Say what is happening. Out loud. To each other. "We have not been intimate in four months, and I need to talk about why." This sentence is terrifying. It is also the door through which every other conversation must pass. The sexless marriage that remains sexless usually does so because both spouses have agreed, implicitly, never to name what is happening. Breaking that agreement is the first act of intimacy — the intimacy of truth.

The second is curiosity. Not accusation — curiosity. "What happens for you when I initiate?" "What would feel safe?" "What are you afraid of?" These questions require the desiring spouse to set aside their hurt long enough to listen. They require the reluctant spouse to set aside their shame long enough to answer. Both of these are acts of tremendous courage.

The third is professional help. A good therapist — specifically, a therapist trained in sexual health, not just general marital counseling — can name what the couple cannot name. They can identify patterns, address trauma, explore medical factors, and provide a framework for the conversation that neither spouse can provide on their own. The church that refuses to recommend therapy because it believes prayer should be sufficient is not protecting the sanctity of marriage. It is abandoning couples to a problem they cannot solve alone.

The fourth is patience. Sexual intimacy, once lost, does not return quickly. The couple that expects resolution in weeks will be disappointed. The recovery is measured in months, sometimes years — in small gestures, tentative approaches, setbacks that feel like failures but are actually part of the process. The couple needs to know that the process itself is the faithfulness. The willingness to keep showing up, to keep having the hard conversation, to keep reaching across the distance — that willingness is the covenant in action.

What the Church Must Say

The church must say what it has been afraid to say: that the absence of sexual intimacy in marriage is a serious matter that deserves serious pastoral attention. Not a joke. Not a punchline. Not a footnote in a sermon about something else. A serious matter.

The church must stop treating sex as a reward for spiritual maturity and start treating it as a dimension of the relationship that, like every other dimension, is subject to brokenness, requires grace, and demands honest engagement. The couple in the sexless marriage is not less spiritual than the couple with a flourishing sex life. They are carrying a wound that the church should help them tend, not a sin the church should help them confess.

And the church must make room for the grief. The spouse who has not been touched in years is grieving something real — the loss of a dimension of marriage that they were told would be a gift and that has become an absence. The church that cannot sit with that grief — that rushes to fix it or minimize it or spiritualize it — is not serving these marriages. It is abandoning them.

The sexless marriage is a crisis of intimacy, and the church that claims to know something about intimacy — with God, with neighbor, with spouse — must find the courage to enter this crisis with honesty, compassion, and the willingness to stay for as long as the healing takes.

Which is usually longer than anyone wants it to be.
excerpt: The absence of physical intimacy in a marriage is not a punchline. It is a wound that both spouses carry in silence, and the church's refusal to address it has left generations without language for what they are losing.

title: Marriage and Mental Health
body:
He stopped getting out of bed on a Tuesday in October. Not dramatically — not with an announcement or a crisis or a reason his wife could point to. He just did not get up. And the next day he did not get up. And by Friday she was standing in the bedroom doorway, watching him sleep at two in the afternoon, wondering which version of the question to ask: "Are you okay?" — which he would answer with a lie, or "What is wrong with you?" — which would make her the villain in a story she did not write.

Marriage and mental health exist in a relationship the church has barely begun to explore. We have a theology of marriage. We have, belatedly, begun to develop a theology of mental health. But we have almost no theology of what happens when these two realities collide — when the person you married disappears into depression, when anxiety turns your spouse into someone you do not recognize, when the illness that lives in your partner's brain moves into your house and takes up permanent residence.

This is not a marginal issue. The National Institute of Mental Health estimates that nearly one in five American adults lives with a mental illness in any given year. In a congregation of two hundred, that is forty people — and forty spouses trying to love someone through something the church has historically treated as a spiritual problem rather than a medical one.

The Spouse Who Is Ill

Depression does not announce itself as depression. It announces itself as fatigue, as irritability, as a loss of interest in things that used to matter. The spouse who is sinking into a depressive episode does not think, "I am depressed." They think, "I am tired." They think, "Nothing sounds good." They think, "I do not know why I cannot make myself care about this." And because they do not name it as illness, they do not seek treatment for illness. They try harder, or they withdraw further, and the marriage absorbs the impact either way.

Anxiety operates differently but with similarly devastating marital effects. The anxious spouse lives in a state of perpetual vigilance — scanning for threats, catastrophizing outcomes, needing reassurance that cannot reassure because the problem is not the specific fear but the fear itself. The anxious spouse may become controlling — not out of malice but out of terror. If I can control enough variables, the thinking goes, I can prevent the disaster I feel is always imminent. The marriage becomes a system organized around the management of one spouse's anxiety, and neither person chose this arrangement or knows how to dismantle it.

Bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, PTSD, personality disorders — each of these conditions shapes a marriage in specific and predictable ways, and the church has naming language for almost none of them. We say "spiritual warfare" when we mean panic attacks. We say "lack of faith" when we mean clinical depression. We say "selfishness" when we mean the executive-function deficits that accompany ADHD. Our language is not just inadequate. It is harmful, because it locates the problem in the sufferer's character rather than in their neurology, and it makes the illness worse by adding guilt to every other symptom.

The Spouse Who Is Well

The well spouse — and the term is relative, because no one remains entirely well while living with someone who is ill — occupies a position of extraordinary difficulty that the church rarely acknowledges. They are simultaneously a partner and a caregiver, and the two roles exist in perpetual tension.

As a partner, they want reciprocity. They want the marriage to be a mutual exchange of support, affection, and engagement. As a caregiver, they provide support that is not reciprocated, manage logistics their spouse cannot manage, and absorb emotional weight that was supposed to be shared. Over time, the caregiver role begins to crowd out the partner role, and the marriage shifts from a relationship between equals to a relationship between a patient and a provider.

This shift is not anyone's fault. It is the natural consequence of chronic illness in a closed system. But it is devastating, and the well spouse is not allowed to say so — because who complains about a sick person? Who resents someone for being ill? The well spouse does. And the guilt of that resentment — the sense of being a bad person for feeling what they feel — is one of the heaviest burdens in marriage.

I have sat across from well spouses who whispered their truth as if confessing a crime: "I am angry at him for being depressed." "I resent her anxiety." "Sometimes I wish I had married someone else." These are not sins. They are the honest expressions of a person who is carrying more than they signed up to carry and who has no one to help them set the weight down. The church must be the place where those words can be spoken without judgment. If it is not, it is not serving these marriages at all.

The Myth of Prayer as Treatment

The church's most damaging contribution to the intersection of marriage and mental health has been the persistent suggestion that mental illness is, at root, a spiritual problem — that depression is a failure of faith, that anxiety is a failure of trust, that the right combination of prayer, Scripture, and spiritual discipline will heal what medication and therapy cannot.

This is not just wrong. It is dangerous. The depressed spouse who is told to pray harder instead of seeing a psychiatrist may die. This is not hyperbole. Untreated depression is a leading risk factor for suicide, and the church that substitutes spiritual counsel for medical treatment is, in the most literal sense, putting lives at risk.

Prayer is not treatment. Prayer is prayer. It is communion with God, it is the soul's honest cry, it is the practice of placing oneself in the presence of the One who made us. It is vital and irreplaceable and it does not adjust serotonin levels. The God who created the brain also created the science that understands the brain, and the faithful response to mental illness is not to choose between prayer and psychiatry. It is to use both, grateful for both, and to stop treating one as a betrayal of the other.

The marriage in which one spouse is mentally ill and untreated is a marriage under unbearable strain. The church that discourages treatment — actively or passively, explicitly or by omission — is complicit in that strain. This must be said clearly, because it is not said clearly enough: if your spouse is suffering from a mental health condition, getting them to a qualified professional is not a failure of faith. It is an act of love.

What Mental Illness Does to Intimacy

The most insidious effect of mental illness on marriage is the erosion of intimacy — not just physical intimacy, though that is often affected, but the deeper intimacy of knowing and being known. The depressed spouse withdraws into a private darkness that the well spouse cannot enter. The anxious spouse is so consumed by their fears that they cannot be present to anyone else's experience. The spouse with PTSD may be triggered by touch, by certain words, by situations that the well spouse cannot predict or understand.

Over time, both spouses become lonely. The ill spouse is lonely because their illness isolates them — because the interior country of depression or anxiety or psychosis is, by its nature, inaccessible to anyone who is not inside it. The well spouse is lonely because the person they married is present in body and absent in every other way that matters. They live together and they are alone.

This loneliness is the real crisis of the mentally ill marriage, and it is the crisis the church is most equipped to address — if it will. The church knows something about presence in darkness. The church has a liturgical tradition built around sitting with suffering, naming what is broken, and refusing to abandon the sufferer. Holy Saturday — the day between crucifixion and resurrection, the day when God was dead and nothing had been resolved — is the patron feast of the mentally ill marriage. It is the day that says: sometimes faithfulness looks like sitting in the dark with no assurance that the light is coming.

Medication, Therapy, and the Marriage

When the ill spouse begins treatment — medication, therapy, or both — the marriage enters a new phase that is often more difficult than anyone anticipates. Medication may help, but it also changes things. The depressed spouse who starts an SSRI may find their mood lifting and their libido disappearing. The anxious spouse who begins a benzodiazepine may feel calmer and also flatter — less anxious but also less joyful, less present, less themselves. The well spouse, who prayed for their partner to get help, may discover that the medicated version of their spouse is not the version they fell in love with.

Therapy introduces its own complications. The ill spouse may begin to understand their condition in ways that reframe the marriage — recognizing patterns, naming dynamics, gaining language for things they could not previously articulate. This is good. It is also destabilizing, because it changes the rules of a game both spouses had learned to play. The well spouse may feel left behind, or threatened, or resentful that a therapist seems to understand their partner better than they do.

These are not signs that treatment is failing. These are signs that treatment is working — that the marriage is being disrupted by health, which is just as disorienting as being disrupted by illness. The church must prepare couples for this disruption and normalize it. Getting better does not mean getting easier. It means getting more honest, and honesty is always harder before it is better.

What the Marriage Needs

The marriage in which one spouse is mentally ill needs what every marriage needs, but more of it: honesty, patience, professional support, and a community that will not abandon them when the crisis extends past the casserole phase.

It needs the ill spouse to accept their illness as illness — not as identity, not as punishment, not as a character defect, but as a condition that requires treatment and management and the humility to accept help. It needs the well spouse to accept that their role will, for seasons, be disproportionate — that they will give more than they receive, carry more than they should, and need their own support system to sustain them. It needs both spouses to grieve together what the illness has taken from their marriage, without pretending the grief is faithlessness.

And it needs the church to show up. Not with platitudes. Not with Bible verses offered as prescriptions. With presence. With meals. With the willingness to watch someone's children so the well spouse can go to their own therapy appointment. With the honesty to say, "I do not understand what you are going through, but I am here, and I am not leaving."

The marriage that carries mental illness is carrying one of the heaviest crosses two people can share. The church that calls itself the body of Christ — the community that claims to know something about bearing one another's burdens — must learn to help them carry it.

We have been silent too long. The silence has not protected anyone. It has only made the carrying lonelier.
excerpt: When one spouse lives with depression, anxiety, or any other mental health condition, both spouses carry the weight. The church has been slow to acknowledge this, and marriages have suffered for it.

title: When Divorce Is the Faithful Option
body:
I need to say something the church does not want to hear, and I need to say it without qualification or hedge: there are marriages in which divorce is not the failure of covenant but the recognition that the covenant has already been destroyed — by violence, by sustained cruelty, by a pattern of behavior so destructive that remaining in the marriage requires the annihilation of the person God made you to be.

I say this as a pastor. I say this as someone who has performed weddings and meant every word of the liturgy. I say this as someone who believes marriage is a covenant, not a contract, and that covenants are meant to be kept. But I also say it as someone who has sat across from people — mostly women, though not exclusively — who stayed in marriages that were destroying them because the church told them that God required it. Who endured abuse because their pastor said suffering was redemptive. Who watched their children absorb patterns of cruelty because leaving was a sin and staying was faithfulness.

That theology is wrong. It is not just pastorally insensitive. It is theologically wrong. And the damage it has done — the lives it has diminished, the children it has harmed, the image of God it has defaced in the name of preserving the image of God — demands a reckoning that the church has been too comfortable to undertake.

What Scripture Actually Says

The church's case against divorce rests primarily on two texts: Malachi 2:16, traditionally translated "I hate divorce, says the Lord," and Jesus's statement in Matthew 19:6, "What God has joined together, let no one separate." Both texts are real. Both are authoritative. And both have been read with a selectivity that borders on dishonesty.

The Malachi passage, in its fuller context, is not a blanket prohibition against divorce. It is a prophetic indictment of men who were divorcing their wives to marry younger women — a specific cultural practice in which powerful men discarded faithful wives. The prophet is not addressing the woman fleeing an abusive husband. He is addressing the husband who treats his wife as disposable. To read this passage as a command that the discarded wife must remain discarded is to invert the text's own moral logic.

Jesus's statement in Matthew 19 is similarly contextual. He is responding to Pharisees who ask whether a man can divorce his wife "for any cause" — a reference to the debate between the schools of Hillel and Shammai over the interpretation of Deuteronomy 24:1. The school of Hillel permitted divorce for almost any reason, including burning dinner. Jesus sides against this permissiveness, insisting that marriage is a covenant, not a convenience. But in the same passage, he names an exception: porneia — sexual immorality. And in Matthew 5:32, he uses the same exception, indicating that this was a consistent element of his teaching, not a one-time concession.

Paul adds another exception in 1 Corinthians 7:15: if an unbelieving spouse departs, the believing spouse "is not bound." The word Paul uses — dedoulotai — is a slavery term. The believing spouse is not enslaved to the marriage. This is strong language, stronger than the church typically acknowledges.

The point is not that Scripture takes divorce lightly. It does not. The point is that Scripture's treatment of divorce is more nuanced, more contextual, and more compassionate than the church's treatment of divorce. The Bible knows what the church often refuses to know: that some marriages should not continue. That the preservation of the institution is not always the preservation of the people within it. That a God who liberates slaves and defends the oppressed does not require the oppressed to remain in bondage to a covenant that has become a weapon.

The Covenant That Was Already Broken

The deepest error in the church's theology of divorce is the assumption that the person who files for divorce is the person who broke the covenant. In many cases, the covenant was broken long before the paperwork was filed. It was broken by the first act of violence. It was broken by the sustained pattern of contempt. It was broken by the addiction that the addicted spouse refused to address. It was broken by the infidelity that the unfaithful spouse refused to end.

Divorce, in these cases, is not the breaking of the covenant. It is the legal recognition that the covenant has already been broken — by someone else. The spouse who files for divorce after years of abuse is not violating their vows. They are acknowledging that their vows were violated — by the person who promised to love, honor, and cherish and instead chose to harm, demean, and destroy.

This distinction matters enormously, and the church's failure to make it has caused incalculable suffering. The abused spouse who stays because "I made a vow" is keeping a vow to a covenant that no longer exists. The other party destroyed it. What remains is not a covenant. It is a cage dressed in the language of covenant, and no theology worth the name should require anyone to remain in it.

The Children Question

The church's strongest argument against divorce — the one that gives even the most progressive pastors pause — is the children. "Stay together for the kids." The research is cited, usually selectively: children of divorce have worse outcomes on a range of measures. This is true, as far as it goes. But the research the church does not cite is equally clear: children raised in high-conflict marriages have outcomes that are as bad or worse than children of divorce. The child who watches one parent belittle, control, or strike the other is not being protected by the preservation of the marriage. They are being educated in what marriage looks like, and the lesson they are learning will shape every relationship they have for the rest of their lives.

The question is not whether children suffer when their parents divorce. They do. The question is whether they suffer more from the divorce or from the marriage — and in cases of abuse, addiction, or sustained high conflict, the answer is clear. The most loving thing a parent can do for their child is not to preserve the marriage at all costs. It is to show the child what health looks like, what dignity looks like, what it means to refuse to accept destruction as normal.

I have watched children bloom after a divorce — children who had been anxious, withdrawn, hypervigilant, who began to relax when the household that had been a war zone became two households that were peaceful. I do not celebrate this. I grieve that it was necessary. But I refuse to pretend that the marriage was better for them than the divorce, because I watched what the marriage was doing to them, and it was not good.

The Stigma the Church Creates

The divorced person in the church occupies a particular kind of exile. They are present but marked. Their status is known. In some congregations, they are explicitly barred from leadership, from teaching, from serving communion. In others, the exclusion is subtler — a certain distance in conversation, an absence of invitations, the sense that they have been reclassified from full member to cautionary tale.

This stigma is not biblical. It is cultural. It is the church's anxiety about its own failure to prevent the divorce, projected onto the person who had the courage to end a destructive marriage. And it is devastating to people who are already carrying the weight of a life they did not plan — who are already grieving, already questioning, already wondering whether God has abandoned them the way the church seems to have.

Jesus was remarkably gentle with divorced people. His conversation with the Samaritan woman at the well — a woman who had been married five times and was now living with a man who was not her husband — contains not a single word of condemnation. He sees her. He knows her. He offers her living water. The church that claims to follow Jesus should follow him here: into the conversation with the divorced person that begins not with judgment but with presence.

When Staying Is the Unfaithful Option

I want to push further than the church typically allows. I want to say not just that divorce is sometimes permissible but that staying is sometimes wrong. Not just inadvisable. Wrong.

When a spouse is being physically abused, staying puts them and their children at risk of serious harm or death. Staying is not faithfulness. It is complicity in one's own destruction, and God does not require it.

When a spouse is being systematically degraded — told they are worthless, stupid, ugly, incompetent — staying cooperates with the destruction of the image of God in a human person. The imago Dei is not merely a theological concept. It is the most fundamental truth about every human being, and the marriage that systematically assaults it is not a covenant worth preserving.

When a spouse is addicted and refuses treatment, staying enables the addiction. The language of enabling is not therapeutic jargon. It is a description of a real dynamic: the spouse who stays, who covers, who compensates, who absorbs the consequences — that spouse is making it possible for the addiction to continue. Sometimes the most loving thing you can do for an addict is to leave, because leaving is the only thing that might make the cost of the addiction high enough to motivate change.

When a spouse is unfaithful and unrepentant — not a single transgression met with genuine remorse, but a pattern of infidelity accompanied by blame-shifting, gaslighting, and refusal to change — staying teaches the unfaithful spouse that their behavior has no consequences. Forgiveness without repentance is not grace. It is permission.

In each of these cases, staying is not the faithful option. It is the option that protects the institution at the expense of the person. And no institution — not even marriage — is more valuable than the person God made.

The Grace on the Other Side

I have walked with people through divorce. I have sat with them on the night they signed the papers. I have listened to them grieve the life they thought they would have and did not get. And I have watched many of them — not all, but many — emerge on the other side into a life that is quieter, healthier, and more honest than the one they left.

This does not mean the divorce was easy. It was not. It does not mean the divorce was painless. It was excruciating. But it means that the God who promises to make all things new does not limit that promise to people who stayed married. The divorced person is not damaged goods. They are a person who survived something, who made a terrible and necessary choice, and who is now standing in a place they never planned to stand, looking for the grace that the church has told them they forfeited.

They did not forfeit it. Grace is not forfeited by divorce any more than it is forfeited by any other human brokenness. The entire point of grace — the entire scandal of grace — is that it goes to the places where human effort has failed and human plans have collapsed and human covenants have been broken. If grace does not go there, it does not go anywhere that matters.

The church must learn to say this. Not mumble it. Not whisper it in private conversations while maintaining the public theology that divorce is always a failure. Say it: sometimes divorce is the faithful option. Sometimes it is the only faithful option. And the God who hates divorce also hates the conditions that make divorce necessary, and the person who chose divorce over destruction chose well.

They chose life. And the God who sets before us life and death and says "choose life" — that God is not ashamed of them.

Even if the church is.
excerpt: The church has spent centuries telling people that divorce is always a failure. It is time to say what the church has been afraid to say: sometimes divorce is the most faithful thing a person can do.

title: Marriage and Addiction
body:
She found the bottles behind the dryer. Not one — seven, lined up like a small army of empty soldiers. She stood there holding one, turning it in her hands, and the feeling that came was not surprise. It was confirmation. She had known for months — known in the way spouses always know, which is to say she knew and did not know simultaneously, holding the knowledge at arm's length because looking at it directly would require her to act, and she was not ready to act.

Addiction enters a marriage the way water enters a basement — slowly, through cracks you did not know existed, until the day you go downstairs and find everything ruined. By the time the addiction is visible, it has already been at work for months or years, reshaping the marriage from the inside. The finances have shifted. The schedule has been reorganized around the substance or the behavior. The conversations have narrowed to the safe topics — the ones that do not lead to the argument, the denial, the look in the addicted spouse's eyes that says, "I know and I cannot stop and I need you not to say it out loud."

The church has gotten better at talking about addiction in the abstract. We have recovery ministries and Celebrate Recovery programs and sermons that acknowledge that addiction is real and that Christians are not immune. But we have gotten almost no better at talking about what addiction does to a marriage — the specific, daily, grinding destruction that addiction inflicts on the person who shares a life with an addict.

What Addiction Does to the Addicted Spouse

The addicted spouse is not the villain the church sometimes makes them. They are a person in bondage — the biblical language is more accurate than the clinical language here — caught in a cycle of compulsion, temporary relief, shame, and renewed compulsion that they cannot break by willpower alone. The addicted spouse did not choose addiction any more than a person chooses cancer. They may have chosen the first drink, the first pill, the first click on the screen. But the disease that followed the choice has its own logic, its own demands, its own relentless progression.

This does not absolve the addicted spouse of responsibility. It contextualizes their responsibility. They are responsible not for having a disease but for seeking treatment for it. They are responsible not for the compulsion but for the deception — the lies, the hidden bottles, the secret accounts, the elaborate architecture of concealment that addiction requires. The disease explains the craving. It does not explain the dishonesty. And the dishonesty is what destroys the marriage.

Every addicted spouse I have counseled has told a version of the same story: "I was going to stop. I kept meaning to stop. I told myself every morning that today would be the day." And every one of them knows, somewhere beneath the denial, that meaning to stop and stopping are not the same thing. The road to relapse is paved with sincerity. The addicted spouse is often genuinely sincere — genuinely sorry, genuinely committed to change — and genuinely unable to produce the change they commit to. This is the nature of addiction, and the church must understand it before it can address it.

What Addiction Does to the Sober Spouse

The sober spouse undergoes a transformation that is as predictable as it is devastating. They become a manager — managing the addict's behavior, managing the household, managing the public image of a marriage that is collapsing behind closed doors. They learn to read their spouse's eyes for signs of intoxication. They learn to check the browser history, the credit card statements, the odometer. They learn to lie — to their parents, their children, their friends, their pastor — because the truth is too humiliating and the consequences of the truth are too frightening.

This is codependency, and it is its own form of sickness. Not a moral failure — a predictable human response to living with someone who is out of control. The sober spouse compensates for what the addicted spouse cannot do. They cover for the missed days at work. They explain away the erratic behavior. They absorb the financial damage. And in doing so, they make it possible for the addiction to continue without consequences — which means they are, with the best of intentions, participating in the destruction of the person they love.

The church must speak to this dynamic honestly, without cruelty. The sober spouse who enables is not weak. They are terrified. They are terrified of what will happen if they stop covering — if the addiction becomes visible, if the consequences land, if the marriage they have been holding together with lies and effort finally falls apart. They enable because they love, and because the alternative to enabling feels like abandoning the person they love to destruction.

But enabling is not love. It is the counterfeit of love — the thing that looks like love from the outside and functions, from the inside, as permission. The sober spouse must eventually learn the hardest lesson in addiction: that the most loving thing they can do is to stop protecting the addicted spouse from the consequences of their addiction. This is not punishment. It is honesty. And honesty, in the context of addiction, is the only soil in which recovery can grow.

The Children in the Addicted Home

The children of addicted parents learn lessons that no child should have to learn. They learn to read a room before they enter it — to gauge the mood, to assess the danger, to calibrate their behavior to the most volatile person present. They learn that the parent they love cannot be trusted — not because the parent does not love them, but because the parent's love is held hostage by something the child cannot see and cannot understand.

These children often appear remarkably mature. They are the helpers, the peacemakers, the ones who get straight A's and never cause trouble. This maturity is not a gift. It is a survival strategy — the child's attempt to create order in a disordered home, to earn approval from a parent who is emotionally unavailable, to be so good that the bad thing stops happening. It never works, because the bad thing is not about them. But they keep trying, because trying is the only agency they have.

The church that wants to serve addicted families must see these children. Not as the collateral damage of their parents' problems. As people in their own right, carrying burdens they should not be carrying, developing patterns that will follow them into their own marriages and their own parenting unless someone intervenes. The church can be that intervention — a stable adult presence, a consistent community, a place where the child does not have to manage the room because the room is already managed.

The Question of Ultimatums

Every sober spouse eventually faces the question of ultimatums: should I threaten to leave if my spouse does not get help? The church's instinct is to recoil from this — ultimatums feel coercive, un-Christlike, incompatible with unconditional love. But unconditional love does not mean unconditional tolerance. God's love for Israel was unconditional. God's tolerance of Israel's idolatry was not. There came a point when the consequences landed — not because God stopped loving Israel, but because love without consequences is not love. It is indulgence.

The ultimatum, properly understood, is not a threat. It is a boundary. It says: I love you, and I will not participate in your destruction. I love you, and I will not allow our children to grow up in a home organized around your addiction. I love you, and I will not lie for you anymore. These are not acts of cruelty. They are acts of desperate, costly, terrifying love — the love that risks losing the person in order to save them.

Not every ultimatum leads to recovery. Some addicted spouses choose the substance over the marriage. This is devastating, and it is not the sober spouse's fault. The sober spouse who sets a boundary and enforces it has not failed the marriage. They have honored it — honored what the marriage was supposed to be, honored the person the addicted spouse was before the addiction consumed them, honored the children who deserve to see what health looks like.

Recovery and the Marriage

If the addicted spouse enters recovery, the marriage enters its own recovery — and this process is often more difficult than either spouse anticipated. The sober spouse expects to feel relief. Instead, they often feel rage — the accumulated anger of years of deception and codependency, finally released now that it is safe to feel it. The addicted spouse, newly sober and fragile, is bewildered: "I thought you wanted me to get help. I got help. Why are you angry?"

This anger is not irrational. It is delayed. It is the anger the sober spouse could not afford to feel while the crisis was active — the anger that had to be suppressed in favor of managing, covering, surviving. Now that the crisis has passed, the anger surfaces, and it is enormous, and it must be felt. The addicted spouse who dismisses this anger — who says, "I am in recovery now, we should be moving forward" — does not understand what their addiction cost. They must learn to understand, and the learning will be painful.

The marriage in recovery also faces the practical challenge of rebuilding trust that was systematically destroyed. Every lie told during the addiction is a brick removed from the foundation. Rebuilding means replacing every brick — which means the addicted spouse must become radically transparent, radically accountable, radically patient with a partner who has every reason to doubt them. This is the work of years, not weeks. The twelve steps call it "making amends," and the ninth step — the one about direct amends — is specifically about repairing what was broken. The marriage is usually the most broken thing.

What the Church Must Offer

The church must offer addicted families three things: honesty, community, and the long view.

Honesty means calling addiction what it is — not a weakness, not a phase, not something that will resolve itself with prayer and willpower. It is a disease. It requires treatment. And the church that tells the sober spouse to pray harder while the addicted spouse drinks themselves to death is not being faithful. It is being negligent.

Community means walking with the family for the duration — not just through the crisis of intervention, not just through the first month of rehab, but through the years of recovery, relapse, recovery again. Addiction is a chronic condition. It does not end with the last drink. It continues in the daily, undramatic discipline of sobriety, and the marriage that carries it needs a community that understands this and stays present through it.

The long view means accepting that the outcome is uncertain. Not every addicted spouse gets sober. Not every marriage survives addiction. The church must learn to hold these possibilities simultaneously — hope for recovery and acceptance that recovery may not come — without collapsing into either despair or false optimism. The church's job is not to guarantee outcomes. It is to be present in the uncertainty, to say to the sober spouse and the addicted spouse alike: we are here. Whatever happens, we are here.

That presence — steady, honest, unshockable — is the most powerful thing the church can offer to a marriage that addiction is trying to destroy.

It may not save the marriage. But it will save the people in it from the loneliness that makes everything else worse.
excerpt: Addiction does not happen to one person. It happens to a marriage. And the church that wants to serve addicted families must learn to see both the addict and the spouse who loves them.

title: Long-Distance Marriage and Maintaining Connection
body:
The hardest part of a long-distance marriage is not the longing. Longing has its own energy — it pulls you toward the person you love, it keeps the relationship charged, it gives the reunion its gravity. The hardest part is the ordinariness. It is eating dinner alone and knowing that your spouse is eating dinner alone in another city, and the meal is not a crisis and the evening is not dramatic and there is nothing to report except that you microwaved leftover pasta and watched something forgettable and went to bed in a room that has your things in it but not the person those things are supposed to surround.

Long-distance marriage is more common than the church acknowledges. It is not only the military marriage, though that is the version with the most public narrative. It is the marriage in which one spouse took a job in another city because the alternative was no job at all. It is the marriage in which immigration status separates a couple across a border. It is the marriage in which a spouse is incarcerated, or hospitalized for extended treatment, or caring for an aging parent in another state. It is any marriage in which the two people who promised to share a life are, for a season, sharing it in separate locations.

The church has almost nothing to say about this. Our theology of marriage assumes proximity. It assumes shared meals, shared beds, shared space. "The two shall become one flesh" — and what happens when the one flesh is divided by eight hundred miles and a three-hour time difference?

What Distance Reveals

Distance does not create problems in a marriage. It reveals them. The couple that communicates well in person will find ways to communicate across distance. The couple that avoids hard conversations in person will find that distance makes avoidance even easier — the phone call can always be cut short, the video chat can always be interrupted by a bad connection, and the text message is the perfect medium for saying nothing while appearing to say something.

Distance also reveals what the marriage is actually built on. If it is built on physical proximity — on the comfort of sharing a couch, on the reassurance of a body in the bed — then distance will expose the absence of deeper foundations. If it is built on companionship and shared activity, distance will reveal how little the couple has invested in the kind of intimacy that does not require the same room. And if it is built on genuine knowledge of and commitment to each other — the kind of commitment that Paul describes as bearing all things, believing all things, hoping all things, enduring all things — then distance, while painful, will not be fatal.

This does not mean that distance is good for marriage. It is not. Marriage is designed for proximity, for the daily friction and comfort of two lives intertwined. But the marriage that survives distance learns something about itself that the proximate marriage may never discover: it learns what its foundations are made of. And that knowledge, however painfully acquired, is a gift.

The Daily Practice of Connection

The long-distance marriage lives or dies on the practice of intentional connection — and the word "practice" is chosen deliberately. Connection across distance is not spontaneous. It cannot be. The spontaneous connection that happens in a shared home — the conversation that starts while unloading the dishwasher, the touch as you pass in the hallway, the shared reaction to something on the news — all of that is lost when you live apart. What replaces it must be deliberate, scheduled, and protected from the hundred small erosions that will try to reduce it.

This means a daily phone call that is not optional. Not a check-in — not "how was your day, fine, how was yours, fine." A real conversation, with space for silence and space for honesty and space for the mundane details that, in a proximate marriage, you absorb without effort. What you ate. What the weather was. What your coworker said that annoyed you. Who you ran into at the grocery store. These details feel trivial, and they are essential. They are the raw material of a shared life, and the long-distance marriage that stops exchanging them will find, when reunion comes, that it has two separate lives instead of one shared one.
