It means finding ways to be present in each other's daily environment. Sending a photograph of your desk. Leaving a voicemail that your spouse will hear when they wake up. Ordering delivery to their apartment on a night you know they will be too tired to cook. These are not grand gestures. They are the long-distance equivalents of the small, unremarkable acts of care that sustain every marriage — the coffee made before they wake up, the blanket pulled over them when they fall asleep on the couch. The medium changes. The intention is the same.

The Loneliness That Must Be Named

The long-distance spouse is lonely. This must be said plainly, because the long-distance marriage generates a particular expectation that the spouse should not be lonely — should be grateful for the job, or the opportunity, or the visa that makes reunification possible someday. Gratitude and loneliness are not mutually exclusive. You can be thankful for the arrangement and devastated by it simultaneously. The church must make room for both.

The loneliness of the long-distance marriage is different from the loneliness of being single. The single person is lonely for a relationship they do not have. The long-distance spouse is lonely for a relationship they do have — that exists, that is real, that they can see on the screen of their phone but cannot reach through it. This is its own particular torment. The absence is not the absence of love. It is the absence of love's physical expression — the touch, the presence, the body in the next room that means you are not alone even when you are not talking.

The church can serve the long-distance spouse by being the community that fills some of the relational space that distance has emptied. Not as a replacement for the marriage — nothing replaces the marriage — but as a presence that says: you are not invisible here. You are known. You have a place. The long-distance spouse who disappears from community — who stops going to church, stops accepting invitations, stops reaching out — is a spouse in danger. Not of infidelity, necessarily, though that risk is real. In danger of the deeper loss, which is the loss of the self that exists in relationship. We are made for community. The long-distance spouse who loses community loses a part of themselves, and the marriage absorbs that loss whether it knows it or not.

The Temptation That Proximity Creates

The long-distance marriage must be honest about temptation. Not in the anxious, surveillance-driven way the church usually discusses it — not the purity culture framework of walls and boundaries and accountability software. In the honest way. Which is this: when you are lonely, and someone is kind to you, and that someone is physically present in a way your spouse is not, the kindness can become something else before you notice the transition.

This does not happen because the long-distance spouse is morally weak. It happens because human beings are wired for connection, and the absence of connection with the person you are committed to creates a vulnerability that presence would have prevented. The affair that begins with "we are just friends" is not a lie — not at the beginning. It becomes a lie gradually, as the friendship fills the space that the marriage cannot fill from a distance, and by the time the transition is visible, it is already well advanced.

The antidote to this is not more vigilance. It is more honesty. The long-distance spouse who tells their partner, "I have a coworker I am becoming friends with, and I want you to know about it," is practicing the kind of transparency that prevents the slow drift toward infidelity. The long-distance spouse who hides the friendship — who tells themselves it is nothing, it is innocent, there is nothing to report — has already begun the concealment that every affair requires.

Reunion and Its Discontents

The reunion is supposed to be the reward — the homecoming, the embrace, the restoration of everything that distance took away. And sometimes it is. But often it is harder than either spouse anticipated. The spouse who has been living alone has developed routines, habits, a way of organizing the household that works for one person. The returning spouse disrupts those routines simply by being present. The refrigerator is suddenly wrong. The bathroom schedule is suddenly complicated. The bed that was spacious is suddenly shared.

These are trivial complaints, and they are not trivial at all. They are the friction of two people who have been living separate lives trying to reintegrate into one life, and the friction generates heat that neither person expected. The reunion that was supposed to feel like homecoming feels, instead, like hosting a guest — a beloved guest, a wanted guest, but a guest nonetheless. The house has to be rearranged. The rhythms have to be renegotiated. The self that learned to be alone has to learn, again, to be accompanied.

The church must normalize this. The reunion is not a failure if it is difficult. It is difficult because it is real — because two real people with real habits and real lives are trying to merge those lives again, and merging is always harder than separating. The couple needs permission to struggle with the reunion without interpreting the struggle as evidence that the marriage is broken. The marriage is not broken. It is doing a hard thing. Again.

The Faithfulness of Distance

The long-distance marriage teaches a truth the church needs to hear: faithfulness is not guaranteed by proximity. The couple that shares a house can be faithless to each other in a thousand ways that do not involve physical separation. And the couple that is separated by distance can be faithful in ways that the proximate couple never has to demonstrate — faithful in the daily choice to connect, to prioritize, to remain committed to a person who is not present and whose absence would make abandonment easy and invisible.

This faithfulness is not romantic. It is mundane. It is the phone call made when you are tired. It is the financial transparency maintained when no one is checking. It is the decision to go home after the work dinner instead of accepting the invitation to stay for another round. It is small and repetitive and nobody sees it, and it is the substance of which marriage is actually made.

The long-distance marriage that endures has learned that love is not a feeling sustained by presence. It is a practice sustained by will. And the will is sustained by something deeper than either feeling or will — by the covenant itself, which holds even when the feeling fades and the will falters and the distance feels like it will never end.

It does end. Or it does not. Either way, the faithfulness was real. And faithfulness that is real in the absence is faithfulness of the deepest kind.
excerpt: The marriage that exists across distance must learn to be sustained by what most marriages take for granted: the daily, unremarkable acts of presence that add up to a life together.

title: Second Marriages: Grace, Baggage, and Starting Again
body:
The second wedding is different from the first. Not necessarily smaller or less festive, though it often is both. Different in texture. The vows land differently in a mouth that has spoken them before. The promise to love until death do us part carries a different weight when you know, from experience, that the part can come long before death. The guests clap and smile, and some of them are thinking what the couple is thinking but will not say: we hope this one works.

Second marriages are the church's most awkward category. We do not quite know what to do with them. We believe in the permanence of marriage, and here are two people whose first marriages were not permanent. We believe in new beginnings, and here is a beginning that is not entirely new — it is built on the foundation of something that ended, and the ending is part of the structure whether we acknowledge it or not. We believe in grace, but we are not sure how far grace extends. Does it extend to a second chance at the thing you failed at the first time? Does it extend to happiness after the covenant was broken? Does grace have a statute of limitations?

It does not. But the church has often acted as though it does, and second marriages have paid the price.

What the Second Spouse Inherits

The person who marries someone with a previous marriage inherits more than a partner. They inherit a history — a history that includes wounds they did not inflict, patterns they did not create, and sensitivities they will trip over in the dark for years before they learn where they are.

The previously married spouse carries reflexes from the first marriage. If the first marriage ended because of criticism, they will flinch at anything that sounds like criticism in the second. If the first marriage ended because of emotional withdrawal, they will panic at any sign of distance. If the first marriage ended because of infidelity, they will scan for threats with a vigilance that feels, to the new spouse, like mistrust. And it is mistrust — not of the new spouse, but of marriage itself. The first marriage taught them that marriage can fail, and they carry that knowledge into the second marriage like a scar that aches before rain.

The second spouse did not cause these reflexes. They did not earn this mistrust. But they must live with it, and the living-with-it requires a patience that nobody warns them about. "I am not your ex" is the sentence that every second spouse eventually says, and it is true and it is necessary and it does not solve the problem, because the problem is not rational. It is somatic. It lives in the body, in the nervous system, in the place where the first marriage wrote its lessons in a language the conscious mind cannot always read.

The Baggage Everyone Mentions and Nobody Defines

People speak of "baggage" in second marriages the way they speak of "issues" in therapy — vaguely, as if the word itself explains something. It does not. Baggage, in the context of second marriage, means specific things, and naming them is the beginning of dealing with them.

Financial baggage: the debt from the first marriage, the alimony or child support payments, the lifestyle adjustment that comes with dividing one household into two. The second marriage starts with less than the first marriage had, and the disparity between expectation and reality can generate resentment before the honeymoon is over.

Relational baggage: the ex-spouse who is still in the picture because children require co-parenting, the in-laws from the first marriage who are now the grandparents of the new spouse's stepchildren, the friendships that were forged during the first marriage and may not survive the transition to the second. The second marriage does not begin with a clean relational slate. It begins in the middle of a relational web that was already in place.

Emotional baggage: the grief of the first marriage's failure, the guilt (whether warranted or not) about the role one played in that failure, the fear that history will repeat itself, the defensive patterns developed during the worst of the first marriage that now get deployed in the best of the second. The second spouse reaches for their partner's hand and the partner pulls away — not because they do not want to be touched, but because the last person who reached for their hand used touch as a prelude to a fight.

The church cannot remove this baggage. But it can stop pretending it does not exist. The pastoral preparation for a second marriage should differ substantially from the preparation for a first marriage — not because second marriages are less holy, but because they face different challenges. The couple entering a second marriage needs to name their baggage explicitly, to each other and to their community, and they need a community that can hold that naming without judgment.

The Ghost of the First Marriage

Every second marriage has a ghost. The ghost is the first marriage — not the ex-spouse as a person, but the first marriage as a template, a reference point, an invisible standard against which the second marriage is constantly measured.

The measurement works in both directions. Sometimes the second marriage is measured favorably: "He never listened to me the way you do." "She was never this affectionate." These comparisons feel like compliments, but they are not. They are reminders that the new spouse exists in relation to the old one, that their virtues are defined not on their own terms but in contrast to someone else's failures. No one wants to be loved as the correction of a previous mistake.

Sometimes the measurement works unfavorably, and this is worse. "My first husband always remembered my birthday." "My first wife kept a cleaner house." These comparisons, even when unspoken, create an impossible standard — a standard defined by selective memory, because the first marriage is now remembered not as it was but as it is wished it had been. The dead marriage, like the dead in general, gets idealized. Its faults fade. Its virtues sharpen. And the living spouse — the one who is present, imperfect, doing their best — cannot compete with a memory.

The second marriage must exorcise this ghost, and the exorcism is simple to describe and difficult to execute: stop comparing. Not "stop saying it out loud." Stop doing it. This requires a discipline of the mind that borders on spiritual practice — the deliberate choice, repeated hundreds of times, to judge the current marriage on its own terms rather than against the template of the previous one. It is the decision to let this marriage be this marriage, with its own shape, its own rhythms, its own particular combination of strengths and weaknesses that has never existed before and will never exist again.

Grace and the Second Chance

The theological question at the heart of the second marriage is whether grace extends to second chances — and if so, what that grace looks like. The church has historically been ambivalent about this, and the ambivalence shows in the way we treat second marriages: we perform them, but with less enthusiasm. We celebrate them, but with a footnote. We welcome them, but we wonder, privately, whether God blesses what God did not originally intend.

This ambivalence is understandable. It is also unnecessary. The entire narrative of Scripture is a story of second chances — of God who makes covenant, watches the covenant broken, grieves the breaking, and makes covenant again. Abraham lied about Sarah. Twice. God renewed the covenant. David committed adultery and murder. God did not abandon the Davidic line. Peter denied Jesus three times. Jesus restored him three times. The pattern is relentless: human beings break things, and God, instead of writing them off, offers them another chance to build something faithful.

If this is the pattern of God's dealing with humanity, then the church must stop treating the second marriage as a concession and start treating it as an instance of the pattern. Grace does not erase the past — the first marriage happened, the failure happened, the pain happened, and none of it is undone by the second ceremony. What grace does is make the past usable. It transforms the failure from a disqualification into a teacher. It says: what you learned in the fire, bring it into this new thing. Let the scars inform the love. Let the grief deepen the gratitude. Let the failure make you humble enough to succeed.

What the Second Marriage Needs from the Church

The second marriage needs the church to do four things.

First, welcome without asterisk. The couple entering a second marriage does not need to be reminded that their first marriage failed. They know. They carry it every day. What they need is a community that receives them as they are — with their history, their children, their complications — and says, "You are home here."

Second, pastoral care that acknowledges the complexity. Second marriages face challenges that first marriages do not: blended family dynamics, co-parenting with ex-spouses, the integration of different family cultures, the management of financial obligations from previous relationships. The church that applies its standard first-marriage counseling to a second marriage is not being efficient. It is being lazy.

Third, patience with the timeline. Second marriages take longer to reach their stride. The couple is not just learning each other — they are learning each other while unlearning the patterns of a previous relationship. This takes time. More time than the church usually offers before it starts asking, "How are things going?" with that particular pastoral inflection that means, "Are you sure this was a good idea?"

Fourth, the freedom to grieve. The second marriage does not erase the grief of the first marriage's ending. That grief will surface — at unexpected times, triggered by unexpected things — and the second spouse must be allowed to feel it without the new partner interpreting it as a commentary on their relationship. The person who grieves their first marriage while building their second is not being unfaithful to the second. They are being human. And the church must make room for the grief alongside the new beginning.

The second marriage is an act of courage that the church does not always recognize as such. It is the decision to try again — knowing what failure costs, knowing what the odds are, knowing that the scars of the first attempt will ache in weather they cannot predict. It is the most human thing in the world: to be broken and to choose, despite the brokenness, to love again.

The God who makes all things new does not require that the old things never happened. God requires only that we bring them — all of them, the joy and the wreckage — and lay them down, and begin.
excerpt: The second marriage carries everything the first marriage taught — including things both spouses wish they had not learned. Grace does not erase the past. It makes the past usable.

title: Marriage Across Cultural Lines
body:
They met at a conference. She was Korean American, second generation, fluent in both languages but at home in neither — too American for her parents' expectations, too Korean for her college friends' assumptions. He was from a small town in Indiana, where the only Korean restaurant was a buffet next to the Walmart and culture meant whether you rooted for Purdue or IU. They fell in love the way people do — gradually, then all at once — and they married, and then they discovered that falling in love across cultures is the easy part. Building a life across cultures is the work that never ends.

The intercultural marriage is not a special category of marriage. It is marriage with the volume turned up — every negotiation that every marriage requires, amplified by the fact that the two people negotiating come from different assumptions about what negotiation looks like, what marriage requires, what family means, and what love is supposed to feel like when it is expressed.

The church has been slow to develop a theology of intercultural marriage, partly because the church has been slow to develop a theology of culture at all. We speak of "the culture" as if it were a monolith — a single, secular, threatening force that the church must resist. This is lazy thinking, and it is particularly unhelpful for the couple sitting in the pew whose marriage is the daily encounter of two cultures, neither of which is monolithic, neither of which is the enemy, and both of which are the water they swim in.

What Culture Means in a Marriage

Culture is not cuisine and holidays. It is the invisible architecture of assumptions — assumptions about who speaks first, who speaks loudest, who defers, who decides. It is what you learned, before you were old enough to learn it consciously, about how emotions are expressed, how conflict is handled, how respect is shown, and how love is communicated.

In some cultures, love is expressed through words — through verbal affirmation, through the direct statement of feeling. In others, love is expressed through action — through provision, through labor, through the silent, unremarked acts of care that speak louder than any declaration. When a spouse from one tradition says "I love you" and waits for the reciprocal statement, and the spouse from the other tradition shows their love by waking up early to pack lunch and says nothing, both are loving. Neither feels loved. And the gap between the two — the gap that is cultural, not personal — can become a wound if it is not named.

Conflict management is equally culturally determined. Some cultures prize direct confrontation — the problem is named, the argument is had, the resolution is reached, and life continues. Others prize harmony — the problem is acknowledged indirectly, the confrontation is avoided, the resolution is reached through mediation or the simple passage of time. When a spouse from a direct-conflict culture marries a spouse from a harmony culture, the direct spouse feels that their partner is evasive, dishonest, unwilling to engage. The harmony spouse feels that their partner is aggressive, disrespectful, incapable of reading the room. Both are wrong about each other. Both are right about their own cultural logic.

The intercultural marriage must develop a third culture — a culture that belongs to neither spouse's origin but is created, negotiated, revised, and reinvented by the couple together. This third culture is the marriage's own creation, its unique contribution to the world. It does not require either spouse to abandon their culture of origin. It requires both spouses to hold their culture of origin with open hands — to keep what serves the marriage and release what does not, and to do this without interpreting the release as a betrayal of who they are.

The Family Systems Behind the Couple

The intercultural couple does not marry in isolation. They marry into each other's families, and the families bring their own cultural expectations to the marriage with a force that the couple may not have anticipated.

In many cultures, marriage is not primarily a union of two individuals. It is a union of two families. The expectations that come with this understanding — expectations about where the couple will live, how often they will visit, what role the parents will play in child-rearing, how financial resources will be shared with the extended family — can be radically different from the individualistic assumptions that dominate American culture. The spouse who sends a significant portion of their income to family overseas is not being irresponsible. They are fulfilling an obligation that their culture has wired into them as deeply as the American culture has wired self-sufficiency into their partner.

These family expectations can become flashpoints in the marriage, particularly when they are unspoken. The spouse who assumes that their parents will live with them in old age and the spouse who assumes that their parents will move to assisted living are not just disagreeing about logistics. They are disagreeing about the fundamental meaning of family obligation, and the disagreement goes deeper than either of them can articulate because it is not a conclusion they reached. It is a world they were raised in.

The church must help intercultural couples surface these assumptions before they become conflicts. Not to adjudicate which culture is right — both are right, within their own logic — but to make the invisible visible, to give the couple a framework for understanding why they disagree, and to create space for the negotiation that must follow.

Race, Power, and the Marriage

When the intercultural marriage is also an interracial marriage, the dynamics of race and power enter the household with a weight that the church has been reluctant to address. The white spouse who has never thought about race in a sustained way marries a person for whom race is an inescapable daily reality — a reality that shapes where they feel safe, how they are perceived, what they must teach their children about the world.

The interracial couple will face external pressures that same-race couples do not. Stares in restaurants. Comments from strangers. The family member who accepts the marriage publicly and makes racist remarks privately. The church member who says "I do not see color" and means it as a compliment and does not understand why it is not. These external pressures are exhausting, and they create an internal dynamic in the marriage: the minority spouse carries the weight of explaining, educating, and managing the emotional impact of racism, while the majority spouse either shares the weight or — more commonly — does not fully perceive it.

The intercultural, interracial marriage needs a church that takes race seriously — not as a political issue but as a human one. The church must be the community where the minority spouse does not have to be the sole educator, where the majority spouse can learn without requiring their partner to be the teacher, and where the children of the marriage — the children who belong to both cultures and are often claimed fully by neither — can see their identity reflected in the community that claims to worship a God who created every ethnicity and called all of them good.

The Children Between Worlds

The children of intercultural marriages are the inheritors of complexity. They are biracial, bicultural, bilingual — or they are none of these things, because the parents chose, consciously or by default, to raise them in one culture rather than two. Either way, the children carry questions about identity that monocultural children do not: Who am I? Which half of me is real? Do I have to choose?

The church must speak to these children with care. Not with the easy assurance that "we are all one in Christ" — which is true but which, spoken prematurely, can function as an erasure of difference rather than a celebration of unity. The children of intercultural marriages need a community that names their complexity as a gift — that says, "You hold two worlds in one body, and both worlds are good, and neither world requires the erasure of the other."

This is, if we think about it, a profoundly Christian vision. The incarnation itself is intercultural — the divine entering the human, the infinite taking on the finite, two natures united in one person without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The Chalcedonian formula, that ancient attempt to describe how Christ can be fully God and fully human, is the best theological model the church has for the intercultural child: fully one thing and fully another, with no contradiction.

What the Marriage Teaches the Church

The intercultural marriage is not a problem for the church to solve. It is a gift the church needs to receive. Because the intercultural marriage does, in miniature, what the church is supposed to do on a global scale: it brings different peoples together into one body, not by erasing their differences but by holding those differences in a unity that is deeper than sameness.

Paul wrote to the Galatians that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. He did not mean that the categories disappear. He meant that the categories no longer divide. The intercultural marriage embodies this vision — two people from different cultures who refuse to let culture divide them, who build a third thing that is neither one nor the other but both, held together by a love that is stronger than the differences it spans.

The church that learns from the intercultural marriages in its congregation will learn something about itself: that unity does not require uniformity, that diversity is not a problem to be managed but a reality to be celebrated, and that the God who created a world of astonishing cultural variety probably did not intend the church to reduce that variety to a single way of being.

The intercultural marriage, in all its difficulty and beauty, is a prophetic sign — a small, daily demonstration that the wall of hostility has been broken down, and that two can become one without either ceasing to be who they are.

The church should pay attention. There is a sermon in every intercultural marriage. And the church needs to hear it.
excerpt: The intercultural marriage does not simply blend two people. It brings two worlds into a single household, and the household must learn to hold them both without asking either to disappear.

title: The Marriage That Lost Its Friendship
body:
There was a time when they talked. Not about the children's schedules or the broken dishwasher or who was picking up the prescription. They talked about ideas, about memories, about the article one of them read that morning. They talked about nothing in particular for hours, the way you do with someone whose company you enjoy — not because the conversation was important, but because the person was.

They cannot remember when that stopped. It was not a moment. It was an erosion — so gradual that neither of them noticed until the evening came when they sat across from each other at dinner and realized they had nothing to say. Not nothing worth saying. Nothing. The well was dry. The friendship that had been the foundation of the marriage — the thing that made them choose each other in the first place — had been replaced by a management partnership. They were efficient together. They ran the household. They divided the labor. They were, by every functional measure, a successful team. And they were lonely in a way that only people who share a life with someone they no longer know can be lonely.

This is the marriage that lost its friendship. It is not dramatic. There is no affair, no addiction, no crisis that would justify a counselor's appointment or a pastor's intervention. It is simply two people who like each other less than they used to — or, more precisely, two people who have forgotten how to like each other, because liking requires attention, and attention has been directed elsewhere for so long that neither of them knows how to redirect it.

How Friendship Dies in Marriage

The friendship in a marriage dies by neglect, and the neglect has identifiable stages. The first stage is the prioritization of function over connection. This begins, usually, with the arrival of children. The couple that used to spend Saturday mornings in bed talking now spends Saturday mornings at soccer games and grocery stores. The couple that used to cook together now eats in shifts. The couple that used to read aloud to each other now reads separately, in different rooms, after the children are in bed — if they read at all, if they have the energy, if they are not already asleep.

This is understandable. Children require attention, and the attention must come from somewhere. But what the couple does not realize, in those early years of parenting, is that they are making a withdrawal from an account they are not replenishing. The friendship was built by hours of shared attention. It is being starved by the redirection of that attention to the demands of the household. And when the demands eventually subside — when the children are older, when the schedule loosens — the couple discovers that the friendship they assumed would be waiting for them has died in their absence.

The second stage is the replacement of curiosity with assumption. In the early years, you asked your spouse questions because you did not know the answers. What do you think about this? How do you feel about that? What would you do if? Over time, you stop asking because you think you already know. You assume you know what your spouse thinks about politics, about faith, about the neighbor's new car. And in most cases, you are right — you do know. But the act of asking was never primarily about acquiring information. It was about expressing interest. It was the verbal equivalent of turning toward someone and saying, with your attention, "You matter to me. Your inner life is worth my curiosity." When the asking stops, the message that replaces it is: I already know everything about you. There is nothing new to discover. You are a solved equation.

Nobody wants to be a solved equation.

The third stage is the accumulation of unprocessed grievances. Every marriage generates friction, and healthy marriages process the friction through conversation — through the small, ongoing negotiations that keep two people calibrated. But the marriage that has lost its friendship has also lost the channel through which friction is processed. The conversation that should happen — "It bothered me when you said that" — does not happen, because the couple no longer has the relational credit to absorb the vulnerability that honest conversation requires. Instead, the grievances accumulate. They pile up like snow on a roof, invisible from the outside, adding weight that the structure was not designed to carry.

Eventually, the roof collapses — not under the weight of any single grievance, but under the accumulated weight of years of unspoken ones. And both spouses are bewildered, because none of the individual grievances seem heavy enough to explain the collapse. They are not heavy enough. Individually. Together, they are crushing.

What John Gottman Found

The research of John Gottman — the psychologist who has studied marriage with more rigor and over a longer period than anyone else in the field — consistently identifies friendship as the most important predictor of marital satisfaction and stability. Not passion. Not compatibility. Not shared values or shared interests or shared faith. Friendship. The simple, unspectacular reality of two people who know each other, like each other, and turn toward each other when the world turns against them.

Gottman's concept of "bids for connection" is particularly illuminating. A bid is any attempt by one spouse to connect with the other — a comment, a question, a touch, a look. "Look at that bird" is a bid. "How was your meeting?" is a bid. Reaching for your spouse's hand while watching television is a bid. Gottman found that couples who stayed together turned toward their partner's bids 86 percent of the time. Couples who divorced turned toward only 33 percent of the time.

The numbers are stark, but the mechanism is intuitive. Every bid is a test — a small, often unconscious test of whether the other person is available, interested, present. When the bid is met — when the spouse looks at the bird, answers the question, takes the offered hand — the message is: I am here. You are not alone. We are connected. When the bid is ignored — when the spouse does not look up, does not answer, does not take the hand — the message is: you do not matter enough to interrupt what I am doing. And enough of those messages, received over enough years, will kill the friendship as surely as oxygen deprivation kills a flame.

What the Church Can Say

The church has a theology of marriage as covenant, as sacrament, as a reflection of Christ and the church. What it lacks is a theology of marriage as friendship — a framework that takes seriously the daily, unglamorous, absolutely essential practice of liking the person you love.

The Song of Solomon provides the raw material. "This is my beloved and this is my friend," the woman declares. The two categories are not separated. They are held together, and the holding together is the point. The beloved is the friend. The friend is the beloved. The marriage that loses the friendship has not merely lost a convenience. It has lost a constitutive element — the element without which the covenant, however intact, is hollow.

The church should say this: friendship in marriage is not optional. It is not a bonus that some couples enjoy and others manage without. It is the soil in which everything else — sex, parenting, conflict resolution, spiritual growth — takes root. Without it, the marriage can function, but it cannot flourish. And God did not institute marriage so that two people could function together. God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone," and the solution was not a business partner or a roommate. It was a companion. A friend.

The Recovery of Friendship

Friendship in marriage can be recovered, but the recovery requires intentionality that feels, at first, artificial. The couple that has not had a real conversation in months cannot simply decide to start having real conversations. They have to relearn the skill — and it is a skill — of being curious about each other, of turning toward bids, of carving out time that is not functional but relational.

This means dates. Not the performative date night that the church has elevated to a sacrament — not the expensive dinner where both people sit across from each other trying to remember how to talk. Simple dates. A walk. A drive. An errand done together instead of divided for efficiency. The goal is not romance. The goal is proximity without agenda — the condition in which friendship naturally grows.

It means questions. Real questions, not the questions you already know the answers to. "What are you worried about that you have not told me?" "What is the best part of your life right now?" "If you could change one thing about our daily routine, what would it be?" These questions require vulnerability from the asker and the answerer, and vulnerability is the currency of friendship.

It means turning off the screens. The phone, the laptop, the television — these are the enemies of friendship, not because technology is evil but because technology provides an endless supply of stimulation that requires nothing from you. Friendship requires something from you. It requires your attention, your presence, your willingness to be bored together — because boredom, shared, is the precondition for the spontaneous conversation, the unexpected discovery, the moment of connection that no algorithm can engineer.

What Friendship Makes Possible

The marriage that recovers its friendship does not merely become happier. It becomes more resilient. The friendship is the shock absorber — the thing that cushions the marriage against the inevitable impacts of life in a fallen world. The couple that likes each other can survive a financial crisis. The couple that has lost its friendship may not survive a bad week.

Friendship also makes the hard conversations possible. The couple that is friends can say, "I need to tell you something difficult" without the other person bracing for catastrophe. The friendship creates a context of safety — a confidence that the person across from you is for you, not against you, and that the difficult thing they are about to say comes from a place of care rather than contempt.

And friendship makes the marriage worth fighting for. The couple in crisis who can still say, "I like this person — I have forgotten how to show it, but I like who they are" — that couple has something to build on. The couple who cannot say it, who have not liked each other in years, who stay together out of obligation or fear or inertia — that couple has a harder road, though not an impossible one.

The recovery of friendship in marriage is not the recovery of the past. You cannot go back to the people you were when the friendship was new. You can go forward to the people you are now — older, more tired, more complicated, and more in need of a friend than you have ever been.

The friend is there. Across the table. Across the silence. Waiting to be rediscovered.

All it takes is turning toward them. And saying something. Anything. Even: "Look at that bird."
excerpt: Before they were lovers, they were friends. Before the mortgage and the children and the routine that replaced conversation, they liked each other. The recovery of friendship may be the most important thing a struggling marriage can do.

title: Submission Revisited: What Ephesians 5 Actually Says
body:
No passage of Scripture has been more weaponized in the history of marriage than Ephesians 5:22-33. "Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord." Those eleven words have been quoted to justify everything from benign patriarchy to outright abuse, from the gentle insistence that the husband should make the final decision to the violent demand that the wife should obey without question. They have been embroidered on pillows, preached from pulpits, and whispered by abusers to their victims as theological justification for cruelty.

And they have been quoted, almost always, out of context. Torn from the passage that surrounds them, stripped of the revolutionary framework in which Paul placed them, and deployed as a proof text for a power arrangement that the passage itself subverts.

It is time to read the text again. Not the eleven words. The whole passage. And not with the assumptions that two thousand years of patriarchal interpretation have layered onto it, but with the eyes of someone encountering Paul's argument for the first time, in the context in which it was written, to the audience that first received it.

What we will find is not what either the complementarians or the egalitarians expect. What we will find is harder, more beautiful, and more costly than either camp has been willing to say.

The Verse They Always Skip

The passage does not begin at verse 22. It begins at verse 21: "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." This verse is the heading — the thesis statement — of everything that follows. Paul's instruction to wives does not emerge from a vacuum. It emerges from a prior, overarching command to mutual submission. Every relationship that Paul addresses in the following verses — wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters — is nested under this controlling statement: submit to one another.

This matters enormously. If verse 22 is read in isolation, it establishes a one-directional hierarchy: wives submit to husbands. But if verse 22 is read as a specific application of verse 21, the hierarchy is reframed. The wife's submission is one expression of a mutual submission that characterizes the entire Christian community. The husband is not exempted from submission. He is included in it by the verse that governs the passage.

The church has, for most of its history, read verse 22 without verse 21. This is not an accident. It is a choice — a choice made by interpreters who benefited from the hierarchical reading and who had every incentive to ignore the verse that complicated it. When you begin at verse 22, you get patriarchy. When you begin at verse 21, you get something else entirely. You get a community in which power is not exercised over others but surrendered for others. You get a marriage in which both spouses are called to the same fundamental posture: submission — not to each other's authority, but to each other's good.

What "Submit" Actually Means

The Greek word translated "submit" is hupotasso. In its military usage, it means to arrange oneself under — to place oneself in a position of subordination within an ordered structure. But Paul is not writing a military manual. He is writing to a community that has been turned upside down by the gospel, in which the first are last and the last are first, in which the greatest is the servant of all. In this context, hupotasso does not mean "obey a superior." It means "orient yourself toward the good of another person, even at cost to yourself."

This is a crucial distinction. Obedience is compelled by authority. Submission, in Paul's usage, is offered by love. It is not the response of an inferior to a superior. It is the response of a free person who chooses, voluntarily, to prioritize another's well-being. It is what Jesus modeled in the foot-washing — the one with all the authority choosing to serve the one with none. The submission Paul calls for is not the submission of weakness. It is the submission of strength voluntarily restrained for the sake of love.

The wife who submits in this sense is not diminishing herself. She is orienting herself — toward her husband's good, toward the good of the marriage, toward the pattern of Christ who submitted himself to death for the sake of those he loved. This is not a demeaning posture. It is the most exalted posture the New Testament knows.

But — and this is where the complementarian reading goes wrong — it is not a posture required only of wives.

What the Husband Is Actually Told

Paul's instruction to husbands occupies three times the space of his instruction to wives. This is not an accident. In a first-century context, the wife's submission was assumed. It was the cultural default. The husband's authority was unquestioned. Paul did not need to spend time establishing what everyone already accepted. What he needed to establish — what required argument, what was genuinely radical — was the limitation and redefinition of that authority.

"Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." This is not a general instruction to be nice. It is a specific instruction to die. The model Paul holds up is not Christ the King, not Christ the Ruler, not Christ the Head who exercises power over the body. It is Christ the Crucified — the one who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was obedient unto death. The husband's love is to look like that.

In a first-century household — in a world where the husband had near-absolute legal authority over his wife, where he could divorce her at will, where he owned her property and controlled her social access — this instruction was not a reinforcement of the status quo. It was its demolition. Paul tells the husband: your authority is real, and it exists for one purpose only — to be spent on behalf of your wife. You do not exercise it over her. You exercise it for her. You do not use your position to get what you want. You use your position to give what she needs. And if the giving costs you everything — if it costs you your comfort, your preferences, your very life — that is precisely the cost Christ paid, and it is the cost you signed up for when you entered this covenant.

The husband who reads Ephesians 5 and concludes that he is in charge has read three verses and missed the other nine. He has seen his authority and missed its purpose. He has claimed the throne and ignored the cross that stands behind it.

The Head-Body Metaphor

Paul says the husband is the "head" of the wife as Christ is the head of the church. The word "head" — kephale in Greek — has generated more scholarly debate than perhaps any other word in the Pauline corpus. Does it mean "authority over," as the complementarian tradition insists? Or does it mean "source," as some egalitarian scholars have argued?

The honest answer is that the debate is not settled, and both sides have legitimate arguments. But what is more important than the precise meaning of kephale is the model Paul attaches to it. Whatever "head" means, it means what Christ's headship means. And Christ's headship, as Paul describes it in this passage, means giving himself up — not exercising authority over the church, but sacrificing himself for the church's good.

If "head" means "authority," then the authority is self-sacrificial. If "head" means "source," then the source is self-giving. Either way, the husband's role is defined not by what he gets from the relationship but by what he gives to it. The head that does not serve the body is not a head in any Christian sense. It is a tumor.

This is not what the complementarian tradition has typically taught. The typical complementarian teaching says: the husband leads, the wife follows. The husband decides, the wife submits. The husband is the head, the wife is the body. These formulations, while they sound like Ephesians 5, actually reverse the passage's logic. The passage does not say the husband leads and the wife follows. It says both submit — the wife through willing orientation toward her husband's good, the husband through self-sacrificial love that takes Christ's death as its model. Both postures are forms of submission. Neither is a claim to power.

What the Passage Does Not Say

Ephesians 5 does not say the husband makes the decisions. It does not say the wife must obey. It does not say the husband has the final word. It does not say the wife cannot lead, teach, earn, think, or speak. It does not say the husband's opinion carries more weight. It does not establish a chain of command. It does not create a hierarchy of value, worth, intelligence, or spiritual capacity.

These are things the church has read into the passage — projecting the patriarchal assumptions of its culture onto a text that was, in its original context, far more subversive than the church has been willing to recognize. First-century wives did not need to be told to submit; the culture already required it. What was revolutionary was the instruction to husbands — the limitation of their authority, the redefinition of their headship, the insistence that their power existed solely for the purpose of self-sacrificial love.

The tragedy of the church's use of Ephesians 5 is that it has taken a passage that originally limited the husband's power and used it to expand it. It has taken a passage that originally elevated the wife's dignity and used it to diminish it. It has turned a revolutionary text into a reactionary one — and in doing so, it has done violence to the text, to women, and to the marriages that the text was meant to serve.

What Mutual Submission Looks Like

If Ephesians 5 is read as Paul intended — beginning at verse 21, with mutual submission as the controlling principle — what does it produce? Not the complementarian hierarchy. Not the egalitarian erasure of all difference. Something harder and more beautiful than either.

It produces a marriage in which both spouses are constantly asking: what does love require me to give up? Not what does love entitle me to. What does love require me to surrender? This is the question that the cross asks every relationship, and it is the question that mutual submission embeds in the daily life of the marriage.

Sometimes love requires the wife to defer to her husband — not because he has authority over her, but because his judgment is sound and her deference serves the good of the family. Sometimes love requires the husband to defer to his wife — not because she has authority over him, but because her wisdom exceeds his and his deference serves the good of the family. The direction of deference is not fixed by gender. It is determined by wisdom, by context, by the specific needs of the specific moment. And both spouses are willing to defer, because both spouses have internalized the same principle: I am here to serve, not to be served.

This is harder than hierarchy. Hierarchy is simple: someone is in charge, someone is not. Mutual submission is complex: both are in charge, both are not, and the negotiation of who leads in which moment requires a level of maturity, trust, and communication that hierarchy does not demand. But the difficulty is the point. Marriage is supposed to be a crucible — a context in which both people are shaped into the image of Christ. And the shape of Christ is not the shape of authority. It is the shape of a cross.

The Cost of Getting This Wrong

The church's misreading of Ephesians 5 has had consequences that cannot be measured. Women who were told that God required their submission to men who were harming them. Men who were told that their authority was divinely sanctioned and therefore beyond question. Marriages in which one person's voice was elevated and the other's was silenced — not by mutual agreement, but by a theological framework that was presented as biblical and was, in fact, a cultural projection onto a text that said something else entirely.

I have sat with the women who were damaged by this misreading. I have heard their stories. I have watched them struggle to disentangle the God they were taught from the God who actually exists — the God who does not require their diminishment, who does not sanction their suffering, who does not use the language of love to enforce the reality of control.

And I have sat with the men who were damaged by it too — men who were told they were the leaders and discovered, to their bewilderment, that the crown was heavy and the authority was isolating and the marriage they were supposed to lead was dying because their wife did not need a leader. She needed a partner. She needed a friend. She needed someone who would submit to her — to her needs, her wisdom, her experience, her voice — the way she had been told, all her life, to submit to him.

Ephesians 5 is one of the most beautiful passages in Scripture. It envisions a marriage in which both people pour themselves out for each other, in which authority is exercised as service, in which the pattern of Christ's self-giving love becomes the pattern of daily life. The church has turned it into a hierarchy. It is time to turn it back.

The cross is not a throne. And the marriage that is built on the cross is not built on power. It is built on the willingness to lay power down.
excerpt: Ephesians 5 has been used to silence women and empower men for centuries. A serious reading of the text reveals something far more radical — and far more costly — than either side of the debate wants to admit.

title: When Abuse Hides Behind Theology
body:
She came to see me on a Wednesday afternoon. She was composed — the careful composure of a woman who had learned to manage her expression the way you manage a budget, allocating exactly enough emotion to seem normal and reserving the rest for the car, the shower, the 3 a.m. hours when no one could see her face.

She told me her husband was a godly man. She said this first, before she said anything else, the way you establish credentials before making an argument that might be dismissed. He led the family devotion. He prayed over meals. He served on the elder board. He was, by every public measure, a man the church admired.

Then she told me what happened at home. The monitoring of her phone. The control of the finances — not shared management, but control: she had no access to the accounts, no knowledge of the balances, no ability to make a purchase without his approval. The criticism that was never direct but always present, delivered as concern: "I am worried about you — you seem scattered lately." The isolation from friends and family, accomplished not by forbidding her to see them but by making every visit so costly — the silent treatment, the interrogation, the theological correction that followed — that she stopped going.

And the theology. Always the theology. "I am the head of this household." "Scripture says you are to submit." "A godly wife does not question her husband's decisions." "If you were more spiritually mature, you would not struggle with this."

She asked me if he was abusive. She did not know. That is the most devastating sentence in this paragraph: she did not know. After years of being told that what she experienced was biblical headship, godly leadership, the natural order of a Christian home — she could not tell the difference between love and abuse. Because the church had never taught her the difference.

How Theology Becomes a Weapon

Abuse does not always look like a fist. The most insidious form of abuse in the church is the form that operates through theology — that uses the language of Scripture, the structures of the church, and the authority of God to control, diminish, and silence.

This is not a distortion of theology. It is theology functioning as designed — or rather, as redesigned by people who have a stake in maintaining power. The theological tools are real: headship, submission, male authority, wifely obedience. These concepts exist in the tradition. They have been taught for centuries. And in the hands of an abuser, they become instruments of control that are almost impossible to resist, because resisting them feels like resisting God.

The abuser who quotes Ephesians 5 is not engaging in biblical exegesis. He is weaponizing a text to serve a purpose the text was never intended to serve. But the victim does not know this — cannot know this — because the church has not equipped her to distinguish between a faithful reading and a predatory one. She hears "submit" and she submits, because she was taught that submission is godliness and resistance is rebellion. She hears "headship" and she defers, because she was taught that the husband's authority is God-given and her questioning of it is sin.

The church created the conditions for this abuse by teaching a theology of marriage that concentrates authority in one person without building in any mechanism of accountability. When the husband is the head and the wife is the body, and the head answers to God and not to the body, there is no check on the head's exercise of power. The system depends entirely on the head being benevolent. And when the head is not benevolent — when the head is controlling, manipulative, cruel — the system has no corrective. It simply tells the body to submit harder.

What Abuse Actually Looks Like

The church needs a clear definition of abuse, because the absence of a definition has allowed abusers to operate in plain sight. Abuse is a pattern of behavior — not a single incident but a pattern — in which one person systematically uses power, control, fear, or intimidation to diminish, isolate, or subjugate another person.

Physical abuse is the form the church recognizes most readily, and even this recognition is inadequate. I have known pastors who counseled women to return to husbands who hit them, on the grounds that the violence was provoked, or infrequent, or the result of stress that would pass. These pastors were not evil. They were untrained, and their training gap had consequences measured in bruises, broken bones, and occasionally in death.

But physical abuse is only one form. Emotional abuse — the systematic degradation of a person's sense of self — is equally destructive and far harder to see. The husband who never hits his wife but tells her, daily, that she is stupid, incompetent, unattractive, and spiritually immature is abusing her. The wife who never raises her hand but controls her husband through shame, manipulation, and the threat of public humiliation is abusing him. These forms of abuse leave no visible marks, and the absence of visible marks has allowed the church to pretend they do not exist.

Spiritual abuse is the form most unique to the church, and it deserves particular attention. Spiritual abuse occurs when one person uses spiritual authority — whether the authority of a pastor, an elder, or a husband exercising "headship" — to control another person's behavior, restrict their freedom, or punish their independence. It includes using prayer as a weapon ("I am praying that God will convict you of your rebellion"), using Scripture as a bludgeon ("The Bible says you are to submit, and your refusal to submit is sin"), and using church discipline as a threat ("If you leave me, I will tell the elders, and they will discipline you").

The abuser who uses theology is particularly dangerous because the victim cannot separate the abuse from the faith. To resist the abuser feels like resisting God. To leave the abuser feels like leaving the church. To name the abuse feels like blasphemy. The victim is trapped not just by the abuser but by their own theology — by the sincere belief that what is happening to them is what God requires.

What the Church Gets Wrong

The church's response to domestic abuse has been, with too few exceptions, a catastrophic failure. The failure is not primarily one of intention. Most pastors want to help. The failure is one of theology, training, and institutional incentive.

The theological failure is the one I have already named: a theology of marriage that concentrates authority without accountability, that treats submission as a one-directional obligation, and that makes the preservation of the marriage the highest priority in every situation. This theology does not cause abuse. But it creates an environment in which abuse can flourish, because it removes the very things — accountability, mutual submission, the willingness to name sin in the powerful — that would otherwise check the abuser's behavior.

The training failure is practical. Most pastors receive little or no training in identifying domestic abuse, assessing danger, developing safety plans, or navigating the legal and social systems that serve abuse victims. The pastor who counsels an abused woman to go home and submit harder is not usually being malicious. He is being ignorant — deploying the only tool he has (marital counseling) in a situation that requires a completely different set of tools (safety planning, legal advocacy, trauma-informed care).

Couples counseling, in particular, is dangerous in abusive situations. The premise of couples counseling is that both parties share responsibility for the relational dynamic and both need to change. In an abusive relationship, this premise is false. The abuser is responsible for the abuse. The victim is not contributing to a "dynamic." They are surviving a pattern of control. Couples counseling in this context gives the abuser information — the victim's vulnerabilities, their complaints, their emotional needs — that the abuser will weaponize in the next argument. Many domestic violence experts identify couples counseling as a contraindication in abusive relationships, and the church must learn this distinction.

The institutional failure is the most painful to name. The church has an institutional interest in keeping marriages together. Divorce is bad for the church's public image. It complicates the community. It raises questions about the church's teaching. And so the church's instinct, when confronted with abuse in a marriage, is to counsel reconciliation — to send the victim back, to give the abuser another chance, to believe the abuser's repentance because believing it is easier than dealing with the alternative.

This instinct kills people. Not metaphorically. Literally. The most dangerous time for a domestic abuse victim is the period immediately after they leave or attempt to leave. The church that counsels a victim to return — that arranges a meeting between victim and abuser, that facilitates "reconciliation" without a comprehensive safety plan — is putting that person at risk. This is not an overstatement. It is the assessment of every major domestic violence organization in the country, and the church must reckon with it.

What Repentance Looks Like — and What It Does Not

The abuser who is confronted will almost always express remorse. He will cry. He will quote Scripture. He will say he has seen the light, that he is a changed man, that God has spoken to him. He may be sincere. He may not. The point is that sincerity, in the moment of confrontation, is not the same as repentance, and repentance is not the same as change.

Genuine repentance in an abuser has specific, observable markers, and the church must learn to identify them. Genuine repentance accepts full responsibility — not "I was wrong, but you provoked me," but "I was wrong." Genuine repentance does not minimize — not "I only raised my voice," but "I used my voice to control and frighten you, and that is abuse." Genuine repentance submits to accountability — not the accountability of a small group that meets weekly and asks how he is doing, but the accountability of a structured program designed specifically for abusive men, led by professionals trained in the dynamics of abuse.

Genuine repentance also takes time. The abuser who changes in a week has not changed. He has adapted. The patterns of abuse are deeply ingrained — they involve beliefs about power, entitlement, and gender that were formed over decades — and they do not shift because of a crisis or a confrontation or a powerful Sunday sermon. They shift, if they shift at all, through years of sustained, difficult, professionally guided work. The church that accepts a quick repentance and sends the victim home is not practicing grace. It is practicing negligence.

What the Church Must Do

The church must do five things, and it must do them now, without further delay or qualification.

First, it must name abuse from the pulpit. Not once. Regularly. The congregation must hear, from their pastor, in the context of worship, that abuse is sin — that it is not headship, not discipline, not a marital problem. It is sin. And the church does not tolerate it.

Second, it must train its leaders. Every pastor, elder, deacon, and small group leader should receive basic training in identifying abuse, responding to disclosures, and connecting victims with professional resources. This training should be mandatory, not optional. The church that does not train its leaders to respond to abuse is a church that will fail its most vulnerable members.

Third, it must believe victims. The default response when someone discloses abuse should be: "I believe you. You are not crazy. This is not your fault. How can I help?" Not: "Have you tried submitting more?" Not: "What did you do to provoke him?" Not: "Are you sure you are not exaggerating?" Believe the victim. The research is clear: false allegations of domestic abuse are rare. The far more common reality is underreporting — victims who do not disclose because they have been taught, by the church's theology and the church's silence, that what is happening to them is normal.

Fourth, it must prioritize safety over marriage. This is the hardest thing for the church to accept, and it is non-negotiable. When a person is being abused, the first priority is their safety — not the preservation of the marriage, not the reputation of the church, not the abuser's feelings. Safety first. Everything else second. If safety requires separation, the church must support the separation without guilt-tripping the victim about their vows. The vows were already broken — by the abuser.

Fifth, it must reform its theology. Not abandon the tradition. Reform it. The theology that has been used to justify abuse — the unchecked headship, the unilateral submission, the concentration of spiritual authority in the husband — must be re-examined in light of the damage it has caused. This does not mean abandoning Ephesians 5. It means reading it honestly, beginning at verse 21, and building a theology of marriage in which both spouses are called to mutual submission, mutual sacrifice, and mutual accountability.

The woman who came to see me on that Wednesday afternoon deserved better than what the church gave her. She deserved a community that could distinguish between headship and control. She deserved a theology that named what was happening to her as sin rather than obedience. She deserved a pastor who had been trained to recognize the signs, to believe her disclosure, and to help her get safe.

She deserved a church that loved her more than it loved the institution of marriage.

Every victim in every pew deserves that. And the church's failure to provide it is not a secondary issue. It is a crisis of faithfulness. The God who liberated Israel from slavery and who announced his mission as "setting the captives free" does not sanction captivity in the home. The theology that permits it is not biblical. It is an abuse of the Bible.

And it must end.
excerpt: The most dangerous abuse is the abuse that calls itself love, that quotes Scripture, that wraps control in the language of covenant. The church must learn to see it, name it, and stop it.

title: The Five-Year Marriage Check: An Honest Assessment
body:
Five years is not a milestone the culture celebrates. There are no special names for a fifth anniversary — no silver, no gold, no diamond. Hallmark makes a card for it, but the card does not know what to say, because five years is an awkward interval: too long to be new, too short to be tested, too ordinary to merit the kind of reflection that longer marriages receive.

But five years is exactly when the reflection is most needed. Because five years is when the marriage you actually have begins to diverge from the marriage you imagined, and the gap between the two — the gap between what you thought this would be and what it is — is either a source of grief or a source of growth, depending on whether you have the courage to look at it honestly.

I have performed enough weddings and counseled enough couples to know that the first two years are consumed by adjustment — by the shock of sharing a bathroom, a budget, a bed with another person whose habits were formed in a different household. Years three and four are consumed by whatever comes next — often a child, sometimes a career change, occasionally a crisis that forces the couple to discover what they are made of before they were ready to find out. But year five — year five is when the dust settles. The patterns are established. The routines are set. The way you fight, the way you make up, the way you spend Saturday mornings — all of it has calcified into a shape. And the question year five asks is: is this a shape you can live in?

The Questions Nobody Asks

The five-year marriage check begins with questions, and the questions must be honest enough to produce honest answers. Not "Are you happy?" — happiness is too vague, too subject to the weather of any given Tuesday, to be a useful diagnostic. The questions must be more specific, more pointed, more willing to cut through the comfortable fictions that five years of shared life inevitably generate.

Do you like this person? Not love — like. Love is a commitment. Like is a preference. You can love someone you do not like, and many five-year marriages are doing exactly that — maintaining the commitment while losing the preference. Do you enjoy their company? Do you look forward to seeing them at the end of the day? Would you choose them again — not in the romantic, cinematic sense, but in the practical sense: if you met them today, knowing what you know, would you want to build a life with this person?

Do you trust this person? Not with the big things — most people trust their spouse not to clean out the bank account or disappear with the children. With the small things. Do you trust them with your feelings? With your failures? With the parts of yourself that you do not show anyone else? Is this person safe? Not safe in the sense of boring. Safe in the sense of: I can be my full self here, including the parts that are weak and foolish and afraid, and I will not be punished for it.

Do you fight well? Not "do you fight" — every couple fights, and the couple that does not fight is a couple that has stopped caring enough to disagree. The question is whether the fighting produces resolution or resentment. Do your arguments end with understanding, even if they do not end with agreement? Or do they end with someone winning and someone losing, with the loser filing the loss away in the growing archive of grievances that will eventually become too heavy to carry?

Are you growing — individually and together? The person you married five years ago is not the person you are married to now. People change. The question is whether you are changing in directions that bring you closer together or further apart. Are your interests diverging? Your values? Your vision of what a good life looks like? Some divergence is natural and healthy. But if the divergence is so great that you cannot find common ground — if you are becoming strangers who share an address — the five-year mark is the time to name it.

The Patterns That Have Set

By year five, the marriage has developed patterns that feel permanent — and that feel permanent because, without intervention, they are. The patterns of communication, conflict, intimacy, and daily life that characterize a five-year marriage are, with minor variations, the patterns that will characterize a fifteen-year marriage and a thirty-year marriage. The couple that does not fight fair at five will not fight fair at twenty. The couple that avoids hard conversations at five will avoid them at fifteen. The couple that has stopped having sex at five will not spontaneously resume at ten.

This is not fatalism. It is observation, supported by decades of marital research. Patterns, once established, have inertia. They persist not because the couple chooses them but because changing them requires more energy than maintaining them. The couple that wants to change a destructive pattern at year five has time and plasticity on their side. The couple that waits until year fifteen has less of both.

The five-year check is, therefore, an opportunity — perhaps the best opportunity the marriage will ever have — to identify the patterns that are not working and to change them before they harden into permanence. This requires honesty that most couples find uncomfortable. It requires saying, "This thing we do — this way we fight, this way we avoid, this way we coexist without connecting — this is not working, and if we do not change it, it will define us."

That sentence is hard to speak. But it is infinitely easier to speak at year five than at year twenty, when the pattern has been reinforced by fifteen additional years of repetition and the prospect of change feels not just difficult but impossible.

The Myth of Effortless Marriage

The five-year mark is often the point at which the couple confronts one of the church's most damaging myths: that a good marriage is an effortless marriage. The myth says: if you married the right person, and if you are both walking with God, the marriage should be natural, easy, a source of joy rather than work. And when the marriage is not easy — when it requires effort, negotiation, compromise, and the daily decision to choose patience over frustration — the myth whispers: something is wrong. You married the wrong person. God is not in this marriage. A good marriage would not be this hard.

This is a lie. Every good marriage is hard. It is hard because it requires two selfish people — and all people are selfish, at bottom, no matter how sanctified — to share a life in which their selfishness is constantly confronted, constantly challenged, constantly required to yield to the needs and desires of another person. This is not a sign that the marriage is failing. It is a sign that the marriage is doing what marriage is supposed to do: sanctifying the people in it. And sanctification is never comfortable.

The couple that reaches year five and finds their marriage difficult has not failed. They have arrived at the real marriage — the one that exists after the honeymoon fades and the infatuation wears off and the person across the table is revealed as a human being with morning breath and bad habits and a capacity for annoyance that the dating period mercifully concealed.

The real marriage is better than the imagined one. Not easier. Better. Because the real marriage is the place where actual love — not the feeling, but the practice — happens. The feeling of love is a gift. The practice of love is a discipline. And the five-year marriage is the place where the discipline either takes root or is abandoned in favor of the fantasy that somewhere, with someone else, the feeling would have lasted.

What to Do with What You Find

The five-year check may reveal that the marriage is healthier than you realized — that the daily frustrations had obscured a foundation of genuine affection, trust, and shared purpose. If so, name it. Gratitude is not a feeling. It is a practice, and the marriage that practices gratitude is a marriage that reinforces its own health.

The check may reveal problems that are serious but addressable — communication patterns that need repair, intimacy issues that need attention, unresolved conflicts that have been avoided for years and need to be engaged. If so, address them. Now. Not next month, not next year, not when things settle down. The things will not settle down. There will always be a reason to postpone the hard conversation. Do not wait for the reason to run out. The reason will never run out. The marriage might.

The check may reveal that the marriage is in genuine trouble — that the foundation is weaker than either person knew, that the distance between them is greater than adjustment can bridge, that professional help is not optional but urgent. If so, get the help. Not the book. Not the podcast. Not the marriage retreat that costs five hundred dollars and produces a temporary emotional high that fades by Tuesday. A therapist. A skilled, trained, experienced therapist who will sit with you for months and help you rebuild what the marriage requires and that you cannot do alone.

And the check may reveal, in rare cases, that the marriage is not viable — that it was built on a foundation that cannot support what a marriage needs, and that the most honest thing both people can do is to name this truth and reckon with its consequences. This is the hardest outcome, and the church must not treat it as the only possible outcome of honest assessment. Most marriages at year five are not beyond repair. They are under-maintained. And under-maintained is a fixable condition.

An Invitation, Not a Judgment

The five-year marriage check is not a test you pass or fail. It is an invitation to look — honestly, without flinching, without the optimistic distortions that protect you from reality and prevent you from change — at what you have built together, and to decide, with open eyes, whether to continue building it.

The couples I admire most are not the couples with the easiest marriages. They are the couples who looked honestly at what they had, named what was working and what was not, and chose — deliberately, sacrificially, with full knowledge of the cost — to keep building. They chose the marriage. Not because it was perfect. Because it was theirs, and because they believed that what could be built on the existing foundation was worth the effort of building it.

Five years is not a milestone. It is a crossroads. And the couple standing at it has a choice: drift forward on inertia, hoping that time will fix what attention has not, or stop, look, assess, and choose the marriage again — this time with the honesty that the first time lacked, because the first time was a promise about the future and this time is a decision about the present.

The decision about the present is always harder. It is also the only one that matters.
excerpt: Five years into a marriage, the adrenaline of the beginning has faded and the shape of what you are actually building becomes visible. This is the moment to look honestly at what you have made.

title: What Song of Solomon Teaches About Desire
body:
The Song of Solomon is the embarrassment of the biblical canon. It sits between Ecclesiastes and Isaiah — between the philosopher's despair and the prophet's fire — and it talks about bodies. It talks about breasts and thighs and lips and the curve of a waist. It talks about desire with an explicitness that has made the church uncomfortable for two thousand years and that has produced, in response, one of the most extraordinary feats of interpretive avoidance in the history of religious thought.

For most of the church's history, the Song was read as an allegory. The woman was the church. The man was Christ. The desire was spiritual longing. The bodies were metaphors. This reading allowed the church to include the Song in the canon without actually reckoning with what it said — to keep the book without keeping its meaning.
