The parents of faithful children are not necessarily better parents than the parents of prodigals, and to believe otherwise is to lay a burden on grieving mothers and fathers that God never laid on them, and that the gospel explicitly removes.

The stories we do not know

When we grieve a child who has left the faith, we tend to write the story as finished. He left. She walked away. It is over. But we do not know the story. We are standing in the middle of a narrative we cannot see the end of, and we are treating chapter twelve as though it were the final page. The father in the parable did not know his son would return. He simply watched the road. The whole force of that story is that it was told from inside the not-knowing.

I have known too many people who left the faith at twenty-two and returned at forty, transformed, deeper than they ever were before, to believe that a young adult's departure is a verdict. The brain of a twenty-two-year-old is not finished. The life of a twenty-two-year-old has barely begun. What looks like a permanent exit is often a long detour, and the detour is sometimes exactly the road by which a person comes to a faith that is genuinely theirs, purged of the secondhand quality that was all they had when they left.

Augustine left. He spent years in philosophies and practices that broke his mother's heart, and Monica wept and prayed through a departure that must have looked, at the time, absolutely final. It was not final. But she did not know that while she was living it. She lived, as we live, inside the not-knowing, and the faithfulness of her waiting was not validated by the outcome she could not see. It was faithful in the waiting itself. Your child's story is not finished, and neither is your part in it, and the God who wrote Augustine's turning is not finished writing your child's.

Distinguishing what they left from why

It is worth asking, painfully, what exactly your child left. Sometimes what a young adult rejects is not Christ but a distortion of Christ that we, the church and the parents, handed them. They leave a faith that was political tribalism, and we mourn as though they left Jesus. They leave a faith that was rigid and joyless and afraid, and we grieve as though they abandoned the gospel, when in fact they may have rejected something that deserved rejecting.

This is not comfortable to consider, because it implicates us. If my child left because the faith I modeled was more fear than grace, more control than love, more certainty than trust, then part of what they walked away from was my own failure to embody the thing I was preaching. I have had to sit with that. I have had to ask whether the version of Christianity my children saw in me was one worth keeping, and to confess that in some seasons it was not. The departure of a child can be, among other things, an accountability I would rather avoid.

Before you mourn what your child rejected, ask what they actually saw. Sometimes they did not leave Christ. They left the counterfeit we handed them and called by his name.

This is a hard grace, but it is a grace, because it opens a door. If what my child rejected was a distortion, then the real Christ is still available to them, still unencountered, still capable of drawing them in a way the counterfeit never could. My job is not to defend the version of faith they rejected. My job is to live, from now on, a faith so marked by grace and joy and honesty that it becomes a quiet argument against the distortion, a living demonstration that there is more to this than what drove them away.

The temptation to make every conversation about it

When a child leaves the faith, the parent is tempted to turn every interaction into an intervention. Every phone call becomes an opportunity to plant a seed, every visit a chance to raise the issue, every holiday a battleground. And the child, sensing that they are now a project rather than a person, withdraws further, because no one wants to be someone else's unfinished business.

The most counterintuitive discipline for a grieving parent is to stop bringing it up. Not because you have stopped caring, but because your constant raising of the subject communicates that your love is conditional on their return, that they are unacceptable as they are, that the relationship is a means to an end. A child who feels loved only as a target of conversion will flee the love. A child who feels loved simply for existing, whose parent can enjoy their company without an agenda, may one day find in that unconditional love a living argument for the God they abandoned.

I had to learn to shut my mouth. I had to learn that my sermons, delivered at my own dinner table to my own children, were not evangelism but self-soothing, a way to feel I was doing something. The doing something was mostly for me. What actually served my children was the harder discipline of loving them without agenda, of letting the relationship be about them rather than about my need to fix them. The most persuasive thing I could offer was not another argument but a love that refused to be conditional, a welcome that did not depend on their coming around, a father who was glad to see them exactly as they were.

Praying without controlling

Prayer becomes complicated when you are praying for a specific outcome you desperately want and cannot secure. It is easy for prayer to curdle into anxiety, into a bargaining with God, into a demand disguised as devotion. You pray for your child's return, and you check for evidence, and finding none, you pray harder, as though volume could move the hand of God.

I have had to learn a different kind of prayer, a prayer that releases rather than grasps. A prayer that says, this child was yours before they were mine, and you love them more than I do, and I entrust them to a love and a patience deeper than my own. This is not resignation. It is the opposite. It is the deepest form of hope, because it places the outcome in hands stronger than mine, and frees me to love my child without the crushing weight of believing their eternity depends on my strategy. It does not. It never did.

There is a strange freedom that comes when you finally stop trying to be your child's savior. For years I carried the unconscious belief that if I just found the right argument, the right approach, the right combination of pressure and love, I could secure my child's faith. It was an exhausting belief, and it was also, if I am honest, a kind of idolatry, a belief that I could do for my child what only God can do. When I released that, when I confessed that I am not my child's savior and never was, something in me could finally rest, and something in the relationship could finally breathe. My child stopped being a project I was failing at and became, again, simply my child, whom I love. The releasing did not mean I stopped caring or stopped praying. It meant I stopped carrying a weight that was never mine to carry, and handed it back to the God who is actually able to bear it.

Keeping the door open

The single most important thing you can do for a child who has left the faith is to remain a door they can walk back through. This means the relationship must survive the departure. It means that when they visit, they encounter warmth and not a lecture. It means that your love is durable enough to outlast their unbelief, so that if the day comes when they turn around, the road home is not blocked by your bitterness or their fear of your judgment.

The father in the parable ran. He did not wait for an apology, did not demand an explanation, did not make the son grovel through the account of his failures. He ran, and he embraced, and he restored, before a word of repentance was fully spoken. That running is the posture. You keep the road clear. You keep your heart soft. You refuse to let the years of grief harden into a resentment that would make return impossible. You watch the road, and you wait, and you keep the door open, no matter how long.

Keeping the door open is not passive, and it is not easy. It requires a discipline of the heart that most of us underestimate, because bitterness accumulates almost without our noticing, one small resentment at a time, until one day we discover that the door we thought we were keeping open has quietly closed. The grieving parent must tend the door actively, must forgive in advance the wounds that have not yet healed, must refuse the temptation to keep a ledger of the pain their child has caused. This is spiritual work, and it cannot be done in our own strength. It requires the same grace we are asking God to extend to our children, extended first to our own hardening hearts, so that when the child appears on the road, they find not a parent who has been rehearsing the accusation, but a parent whose long waiting has softened rather than soured, whose heart is ready to run.

The grief that has no timeline

Let me be honest about the cost. This grief does not resolve on a schedule, and it may not resolve at all in this life. Some of us will go to our graves with children who never returned to the faith, and I will not pretend otherwise to make you feel better. But even then, the love was not wasted, and the prayers were not lost, and the story is not necessarily over just because your part in it ended. You planted things you may never see bloom. That is the condition of every gardener and every parent and every believer. We plant in hope, and we release the harvest to a God whose timeline is not ours.

If you are in this room tonight, holding this grief, I want you to hear that you are not a failure, and your love was not in vain, and your child is not beyond the reach of a God who pursues across every distance. Keep the door open. Love without agenda. Pray without controlling. And trust that the One who loves your child more than you do is still writing a story you cannot see the end of. The road is not closed. Keep watching it. Keep your heart soft. And do not let the grief steal the hope, because the hope, unlike the grief, is anchored in something that does not depend on you.
excerpt: It is the fear every believing parent carries in the dark. The child you raised in the faith walks away from it. What do you do when you cannot fix it and cannot force it?

title: Parenting in the Digital Age: Screens, Souls, and Boundaries
body:
I raised my older sons before the smartphone and my younger sons after it, and the difference is one of the starkest natural experiments I have ever lived inside. The world my oldest navigated as a teenager and the world my youngest navigates are not the same world, and anyone who tells you the difference is merely a matter of new tools has not paid attention. The screen did not just give our children new things to do. It rewired the environment in which their souls are being formed.

I want to resist two easy responses here, because both let us off the hook. One is the panic that treats every screen as poison and every parent who allows one as negligent. The other is the shrug that treats the technology as neutral, just a tool, no different in kind from a book or a telephone. Neither is honest. The screen is not neutral, but the answer is not panic. The answer is formation, and formation is much harder than either fear or indifference.

The screen is designed, and not for your child's good

Let us begin with what we would rather not say. The devices in our children's hands were designed by some of the most brilliant minds of our time, funded by some of the largest fortunes ever assembled, for a single purpose: to capture and hold human attention. Not to inform. Not to connect. To capture. The business model depends on it. Every feature that keeps a child scrolling was engineered to keep them scrolling, and the engineers know exactly what they are doing, because they measure it.

This matters theologically, because attention is not a trivial thing. Attention is close to the center of the spiritual life. What we attend to shapes what we love, and what we love shapes who we become. Simone Weil said that attention, absolute unmixed attention, is prayer. And here is a machine, in your child's hand, engineered by an industry to fragment attention into ten-second pieces and sell those pieces to advertisers. We are not fighting a neutral tool. We are fighting a deliberate assault on the very faculty by which a soul learns to love God and neighbor.

The screen is not competing with your child's boredom. It is competing with their capacity for attention, and attention is the faculty by which they will one day learn to pray, to love, and to be present. This is a battle for something sacred.

The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt has documented the sharp inflection that arrived when the smartphone and the social platform reached the hands of adolescents, and the timing of the rise in anxiety, depression, and self-harm that followed it. Correlation is not the whole story, and honest people can argue about mechanisms. But the pattern is stark enough that no thoughtful parent can dismiss it, and it lines up with what any of us can observe in our own homes. Something has changed in the inner lives of the young, and the device in their pocket is somewhere near the center of it.

Filters are not formation

The first instinct of the anxious Christian parent is technical. Install the filter. Set the controls. Monitor the usage. And there is a place for these things, especially with younger children, because you do not hand a child a loaded environment and call it freedom. But filters address the wrong problem. Filters keep bad content out. They do nothing to form the soul that will one day, inevitably, encounter the bad content without a filter.

The goal is not a child who cannot access harm because you blocked it. The goal is a child who has been formed into a person who can navigate a world full of harm with wisdom and self-possession. And that formation does not come from software. It comes from the slow, relational work of teaching a child to understand what the screen is doing to them, to notice the pull, to develop the internal muscles of restraint that no external filter can substitute for. A child raised only on filters arrives at eighteen with no filter and no internal formation, which is the worst of both worlds.

This is not an argument against filters. It is an argument against relying on them. The filter buys time, and time is valuable, because it delays exposure until a child is more capable of handling it. But the time must be used, not merely bought. If the years behind the filter are not spent forming a child's judgment, their appetites, their capacity for self-restraint, then the filter has only postponed the reckoning, and the reckoning will arrive against a soul no more prepared for it than before.

What the screen displaces

The real cost of the screen is often not what it shows but what it displaces. Every hour on the device is an hour not spent in the activities that form a healthy soul. Boredom, which is the seedbed of imagination, is now instantly abolished at the first flicker of discomfort. Solitude, which is where a person learns to be at peace with their own company and, eventually, with God, is now impossible, because the device ensures no one is ever alone with their thoughts.

Face-to-face relationship, with all its friction and its irreplaceable richness, is thinned out and replaced by mediated connection that feels like relationship but delivers a fraction of its nourishment. And the developing brain, which needs deep rest, is instead kept in a state of low-grade stimulation late into the night. What the screen displaces is often more damaging than what it delivers. A childhood without boredom, without solitude, without unhurried presence, is a childhood missing the very conditions in which depth grows.

Ask not only what your child is consuming on the screen. Ask what the screen is preventing them from ever experiencing. The absence of boredom is not a gift. It is the theft of imagination.

Boredom is not the enemy we have made it out to be. Boredom is the doorway to imagination, to creativity, to the interior life. A child who is never bored never learns to generate their own inner world, never discovers that the most interesting thing available is not on a screen but inside their own restless, God-given mind. When we rush to eliminate every moment of boredom with a device, we are not being kind. We are amputating a faculty, and the child will grow up unable to be alone with themselves, terrified of the silence in which God is most often found.

The parent in the mirror

Here is where I must implicate myself, and where most of the parenting advice on this subject goes quiet, because it is more comfortable to talk about the children's screens than our own. My children learned their relationship with the screen partly by watching mine. When I checked my phone at dinner, I taught them that the meal was less important than whatever was in my hand. When I responded to a text mid-conversation with my son, I taught him that his father's attention was always provisional, always interruptible, always available to be claimed by someone else.

I cannot count the times a son was telling me something and I was half-present, my eyes drifting to the screen, my thumb already scrolling. I told myself I was listening. I was not. And a child knows the difference between a parent who is present and a parent who is performing presence while their attention is elsewhere. Before I lecture my children about their screen habits, I have to reckon with the fact that I formed those habits, in part, by the example of my own divided attention. The hypocrisy is not lost on them, and it should not be lost on us.

Boundaries as gifts, not punishments

When boundaries do come, and they must, the framing matters enormously. A boundary presented as a punishment, as distrust, as the parent asserting control, invites resistance and teaches the child that the screen is a prize being withheld. A boundary presented as a gift, as a protection of something valuable, as the family together choosing to guard its attention and its presence, invites participation.

The most effective boundaries are the ones the whole family keeps together. The phones that sleep outside the bedroom, all of them, the parents' included. The dinner table where no one, adult or child, brings a device. The stretch of Sabbath where the whole household unplugs together. These are not rules imposed from above. They are practices the family embraces together, and they form everyone, including the parents who most need forming. A child who watches their father put his own phone away for the sake of presence learns something no lecture could teach.

Forming the appetite, not just restricting the intake

Ultimately, parenting in the digital age is about forming an appetite, not just restricting an intake. A child who is only restricted, only blocked, only told no, develops a hunger for the forbidden thing and a plan to access it the moment they are free. A child whose appetites are being formed toward better things, who has tasted the deep satisfaction of a long book, an unhurried conversation, a project made with their hands, a walk with nowhere to be, is developing an internal compass that will serve them when the external controls fall away.

This is the harder work, and the slower work, and the work that no app can do for you. It means providing the alternatives, the analog richness, the family culture in which the screen is not the default but one option among many that are actually more compelling. It means being present enough, unhurried enough, un-distracted enough yourself, that your presence is more attractive than the device. That last one indicts me most of all, because a child will not choose the parent over the screen if the parent is always half inside a screen of their own.

The comparison machine and the young soul

There is a particular harm the screen does to the adolescent soul that deserves naming on its own, because it is more insidious than the obvious dangers we warn about. The platforms our children inhabit are comparison machines. They present, endlessly, a curated highlight reel of everyone else's life, against which the ordinary reality of the child's own life cannot help but look impoverished. A young person scrolling through the polished, filtered, carefully staged images of their peers is being fed, hour after hour, the lie that everyone else is happier, more beautiful, more included, more successful than they are.

This is spiritual poison of a specific kind. Envy has always been a threat to the soul, but never before has a machine been engineered to manufacture envy at industrial scale and deliver it directly into the mind of a developing child. The old wisdom that we should not compare ourselves to others was hard enough to follow when comparison meant the few neighbors we could see. Now the comparison is with a curated infinity, an endless feed of everyone's best moment, and the young soul measures its ordinary Tuesday against a thousand highlight reels and concludes that it is failing. To form a child who can resist this is to form a child who knows their worth does not come from the feed, who can look away, who can be content with an unremarkable life that is nonetheless their own and nonetheless loved by God.

There is another layer to this that cuts even deeper, and it is the way the platforms teach a young person to perform their own life rather than to live it. When every experience is potential content, when the value of a moment is measured by how it will look to an audience, the child learns to stand outside their own life, curating it, packaging it, watching themselves be watched. This is a kind of exile from the self, a loss of the capacity to simply be present in an experience without the running commentary of how it will play. A young person formed this way loses something precious, the ability to have an experience that belongs only to them, unphotographed, unposted, unwitnessed by anyone but God. To give your child moments that are not content, experiences that exist only for their own sake, is to give them back a piece of their own soul that the platforms are quietly stealing. The unposted moment, the memory kept private, the joy that no one else sees, is a form of wealth the comparison machine cannot touch.

The digital age is not going away, and I am not calling you to pretend it is. I am calling you to something more demanding than filters and more honest than panic. I am calling you to form your children, and yourself, into people whose attention is not for sale, whose presence is not fragmented, whose souls are not colonized by an industry that profits from their distraction. That formation begins with the phone in your own hand. Put it down. Look at your child. Be there. The most radical thing you can do in the digital age is to give your child your undivided attention, because you will be teaching them, by doing it, what they are worth.
excerpt: The screen is not neutral. It is designed to capture what we were meant to give to God and each other. Parenting through it requires more than filters. It requires formation.

title: Single Parenting and the Myth of the Complete Family
body:
I was raised without a father. That fact is not a footnote in my life. It is closer to the center of it, and it shapes how I read every Christian conversation about the family, especially the ones conducted by people who have never known its absence. Because the church I eventually joined had a great deal to say about the family, and much of it, however unintentionally, landed on a boy like me as an indictment. Your family was incomplete. Something was missing. The implied conclusion, never quite spoken but always felt, was that I was missing something too.

I want to write toward the single parents, and toward the children of single parents, and toward a church that has too often handed both a burden dressed up as a doctrine. And I want to do it honestly, which means naming the ways the church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly taxed the people who did not fit it.

The myth we mistook for the gospel

Somewhere along the way, a particular arrangement of the family, two parents, a mother and a father, children between them, became elevated in the Christian imagination to the status of a near-sacrament. The nuclear family became the assumed default of every sermon, every ministry, every program. And whatever does not fit that shape came to be seen, however gently, as broken, deficient, a deviation from the design.

But this elevation of the nuclear family is not as biblical as we assume. It owes at least as much to a particular era of Western culture as it does to Scripture. The families of the Bible are a chaotic assortment of arrangements, blended and extended and irregular, held together by covenant more than by tidy structure. The people of God were formed not around the nuclear family but around a covenant community that repeatedly extended itself to the widow, the orphan, the stranger, precisely those whom the nuclear-family ideal leaves out. When we made the intact nuclear family the standard, we quietly abandoned the very people Scripture instructs us to gather in.

The church took a cultural arrangement and baptized it as the divine design, then handed the bill to everyone whose family did not fit the frame. That is not the gospel. That is a preference wearing the gospel's clothing.

The isolated nuclear household, mother and father and children alone in a single dwelling, self-sufficient and turned inward, is a relatively recent development in human history, and a peculiarly modern one at that. For most of human existence, families were embedded in extended networks of kin and community, and children were raised by many hands. When the church made the modern nuclear family the measure of a real family, it did not recover a biblical ideal. It absorbed a cultural accident and gave it the authority of divine command.

What the myth does to a child

I know what the myth does to a child, because it did it to me. When the entire architecture of your church assumes a father in the home, a boy without one absorbs the message that his family is a problem, that his situation is a deficiency, that he is starting the race behind. No one has to say it. The assumption says it. Every Father's Day sermon that celebrated the family I did not have said it. Every ministry built around a structure my family lacked said it.

And the deeper wound was theological. When I was told that God was a father, the metaphor that was meant to comfort me instead named my wound. The very language the church used to describe God's love was borrowed from the relationship I had been denied. It took me years to understand that God being a father was not an insult to my fatherlessness but its answer, that the God who describes himself as father to the fatherless was speaking directly to a boy like me, offering not a reminder of absence but the promise of a presence that would not leave. But no one framed it that way. The church assumed the earthly father and lost the boy who did not have one.

To the single parent carrying it alone

If you are a single parent, I want to say something to you that the church has not said often enough. You are not a broken version of a real family. You are a family. Complete, whole, sufficient, held by the God who has always specialized in the family the world calls incomplete. The exhaustion you carry, the double load of being both provider and nurturer, of making every decision without a partner to share the weight, of falling into bed at night with no one to say you did well today, that exhaustion is holy, and it is seen, even when no one around you seems to see it.

The myth of the complete family did not just wound your children. It wounded you, by teaching you to see your own faithful, sacrificial, exhausting love as somehow second-rate. It is not second-rate. The love you pour out, alone, into your children, is as full and as real and as blessed as any love poured out by two. God does not grade families on a curve of structure. God looks at the love, and your love, single parent, is not diminished by the fact that you carry it alone. If anything, it is magnified by the weight you bear to give it.

Your family is not missing a piece. It is a whole thing, held by a whole God, and the love you give alone is not worth less than the love others give together. The scale God uses does not measure structure. It measures love.

I watched my own mother carry this weight, and I did not understand, as a boy, what it cost her. I understand better now. The single parent lives without the thing every married parent takes for granted, a second set of hands, a second perspective, someone to trade off with when the well runs dry. There is no trading off when you parent alone. The well runs dry and you keep drawing from it anyway, because there is no one else to draw. That is not a lesser love. That is a love that has been tested in a fire most parents never have to enter.

The community that was supposed to be there

Here is where the church must repent, and where I include myself in the repentance, because I have led churches that did this. When Scripture speaks of the fatherless and the widow, it does not merely offer them a metaphor of divine care. It commands the community to become the answer. The people of God are supposed to be the extended family that surrounds the single parent, that provides the men to mentor the fatherless boy and the women to come alongside the exhausted mother, that fills in what a single parent cannot provide alone, not out of pity but out of covenant.

We have largely failed at this. We built programs for the intact families and left the single parents to fend for themselves, and then we had the audacity to lament the state of the fatherless generation, as though the community bore no responsibility for the fathering it was commanded to provide. If the church took seriously its calling to be the family of the fatherless, single parenting would not carry the isolation it carries. The single parent was never meant to parent alone. The community was supposed to show up. The failure of the child is often, at bottom, the failure of a church that would not become the family it was told to be.

The father to the fatherless

Let me speak now to the deepest wound, the one I carry myself. To the child raised without a father, or a mother, there is a specific ache that never fully resolves, a hunger for a presence that was not there. I will not pretend the gospel makes that ache disappear. It does not. I still feel it, decades later, in moments I do not expect. But I have come to know something about that ache that changed my relationship to it.

The God who calls himself a father to the fatherless is not offering a metaphor to paper over the wound. He is offering himself as the presence I was denied. Not a replacement that erases the loss, but a companion who enters the loss and refuses to leave. The fatherlessness was real. The presence of God in the fatherlessness was also real. And I have found, over the long years, that the very wound of my father's absence became the place where I learned most deeply what it means to be fathered by God, because I had nowhere else to put the hunger.

I do not say this to romanticize the wound or to suggest that the absence was somehow good. It was not good. A boy should have a father, and the God who calls himself father to the fatherless would be the first to say so, because the very naming of the wound as something God must answer is an admission that the wound should not have been there. But I have learned that God does not waste our wounds. The hunger my father's absence carved into me became a capacity for God, a place already hollowed out and waiting to be filled, and the God who filled it did not fill it in spite of the absence but by way of it. This is the strange grace at the heart of the gospel, that God enters our worst losses not to explain them away but to be present in them, and that the very places where we were most abandoned can become the places where we are most deeply found.

The temptation to overcompensate

There is a trap that waits for the single parent who has absorbed the myth of the incomplete family, and it is the trap of overcompensation. Believing their child is starting behind, the single parent tries to be both parents at once, to fill every role, to make up by sheer effort for the absence the myth has told them is a deficit. And the effort, however loving, can become its own burden, both for the parent who cannot sustain it and for the child who feels the weight of being someone their parent must heroically compensate for.

You do not have to be two parents. You cannot be, and the attempt to be will exhaust you and communicate to your child that they are a problem being managed rather than a person being loved. What your child needs is not two parents worth of effort from one exhausted person. What they need is one parent who is present, who is at peace, who is not frantically trying to prove that the family is not lacking. A single parent who has made peace with their situation, who is not driven by the shame of the myth, offers their child something far more stabilizing than a parent scrambling to be everything. Let the community be the other hands. Let God be the father to the fatherless. Your job is to be the one parent you are, fully and without shame, and to trust that the rest is held by hands larger than yours.

I have watched single parents pour themselves out until there was nothing left, driven by the fear that any moment of rest, any admission of need, any acknowledgment of their own limits, would confirm the verdict the world had already handed down. This is a cruelty the myth imposes, and it must be resisted, because a depleted parent cannot love well, and a parent who models a life of grinding self-erasure teaches their children that love means the annihilation of the self. It does not. Even God rested. The single parent who guards a measure of rest, who receives help without shame, who tends their own soul as well as their children's, is not failing. They are modeling a sustainable love, a love that can go the distance precisely because it does not pretend to be infinite. Your children do not need a martyr. They need a parent who is still standing years from now, and the way to still be standing is to refuse the myth's demand that you empty yourself completely.

What I want the single parent to hear

You are not raising broken children in a broken family. You are raising loved children in a family God calls whole. The world's myth of completeness is not the gospel's measure. The gospel measures love, and covenant, and faithfulness, and by every one of those measures your family stands complete before God, whatever it lacks by the world's arithmetic.

And to the church, I say we have a debt to pay. We owe the single parents among us the community we were commanded to provide. We owe the fatherless the fathering the covenant obligates us to supply. We owe every family that does not fit the myth an unlearning of the myth, and a return to the God whose own people were never a tidy nuclear arrangement but a gathered community of the broken, the widowed, the orphaned, and the alone, made whole not by their structure but by the God who dwelt among them. That God dwells among the single-parent family too, and calls it not incomplete, but his own.
excerpt: The church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly told single parents they had failed to build it. But the God who raised his own people had no such family either.

title: Adoption Theology: What It Means to Be Chosen
body:
Of all the images the New Testament reaches for to describe what God has done for us, one of the most striking is adoption. Not merely forgiveness, not merely rescue, but adoption, the deliberate act of taking someone who was not yours by birth and making them yours by choice, with all the rights and the inheritance and the name that belong to a child born into the house. Paul returns to this image again and again, and it is worth asking why. Why, of all the metaphors available, did the Spirit inspire the language of adoption to describe the deepest thing about our salvation?

I have watched families formed by adoption up close over many years of ministry, and I have come to believe that adoption is not a lesser or backup way of building a family, a plan B for those who could not do it the ordinary way. It is, if anything, the truer picture of what every family is meant to be, and the clearest earthly enactment of the gospel that I know. To adopt is not merely to add a child to a home. It is to preach, with your whole life, the way God brings the outsider in.

The scandal of chosen belonging

We tend to romanticize biological connection, to treat the tie of blood as the deepest and most natural bond. And there is something real there. But the New Testament does something startling with the family. It relativizes blood. Jesus, asked about his mother and brothers, gestures to those who do the will of God and calls them his family. The community of faith is repeatedly described as a family constituted not by biology but by covenant, by the choosing love of God who calls strangers his children.

Adoption sits at the heart of this reordering. It declares that belonging does not require biology, that a bond chosen and covenanted is as real and as unbreakable as a bond by blood. This is a scandal to a culture that worships genetic connection, and it is meant to be, because it mirrors the deeper scandal of the gospel, that God did not wait for us to be his by nature but chose us, adopted us, brought the outsider into the household and made no distinction between the natural-born and the adopted heir.

Adoption declares that belonging is not something you are born into but something you are chosen for. That is not a lesser belonging. In the gospel, it is the deepest one.

In the Roman world in which Paul wrote, adoption was not a marginal or sentimental arrangement. It was a legal act of enormous weight, by which a person, often an adult, was transferred entirely into a new family, given a new name, made heir to a new estate, released from all former debts and obligations. The adopted son was not a lesser son. Under the law, he was in some respects more securely a son than one born into the family, because his sonship rested on a deliberate act of choosing that could not be undone. When Paul reached for this image to describe our salvation, he reached for the strongest picture of belonging his culture possessed.

Chosen, not settled for

One of the wounds that can attach to an adopted child is the fear of being a second choice, a substitute for the child that could not be, a consolation for a loss. And an adoptive parent must labor against this fear with everything they have, because it is a lie that can poison a life. The truth the gospel offers is precisely the opposite. In adoption, the child is not settled for. The child is chosen.

Think of what God does in adopting us. He does not settle for us because his real children failed to materialize. He deliberately, joyfully, at enormous cost, chooses to make us his own. The language Paul uses is the language of delight, of purpose, of a love that predates our existence and reaches out to claim us not as a fallback but as an intention. To adopt a child in this spirit is to say to them, with your whole life, you were not a substitute. You were the intention. I chose you, and choosing is not less than birthing. In some ways it is more.

There is a particular grief that often precedes adoption, a grief of infertility or loss, and it would be dishonest to pretend that grief plays no part in the story. But the grief that precedes an adoption does not make the child a consolation prize, any more than the grief that precedes a remarriage makes the new spouse a substitute. A parent can have arrived at adoption through sorrow and still choose the child before them with a wholeness and a delight that owes nothing to the sorrow that came before. The child is not the patch over an old wound. The child is a new and complete love, chosen for their own sake.

And there is a deep comfort in this for the child who fears they were second best. The God who adopts us did not do so because his plan for a perfect creation had failed and we were what was left. He chose us from before the foundation of the world, deliberately, with intention and delight, and the language Scripture uses for our adoption is language of purpose and joy, not of resignation. When an adoptive parent looks at their child and says, I did not settle for you, I chose you, and choosing you was one of the great intentions of my life, they are speaking to the child the very words God speaks to every one of us. The fear of being a substitute is answered not by a technique but by a truth, and the truth is that in the economy of grace, to be chosen is the highest form of belonging there is, higher even than to be born, because it rests on nothing but the deliberate love of the one who chose.

Naming the loss honestly

And yet I would be dishonest, and I would fail the adopted, if I painted only the glory and ignored the grief. Adoption is built on loss. Before there is a joining, there is a separation. Before a child is welcomed into a new family, they have lost, in some form, the family of their origin. This loss is real, and it does not disappear because the adoption is loving. To pretend otherwise, to insist that the adopted child should feel only gratitude and never grief, is to add a second wound on top of the first.

The most loving adoptive families I have known are the ones that can hold both truths at once. They can celebrate the joy of the joining and honor the grief of the loss, without asking the child to choose between them. They do not treat the child's questions about their origins as a betrayal. They do not require the child to be grateful in a way that suppresses their sorrow. They make room for the whole story, the loss and the finding, the grief and the joy, because a child who is allowed to grieve their loss is a child who can eventually receive their belonging without the poison of forced gratitude.

An adopted child does not have to choose between grieving what they lost and receiving what they were given. The love that adopts them is large enough to hold both, and so must the family be.

The gospel enacted, not just illustrated

What moves me most about adoption is that it does not merely illustrate the gospel. It enacts it. When a family takes in a child who was not theirs by birth, absorbs the cost, endures the difficulty, and loves the child into belonging, they are not putting on a play about what God did. They are doing, in miniature and in flesh, the very thing God did. They are absorbing the cost of another's brokenness and turning it into belonging. They are making the stranger a son, the outsider a daughter, the one who had no claim into an heir.

This is why adoption is one of the most theologically dense things a family can do. It is the gospel made visible, the abstract doctrine of our adoption in Christ pressed down into diapers and school forms and hard nights and the slow patient work of loving a child into trust. Every adoptive family that perseveres in love is preaching a sermon the watching world cannot ignore, a sermon about a God who welcomes the outsider and calls the stranger his own.

The cost that mirrors the cross

We should not sentimentalize this. Adoption is costly, often far more costly than the glossy version acknowledges. Children who have known loss and disruption sometimes carry wounds that manifest as behavior a family did not anticipate. The love required is often a love that gives and gives and receives, for a long time, resistance and testing rather than gratitude. The child, having learned that attachment leads to loss, may fight the very belonging they most need, testing whether this family too will abandon them when it becomes hard.

And here again adoption mirrors the gospel, because this is exactly the love God shows us. He adopts us knowing we will test the belonging, knowing we will resist the love, knowing we will act out of our brokenness against the very One who welcomed us. And he does not withdraw. The love that adopts is a love that endures the testing, that stays through the resistance, that proves itself precisely by refusing to leave when leaving would be understandable. The cost of adoption is real, and it mirrors the cost of the cross, which is the cost God paid to make us his own.

The testing is not a sign that the adoption has failed. It is often a sign that it is working, that the child is beginning, however painfully, to believe the belonging is real enough to be tested. A child who has learned that love is fragile and abandonment is inevitable will push against a new love precisely to find out whether it too will break. Every act of resistance is, at bottom, a question, and the question is always the same: will you leave me too. And every time the adoptive parent absorbs the resistance without withdrawing, they answer the question, not with words, which the child has learned to distrust, but with presence, which is the only answer a wounded child can finally believe. The staying is the sermon. The refusal to leave, repeated across months and years of testing, slowly rewrites the deepest assumption the child carries, until one day they discover that they have come to trust a love they spent years trying to break, and could not.

The identity questions that must be honored

An adopted child will, at some point, ask the questions that touch the deepest places. Who am I. Where did I come from. Why did they not keep me. Am I really yours. These questions can feel, to an adoptive parent, like a threat, as though the child's very asking is a rejection of the family that loves them. It is not. The questions are not a betrayal. They are the natural work of a person trying to understand their own story, and a child who is forbidden from asking them, or who senses that the questions wound their parents, learns to carry the questions in secret, where they fester.

The adoptive families I most admire have made their homes places where these questions are welcome, where the child's origins are spoken of with honesty and without threat, where curiosity about a birth family is met not with insecurity but with grace. This requires the adoptive parent to have done their own inner work, to be secure enough in the bond that they do not need the child to suppress their story in order to protect the parent's feelings. A child who is free to hold their whole story, the loss and the finding together, is a child who can integrate their identity rather than splitting it, and who can receive their belonging in the adoptive family precisely because they were never asked to deny where they came from. Security, not suppression, is what allows a child to be fully at home.

What the church owes the adoptive family

If adoption is this central to the gospel, then the church ought to be its most fervent supporter, and not merely in sentiment but in substance. Adoptive families need community around them, support through the hard seasons, understanding when their children struggle in ways that are not the ordinary struggles. Too often the church celebrates the adoption at the beginning and disappears when the difficulty comes, leaving the family alone with challenges no one prepared them for.

The community that claims to believe in its own adoption by God should be the community that most surrounds those who adopt, that shares the burden, that provides the extended family every child needs. And it should be a community whose theology of belonging is deep enough that no adopted child in its midst ever feels like a second-class member of the family of God. Because in the gospel, there is no such thing. We were all adopted. Every one of us who belongs to God belongs by the same choosing love, the same welcome of the outsider, the same absorbing of cost that turns strangers into heirs. The adoptive family is not living out a special case of the gospel. They are living out its very center, and the rest of us are more like them than we know.
excerpt: Adoption is not a lesser way to build a family. It is the metaphor the New Testament chose to describe how God brings us home. To adopt is to enact the gospel.

title: Parenting a Child with Special Needs
body:
I want to write about something I have witnessed closely in ministry but have not lived from the inside in the way that parents of children with special needs have lived it. So I write with a particular humility here, aware that there are things about this road that only those who walk it can fully know. But I have sat with enough of these families, in the hospital rooms and the therapy waiting areas and the quiet living rooms after the diagnosis, to have learned some things worth saying, and to have had my own theology broken open and rebuilt by what they taught me.

What I have learned, above all, is that a child with special needs exposes a lie that most of us live inside without ever noticing it. The lie is that human worth is tied to human achievement, that we matter because of what we can do, produce, accomplish, contribute. Our whole civilization is built on this lie, and most of our churches, whatever they say on Sunday, are built on it too. And a child who will never achieve by those measures stands as a living refutation of the whole system, and reveals a gospel that never valued any of us for our productivity in the first place.

The grief no one lets you name

Before anything else, there is grief, and it is a grief the world does not know how to let you have. When a child is born with, or later diagnosed with, a significant disability, a parent grieves. Not the child, who is loved fiercely and completely, but the loss of the imagined future, the expectations quietly assembled during the pregnancy, the life the parent had pictured that will now not be. This grief is real and it is legitimate, and yet parents are often made to feel they cannot voice it, because to grieve the imagined child seems like a rejection of the actual child.

It is not. A parent can love their child completely and still grieve the future they thought they would have. The two are not in conflict. The grief must be allowed to breathe, to be named, to be brought before God honestly, because grief that is suppressed does not disappear. It goes underground and poisons. The parents I have watched flourish in this calling are the ones who were permitted, by their community and by their own honesty, to grieve fully, and then to move through the grief into a love that was not diminished by having grieved. The church that tells such parents they should feel only blessing, only joy, only gratitude, robs them of the honesty their souls require.

You can love your child with your whole heart and still grieve the future you imagined. Do not let anyone shame you out of the grief. Grief honored becomes love deepened. Grief denied becomes love poisoned.

The grief does not resolve once and disappear. It returns, often, at the thresholds, at the birthday parties for other children, at the milestones that will not come, at the moment a younger sibling passes the older child in some capacity the older child will never reach. This recurring grief is not a failure of acceptance or a lack of faith. It is the ongoing cost of loving deeply in a world that is not yet what it will be, and it deserves to be met with tenderness, not with a demand that the parent should be over it by now.

The idol of the productive life

Our society has made an idol of productivity, and the idol demands human sacrifice. We measure a person's worth by their output, their achievement, their contribution to the economy and the accumulation of accomplishments. And this idol reaches into places we do not notice, including the way we love our children, the pride we take in their achievements, the quiet way we treat their accomplishments as a reflection of our own worth as parents.

A child with profound special needs cannot participate in this economy of worth, and their existence therefore functions as a prophetic word against it. Here is a human being, fully and completely a person, made in the image of God, precious beyond measure, who will never produce, achieve, or contribute in the ways the idol demands. And their preciousness is not one bit diminished by that fact. If we can see this clearly, we discover that the idol was always a lie, that human worth was never about productivity, that every one of us was loved by God before we produced anything and would be loved by God if we produced nothing at all.

A child who will never achieve by the world's measures is a prophet against the world's measures. Their worth, undiminished by their limitations, exposes the lie that any of our worth was ever about achievement.

Jean Vanier, who gave his life to communities where those with profound intellectual disabilities lived alongside those without, insisted that such persons were not merely recipients of care but bearers of a gift, that they revealed to the rest of us the poverty of our own hearts and the truth of our own dependence. Whatever we make of the failures that later came to light in his own life, the truth he pointed to remains, and it is a truth the church has been slow to receive. The person the world overlooks is often the one placed among us to heal us of the very blindness that makes us overlook them.

What the image of God actually means

We say that human beings are made in the image of God, but we often smuggle into that phrase an assumption that the image consists in our capacities, our reason, our will, our ability to do things. And if the image of God were located in our capacities, then a person with diminished capacities would bear a diminished image, which is a monstrous conclusion that the Scripture nowhere supports.

The image of God is not a set of abilities we possess. It is a status we are given, a dignity conferred by the Creator, a belonging that does not depend on what we can do. The theologian who taught me this most clearly insisted that the image is about being addressed by God, being in relationship, being held in the divine regard, and none of that depends on cognitive capacity or physical ability. A child who cannot speak, cannot reason as others reason, cannot care for themselves, bears the full and undiminished image of God, and is fully and completely a person whom God addresses and holds and loves. To see this is to have your entire theology of the human person corrected by a child the world would overlook.

The gift hidden in the dependence

There is a gift buried in the profound dependence of a child with severe special needs, though it is a gift wrapped in exhaustion and hard to receive. The gift is a truth about all of us that we spend our lives denying. We are all dependent. We all began in total helplessness and will very likely end there, and in between we sustain the illusion of self-sufficiency that our culture prizes. The child who never outgrows dependence holds up a mirror to the human condition that the rest of us work hard to avoid.

And the dependence, rightly seen, is not a defect but a revelation. It reveals that we were made for relationship, for receiving, for being held, and that the myth of the independent self is exactly that, a myth. The parent who cares for a fully dependent child is living inside a truth about love that the rest of us only glimpse, the truth that love is not a transaction between equals who exchange value, but a giving that asks nothing in return, that finds its meaning in the giving itself. This is, not incidentally, exactly how God loves us. We are all far more dependent on God than we admit, and the child who cannot pretend otherwise teaches the rest of us what we are.

There is a further truth hidden here that our achievement-obsessed culture cannot easily see. The child who receives and cannot repay is not the diminished partner in the relationship of love. In some ways they are the one who gives the greater gift, because they give the parent the chance to love without the corrupting motive of return, to love in the purest form love can take, the form that expects nothing back. We are so trained to think of the caregiver as the giver and the cared-for as the receiver that we miss the reciprocity that runs the other way. The child gives the parent an occasion to become a certain kind of person, a person capable of a love the world barely believes in, a love that most of us, tangled as we are in transactions, never fully learn. The one the world would call a burden is, in the deep economy of the soul, a giver of the rarest gift, the gift of an object for love that asks for nothing in return.

The siblings who also carry it

There is a dimension of this road that is easy to overlook, and it is the experience of the other children in the family, the siblings of the child with special needs. They grow up in a home where an enormous share of the family's time, energy, and attention is necessarily directed toward one child, and they learn, often, to ask for little, to make themselves easy, to carry needs of their own that go unspoken because they can see that their parents are already stretched to the breaking point.

These siblings often become remarkable people, marked by a compassion and a maturity beyond their years. But they also carry a hidden weight, and they need to be seen in it. They need a parent who notices that they too are children with needs, who finds moments to give them undivided attention, who does not allow their goodness and their ease to become an excuse for their neglect. And they need permission to feel the complicated things they feel, the love for their sibling tangled up with resentment, guilt, embarrassment, and grief, without being shamed for the feelings that are the honest fruit of a hard situation. A family raising a child with special needs is raising all its children in the shadow of that reality, and the ones without the diagnosis are shaped by it just as deeply, and deserve to be seen just as clearly.

The community that must show up

Here again the church is tested and often found wanting. Families raising children with special needs frequently find themselves isolated, exhausted, and quietly excluded from the life of a church that was not built with their child in mind. The service that cannot accommodate a child who makes noise. The children's ministry with no place for a child who does not fit the standard program. The well-meaning members who do not know what to say and so say nothing, and by their silence communicate that this family is a burden rather than a gift.

A church that believes what it says about the image of God will move heaven and earth to include these families, will build the ramps and train the volunteers and make the space, will treat the child with special needs not as a challenge to be accommodated but as a member of the body whose presence blesses the whole. The measure of a church's theology is not what it says about human dignity in the abstract but how it treats the child who cannot contribute in the currency the world values. If we cannot make room for that child, we have not understood the gospel we claim to preach.

The love that reveals God

I have watched parents of children with special needs love in a way that has taught me more about the love of God than most sermons I have heard, including my own. Because it is a love that expects nothing back, that gives and gives to a child who may never say thank you, may never understand the sacrifice, may never be able to reciprocate. And in that one-directional, cost-absorbing, expecting-nothing love, I have seen the clearest earthly picture of how God loves us.

God's love for us is not a response to our achievements or a reward for our contribution. It is a love that gives to those who can give nothing back, that pours out on the helpless and the dependent, that asks nothing and offers everything. The parent who loves a profoundly disabled child is not merely enduring a hardship. They are participating in the very heart of God, living out the divine love in the flesh, teaching the watching world what love actually is when it is stripped of transaction and reduced to its essence. If you are that parent, know this: you are not merely surviving. You are revealing God. And the child you love, whom the world would overlook, is one of the clearest windows into the kingdom that I know.
excerpt: The world measures children by what they achieve. A child with special needs exposes that measure as a lie, and reveals a gospel that never valued us for our productivity at all.

title: When Your Child Comes Out
body:
This is among the hardest subjects I could write about, and I want to be honest at the outset about why. It is hard because it touches convictions people hold deeply and disagree about sharply, and because whatever I say, some will feel I have said too much and others too little. But it is hard most of all because it is not, in the moment it actually happens, an abstract debate about theology. It is a child, your child, standing in front of you, having gathered every ounce of their courage to tell you something true about themselves, watching your face to see what happens next.

I am a pastor with settled theological convictions, and I am not going to pretend I do not have them. But I have also sat with too many families in the aftermath of that moment, watched too many relationships shatter and a few survive, to believe that the most important thing in that moment is winning a theological argument. I want to write about what happens when your child comes out, and about the difference between what you believe and how you love, and about why the relationship must survive whatever else is true.

The moment before the moment

By the time a child tells you, they have usually been carrying it, alone, for a long time. Often years. They have rehearsed the conversation a hundred times, imagined every reaction, braced for rejection. What you are seeing when they finally speak is not an impulsive announcement but the end of a long and lonely internal ordeal, and the courage it took to speak is enormous, especially in a home where they have reason to fear the response.

This matters because it should reframe how we understand the moment. Your child is not attacking your beliefs. They are trusting you with the most vulnerable truth about themselves, at real risk, hoping against their fear that your love is bigger than whatever they expect your judgment to be. And the first thing they will learn, in the first seconds of your response, is whether that hope was justified. Long before any conversation about theology, they will read your face and know whether they are still safe with you. That reading happens before a word is spoken, and it may determine everything that follows.

Your child did not come to debate you. They came to be known by you, at the risk of being rejected by you. The first thing they will learn from your response is not what you believe. It is whether they are still safe.

Consider what it took for them to reach this moment. Consider the nights they lay awake wondering whether telling you would cost them your love. Consider that they chose you, chose to risk it, chose to bring you into the truth rather than hiding it from you forever. That choice is itself an act of trust and of love, an offering, and how you receive it will tell your child, more than any words, whether the trust was well placed. The moment is not primarily a test of your theology. It is a test of your love, and your child already knows which one they are hoping to find.

The distinction that saves relationships

There is a distinction that I have come to believe is the difference between families that survive this moment and families that do not. It is the distinction between what you believe and how you love. These are not the same thing, and the great error of the anxious parent is to collapse them, to believe that loving their child requires either abandoning their convictions or enforcing them, when in fact love and conviction operate on different planes entirely.

Consider how God relates to every one of us. God holds convictions about how we ought to live that not one of us fully meets, and yet God's love for us is not withdrawn pending our compliance. God does not make his welcome conditional on our getting everything right first. The gospel is precisely that we are loved before we are fixed, welcomed before we are worthy, embraced in the midst of everything about us that falls short. If God, who has every right to make love conditional on agreement, does not do so, then a parent has no ground to make their love for their child conditional on the child's agreement with them.

You can hold your convictions and love your child without condition at the same time. In fact, you must, because that is exactly how you yourself are loved by God. The parent who says I cannot love you fully unless you agree with me has departed from the gospel they claim to defend, and has substituted for it a conditional love that the God of the gospel never once showed them. The whole scandal of grace is that God's love reaches us in the middle of our disagreement with him, and does not wait for us to come around before it embraces us.

What rejection actually accomplishes

Let me speak plainly about what happens when a parent responds to a child coming out with rejection, with coldness, with the ultimatum that the relationship is contingent on the child changing. It does not accomplish what the parent hopes. It does not draw the child toward the parent's convictions. It does the opposite. It drives the child away, not only from the parent but very often from the faith the parent holds, because the child now associates that faith with the rejection they experienced from the person who was supposed to love them most.

I have watched this happen more times than I can bear to remember. A parent, acting out of what they believed was faithfulness, rejected a child, and in doing so taught the child that the God of that parent was a God of rejection, and the child walked away from both. The rejection did not protect the child's soul. It endangered it. It took whatever openness the child might have retained toward faith and slammed it shut, and it did so in the name of the very faith it destroyed. Whatever you believe about the questions involved, rejection is a catastrophic strategy, and it fails on its own terms.

Rejection does not draw a child toward your convictions. It drives them away from you and from the God you hoped they would find, and it does its damage in the name of the very faith it destroys.

The statistics on what happens to young people rejected by their families are grim, and I will not sensationalize them, but neither will I hide from them. A young person who loses their family's love in the moment they most needed it does not simply lose a relationship. They lose a foundation, and the loss reverberates into every corner of their life and their faith. If we say we care about our children's souls, then we must reckon with the fact that rejection is among the surest ways to imperil the very soul we claim to be protecting.

The relationship must survive

If I could say one thing to a parent in the moment their child comes out, it would be this: whatever else happens, the relationship must survive. Not because the relationship is more important than truth, but because the relationship is the only vessel in which anything true can be received. A child who is cut off cannot hear anything you have to say. A child who remains in relationship with you, who knows your love is durable, who trusts that you will not abandon them, remains someone with whom every conversation is still possible.

The father in the parable did not stand at the edge of the property and shout his convictions at the departing son. He let the relationship hold across the distance, kept the door open, watched the road, and when the son returned, he ran. The whole possibility of that reunion depended on the father not burning the relationship down in the name of being right. Keep the relationship alive. Keep the door open. Whatever you believe, do not let your convictions become the reason your child is no longer in your life, because a child you have lost is a child you can no longer love in any way that reaches them.

The temptation to make it about you

I have to name something uncomfortable, because it is true and because avoiding it would be dishonest. When a child comes out, many parents make the moment about themselves. About their disappointment. About their reputation. About the future they had imagined. About what people at church will think. And the child, who came to be known and loved, instead finds themselves managing their parent's grief, apologizing for the pain they have caused, comforting the very person who was supposed to comfort them.

This is a failure of love, and I say that as someone who understands the parent's genuine grief. Your feelings are real, and they deserve a place to be processed, but that place is not in front of your child in the moment of their vulnerability. To make their coming out about your loss is to abandon them in the moment they most needed to be received. There will be time to work through your own response, with God and with trusted others. In the moment itself, the work is to receive your child, to communicate that they are loved and safe, to keep your own grief from becoming a burden you lay on the shoulders of a child who is already carrying enough.

I want to be careful and compassionate here, because I am not saying your grief is illegitimate. If you had imagined a certain future for your child, and that future is now shifting, you may feel a genuine loss, and that loss is real, and pretending it away helps no one. But grief has an appropriate place and an inappropriate one, and the appropriate place is not on the shoulders of the child who has just entrusted you with their truth. Take your grief to God. Take it to a friend, a counselor, a pastor who can hold it. Examine it honestly, of asking how much of it is genuine loss and how much is wounded expectation, disappointed image, fear of what others will think. But do that work away from your child, so that when you are with your child, what they encounter is not your grief but your love. The order matters enormously. Receive first. Grieve elsewhere. Return to your child with a love that has done its own work and is therefore free to be wholly about them.

The long view of the relationship

One of the traps in this moment is to treat it as a single decisive event, a fork in the road where everything is settled once and for all. It is not. The moment your child comes out is the beginning of a relationship that will unfold over years and decades, and the pressure to resolve everything in the first conversation is a pressure to force what only time can work out. You do not have to have all your responses figured out. You do not have to deliver a definitive statement of where you stand. In the moment, you have to love, and to keep loving, and to leave the longer conversations for the longer relationship.

Parents who survive this well tend to be the ones who took the long view, who resisted the urge to make the first conversation carry all the weight, who trusted that a relationship kept warm over years has room for many conversations, many disagreements, many gradual understandings. The child who knows they are loved does not need every question answered on the first night. They need to know the relationship will hold, that there will be a second conversation and a hundredth, that they have not lost their parent by telling the truth. Give the relationship time. The things that cannot be resolved in a moment can often be held, together, over a lifetime, if the relationship is allowed to survive the moment.

Holding conviction with humility

For those who hold traditional convictions, and I do not hide that I count myself among those who take Scripture's teaching seriously, there is a way to hold conviction that leaves room for love, and a way that does not. Conviction held with humility remembers that the person holding it is also a sinner in need of grace, is also someone who falls short of what they believe, is also loved by God in the midst of their own failures. Conviction held with humility does not weaponize itself against a child.

The parent who approaches their child from a posture of moral superiority, who treats their conviction as a stone to throw rather than a burden they too carry, has misunderstood the gospel entirely. We are all people who fall short. The parent stands before God on exactly the same ground as the child, both of them recipients of a grace neither has earned. To love your child while holding your convictions is not compromise. It is simply to treat your child the way God has treated you, which is to say, with a love that precedes and outlasts every question about whether they have gotten everything right. Hold what you believe. But hold your child first, and hold them always, and never let go.
excerpt: The moment your child comes out, everything you believe meets everyone you love, and the two seem to collide. What matters most in that moment is whether the relationship survives it.

title: The Prodigal Child: Waiting Without Controlling
body:
The parable we call the prodigal son is misnamed. It is not chiefly about the son. It is about the father, and about the almost unbearable discipline of a particular kind of love, a love that lets go, that waits, that watches the road, that does not chase and does not control and does not force the return. If you have a child who has wandered, into rebellion, into a life that breaks your heart, into a distance you cannot close, then this parable is not an inspirational story to you. It is an unbearably accurate description of where you live.

I write as a father who has watched a child walk toward a far country, and who has stood at the window in the way the parable describes, and who has had to learn, against every instinct in my body, the discipline of waiting without controlling. It is the hardest thing love has ever asked of me. And I want to be honest that I have not always done it well, because the temptation to control, to chase, to force the outcome, is nearly overwhelming when the person you love is destroying themselves and you cannot stop them.

The father who let him go

The first thing the father does in the parable is the thing we least want to notice. He lets the son go. The son demands his inheritance, which in that culture was a shocking insult, essentially wishing the father dead. And the father, who had every right and every power to refuse, gives it. He releases the son to a journey he knows will end in ruin. He does not lock the door. He does not withhold the means. He lets his son walk into the far country with his eyes open, knowing what likely awaits.

This is the part that undoes me, because it runs against everything a protective parent wants to do. We want to prevent the disaster. We want to lock the door, cut off the means, make the destructive choice impossible. And there is a place for boundaries, for refusing to fund a child's self-destruction. But the deeper truth of the parable is that love, real love, does not imprison. The father lets the son go because a son who is not free to leave is not a son but a captive, and a love that will not permit departure is not love but control. The releasing was itself an act of love, though it looked like the opposite, and though it must have cost the father everything.

A love that will not let your child leave is not love. It is captivity. The father released his son to a journey he knew would end in ruin, because a child who cannot leave cannot ever truly return.

Notice that God parents the same way. From the very beginning, God gives his children a freedom that includes the freedom to walk away, to choose the far country, to squander the inheritance. God does not compel love, because compelled love is not love at all. The whole story of Scripture is the story of a God who lets his people go into their wandering and then pursues them, not by force, but by a love that keeps the way home open. The father in the parable is not being negligent when he releases his son. He is loving him the way God loves us, with a love that respects the terrible dignity of our freedom.

The discipline of the window

We are told that the father saw the son while he was still a long way off, which means the father was watching. He had not moved on, had not hardened his heart, had not decided the son was dead to him. He was at the window, or on the road, scanning the horizon, keeping vigil for a return that had not come and might never come. This is the posture the parable holds up, and it is a discipline more demanding than either chasing or forgetting.

To chase would be easier in a way, because it would feel like doing something. To forget would be easier too, because it would end the pain of hoping. But the father does neither. He does not chase the son into the far country, dragging him home against his will, which would produce only resentment and another departure. And he does not close his heart and move on, which would mean the son had no home to return to even if he wanted one. He holds the terrible middle ground of active waiting, of a hope that keeps watch without controlling, and this is the exact ground where the parents of prodigals are called to stand.

Why chasing fails

Every instinct in a loving parent, when a child is destroying themselves, is to chase. To intervene. To manage. To do whatever it takes to force the outcome we know is right. And I have tried it. I have chased. I have managed. I have deployed every tool of persuasion, pressure, and control I possessed. And I have learned, at great cost, that chasing a prodigal almost never works, and often makes it worse.

Chasing fails because it removes from the child the very thing they most need, which is to feel the full weight of their own choices. The son in the parable did not come to himself in his father's house, protected from consequences. He came to himself in the pigsty, at the bottom, having spent everything and hit the floor. It was the consequences, not his father's intervention, that turned him. Every time a parent rushes in to soften the consequences, to rescue the prodigal from the bottom, they may be delaying the very moment of reckoning that alone can produce a genuine return. Love that cannot bear to let a child hit bottom sometimes keeps them from the only thing that could bring them home.

The son did not come to himself in his father's house. He came to himself in the pigsty. Sometimes the most loving thing a parent can do is stop cushioning the fall that alone can wake their child up.
