Chasing fails for another reason too. It communicates to the wandering child that the parent has taken responsibility for a choice that belongs to the child. When a parent chases, pleads, and manages, they take the burden of the outcome onto themselves, and the child feels it, and the child resents it, because no one wants their life to be someone else's project. The paradox is that the more responsibility a parent takes for a prodigal's return, the less the prodigal is able to take responsibility for their own life, and the return, when it comes, must be the prodigal's own act, undertaken in freedom, or it is not a return at all.

The line between waiting and enabling

I want to be careful here, because the discipline of waiting can be counterfeited by mere passivity, and worse, by enabling. There is a difference between waiting for a prodigal to come to themselves and funding the far country. The father gave the son his inheritance and then let him spend it and hit bottom. He did not send monthly checks to sustain the son's life in the pigsty. He did not keep the destruction comfortable.

This is a crucial and painful distinction. Some parents, unable to bear the sight of their child's suffering, keep intervening in ways that remove the natural consequences and thereby prolong the very destruction they grieve. They pay the debts, cover the failures, cushion every fall, and in doing so they keep their child from ever reaching the bottom where the turning happens. This is not the patient love of the father. It is a fear dressed up as love, and it can trap a child in the far country indefinitely. Real waiting sometimes requires the agonizing discipline of letting your child feel the full weight of a life you would give anything to spare them.

The hardest part of this distinction is that it cannot be reduced to a formula. There is no rule that tells you exactly when help is genuine love and when it is enabling, when a boundary is faithful and when it is punitive, when to step in and when to stand back. Every prodigal is different, every situation is different, and the discernment required is agonizing precisely because the stakes are so high and the line is so unclear. What I can say is that the question to ask is not whether an intervention would relieve your child's suffering in the moment, but whether it would serve their turning in the long run. Sometimes relieving the suffering short-circuits the very reckoning that could save them. Sometimes it is exactly the help they need to survive long enough to turn. Only love, prayerful and honest and willing to be wrong, can tell the difference, and even then it will get it wrong sometimes, and will have to trust the God who works through our mistakes as well as our wisdom.

The running father

And then, when the son does return, the father runs. This detail would have scandalized the original hearers, because a dignified man of that culture did not run, did not hike up his robes and sprint down the road like a boy. But the father runs, abandoning his dignity, covering the distance himself, reaching the son before the son can finish the rehearsed speech of repentance. He does not wait for the full apology. He does not extract the groveling. He runs, and embraces, and restores, before a word of the confession is complete.

This is the heart of the thing, and it is what makes the waiting bearable. The father waits not with a cold heart, keeping score, preparing his conditions for the son's return. He waits with a heart so ready to forgive that the moment the son appears, all the waiting collapses into running. The waiting was never resentment. It was love holding itself in readiness, love keeping the door open and the heart soft, so that when the moment came, there was no barrier, no lecture, no probation, only embrace. The parent of a prodigal must wait with that kind of heart, a heart that is not hardening in the waiting but softening, so that the return, whenever it comes, meets running rather than judgment.

The elder brother in the mirror

There is a second son in the parable, and we forget him at our peril, because he is often the one the parent of a prodigal most resembles without knowing it. The elder brother never left, never squandered, never wandered. And when the younger son returned to celebration, the elder brother was furious, standing outside the party, refusing to come in, nursing a resentment built on years of dutiful compliance that had never softened into love. He had stayed in the house, but his heart had never been in the same place as his father's.

The danger for the faithful parent of a prodigal is to become the elder brother, to let the years of grief harden into a resentment that poisons the very welcome the returning child would need. To keep a mental ledger of the wrongs done, the pain caused, the years wasted, and to stand ready, when the child returns, not to run but to demand an accounting. If your heart is hardening in the waiting, if your grief is curdling into bitterness, if you find yourself unable to imagine celebrating a return you have decided the child does not deserve, then the parable has a word for you as sharp as any it has for the prodigal. Do not become the elder brother. Keep your heart soft. The father in the story loved both sons, and both sons needed to come home, and one of them was standing in the yard the whole time, lost in plain sight.

The waiting that has no guarantee

I have to end honestly, because the parable ends with a return, and not every real story does. Some prodigals come home. Some do not, at least not in the time their parents are given to see. And the discipline of waiting without controlling is hardest of all when there is no guarantee, when you keep the door open for years with no sign of return, when you watch the road and the road stays empty.

What I have come to believe, in that hardest place, is that the waiting itself is faithful whether or not it is rewarded in this life. The father's love was not made valid by the son's return. It was valid in the waiting, in the keeping vigil, in the refusal to harden. Even had the son never come back, the father's love would have been no less real, no less an image of the God who waits for all of us with a patience that outlasts our wandering. So keep watching the road. Keep your heart soft. Refuse both the chasing that controls and the forgetting that hardens. And trust that the God who is himself the waiting Father loves your prodigal more than you do, and is watching a road you cannot see, with a patience deeper than yours, ready to run.
excerpt: The parable is usually preached about the son. But it is really about the father, and the almost unbearable discipline of a love that waits, watches the road, and refuses to chase.

title: Discipline Without Domination
body:
Few subjects have been more distorted in Christian parenting than discipline. A handful of verses, torn from their context and hardened into a system, have been used to justify practices that owe more to a will to dominate than to anything in the heart of God. And the tragedy is that in the name of raising godly children, we have sometimes formed in them exactly the wounds that make faith hardest, teaching them that authority is arbitrary, that love is conditional, that the powerful may impose their will on the weak and call it righteousness.

I write as a father of five who got this wrong before I got it right, if I have even fully gotten it right yet. I disciplined out of anger and called it correction. I imposed my will and called it godliness. I confused my need to control with my duty to form, and it took years, and the honest testimony of my own children, to teach me the difference. So I do not write from a position of mastery. I write as someone who did damage and is still learning to repair it.

Discipline and punishment are not the same

The first confusion to clear away is the collapse of discipline into punishment. They are not the same thing, and the difference is everything. Punishment looks backward. It focuses on the offense, extracts a penalty, balances a scale. Its logic is retributive: you did wrong, so you must suffer proportionally. Discipline looks forward. The word itself is rooted in discipleship, in the making of a disciple, in formation toward a goal. Its logic is not retributive but developmental: you did wrong, so let us form you toward what is right.

Most of what happens in Christian homes under the banner of discipline is actually punishment, and often punishment driven by the parent's anger rather than the child's formation. The child does something wrong, the parent feels the flash of frustration, and the correction that follows is essentially the discharge of the parent's emotion dressed up as moral instruction. This is not discipline. It is the parent using their power to make themselves feel better, and the child learns nothing about righteousness and everything about the fact that the powerful take out their anger on the weak.

Discipline makes a disciple. Punishment balances a scale. Most of what we call discipline is really our own anger, given a moral costume and discharged onto a child who learns only that power hurts.

The test of whether you are disciplining or merely punishing is often the state of your own heart in the moment. If you are calm, aimed at your child's formation, willing to bear the cost of the slower and harder path, you are likely disciplining. If you are angry, aimed at making your child feel the weight of your displeasure, eager to discharge the emotion that is building in you, you are likely punishing, whatever you tell yourself. The child can feel the difference even when the parent cannot, and what forms them is not primarily the action but the spirit behind it.

The domination we baptized

There is a version of Christian parenting that treats the breaking of a child's will as the goal. It speaks of dominance, of unquestioned authority, of the parent's absolute right to command and the child's absolute duty to obey without hesitation or question. It reads the biblical instructions to children as a warrant for total control, and it reads the biblical instructions to parents, which come right alongside and command them not to provoke or exasperate their children, as though they were not there at all.

This is domination baptized in Scripture, and it produces predictable fruit. A child whose will is broken does not become godly. They become either crushed, having learned that their inner life does not matter and that survival requires the suppression of the self, or they become rebellious the moment the external control is removed, having complied only under duress and stored up years of resentment. Neither outcome is the formation of a disciple. Both are the products of domination, and both leave wounds that follow a person into adulthood and often into their relationship with God, whom they now imagine as the ultimate dominator, arbitrary and demanding and impossible to please.

It is worth noticing what the Scripture actually commands the parent, because the domination model quietly ignores it. The instruction to children to obey is immediately paired with an instruction to fathers not to exasperate or embitter their children. This is not a footnote. It is a direct limit placed on parental authority, a recognition that the power a parent holds over a child can be misused in ways that provoke and wound and embitter, and that God holds the parent accountable for that misuse. The domination model reads the child's obligation and forgets the parent's, which is exactly backward, because the parent is the one with the power, and power is what Scripture is most concerned to restrain.

How God disciplines

If we want to know what discipline should look like, we should look at how God disciplines his own children, because Scripture explicitly frames God's discipline as the model for ours. And what we find there is not domination. We find a discipline that is always aimed at our good, always proceeds from love, always has our formation and flourishing as its goal. God does not discipline us to discharge his anger or to break our will. He disciplines us as a good father, to form us into the people we were made to be.

Notice too that God's discipline is patient, that it works with us over long stretches, that it does not demand instant perfection or crush us when we fail. God bears with our slow growth, our repeated failures, our two-steps-forward-one-step-back progress, with a patience that ought to shame the impatience of our own parenting. If God disciplined us the way many of us discipline our children, with the flash of anger, the impatience, the harshness, the domination, none of us would survive it. But God does not, and God's way is the pattern we are given, not the harsh authoritarianism that has too often claimed the name of Christian discipline.

God bears with our slow growth, our repeated failures, our halting progress, with a patience that shames our own. If God disciplined us the way we discipline our children, none of us would survive it.

The role of consequences

None of this means the absence of correction or the removal of consequences. A child who never experiences consequences is not being loved. They are being abandoned to a fantasy in which actions have no results, and reality will eventually correct that fantasy far more harshly than any parent would. Consequences are a form of love, because they teach a child the true shape of the world they must live in, where choices have weight and actions matter.

But there is a world of difference between consequences that teach and punishments that dominate. A consequence connected naturally to the offense, delivered calmly, aimed at formation, teaches a child about cause and effect and helps them internalize wisdom. A punishment disconnected from the offense, delivered in anger, aimed at making the child suffer, teaches a child only about the parent's power and mood. The same external act, the same removal of a privilege, can be either, depending entirely on the spirit in which it is done and the goal toward which it aims. The child always knows the difference, even when the parent has convinced themselves otherwise.

The repair that teaches most

Here is what I have learned that no parenting book taught me: the most formative moment is often not the discipline itself but the repair afterward, especially the repair of the parent's own failures. Because I did discipline in anger. I did dominate at times. I did provoke and exasperate my children in exactly the ways Scripture warns against. And the question that determined the effect was not whether I failed, since every parent fails, but whether I repaired.

When I went back to a son and said, I was wrong to speak to you that way, my anger was about me and not about you, will you forgive me, something happened that all my correct discipline could never have accomplished. I taught him that authority can be wrong and admit it, that power can humble itself, that love is bigger than the need to be right, that a relationship is worth more than a parent's pride. This is the gospel enacted in the ordinary failures of family life, and it forms a child more deeply than flawless discipline ever could, because flawless discipline is not available to any of us, but faithful repair is.

There is a fear among some parents that admitting fault to a child undermines authority, that a parent who apologizes loses the standing they need to lead. The opposite is true. A parent who can admit fault models the very thing they are trying to teach, which is that we are all under a truth larger than ourselves, all accountable, all in need of grace. The parent who never apologizes teaches the child that power means never having to be wrong, which is a lie about authority and a lie about God. The parent who apologizes teaches the child that even those with power live under grace, which is the truest thing a child can learn.

I think often of what my apologies to my sons actually accomplished, beyond repairing the specific rupture. They dismantled, brick by brick, a false picture of authority that I had inherited and was passing on without meaning to, the picture of authority as infallibility, as the right to never be questioned, as power that admits no error. Every time I got down to my son's level and owned my failure, I replaced that false picture with a truer one, the picture of authority as service, as accountability, as a stewardship exercised under a higher authority to whom even the parent must answer. This is the biblical picture of authority, and it is nearly the opposite of the domination model, which imagines authority as the freedom to command without accountability. My children learned more about godly authority from my apologies than from my commands, because my apologies showed them an authority that was itself under authority, a power that bowed to a truth larger than itself. That is the only kind of authority worth teaching a child to respect, and the only kind that points them toward the God who is himself the source of it.

Anger is the tell

If there is one signal that discipline has crossed into domination, it is the presence of anger in the disciplining parent. Not the fleeting frustration that any parent feels, but the settled anger that drives the correction, that wants the child to hurt, that discharges itself in the raised voice, the harsh grip, the words meant to wound. I know this anger from the inside, because I disciplined my sons in it more than I want to admit, and I have watched the effect it had, the way it taught them to fear me rather than to love the good, the way it wrote something into them that grace had to labor for years to overwrite.

The wisdom here is old and simple, and I ignored it for too long. Do not discipline in anger. When the anger is hot, wait. Step away. Let the fire cool before you correct, because correction delivered in anger is almost never about the child's formation and almost always about the parent's emotion. The child cannot receive formation through a cloud of your rage. They can only receive the message that you are frightening, that authority is dangerous, that love disappears when they fail. Wait until you are calm, and then correct from a place of steadiness and love, and you will discipline as a father rather than as a tyrant. The pause between the offense and the correction is where the difference between discipline and domination is decided.

The goal was never control

The deepest error underneath the domination model is a confusion about the goal. It assumes the goal of parenting is control, a controlled child now and a controlled adult later. But control was never the goal. The goal was always formation, the raising of a person who does what is right not because they are forced to but because they have been formed to love the good and choose it freely.

A controlled child is not a formed child. Control produces compliance under supervision and collapse without it. Formation produces character that holds when no one is watching, because it has been written into the person rather than imposed upon them. And formation, unlike control, cannot be achieved by domination. It can only be achieved by the patient, loving, relational work of discipling a child toward wisdom, the same work God does in us, with the same patience, the same aim at our good, the same refusal to break us in the name of forming us. Discipline your children. But discipline as a disciple-maker, not as a dominator. Aim at their formation, not your control. Repair when you fail, because you will. And model for them, in every correction, the God who disciplines those he loves not to crush them, but to raise them into the fullness of who they were made to be.
excerpt: Discipline and punishment are not the same thing, and much of what passes for Christian discipline is really domination baptized in Scripture. The goal was never control. It was formation.

title: Teaching Kids to Pray (Not Perform)
body:
The first prayer my son ever prayed out loud was a lie, and I taught it to him. Not on purpose. But I taught it just the same. He was four, sitting at the dinner table, and I asked him to thank God for the food. He folded his hands the way he had seen me fold mine, closed his eyes the way he had seen me close mine, and said the words he had heard a hundred times: "Thank you God for this food and this day and my family, amen." Perfect. Fluent. And empty. He was not talking to God. He was performing a shape he had learned from watching me, and I applauded, because the shape was correct.

I want to be careful not to make this sound worse than it was. He was four. Four-year-olds imitate everything, and imitation is how children learn most of what they know, including how to speak to God, so there was nothing sinister in the moment itself. The problem was not that he imitated. The problem was what he was imitating, and the fact that I could not tell the difference between a child learning to pray and a child learning to sound like he was praying, because I had long since lost the ability to tell that difference in myself.

I did not notice for years what I had done. I thought I was teaching him to pray. I was teaching him to sound like someone who prays. Those are not the same skill, and the second one is easier to teach, easier to measure, and quietly poisonous.

The Prayer That Impresses the Room

Every church has a child who prays beautifully. Composed, articulate, theologically tidy, the kind of prayer that makes grandparents cry and other parents feel behind. And every one of us who has raised such a child knows the private truth that we do not say out loud: we coached it. We praised the eloquence. We beamed when the prayer landed well in front of company. And in doing so we taught the child that prayer has an audience, and the audience is not God.

Jesus said something about this that we have managed to file under "the Pharisees" so we never have to file it under "us." He said that when the hypocrites pray, they love to stand and be seen, and that they have their reward already. The reward is the being-seen. That is the whole transaction, closed and settled. He was not describing a first-century sect. He was describing what happens to any human being, at any age, who discovers that religious language earns approval. My four-year-old discovered it before he could read. I handed him the discovery.

I have had to sit with this. The performance prayer is not a failure of my child's heart. It is a reflection of mine. He learned to perform because he was watching a father who performs. The public prayer at the church potluck, warm and rounded and slightly better than my private prayers deserve to sound. The grace before the meal that gets more graceful when guests are present. He absorbed the whole grammar of it, and he was faithful to what he absorbed. Children are not fooled by our prayers, but they are formed by them, and what forms them is not the words we choose but the direction our attention is actually facing while we say them.

What Prayer Actually Is

Before we can teach a child to pray, we have to remember what the thing is. Prayer is not a performance and it is not a technique. It is a relationship conducted in words, and sometimes without them. Eugene Peterson spent a career insisting that the Psalms are the school of prayer precisely because they are so unpolished. They complain. They rage. They accuse God of sleeping. They ask, in Psalm 88, and receive no comfort by the end, and the psalm just stops in the dark. That is in the prayer book. That is what God included when he taught his people to talk to him.

We have handed our children a prayer life with the complaints edited out, and then wondered why it feels fake to them. It feels fake because we made it fake. We removed everything true and kept everything nice.

A child who is only allowed to pray gratitude and requests has been given half a language. The Psalms give the whole language. They give lament, which is the honest naming of pain in the presence of God. They give confession, which is the honest naming of failure. They give the raw questions that a well-behaved prayer is not permitted to ask. If I want my sons to pray for real, I have to let them pray angry. I have to let them tell God they do not understand and are not sure he is listening. That is not irreverence. That is Psalm 13, four times over, "How long, O Lord."

Consider what it means that God gave his people a book of prayers to pray, rather than leaving them to invent prayer from scratch. It means that the human heart, left to itself, will pray too small. It will pray only the acceptable things. God knew this, and so he gave a hundred and fifty prayers that include cursing and despair and confusion and the wild swings of a real interior life, and he said, here, pray these, this is how my people talk to me. A child raised only on the sunny prayers has been quietly told that half of their actual heart is not welcome in the conversation. And a child who learns that half their heart is unwelcome will eventually take the whole heart elsewhere.

The Silence I Was Afraid Of

One of my sons went through a stretch where he did not want to pray at all. He was maybe eleven. And my first instinct, the instinct of the performer, was to fix it, to find the right encouragement, to get him praying again so that the household would look right and I would feel like I had done my job. What I did instead, mostly by accident and partly by exhaustion, was let it be. I said something like, God is patient, and he is not keeping score, and when you have something to say you can say it. Then I stopped managing it.

That was the most honest thing I ever taught him about prayer, and I taught it by not performing a solution. Because a God who requires you to pray on schedule, in the right tone, with the right words, or else, is not the God of the gospel. He is a manager. And a child raised to pray to a manager will either become an anxious performer or walk away from the whole thing the moment he is free to. I have watched both happen, in other families and nearly in mine.

The stretch of not praying lasted longer than I would have liked, and I will admit that I checked on it more than I let on, watching for signs that the faith was still there underneath the silence. It was. What returned, eventually, was not the fluent little prayers of his early childhood but something quieter and more his own, a few honest words at night, sometimes nothing, occasionally a real question thrown at the ceiling. I would not trade that hard-won, halting, genuine prayer for a hundred of the polished ones I used to be so proud of. The silence, it turned out, was not the death of his prayer life. It was the death of his performance, and what grew up in the cleared ground was the real thing.

Praying in Front of Them, Badly

The most useful thing I have done as a father is to let my children hear me pray when I am not doing well. Not the composed dinner grace. The stumbling one. The one where I stop in the middle because I do not know what I am asking for. The one where I say, God, I am angry about this, and I am not going to pretend I am not.

My son once heard me pray after a hard day at the church, a day involving a family in the congregation coming apart, and I prayed badly and briefly and I did not tie it up. I said something like, I do not know what you are doing here and I hate it. Amen. And I worried afterward that I had modeled irreverence in front of my boy. What I had actually modeled was faith. Because only someone who believes God is real talks to him like that. You do not complain to a fiction. The child who hears his father complain to God is watching a father who is convinced God is in the room.

A polished prayer teaches a child that God wants your best performance. A broken prayer teaches a child that God wants you. Those two lessons produce two completely different adults.

There is a risk here, and I do not want to pretend there is not. A parent can tip from honest lament into a kind of performative brokenness, a display of raw prayer that is just as much a show as the polished version, only aimed at looking authentic instead of looking pious. Children can smell that too. The point is not to perform brokenness any more than to perform composure. The point is to actually pray, in front of them, as the person you actually are on that particular day, which some days is grateful and some days is furious and some days has nothing to say at all. What forms them is not the tone. It is the reality.

The Words We Give Them

None of this means we abandon form. Children need words to borrow before they have words of their own, the same way they need to hear a language spoken before they can speak it. The Lord's Prayer is not a performance script. It is training wheels for the heart, given by Jesus himself to people who asked, teach us to pray, because they did not know how either. Written prayers, the ones the church has prayed for centuries, are not the enemy of sincerity. They are a scaffold for it. A child who prays the words of a saint who died a thousand years ago is not performing. He is joining a chorus.

The difference is not written versus spontaneous. The difference is whether the child understands that the words are aimed at a real Person who is actually listening, or whether the words are aimed at the people in the room. You can pray the Lord's Prayer as a performance. You can pray a stumbling, made-up prayer as a performance. The form is not the problem. The audience is the problem. And children learn who the audience is by watching where our eyes go, literally and otherwise, when we pray.

So I have kept the forms in our house. We still pray the Lord's Prayer. We still say grace, most nights, though I have loosened my grip on how it sounds. What I have tried to change is not the presence of form but the presence of God underneath it, the sense in the room that we are actually addressing Someone and not reciting for one another. That is harder to teach than a formula, because it cannot be taught directly at all. It can only be caught, from a parent who is actually doing it, which means the whole thing comes back, as it always does, to whether the father in the room is praying to God or to the table.

What I Am Trying to Undo

I have five sons. I have taught all of them to pray, and I have taught some of them to perform, and the honest work of the last several years has been distinguishing the two after the fact and trying to loosen what I tightened. I have told them, more than once, that I got this wrong early. That when they were small I liked it too much when their prayers sounded good. That a prayer that sounds good in front of Grandma and a prayer that God hears are not automatically the same prayer, and I confused them, and I am sorry.

Telling your children you were wrong is itself a form of prayer, or close to it. It is the confession of a father who performed, spoken to the people he performed in front of. And it does something the performance never could. It tells them that the man teaching them to pray is himself still learning, still stumbling, still not fluent. Which means the whole enterprise is not about arriving at a polished product. It is about staying in the conversation.

The goal was never a child who prays impressively. The goal is a child who, at fifty, in the dark, when everything has gone wrong and no one is watching and there is nothing to perform, still believes there is Someone on the other end of the silence, and talks. That child will not need the right words. That child will need to know he was never performing in the first place. I am not sure I have given my sons that yet. I am sure it is the only thing worth giving them.

So I am still at the table. Still asking them to pray. But I have stopped grading it. And when one of them prays something clumsy and true, something that would embarrass me at a potluck, I have learned to be more grateful for that than for all the fluent, empty, correct prayers I used to applaud. The clumsy true one is the one God is in. I taught them the other kind first. I am trying, late, to teach them this one.
excerpt: The first prayer my son ever prayed out loud was a lie, and I taught it to him. Not on purpose. But I taught it just the same.

title: Death, Grief, and Children: How to Talk About Hard Things
body:
My son asked me if he was going to die, and I lied. He was five, in the bath, and he asked it the way children ask everything, with no warning and full attention. And I said, not for a very long time, buddy. Then I changed the subject to something about a boat. I do not know that he will not die soon. No parent knows that. I said it because I could not bear the alternative, which was to sit in the bathwater with my son and tell him the truth, that everyone dies, that I do not control when, and that this is the one certainty I cannot protect him from.

We think we are protecting our children from death. We are usually protecting ourselves from their questions.

The Death We Hide

Ours is the first culture in human history to keep children away from death almost entirely. For most of human history a child would see death by the time they were old enough to remember anything, a grandparent laid out in the front room, a sibling lost to fever, animals slaughtered for the table. Death was in the house. It was terrible, but it was known. We have moved death to hospitals and hospices and funeral homes, sanitized it, professionalized it, and in the process we have raised children who reach adulthood without ever having stood next to a body. We think this is mercy. It may be the opposite.

Because the child still knows. Children figure out death astonishingly early, usually around four or five, when they realize that dead is not a temporary condition, that the goldfish is not coming back, that this applies to grandparents and eventually to parents and eventually to them. They know. What they do not have, if we have hidden it, is any framework for what they know. They have the terror without the words and without the presence of an adult who will stay in the room while they feel it.

What we have actually done, by removing death from the ordinary landscape of childhood, is not spare our children from it but abandon them to it. The knowledge arrives anyway. It arrives through a dead pet, a news story, a classmate's grandmother, and it arrives to a child who has never once seen an adult handle death with steadiness and faith and tears all at the same time. So the child handles it alone, in the dark, at three in the morning, constructing whatever terrifying theory a five-year-old constructs when the biggest fact in the universe lands on them and the adults have quietly agreed not to discuss it. We did not protect them. We left them to face the largest thing there is without a guide.

What Not to Say

The church has developed a set of phrases we deploy at children in grief, and most of them are quietly damaging. We tell a child that Grandpa went to sleep, and then we wonder why the child develops a terror of bedtime. We tell a child that God needed another angel, and we hand them a picture of a God who kills people because he is lonely, a God to be feared and resented rather than trusted. We tell a child that Grandma is in a better place, before the child has had a single second to be angry that she is not in this place, at this table, where she belongs.

Every comforting lie we tell a grieving child is really a comfort we are giving ourselves. The child does not need the metaphor. We need it, because the truth is unbearable and the metaphor lets us leave the room.

The worst one, the one I have heard from well-meaning saints a hundred times, is do not cry, she is in heaven. This tells a grieving child that their grief is a theological error. That if they had more faith they would not be sad. It weaponizes the resurrection against the natural, God-given, entirely appropriate response of a heart that has lost someone it loves. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, a man he was about to raise from the dead. He knew Lazarus was coming back in five minutes and he still wept. If the certainty of resurrection did not cancel the tears of Christ, it does not get to cancel the tears of my child.

These phrases are not malicious. They come from adults who are themselves frightened, reaching for something to make the moment stop hurting, for the child and for themselves. But a frightened adult reaching for a comforting formula is exactly what a grieving child does not need. What the child needs is an adult who is not so frightened of death that they have to paper over it instantly, an adult who can say the true and terrible thing gently and then stay in the room while it lands. That adult is rare, because it requires the adult to have made some peace with death themselves, and most of us have not, and the phrases are how we hide that we have not.

Grief Is Not the Enemy of Faith

Somewhere we absorbed the idea that a faithful Christian does not grieve, or grieves only briefly and then rallies to the resurrection. Paul says the opposite. He says we do not grieve as those who have no hope, which is not the same as we do not grieve. We grieve. We grieve hard. We just grieve toward something. The hope does not delete the grief. It gives the grief a direction.

When I teach my children about death, the most important thing I can give them is permission to be devastated. That the sadness is not a lack of faith, it is love with nowhere to go. That God is not offended by their tears, he collects them, the psalm says he keeps them in a bottle. A child who is allowed to grieve fully, in the presence of a parent who is also grieving and not pretending otherwise, learns something they cannot learn any other way, that the worst thing is real, that it can be survived, and that they are not alone in it. A child who is rushed past grief to the tidy comfort learns to distrust their own heart and to distrust the comfort.

There is a long-term cost to teaching a child that grief is faithlessness, and I have seen it in grown adults sitting in my office decades later. They lost a parent as a child, were told to be strong, were praised for how well they were handling it, and so they buried a grief that had nowhere to go, and it went underground, and it shaped them into adults who cannot feel loss, cannot cry, cannot let anything reach the buried place. They were faithful children. They were also, without knowing it, wounded ones, wounded not by the death but by the instruction to skip the grief. The resurrection does not require us to skip the grief. It promises to meet us on the far side of it, which is a different thing entirely.

Telling the Truth About What We Do Not Know

Children ask the questions we have spent our whole adult lives avoiding. Where is Grandpa now. What is it like to be dead. Will it hurt. Will you die. Will I die. Why did God let it happen. And the temptation, always, is to answer with false certainty because false certainty feels like strength and the truth feels like abandoning them.

But false certainty is a debt that comes due. The child who is told exactly what heaven is like, in confident detail, will one day discover that we were guessing, and will wonder what else we were guessing about. The stronger answer, the one that actually holds up over a lifetime, is honest uncertainty inside a larger trust. I do not know exactly what it is like to be with God. The Bible gives us pictures, not a map. But I know God is good, I know Jesus went there first, and I know that wherever Grandpa is, he is not lost, because God does not lose people. I can say that and mean it. I cannot say Grandpa is watching over you from a cloud and mean it, so I do not say it.

Children can carry the words I do not know if you carry them for them. It is not uncertainty that terrifies a child. It is uncertainty in the arms of a parent who is also terrified and pretending not to be.

This is the discipline that costs the most, because it requires the parent to tolerate their own not-knowing in front of a child who is begging for certainty. Every instinct in a parent's body wants to end the child's distress with a confident answer. But the confident answer we do not actually possess is a loan against a future the child will have to repay, and the honest answer, held steadily and warmly, is a gift they can keep. I do not know, but I trust him, and here is why. That sentence, from a parent who is clearly not panicking, does more for a child's faith than a dozen confident descriptions of the geography of heaven that the parent secretly made up.

Let Them See You Grieve

My father died, and I made a decision, half-conscious, that my sons would see me cry. Not perform grief for their benefit, but not hide it either. Because I had been raised to believe that a man does not let his children see him break, and I have spent decades unlearning the damage of that belief, and I was not going to hand it down.

So they saw me cry at the funeral. They saw me quiet for weeks. They saw their father, the pastor, the one who is supposed to have answers, sit at the kitchen table and not have them. And I have come to believe that this was one of the most important things I ever gave them. Because now they know that grief does not end a man. That you can be shattered and still make breakfast. That faith is not the absence of tears, it is what you hold onto while you cry. If I had hidden my grief to protect them, I would have taught them that grief must be hidden, and I would have handed them, wrapped in love, the exact loneliness that nearly broke me at their age.

I grew up without a father, which means I never saw a man grieve, never saw a father cry, never had a model for how a man survives loss. I had to build that model from nothing, badly, in real time, in front of my own sons. And the thing I most wanted them to see was the thing I had never seen: a man who feels the full weight of a loss and does not pretend otherwise and does not let it destroy him and does not hide it from the people who love him. I do not know if I gave them that. I know I tried, at my father's funeral, with my own sons watching, to be the man I had needed and never had.

The Long Conversation

Death is not a single conversation. It is a conversation that reopens at every age with new questions. The five-year-old asks if you will die. The nine-year-old asks what it means that a classmate's parent died. The thirteen-year-old asks whether heaven is even real. The seventeen-year-old, sitting up late after a friend's suicide, asks the question underneath all the others, whether anything means anything if it all ends. Each of these is the same child, coming back to the same edge, needing to know that the parent is still standing there, still honest, still unafraid to say I do not know and still sure that God is good.

What ruins this is a single early lie, delivered with confidence, that later gets exposed. The bathtub lie I told my son, not for a very long time, buddy, was a small one, and I have since gone back and told him a truer version, that I do not control when anyone dies, that I hope for a long life for him and cannot promise it, and that whatever happens, God does not lose the people he loves. He took it better than the lie deserved. Children usually do. They are stronger than our fear of their fear.

What the Resurrection Actually Offers a Child

At the end, after all the honesty about grief and uncertainty, there is a thing we get to say to our children that no other worldview gets to say. Not that death is not sad. It is. Not that we know all the details of what comes after. We do not. But that death is not the last word. That the tomb was empty. That the God who wept at the grave of his friend is the same God who called him out of it. That the story does not end in the dark, even when the psalm does, even when the funeral does, even when the bathwater conversation does.

We do not give children this by skipping the grief. We give it to them by walking through the grief with them, all the way down, and then, from the bottom, pointing east. The hope is not a shortcut around the sorrow. It is a light that only makes sense once you have been in the dark long enough to need it. Our job is not to keep our children out of the dark. It is to be in there with them, holding their hand, telling the truth, and refusing to let go until the light comes up. It will come up. That is the one thing I am willing to promise them. It is the only thing I know for certain, and it is enough.
excerpt: My son asked me if he was going to die, and I lied. I said not for a very long time. I do not know that. No parent knows that.

title: Blended Family Parenting
body:
There is a moment in every blended family when a child says you are not my real parent, and it is true, and it lands like a verdict. The child is not wrong. That is what makes it unbearable. You have fed them, driven them, stayed up with them, and paid for them, and in one sentence they have named the thing you cannot argue with. You are not their real parent. And the whole fragile architecture of the household seems to shudder around that one true, cruel sentence.

I want to say at the outset that I speak here partly as a pastor and partly as a man who was raised without his own father, which means I know the particular weight a father-shaped hole puts on a child, and I have watched families try to fill it, or fail to, or make it worse. Blended families are not a lesser thing. But they are a harder thing, and the church has been dishonest about that for too long, treating the stepfamily as either a scandal to be quietly mourned or a triumph to be celebrated without cost. It is neither. It is a family built on the site of a loss, and the loss does not disappear because a new family stands on top of it.

The Loss Underneath

Every blended family is founded on grief. This is the fact we skip. Whether the first marriage ended in death or divorce, a child in a blended family has lost the family they were born into. Even when the new arrangement is happier, safer, and more stable, even when the previous situation was genuinely bad, the child has lost something. And you cannot build well on ground you refuse to acknowledge is a grave.

We keep trying to make blended families work by pretending the first family did not matter. The child cannot pretend that. The first family is written into their body. Every attempt to overwrite it is felt as a second loss.

The stepparent who arrives cheerful and eager, ready to be loved, ready to blend, is often walking straight into a child's grief without seeing it. The child is not rejecting the stepparent because the stepparent is bad. The child is grieving a family that this new person, however kind, represents the end of. To love the stepparent fully can feel, to the child, like betraying the parent who is gone or the family that broke. This is not a discipline problem. It is a loyalty bind, and it will not yield to firmness. It yields, slowly, to patience and to being seen.

The first task of anyone entering a blended family, then, is not to build the new thing but to honor the grief the child is carrying about the old thing. This feels backward. Everyone wants to move forward, to make the new family work, to leave the painful past behind. But a child cannot move forward over a grief that no one will acknowledge. The stepparent who says, out loud, I know this is hard, I know you miss how things were, I am not trying to replace anyone, has done more to eventually win the child than the stepparent who arrives with forced cheer and a schedule of bonding activities. You cannot skip the funeral to get to the wedding. The child is still at the funeral. Sit down next to them there first.

Do Not Compete With the Ghost

The most common mistake I have watched stepparents make, and watched wreck households, is competing with the absent or deceased biological parent. The stepfather who subtly undermines the dad every other weekend. The stepmother who cannot hide her irritation when the kids talk about their mom. It is human. It comes from insecurity, from wanting to be chosen, from the exhausting experience of doing the daily work of parenting while some idealized ghost of the "real" parent gets the child's loyalty. But it is fatal.

Because a child cannot betray one of their parents to satisfy another without splitting in half. When you make a child choose between you and their biological parent, you do not win. You teach the child that love is a war and that they are the battlefield. The most powerful thing a stepparent can do, the thing that eventually, years later, produces real love, is to honor the biological parent openly, even when that parent does not deserve it, even when that parent is failing, even when honoring them costs you. You are not competing for the throne. You are adding a room to a house that already had a foundation.

This is especially brutal when the biological parent is genuinely bad, unreliable, absent, or cruel, and the stepparent, who is actually doing the work, has to watch the child pine for someone who does not show up. Everything in you wants to say what you can see, that the absent parent is failing them. Do not. The child has to reckon with that themselves, in their own time, and if you force the reckoning you become the villain who attacked their parent, and the child's loyalty snaps back to the failing parent with a vengeance. Your job is to be the steady presence that is actually there, day after day, without demanding that the child renounce the one who is not. Over years, the contrast makes its own argument, and you do not have to make it for them.

The Discipline Trap

Nothing detonates a blended family faster than the stepparent who tries to discipline too early. The instinct is understandable, especially for men, especially for men who were raised to believe that a household needs a firm hand. You move in, you see a child behaving in ways you would never have permitted, and you step in to correct it, and the whole thing explodes, because you have not yet earned the standing.

Authority is not conferred by a marriage certificate. It is earned by relationship, over time, in that order, always. The biological parent has years of accumulated trust that gives their correction weight. The stepparent has none of that yet, and a correction delivered without relationship is experienced not as guidance but as invasion. Who are you to tell me what to do. And again, the child is not entirely wrong. You are, at first, someone who married their parent. The relationship that makes discipline bearable has to be built before the discipline can be received, and building it takes years, not months.

The stepparent's first job is not to lead. It is to love without requiring love in return. Authority follows relationship. It never leads it. Every family that got this backward is a family I have watched come apart.

In the early years, the wisest arrangement is usually that the biological parent carries the discipline and the stepparent carries the relationship. The stepparent supports the household rules without being the primary enforcer of them. This feels unfair to the stepparent, who is doing the work of a parent without the authority of one. It is unfair. It is also the price of building something that lasts, and the parents who pay it early are the ones whose children, at twenty-five, call the stepparent to ask advice.

The Marriage Comes First, and It Is Hard to Believe That

In a first-marriage family, the marriage precedes the children and everyone knows it. In a blended family, the children precede the marriage, and this inverts everything. The biological parent has a bond with their child that is older and, in the raw moments, stronger than the bond with the new spouse. And children, especially wounded children, will test whether they can split the marriage, not out of malice, but because a child who has already watched one family dissolve is checking, constantly, whether this one will hold.

The couple that survives is the couple that decides, together, that the marriage is the load-bearing wall of the new house. Not more loved than the children. Load-bearing. If the marriage fails, the children lose a second family, and no child should have to survive that twice. Protecting the marriage is not selfishness in a blended family. It is the single most protective thing the parents can do for the children, and it is the thing the children will fight hardest against, and both of those are true at once.

This requires the biological parent to do something excruciating, which is to sometimes side with the new spouse against their own child, on matters of respect and household order, when the child is testing the seam. Not on everything, and not against the child's genuine interests, but on the basic question of whether the marriage is a real thing that will not be split. A child who learns that they can drive a wedge between the parent and the stepparent will keep driving it, not because they are wicked but because the wedge feels like power in a life where they have felt powerless. Closing that gap, gently but firmly, is a gift to the child, even as they rage against it. It tells them the new family will hold, which is the thing they most need and most fear to find out.

The Long Timeline

The research and the pastoral experience agree on a number that no one wants to hear. A blended family takes years to actually blend. Not months. Years. Somewhere between four and seven, on average, before the household feels like a family rather than a merger. And most couples give up, or nearly do, in year two, because they measured against the wrong timeline. They expected the Brady Bunch by Christmas and got resentment and slammed doors and a child who would not call them anything, and they concluded they had failed.

They had not failed. They were on schedule. The schedule is just brutally long. The blended families that make it are the ones that stopped expecting instant love and started playing the long game, offering steady, non-anxious, unconditional presence year after year, weathering the rejections without retaliating, being the adult who does not leave. Love in a blended family is not a feeling that arrives. It is a track record that accumulates. You earn it in the years when it is not returned.

The couples who quit in year two almost always quit because they were measuring the wrong thing. They were measuring the feeling, checking each week to see whether love had bloomed yet, whether the stepchild had warmed, whether the household finally felt like the family in their imagination. And when the feeling did not come on schedule, they concluded the whole thing was a mistake. But the feeling was never the metric. The metric was faithfulness, whether you kept showing up, kept honoring the biological parent, kept loving without demanding return, kept being the adult who does not leave. Measured that way, a family that feels nothing but strain in year two can be succeeding beautifully, because success in year two is not warmth, it is presence, and presence is a thing you can choose even when the warmth has not arrived. The couples who understood this survived to see the warmth eventually come. The couples who demanded the warmth first left before it could.

Grace as the Only Foundation That Holds

Here is where the gospel does something no parenting technique can. The whole logic of a blended family, done well, is the logic of adoption, which is the logic at the center of the Christian faith. God did not father us because we were his by blood. We were not his. He chose us, brought us into a family we had no birthright to, and loved us before we returned it, and called us sons and daughters with full inheritance, no asterisk. That is a stepfather's love, raised to the divine. The stepparent who loves a child who is not theirs by blood, who chooses that child daily, who honors what came before while building what comes next, is doing in miniature what God did for all of us who were not his by blood either.

This is why the years of unreturned love are not wasted years, even when they feel like it, even when the stepchild is cold and the effort seems to vanish into nothing. Adoption love always precedes the response. God loved us while we were still his enemies, still turned away, still incapable of loving him back, and that love was not wasted in the years before we returned it, it was the very thing that eventually made the returning possible. The stepparent loving a resistant child is standing in exactly that position, pouring out a love that is not yet reciprocated, planting something whose harvest may be years away and may, honestly, never come in a form they can see. That is a hard place to stand. It is also the most Christlike place a parent can stand, because it is precisely where God stood toward all of us, loving first, loving unreturned, loving at cost, and calling it not foolishness but family.

I was raised without a father, and I have spent my life aware of the shape of that absence, and I will tell you that the men who step into a fatherless child's life, who choose a child the world would say is not theirs, are doing holy work, whether or not the child ever thanks them, whether or not the love is returned on schedule, whether or not it is returned at all in the years when it costs the most. You are not their real parent. That sentence is true. And the deeper truth, the one that takes years to prove and is worth every one of them, is that real is not only a thing you are born into. Real is also a thing you build, in the ruins of a loss, with a love that does not quit. God built his family that way. You can too.
excerpt: There is a moment in every blended family when a child says you are not my real parent, and it is true, and it lands like a verdict.

title: Parenting Through Divorce
body:
You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice, feels like protecting them from a distorted version of events, feels like the truth they deserve. It is a knife, and you are handing it to your child to carry, and it will cut them for the rest of their lives, not the parent you aimed it at.

I am a pastor. I believe marriage is meant to last, and I do not write this to make divorce comfortable. I write it because divorce happens, it happens in the church, it happens to people who fought for their marriages and to people who did not, and when it happens there are children in the house, and those children did not choose any of it, and how the parents behave in the wreckage will shape those children more than the divorce itself. The divorce is a wound. The way you handle it is either a bandage or salt.

The Thing Children Actually Fear

Ask children of divorce what they were most afraid of, and it is almost never the logistics. It is the fear that it was their fault, and the fear that a parent who left the marriage might leave them too. Children are natural egocentrists, not out of selfishness but out of developmental necessity, and a young child genuinely believes the world revolves around them, which means when the world breaks, they assume they broke it. If I had been better, if I had not fought with my brother, if I had been easier, they would have stayed together.

The child is not asking whose fault the divorce was. The child is asking whether the divorce was their fault. And every argument you win in front of them about the other parent confirms their worst fear, that the family is a war and they are somewhere near the cause.

You have to say it, out loud, more than once, in words a child can hold. This is not your fault. Nothing you did caused this and nothing you could have done would have prevented it. This is between the adults, and both of us still love you, and that is never going to change. You will feel like you are stating the obvious. You are not. The child does not know it. The child needs to hear it from both parents, repeatedly, over years, because the fear is not defeated in one conversation. It comes back at every developmental stage in a new disguise.

The second fear, that a parent who left the marriage might leave the child, is subtler and just as real. A child watches one parent walk away from a relationship they thought was permanent, and the child does the math. If that bond could break, what about mine. This is why divorced parents have to be almost obsessively reliable about the small things, the pickups, the promises, the phone calls, the being where you said you would be when you said you would be there. Every kept promise is evidence against the fear. Every broken one confirms it. The child is running an experiment, mostly unconsciously, on whether the adults in their life can be counted on, and the divorce has already returned one frightening result. Your reliability is how you argue with it.

Do Not Make Them a Messenger

The single most damaging habit in a divorce is turning the child into a courier. Tell your father he still owes for the field trip. Ask your mother why she was late again. Every message you send through the child forces the child to carry your conflict on their small back, across the demilitarized zone, into the other parent's house, where they will absorb the return fire. You have made your child a diplomat in a war they did not start and cannot end.

Children are not messengers. They are not spies, either, though divorced parents interrogate them constantly, what did your mother say, is there a new man there, how much did that cost, framed as concern, functioning as reconnaissance. The child learns to manage information between two hostile powers, to say different things in different houses, to survive by becoming a small deceiver. This is corrosive to the soul of a child. The adults have to communicate with each other, directly, even when it is excruciating, so that the child can just be a child in both houses instead of a courier in neither.

I know how hard the direct communication is, because the whole reason you divorced is often that direct communication became unbearable. But the alternative, routing your conflict through a child, does not spare the child the conflict. It embeds them in it. If you cannot talk to your former spouse without it becoming a fight, then use writing, use a scheduling app, use a mediator, use anything that is not your nine-year-old. The child is not a neutral channel. The child loves both of you, which means every message they carry costs them something in loyalty and every hostility they witness lands on a heart that is already divided in half.

Do Not Recruit Them

There is a deeper betrayal than using a child as a messenger, and it is using a child as a confidant. The lonely, wounded parent who, out of genuine pain, begins to lean on the child emotionally, to share adult grievances, to make the child their support system, their ally, their friend. It feels like closeness. The child even seems to want it, seems mature enough for it, rises to it. It is one of the most damaging things a parent can do.

When you make your child your emotional support, you have not gained an ally. You have lost a child. You have handed them a weight they were never built to carry, and they will carry it, because they love you, and it will bend them.

The child who becomes the parent's confidant loses their childhood. They become anxiously attuned to the adult's emotional state, responsible for a grief they cannot fix, and torn in half when the confided-in grievance is about the other parent they also love. They are being asked to take a side in the destruction of their own family. Some of them do take a side, and it looks like loyalty, and it is really a child being conscripted. Your grief is real and it deserves support. It deserves support from other adults. Your child is not a peer, no matter how mature they seem, and treating them as one steals something from them they do not get back.

This is hardest for the parent who is genuinely alone, whose marriage ended and whose support system thinned out at the same time, and whose most available, most sympathetic listener is the child sitting across the table. I understand the pull. But the pull has to be resisted, precisely because it is so strong and the child is so willing. A twelve-year-old who has become their mother's best friend is not being honored by the closeness. They are being robbed of the freedom to be twelve, to have their own problems be the big problems, to lean on the adult instead of propping the adult up. Find adult support, however hard that is to find, so that your child gets to keep being your child.

Two Houses, One Childhood

The practical work of parenting through divorce is the work of protecting the child's world from becoming a battlefield of contrasts. Two households, run by two hurt people, will differ. But the more the child experiences the two houses as opposed camps with opposed values, the more the child has to fracture themselves to belong in both. Consistency between houses, on the things that matter, bedtimes, expectations, the basic sense of what is right, is a gift to the child's coherence. You are not doing it for your ex. You are doing it so your child does not have to be two different people.

This requires something almost impossible, a working relationship with the person who broke your heart. Not friendship. Not forgiveness on any timeline that can be rushed. A working relationship, businesslike, focused entirely on the child, in which you can sit at the same graduation and the same wedding decades later without the child having to manage your feelings. The parents who achieve this, and some do, give their children something worth more than the intact marriage would have given a different family, proof that love for a child can outlast the love between the adults.

Your Anger Is Real, and It Is Not the Child's to Hold

None of this means your anger is wrong. If you were betrayed, abandoned, or wounded, the anger is righteous and it deserves a place. It deserves a therapist, a pastor, a friend, a journal, the psalms of lament that were written by people who wanted God to break the teeth of their enemies. God can hold your rage. Your congregation can hold your grief. What cannot hold it, what must not be asked to hold it, is a nine-year-old who loves both of the people you are enraged at each other about.

I have sat with divorced parents who were doing everything right in every visible way and were still leaking their bitterness into the child through a thousand small tells, the tone when the other parent's name comes up, the tightness at drop-off, the sigh. Children read these fluently. The work is not to feel nothing. That is impossible. The work is to find adult places for the adult feelings so that the child gets a parent instead of a co-belligerent.

There is a particular temptation that deserves naming, because it is so easy to justify. It is the temptation to let the child see just a little of the truth about the other parent, to plant one small correction, to make sure the child knows, quietly, who was really at fault. It never feels like weaponizing the child. It feels like honesty, like fairness, like refusing to let a lie stand. But the child does not experience it as fairness. The child experiences it as being asked to hold their parent in contempt, and every such request, however small, however justified, tears at the child's own sense of self, because the child is made of both of you. To ask a child to despise one parent is to ask them to despise half of themselves. Whatever the other parent did, and it may have been genuinely terrible, the child's need to love both of you intact is more important than your need to be proven right, and the parent who grasps this, and holds their tongue at the cost of never getting the vindication they crave, is giving the child something worth more than the truth about who broke the marriage.

What Grace Looks Like in the Wreckage

I said I am a pastor and I believe marriage is meant to last. I also believe in grace, and grace is not a doctrine that lives in the abstract, it is a way of behaving toward people who have hurt you. The parent who, in the wreckage of a divorce, refuses to weaponize the children, who honors the other parent in front of them even while grieving privately, who absorbs the messenger role instead of assigning it, who finds adult support instead of conscripting the child, is doing something profoundly Christlike. They are absorbing cost so that someone smaller does not have to. That is the shape of the cross, transposed into custody arrangements and drop-off schedules.

None of this is possible in your own strength, and I will not pretend it is. To honor the person who betrayed you, to hold your tongue when you could win the child to your side, to absorb the messenger role and the loneliness and the rage without leaking any of it onto a child, is genuinely beyond the natural capacity of a wounded human heart. It requires grace poured into you before you can pour it out, the grace of a God who himself absorbed betrayal and did not retaliate, who was wronged past all measure and answered with forgiveness. You will not manufacture this behavior by trying harder. You will only find it by going to the God who did it first and asking him to do it in you, over and over, on the hard mornings, at the drop-offs, in the moments when everything in you wants to make the child understand who the real villain was. The grace you extend to your former spouse for the sake of your children is not something you generate. It is something you receive and pass through, and the passing through is itself the healing, both for you and for the children who are watching.

Your children are watching how you treat the person who hurt you most. They will learn, from that, more about the gospel than from every sermon they hear, because they will see whether grace is real or only spoken. The divorce is not the last word over your children. The way you carry them through it can be a testimony louder than the marriage would ever have been. Not because the divorce was good. It was not. But because grace does its best work exactly where things have broken, and your children are old enough to see, in you, whether you believe that or only preach it. Show them. It is the most important sermon you will ever give, and you will give it without words, in the years when it costs the most.
excerpt: You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice. It is a knife you are handing your child.

title: When Your Teenager Calls You a Hypocrite
body:
My son called me a hypocrite, and my first reaction was rage, and my rage proved his point. He had watched me preach patience on Sunday and lose it in the car on Tuesday. He had heard me talk about grace from the pulpit and had felt precious little of it at the dinner table. And when he finally said it, sixteen years old and furious, you are a total hypocrite, Dad, the thing that rose up in me was not humility. It was the urge to crush him for saying it. Which was, of course, exactly the hypocrisy he had named.

He was right. That is the part I could not stand. It was not a cheap shot from a rebellious kid trying to wound. It was a true observation from someone who had been watching me closely for sixteen years and had finally worked up the nerve to report what he saw. And the fact that it was true is the only reason it hurt that much. We are not wounded by accusations we know to be false. We are wounded by the ones that land.

The Charge Is Usually Accurate

Let us start with the thing no parenting book wants to admit. When your teenager calls you a hypocrite, they are usually right, at least about the specific instance. You do say one thing and do another. Everyone does. But you, the parent, have set yourself up as the teacher of a way of life, and your teenager has been in the classroom their entire existence, and they have a mountain of data, and somewhere in that mountain is every gap between your words and your life.

The teenager is not inventing your hypocrisy. They are reporting it. The question is not whether the charge is true. The question is what you do with a true charge delivered by a child who is furious and, for once, correct.

The temptation is to defend, to distinguish, to explain why this instance was different, why the standard I hold you to is not the standard I failed. All of that is true, some of the time. Sometimes there really is a distinction. But if the first thing out of your mouth is a defense, you have confirmed the diagnosis. Because the non-hypocrite, the person of genuine integrity, is the person who can hear I do not live up to my own words and say, you are right, without collapsing and without counterattacking. The defensive rage is the hypocrisy. The teenager just held up a mirror.

What makes this so hard for parents, and especially for parents who are church people, is that we have staked our authority on our example. We have said, in effect, do as I do, follow my lead, watch how I live. So when the teenager points out that our living does not match our teaching, it feels like the whole foundation of our authority is being pulled out. And in a sense it is, if our authority was ever really based on our performance. But it never should have been. A parent whose authority depends on never being caught failing is a parent building on sand, because the failures are coming, and the teenager has a front-row seat, and the sand is going to wash out from under exactly the parent who most needed it to hold.

Why This Moment Matters More Than It Feels Like It Should

Something specific is happening developmentally when a teenager starts leveling this charge. They are individuating, which is a clinical word for the process by which a child stops taking your worldview on faith and starts examining it. This is not rebellion in the sinful sense. It is the necessary work of becoming a person who owns their own convictions rather than inheriting them like furniture. And part of that work is testing whether the people who taught them the convictions actually believe them, actually live them, or were just handing down a script.

The hypocrisy accusation, then, is not the enemy of your child's faith. It is the crucible of it. They are asking, underneath the anger, a real question, is this thing you taught me real, or is it a costume you wear on Sundays. And your response to being called a hypocrite is the answer. If you defend the costume, you confirm that it is a costume. If you take off the costume, if you say, you are right, I fail at this, and here is why I still believe it anyway, you show them something a script could never show, a faith that survives the failure of the person holding it.

The Difference Between a Hypocrite and a Sinner

Here is a distinction I have had to learn to make, for my own soul as much as for my son's. A hypocrite is not simply a person who fails to live up to their standards. By that definition, every honest human being who has ever held a standard is a hypocrite, and the word means nothing. A hypocrite, in the original sense, is a play-actor, someone who performs a virtue they do not actually possess, who pretends. The sin is not the gap between belief and behavior. The sin is pretending the gap is not there.

I am not a hypocrite because I fail to be patient. I am a hypocrite if I pretend I have arrived at patience while failing at it. The failure is human. The pretense is the lie. My teenager can forgive the failure. He cannot respect the pretense, and he should not.

This distinction is a lifeline for a parent, because it means the answer to the hypocrisy charge is not to become perfect, which is impossible, but to stop pretending, which is possible today. When my son called me a hypocrite, the true and honest and even godly response available to me was, you are right that I fail at this, and you are right to be angry, and I am sorry, and hear me, I never claimed to have arrived, I claimed that this is worth aiming at, and I am still aiming, badly, and I always will be. That is not hypocrisy. That is the ordinary condition of a Christian, named honestly instead of hidden.

There is a version of the Christian life, common in the kind of church I grew up around, that treats the appearance of holiness as the goal, and this version manufactures hypocrites at an industrial rate, because it rewards the performance of virtue over the honest pursuit of it. A teenager raised in that version is being handed a religion of pretense, and the sharpest ones see through it early, and when they call it out, they are not attacking the faith. They are attacking the counterfeit, and they are right to, and the tragedy is that we so often defend the counterfeit and lose the child rather than admit the counterfeit and keep them.

The Repentance That Preaches

The most powerful thing I have ever done for my sons' faith was not a good sermon. It was an apology. It was going back to my son after I had lost my temper, after I had been the hypocrite he named, and saying, I was wrong, I am sorry, will you forgive me. There is no sermon on the planet that teaches the gospel the way a parent's genuine repentance does, because the gospel is not fundamentally a set of ideas. It is the announcement that failure is not final, that there is a way back, that grace is real. And a teenager cannot learn that from a lecture. They learn it from watching a parent walk it.

When you repent to your teenager, you demonstrate the entire mechanism of the faith you have been trying to teach. You show that you believe you are accountable to a standard higher than your own comfort. You show that being wrong is survivable. You show that relationships are repaired through confession, not through pretending. You model the exact thing you most want them to be able to do, which is to fail and return, fail and return, for the rest of their lives. The parent who cannot say sorry is teaching their child that Christianity is about maintaining an image. The parent who can say sorry is teaching them that it is about grace. Only one of those faiths survives adulthood.

I did not learn to apologize to my children easily. I was raised by no father and a mother doing the work of two, and the model I absorbed was that authority does not explain itself and certainly does not concede. Learning to say I was wrong to a sixteen-year-old required dismantling something in me that ran deep, a belief that a father who admits fault has lost the room. He has not. He has, in the only way that ultimately matters, won it. Because the son who watches his father humble himself learns that humility and strength are not opposites, and that lesson, delivered by example, will outlast every rule I ever enforced.

When the Charge Is Unfair

Sometimes, of course, the teenager is not making a fair observation. Sometimes hypocrite is just the sharpest available weapon and they are wielding it because they are angry that you said no to something, and the charge is a manipulation rather than a mirror.
