The talks I gave about love and commitment, the careful lessons, the things I said on purpose, these have mostly evaporated, and I doubt they could quote a single one. But the way conflict was handled in our house, the temperature of the disagreements, the presence or absence of contempt, the reliability of the repair, these went in deep, below the level of memory, into the place where a person's own instincts about relationship are formed. My sons do not remember what I told them about marriage. They remember, in their bodies, what marriage felt like in the house they grew up in, and they are reproducing that feeling, for better and worse, without ever deciding to. This is humbling and a little frightening, because it means the lesson was never mostly in my control. I could control what I said. I could only partly control what I did in the heat of a real fight, and it was the second thing, not the first, that became their inheritance.

So here is the weight I want to leave with any parent who fights, which is every parent. Your children are learning about love from how you conduct your conflicts, right now, in the fights you think are private. You cannot prevent this lesson. You can only decide what it teaches. Let it teach that love and anger coexist, that people who hurt each other can heal each other, that being wrong is survivable and apology is strength and reconciliation is real. Fight without contempt. Repair where they can see it. Apologize out loud. Those are the marriage lessons that will actually reach your children, and they will reach them not through your words but through your conduct, in the one relationship they are watching most closely and learning from most deeply, the one you may have thought they could not see.
excerpt: My sons learned more about marriage from the fights they were not supposed to hear than from anything I ever said about it on purpose.

title: Raising Kids Who Question (Not Kids Who Perform)
body:
I used to be proud that my children never doubted. They believed what I taught them, cleanly, without argument, and I took this as evidence that I was raising them well, that the faith was taking, that I had transmitted the truth successfully into the next generation. I have come to understand that I was proud of the very thing that would eventually break their faith, because a faith that has never been questioned is not strong. It is untested, and untested faith shatters on first contact with a hard question, and the hard questions always come.

There is a kind of Christian home that produces children who perform belief flawlessly and possess it not at all, and I was building one without knowing it. The child in that home has learned the right answers, the right posture, the right vocabulary, and has learned above all that questions are dangerous, that doubt is failure, that the way to keep the parents' approval and God's is to never let a hard question surface. And so the questions go underground, where they fester, until one day, usually around eighteen or twenty, they erupt, and the performed faith collapses all at once, because it was performance the whole time.

The Faith That Cannot Survive a Question

A faith that cannot survive being questioned is not being protected by our refusal to allow questions. It is being exposed as fragile. When we treat our children's doubts as threats to be shut down, as attacks to be repelled, as evidence of rebellion to be corrected, we teach them that the faith is a delicate thing that cannot bear scrutiny, and children are not stupid, they draw the obvious conclusion, that a belief which cannot be questioned is probably not true.

When you forbid the question, you do not protect the faith. You confirm the child's growing suspicion that the faith would not survive the question. Nothing makes doubt more corrosive than a parent who treats it as forbidden. The forbidding is the confession that we are afraid of the answer.

Contrast this with the God of the Bible, who is remarkably unafraid of questions. Job questions God for chapters, accuses him, demands an answer, and God's response is not to condemn the questioning but to answer it, at length, and then to say that Job spoke rightly, unlike his friends who defended God with tidy pieties. The psalmists question constantly. Thomas doubts and is not cast out but invited to touch the wounds. Jesus fields hostile questions his entire ministry and never once responds by forbidding the question. A God this comfortable with being questioned is not honored by parents who forbid their children to question. He is misrepresented by them.

It is worth sitting with the fact that God answered Job's friends more harshly than he answered Job. The friends did everything a certain kind of Christian parent praises. They defended God, they explained his ways, they refused to entertain the possibility that anything was wrong, they had an answer for every complaint. And God said they had not spoken rightly of him, while Job, who had shaken his fist at heaven and demanded an accounting, had. The honest questioner was closer to God than the confident defenders. If that is how God sorts the wrestlers from the reciters, we should be far more worried about raising reciters than we usually are.

The Difference Between Doubt and Rebellion

We have collapsed two different things into one category and called them both dangerous. Doubt and rebellion are not the same. Rebellion is a turning away from God with the will. Doubt is a wrestling toward God with the mind. And many of the children we accuse of rebellion when they start questioning are not rebelling at all. They are doing the necessary work of making the faith their own instead of merely inheriting it, and they are doing it out loud, in front of us, which is a sign of trust, and we punish the trust as though it were treason.

The child who questions in front of you is honoring you with their honesty. They could hide it. Many do, having learned that questions are unwelcome. The one who brings you the hard question, is the resurrection real, why does God allow suffering, how do we know the Bible is true, why do I have to believe what you believe, is handing you their genuine struggle and asking for help with it. And if we respond with alarm, defensiveness, or discipline, we teach them never to bring us a question again, and the questions do not stop, they just go somewhere we cannot help, which is the worst possible outcome for a parent who wants their child's faith to survive.

I am not pretending the distinction between doubt and rebellion is always clean, because sometimes it is not. Sometimes a child weaponizes doubt, using intellectual questions as a cover for a will that has already decided to do what it wants, and a discerning parent has to be able to tell the difference between a mind that is genuinely wrestling and a heart that is simply looking for permission. But here is what I have learned about telling them apart. You cannot sort the honest questioner from the manipulator by shutting down the questions, because that shuts down both, and drives the honest one into hiding while doing nothing to reach the rebellious one. You can only sort them by welcoming the question, engaging it seriously, and watching what happens. The genuine questioner leans in, wrestles, wants to keep talking. The one using doubt as a cover loses interest the moment the question is actually engaged, because they never wanted an answer, they wanted an exit. Welcome all the questions, and the honest ones will reveal themselves by their hunger, and the manipulative ones by their disinterest, and you will have learned something you could never have learned by forbidding the questions in the first place.

Why Performed Faith Collapses

The tragedy of raising children who perform rather than question is that the performance has an expiration date, and it is usually early adulthood. As long as the child is under our roof and our approval, the performed faith holds, because it is being sustained by our presence and expectations. But the moment they leave, the moment the external scaffolding of the Christian home is removed and they are genuinely free, the performed faith has nothing holding it up, because it was never internalized, it was only enacted, and it falls.

The child who was never allowed to question did not skip the questions. They deferred them. And deferred questions do not weaken with time. They compound. And when they finally come due, all at once, in a dorm room far from home, the faith that could not answer them in childhood cannot answer them now, and it goes.

This is the pattern behind so many stories of young adults abandoning the faith of their childhood. It is often narrated as if the world corrupted them, as if the university stole their faith, as if bad influences pulled them away. Sometimes. But frequently what actually happened is that a performed faith met the first serious question it was never allowed to face, and had no resources, because the resources are built by questioning and this child was never permitted to build them. The world did not take their faith. Their faith was hollow, and the world merely revealed it, and we made it hollow by forbidding the questions that would have made it real.

What Raising a Questioner Requires

Raising a child who questions requires a parent who is not threatened by the question, which requires a parent whose own faith is secure enough to sit with uncertainty. This is the hard part, because our reactions to our children's doubts usually reveal the state of our own. The parent who panics at a child's hard question is often a parent with the same unaddressed question buried in themselves, and the child has poked the wound. If I cannot bear my child's doubt, it is often because I have never made peace with my own.

So the work of raising a questioner begins with the parent's own faith becoming honest. It means being able to say, that is a real question, and I do not have a complete answer, and I have wrestled with it too, and here is what I have found, and here is what I am still not sure about. It means modeling a faith that includes uncertainty rather than pretending to a certainty we do not possess. Children can smell false certainty, and it teaches them that faith requires pretending to know what you do not know, which is a faith they will eventually and rightly reject. A faith honest about its own questions is far more transmissible than a faith that performs certainty it has not earned.

Sitting in the Question With Them

When one of my sons brought me a genuinely hard question, the temptation was always to resolve it quickly, to hand him an answer that would close the question and restore my comfort. I have learned that this is usually the wrong move. Often the more faithful response is to sit in the question with him, to take it seriously, to explore it honestly, to acknowledge its weight, and to resist the urge to prematurely tie it off with an answer that he can tell I reached for out of my own discomfort rather than out of the truth.

Because the goal is not to end the questioning. The goal is to raise a person who can hold hard questions and keep believing, who has learned that faith and questions coexist, who does not experience doubt as the end of faith but as part of its ordinary life. That person is far more durable than the one with all the answers memorized, because when the next question comes, and it will, they will not panic, they will do what they have always done, bring it into the light, wrestle it honestly, and keep walking. That capacity is the thing worth building, and it is built by welcoming questions, not forbidding them.

There is a real discipline in not answering too fast, and it runs against every parental instinct. When your child is troubled by a hard question about God, everything in you wants to relieve the trouble, because you love them and their distress is your distress. But the too-quick answer, even a true one, teaches the child that questions are problems to be eliminated rather than territory to be explored, and it robs them of the muscle they build by staying in the question long enough to find their own footing. Sometimes the most loving thing is to say, that is worth thinking hard about, let us not rush it, and to let the child sit in the discomfort of not-yet-knowing, with you beside them, which is the exact experience they will need to be able to survive when the questions come and you are not there.

The Faith I Actually Want to Leave Them

I came to faith out of atheism, as an adult, through hard questions, not around them. My faith was forged in exactly the kind of relentless questioning I spent years trying to prevent in my own children, which is one of the stranger inconsistencies of my parenting, that I gained my faith by questioning and then tried to give my children a faith that skipped the questioning. My own testimony should have taught me better. The questions did not destroy my atheism's certainties and then leave me with nothing. They carried me, through the wrestling, into a faith that could bear weight precisely because it had been tested.

There is a fear that stops parents from doing this, and I felt it acutely, so I want to name it plainly. The fear is that if you welcome the questions, you might lose the child, that a doubt engaged is a doubt strengthened, that by allowing the questioning you are opening a door the child might walk out of. I understand the fear because I lived inside it for years, and it is exactly backward. The child does not walk out through the door you open by engaging their doubts honestly. The child walks out through the door you slam, the one that tells them their questions are not welcome here, that this faith cannot bear their honesty, that they must choose between their integrity and their belonging. That slammed door is the exit. The open door, the one where a parent says bring me your hardest question and I will not flinch, is not an exit at all. It is the thing that keeps the child in the room, keeps the conversation going, keeps the relationship intact through the very years when so many are lost. You do not lose children by letting them question. You lose them by refusing to.

That is the faith I actually want to leave my sons, not the performed kind that impressed me when they were young, but the wrestled kind that will still be standing when they are fifty and the hard questions have come, as they always come. A faith that has been questioned and survived is not a weaker faith than one that has never been questioned. It is the only strong kind there is. The unquestioned faith is not strong. It is merely untested, and untested is not a virtue, it is a countdown. So I stopped being proud that my children never doubted, and started being grateful when they did, and started welcoming the questions I used to fear, because the questions are not the enemy of their faith. The forbidding of questions is. I forbade them for years. I am trying, now, to be the kind of father a hard question can be brought to, because that father is the one whose children's faith survives him. It is the only inheritance worth leaving, and it cannot be performed. It has to be true, and true things can be questioned, and survive.
excerpt: I used to be proud that my children never doubted. I have come to understand that I was proud of the very thing that would eventually break their faith.

title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
body:
There are two popular versions of the Bible's teaching on money, and both of them are wrong. The first says God wants you rich — that faith is an investment strategy and the Almighty is a venture capitalist who rewards spiritual performance with material returns. The second says money is inherently corrupt — that genuine discipleship requires voluntary poverty, that wealth itself is the sin, and that any Christian who accumulates more than subsistence has already betrayed the gospel. The prosperity gospel and the poverty gospel stand on opposite street corners, shouting past each other, each holding a handful of proof texts and ignoring the rest of the canon.

The actual biblical witness is more demanding than either alternative. It does not condemn wealth. It does not promise it. It treats money as a diagnostic instrument — a tool of extraordinary precision for revealing what you actually worship. And it does this from the first book to the last, with a consistency that should unsettle anyone who has reduced the Bible's economic teaching to a bumper sticker.

The Torah: Wealth as Covenant Gift

The economic theology of the Old Testament begins not with prohibition but with provision. Genesis 1 presents a God who creates abundance — a world teeming with life, resources distributed across the earth, human beings commissioned to cultivate and steward what has been given. The creation narrative is not ascetic. It does not regard the material world with suspicion. The refrain is not "be careful" but "it was good."

Deuteronomy 8 is the critical text, and it is almost never quoted in full by either side of the prosperity debate. Moses tells Israel that God is bringing them into a good land — a land with streams and springs, wheat and barley, olive oil and honey. "You will eat and be satisfied," he says, "and you will bless the Lord your God for the good land he has given you." This is unambiguous affirmation of material blessing. The prosperity preachers stop here. They should not.

The passage continues with a warning so severe it occupies more space than the promise: "Beware that you do not forget the Lord your God. When you have eaten and are satisfied, when you have built fine houses and settled down, when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all you have is multiplied — then your heart will become proud and you will forget the Lord your God." The danger is not wealth. The danger is the amnesia that wealth produces. You forget who gave it. You begin to believe your own hands produced it. And that forgetting is not a minor theological error. It is idolatry.

Craig Blomberg, in his exhaustive study Neither Poverty nor Riches, argues that the Torah's economic vision is structured around three interlocking principles: God owns everything, human beings are stewards of what has been entrusted, and the community bears collective responsibility for the vulnerable. The sabbatical year laws in Exodus 23 and Deuteronomy 15 — requiring debt cancellation every seven years — are not charitable suggestions. They are structural provisions designed to prevent the permanent concentration of wealth. The jubilee legislation in Leviticus 25, mandating the return of ancestral land every fifty years, goes further still. Whether or not Israel ever fully practiced jubilee is debated among scholars, but its theological function is clear: the land belongs to God, you are tenants, and no family can be permanently dispossessed.

This is not socialism. It is not capitalism. It is a theocentric economy in which property rights are real but limited, wealth is permitted but monitored, and the accumulation of resources at the expense of the poor is treated as a direct offense against the God who owns the vineyard.

The Prophets: Wealth as Indictment

If the Torah establishes the framework, the prophets enforce it. And they enforce it with a ferocity that should make every comfortable Western Christian deeply uneasy. Including me.

Amos, writing in the eighth century BC during a period of unprecedented Israelite prosperity under Jeroboam II, delivers the most sustained economic indictment in the Hebrew Bible. He does not attack wealth in the abstract. He names specific behaviors: selling the poor for a pair of sandals, trampling the heads of the needy, lying on beds of ivory while the nation crumbles. His targets are not pagans. They are the faithful — the people who attend the festivals, offer the sacrifices, sing the songs. "I hate, I despise your religious festivals," God says through Amos. "Away with the noise of your songs. But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream."

The prophetic critique is not that the wealthy are rich. It is that they are rich and religious simultaneously — that they have managed to worship God on the sabbath while exploiting the poor on Monday, and that they see no contradiction. Isaiah 58 makes the same point with devastating clarity: Israel asks why God does not respond to their fasting. God answers: because on the day of your fasting you exploit your workers. The worship is invalidated not by theological error but by economic behavior.

Justo Gonzalez, in Faith and Wealth, traces this prophetic thread through the intertestamental period and into the early church. He demonstrates that by the time of Jesus there existed a robust tradition — in the prophets, in the wisdom literature, in the apocalyptic writings — that linked economic justice to covenant fidelity. Jesus did not invent the connection between money and worship. He inherited it.

Jesus: The Most Uncomfortable Teacher

Jesus talked about money more than he talked about heaven and hell combined. This is not a rhetorical exaggeration. It is a textual fact that anyone with a concordance can verify. And what he said was not comforting.

Luke 6 gives the version of the Beatitudes that prosperity preachers avoid. Matthew softens the language to "poor in spirit." Luke does not. "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort." There is no interpretive escape hatch here. The poor are blessed. The rich are warned. And the warning is not conditional — it does not say woe to you who are rich and also happen to be greedy. It says woe to you who are rich.

The parable of the rich fool in Luke 12 is aimed at a man who has done nothing illegal. He is a successful farmer. His land produces abundantly. He decides to build bigger barns and enjoy his retirement. He is, by every modern financial-planning standard, a model citizen. And God calls him a fool — not because he stole, not because he cheated, but because he stored up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God. The sin is a horizon that ends at the self.

Then there is the rich young ruler, who kept every commandment and still walked away sorrowful when Jesus told him to sell what he had and give to the poor. It is the only recorded instance of someone rejecting a direct invitation from Jesus and being permitted to leave. Jesus does not chase him. He watches him go and says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples are astonished, which tells you they had not yet learned to soften the saying the way we have.

The Bible does not ask whether you have money. It asks whether your money has you. And that is a question the balance sheet cannot answer.

The Early Church: A Community That Shared

Acts 2 and 4 describe a community in which no one claimed that any of their possessions was their own. They had everything in common. Those who owned land or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles, and it was distributed to anyone who had need. This was not enforced by law. Ananias and Sapphira were not judged for keeping their property but for lying about it, for pretending to a generosity they did not have. The problem was hypocrisy, not private ownership. But the direction of the community is unmistakable. The gravitational pull of the gospel is toward open hands.

Paul organized a collection across the Gentile churches for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, and in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 he laid out a theology of giving that has almost nothing in common with modern fundraising. He appeals to the Macedonians, who gave out of extreme poverty and severe affliction, and he grounds the whole enterprise in the self-emptying of Christ: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich. Generosity is not a technique. It is a participation in the movement of the incarnation.

What This Means for a Tuesday Afternoon

I have preached on money for fifteen years, and I have watched my own heart flinch every time. It is easy to stand in a pulpit and denounce the rich when you have quietly decided that rich means the person with more than you. That is the oldest trick in the book, and I have used it. The prophetic word about wealth is not a weapon to aim at the people above you on the ladder. It is a mirror. It implicates the preacher first.

So here is the verdict, and it is not comfortable for me either. The Bible does not tell you how much money you are allowed to have. It tells you that whatever you have will testify against you or for you, and that the testimony will be economic before it is verbal. What you do with money is the most honest sermon you will ever preach. Your bank statement is a spiritual autobiography. It records, line by line, what you feared, what you loved, whom you forgot, and whom you saw.

You cannot serve God and money. Jesus said it plainly, and he used the word serve, which means slave. There is no arrangement in which both are masters. One will be Lord and the other will be tool. The question the Bible presses on every one of us, and it presses hardest on those of us who preach, is which is which. And you will not answer that question with your mouth. You will answer it with your checkbook, quietly, over the course of a life, and the answer will be true.

The Wisdom Literature: Money Without Illusions

Between the Torah and the prophets sits a body of literature that treats money with an almost startling realism, and it is the part of the Bible most likely to disorient someone who has reduced the subject to a slogan. Proverbs praises diligence and warns against sloth; it commends the accumulation of resources through honest labor and treats poverty caused by laziness as folly. There is no romanticizing of destitution here. And yet the same book, sometimes on the same page, warns that the pursuit of riches is a snare, that the rich man's wealth is his imagined fortress, that a good name is worth more than great riches, and that the one who trusts in his wealth will fall.

Agur's prayer in Proverbs 30 is the wisdom tradition's most honest word on the subject, and it is almost never preached: "Give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread. Otherwise I may have too much and disown you and say, Who is the Lord? Or I may become poor and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God." Here is a man who understands that both wealth and want carry spiritual danger — that riches tempt toward self-sufficiency and forgetting God, while poverty tempts toward theft and despair. He asks for enough. Craig Blomberg titled his study after this prayer for good reason: neither poverty nor riches, but daily bread, is the wisdom tradition's answer to the money question, and it undercuts both the prosperity gospel and the poverty gospel at a single stroke.

Ecclesiastes goes further still, pressing on the futility of accumulation with a bleakness that most Christian teaching cannot bear. The Preacher has everything — wealth, projects, pleasure, achievement beyond any of his predecessors — and he finds it all vapor, a chasing after wind. He notices that he must leave everything to someone who did not work for it, and who may be a fool. He observes that the sleep of the laborer is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich permits him no sleep. This is not a rejection of work or wealth; the Preacher commends enjoying the fruit of one's labor as a gift from God. But it is a savage deflation of the idea that accumulation can satisfy. Money cannot fill the hole it promises to fill, and the wisdom literature says so with a candor the modern church rarely matches.

James: The Prophet Returns

The letter of James picks up the prophetic thread and carries it directly into the church, refusing to let the New Testament soften the Old Testament's economic edge. James warns the rich who oppress their workers that the wages they have failed to pay are crying out, and that the cries have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty — an almost verbatim echo of the prophetic tradition. He rebukes the church for showing favoritism to the wealthy visitor and dishonoring the poor. He insists that faith without works is dead, and the works he has in mind are explicitly economic: clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, caring for widows and orphans in their distress.

James is the bridge that proves the economic teaching of the Bible is one continuous stream from Amos to the apostles. The gospel did not spiritualize away the concern for money and the poor; it intensified it. The community formed by the death and resurrection of Christ was to be marked, more than anything, by a radically different relationship to wealth — open-handed, generous, indifferent to status, oriented toward the vulnerable. Where the church has failed to be marked this way, it has not merely fallen short of an ideal. It has departed from the plain and consistent teaching of the book it claims to obey.
excerpt: The Bible neither baptizes wealth nor canonizes poverty — it treats money as a diagnostic instrument that reveals, with unbearable precision, what you actually worship.

title: The Theology of Work
body:
Ask most Christians why they work and you will get one of two answers. The first is grim resignation: work is a necessary evil, the price of keeping the lights on, the thing you do so you can afford the things you actually want to do. The second is only slightly better: work is where you witness, a mission field disguised as a cubicle, the value of which lies entirely in the evangelistic conversations it might produce over the coffee machine. Neither answer takes the work itself seriously. Both treat the eight hours a day you spend laboring as spiritually neutral at best, spiritually contaminating at worst.

This is a theological failure, and it is a recent one. The Bible does not treat work as a curse to be endured or a stage for something more important. It treats work as one of the primary ways human beings image God. Recovering that conviction is not a productivity hack. It changes what a Tuesday means.

The First Worker

Genesis introduces God as a worker before it introduces God as anything else. The opening act of Scripture is labor — God speaking, forming, separating, filling, ordering. The Hebrew verbs are the verbs of craftsmanship. And when God makes human beings in his image, the very first commission he gives them is a job: fill the earth, subdue it, have dominion, cultivate the garden. Work precedes the fall. It is not the consequence of sin. It is the shape of unfallen humanity.

This matters enormously, because if work is a pre-fall reality, then work is intrinsic to what it means to be human, not a penalty imposed after the trouble started. Adam is put in the garden to work it and keep it before the serpent ever appears. Dorothy Sayers, in her essay Why Work?, argued that the medieval church understood this better than we do — that work was seen as a way of glorifying God through the making of good things, and that the modern division between sacred and secular labor would have baffled a stonemason building a cathedral he would never live to see finished.

What the fall did to work was not create it but corrupt it. Genesis 3 tells us the ground is now cursed, that work will involve thorns and thistles and sweat. The frustration is real. The futility is real. Anyone who has ever watched a project collapse, a business fail, a report get buried, knows the thorns are not a metaphor. But the frustration is a distortion of a good thing, not the thing itself. Work was good, then it was broken, and the gospel is in the business of restoration.

Vocation and the Priesthood of All Believers

The recovery of a robust theology of work is one of the great achievements of the Reformation, and it is one the Protestant church has quietly abandoned. Luther attacked the medieval assumption that the monastery was a higher calling than the farm. He insisted that the milkmaid and the magistrate and the merchant were doing holy work when they did their work faithfully — that vocation was not reserved for the clergy but distributed across every honest station of life. "The works of monks and priests," he wrote, "however holy and arduous they may be, do not differ one whit in the sight of God from the works of the rustic laborer in the field or the woman going about her household tasks."

This was revolutionary, and it is worth pausing on how far the modern church has drifted from it. We have re-clericalized the calling. We speak of "full-time ministry" as though it were the premier league and everything else were the minor leagues. We invite the missionary to the front of the church and pray over him and send him out, and we do not do the same for the accountant, the nurse, the electrician, the schoolteacher. We have communicated, without ever saying it directly, that the real Christians go into ministry and the rest support them.

We tell people their work is a mission field. We rarely tell them their work is a form of worship. The difference is the whole gospel.

I have been guilty of this from the pulpit. I have prayed publicly for the people going overseas and forgotten the people going to the office, and in doing so I taught my congregation that God cares more about the sermon than the spreadsheet. That is not the theology of Genesis. It is the theology of a church that has confused the platform with the kingdom.

Work as Neighbor-Love

Here is where the theology of work becomes concrete and stops being abstract. The Reformers understood vocation not primarily as self-fulfillment but as service to the neighbor. Gene Veith, in God at Work, develops this beautifully: the way God feeds the hungry is through the farmer and the grocer and the trucker. The way God heals the sick is through the doctor and the researcher and the janitor who keeps the hospital clean. The way God protects the vulnerable is through the police officer and the social worker and the attorney. Your work is the mask of God — the means through which the Creator continues to provide for a world he has not abandoned.

This reframes the most ordinary labor. The barista is not merely selling coffee; she is a channel through which a tired person receives a small mercy. The programmer is not merely writing code; he is building a tool that will let someone else do their work more faithfully. The garbage collector is doing work without which the city would become uninhabitable. When you begin to see your labor as the way God loves your neighbor through your hands, the question of whether your job is "spiritual" dissolves. All honest work that serves the neighbor is spiritual, because God is the one working through it.

The Problem of Meaningless Work

But we have to be honest, because a theology of work that only celebrates the meaningful jobs is a theology for the fortunate. Much modern work is not obviously ennobling. Some of it is tedious, some of it is exploitative, some of it exists only to generate profit for people the worker will never meet. The person stocking shelves at three in the morning, the worker on the assembly line performing the same motion ten thousand times a shift, the employee whose entire job is to make a wealthy company slightly wealthier — where is the dignity there?

The New Testament speaks directly into this, and it does so from the underside. Paul addresses slaves in Colossians 3 and tells them to work as for the Lord and not for men. This is not an endorsement of slavery, which Paul elsewhere undermines. It is a claim that even labor performed under the most degrading conditions, for a master who does not deserve loyalty, can be offered to God and received by God. The worth of the work is not determined by the worth of the employer. If a first-century slave could work as unto the Lord, then the exhausted retail worker and the underpaid caregiver can too. Their labor is seen by the one who matters, even when it is invisible to everyone else.

This is not a reason to accept exploitation. The same Bible that tells slaves to work faithfully tells masters that they too have a Master in heaven, and it tells the church to defend the wages of the laborer. Naming the dignity of work does not require pretending that all working conditions are just. It requires insisting that the worker's worth survives the injustice.

Rest as the Frame of Work

A theology of work is incomplete without a theology of rest, and this is where the modern Christian, and the modern pastor, most needs correction. The same God who worked six days rested on the seventh and commanded his people to do the same. The sabbath is a declaration that your worth is not your output. You are not a machine whose value is measured in production. You are a creature loved before you have accomplished anything, and the weekly cessation of labor is a physical rehearsal of that truth.

I struggle with this more than anything else in my own life. The pastor's work is never finished; there is always another visit, another sermon, another crisis. And I have used the language of calling to justify a functional atheism in which I behave as though the church will collapse if I stop. It will not. God ran the universe before I was born and will run it after I am gone. My rest is not laziness. It is confession. It confesses that God is God and I am not, and that the work is finally his.

The Cultural Mandate and the Great Commission

There is a debate that runs quietly beneath the theology of work, and it concerns whether ordinary labor has any lasting significance or is merely a temporary necessity until the return of Christ. The pietist instinct treats work as scaffolding — useful for now, but to be torn down and discarded when the real building, the spiritual kingdom, is complete. On this view, the only thing that survives from your working life is the souls you led to Christ; the buildings, the discoveries, the cultivated fields, the good work itself, all burns. This is a widespread assumption, and it drains ordinary work of ultimate meaning.

But the Bible's vision of the end is not a bonfire that consumes the material world; it is a renewal of it. The new creation is not a disembodied heaven but a redeemed earth, a city, with the glory and honor of the nations brought into it. Isaiah pictures a restored world where people build houses and inhabit them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and do not labor in vain. There is work in the new creation, and there is continuity between the labor of now and the world to come. This means your work is not merely scaffolding. In ways we cannot fully trace, the good you make participates in a creation that God intends not to destroy but to renew. The cultural mandate of Genesis and the great commission of Matthew are not rivals. They are two commissions to one people, and neither cancels the other.

The Idol of Work

Having said all this in praise of work, honesty requires the counterweight, because the same work that can be worship can become an idol, and in our culture it is the most respectable idol of all. Timothy Keller observed that work is one of the most common places modern people look for the significance and identity that only God can provide. We ask our careers to tell us we matter, to justify our existence, to give us a name. And work, being a good gift and not a god, cannot bear that weight. It collapses under it, and takes us down with it.

The symptoms are everywhere: the person who cannot rest, who checks messages on vacation, who feels worthless when a project fails, whose whole sense of self rises and falls with performance reviews and quarterly results. This is not diligence. It is idolatry, and it is destroying people who would never bow to a carved image but bow every day to their own achievement. The theology of work must include this warning, or it becomes fuel for the very workaholism it should heal. Good work offered to God is worship. Good work demanded to justify you is a false god that will consume everything you feed it and still leave you hungry.

The Excellence Question

If work is worship, then the quality of the work matters in a way we rarely connect to our faith. Dorothy Sayers made this point with characteristic sharpness: the church has spent centuries telling the carpenter not to get drunk and not to cheat his customers, and almost no time telling him to make good tables. But a shoddy table is a kind of blasphemy for the Christian, because it offers to God and neighbor something less than our best in work that is supposed to be an offering. The first demand that Christianity makes on any worker, she argued, is not that they preach at their bench but that they do good work at it.

This reframes excellence as a spiritual matter rather than a merely professional one. The Christian mechanic who does careful, honest work is worshiping through the wrench; the one who cuts corners and does slapdash work is dishonoring God through the same tool, whatever they say about their faith on Sunday. The work itself is the offering, and God is not honored by an offering thrown together carelessly. This does not mean every Christian must be the best in their field, which is impossible, but it does mean the Christian brings a particular integrity to their labor, a refusal to do bad work, because the work is being done, at the deepest level, unto the Lord. The competence of a believer's work is part of their witness, and often a louder part than their words.

Work and the Body of Christ

There is a final dimension that the individualism of modern work culture obscures: work is meant to be woven into a body, not performed in isolation. The New Testament's vision of the church as a body with many members, each contributing a different function, is fundamentally a vision of interdependent labor. No member does everything; each does their part; and the whole depends on all the parts working together. This is a picture of work as it was meant to be — diverse callings, mutually dependent, contributing to a common good larger than any individual.

Our economy has largely stripped this out, atomizing work into isolated individual careers pursued for individual advancement. But the Christian recovers the truth that their work is part of something larger, that they labor not merely for themselves but as one member serving the whole, that the electrician and the teacher and the nurse and the farmer are all doing their part in a vast web of interdependent service through which God provides for his world. This is dignifying and humbling at once: dignifying, because your work matters to the whole; humbling, because you are not the whole, only a member, and the body does not depend on you alone. To work as a member of the body is to work without the crushing burden of self-importance and without the diminishment of self-contempt, taking your place in a larger service that God is orchestrating.

So work. Work hard, work well, work as the way God loves the person on the other end of your labor. But do not make work your identity, because it is not strong enough to hold you. Work is worship when it is offered to God and rest when it is surrendered to God, and both are needed, and the one who cannot rest has not yet understood who is actually running the world.
excerpt: Work is not a curse we endure to fund the parts of life that matter. It is a form of worship, a participation in God's ongoing creation — and the modern church has almost entirely forgotten how to say so.

title: Tithing: Command, Principle, or Guilt Trip?
body:
Somewhere in the life of nearly every churchgoing Christian there is a low-grade, chronic guilt about the tithe. You know the number — ten percent — and you know you are probably not hitting it, and you know the pastor is going to preach on stewardship sometime around the fall budget season, and you brace for it the way you brace for a dentist appointment. The tithe has become one of the great sources of ambient shame in the Christian financial imagination. And the strange thing is that almost no one can actually tell you where the ten percent comes from, whether it is binding, or what it is supposed to mean.

So let us do the thing the guilt prevents us from doing. Let us actually look at what the Bible says about the tithe, and let us be honest about where the conventional teaching is standing on solid ground and where it is standing on nothing at all.

The Old Testament Tithe Was Not What You Think

Start with the surprise. The tithe in the Old Testament was not a single ten percent. It was a system of multiple tithes that, taken together, amounted to something closer to twenty or twenty-three percent of annual produce. There was the Levitical tithe that supported the priestly tribe who had no land inheritance. There was the festival tithe that funded the annual pilgrimages and feasts. And there was a third-year tithe stored in the towns to feed the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the Levite. The tithe was fundamentally agricultural, tied to the produce of the land and the increase of the flocks, and it functioned as something like a combined religious tax and social welfare system for the covenant nation.

This complicates the modern sermon considerably. When a pastor stands up and says "the Bible commands you to tithe ten percent of your income," he is compressing a complex, multi-layered agricultural system into a single number and applying it to a wage economy the Torah never envisioned. That does not make the compression illegitimate, but it should make the preacher humble about how directly he can wield the word command. I have preached the ten percent as though it fell from heaven with a decimal point already attached. It did not.

Abraham and Jacob: Before the Law

The tithe predates the law of Moses, which is the strongest argument that it reflects something more permanent than the Sinai covenant. Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek in Genesis 14, a spontaneous act of worship after a military victory, long before there was any commandment requiring it. Jacob, fleeing his brother, vowed at Bethel that if God brought him home safely he would give God a tenth of everything.

These two episodes are the favorite proof texts of the pro-tithing preacher, and they carry real weight, but notice what they actually show. Both are voluntary. Both are responses to grace already received — Abraham to victory, Jacob to a promise. Neither is a religious tax paid under obligation. They establish that giving God a proportion of what you have is an ancient instinct of worship. They do not establish that the proportion is legally fixed at ten percent for all people in all times.

Jesus and the Tithe

Here is the text that gets left out of the stewardship sermon. In Matthew 23, Jesus rebukes the Pharisees: "You give a tenth of your spices — mint, dill and cumin. But you have neglected the more important matters of the law — justice, mercy and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former." This is the only place Jesus directly addresses the tithe, and it is a stunning statement. He affirms the tithe — you should have practiced the former — while making clear that it is the least of the commandments, a matter so minor that a person can scrupulously obey it while missing the entire point of the law.

The Pharisees tithed their herb garden and swallowed injustice whole. Jesus did not tell them to stop tithing. He told them the tithe had become a way of not loving anyone.

This is the danger the tithe carries, and it is a danger I have watched play out in my own congregation and my own heart. The number becomes a ceiling instead of a floor. You write the check, you cross the line, you feel the small warm glow of obligation discharged, and you close your hand around the remaining ninety percent as though it were now entirely and unquestionably yours. But the New Testament nowhere teaches that ninety percent is yours. It teaches that one hundred percent is God's, and that you are a steward of all of it.

The New Testament's Silence and Its Meaning

The most important fact about the tithe in the New Testament is how little it appears. Paul, who wrote more about money and giving than any other apostle, never once commands the tithe. When he takes up the great collection for Jerusalem in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, he does not say "remember your ten percent." He says something both freer and more terrifying: "Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." And in 1 Corinthians 16 he asks each person to set aside a sum in keeping with their income — proportional, but not fixed.

Some read this silence as liberation: the tithe is abolished, give whatever you feel like. But that reading gets the direction exactly backward. The New Testament does not lower the bar below the tithe. It removes the bar and replaces it with the whole of your life. Under the old covenant you owed ten percent and the rest was, in a sense, negotiable. Under the new covenant you owe everything, because you have been bought with a price and you are not your own. The tithe was a training-wheel proportion for a people learning to give. The gospel invites you off the training wheels into a generosity with no ceiling at all.

So Should You Tithe?

Here is where I have landed after fifteen years of preaching this, and I offer it as a pastor rather than a lawyer. The ten percent is not a New Testament command, and any preacher who tells you it is has overstated his case. But it is an extraordinarily wise starting place. It is a proportion old enough to predate the law and specific enough to be actionable, and it forces a question that vaguer instructions let us dodge. If you tell people to give as their heart decides, most hearts will decide on very little, because the heart is an accomplished self-deceiver, and mine is the most accomplished of all.

So I teach the tithe not as law but as trellis — a structure to grow on. For the person who has never given systematically, ten percent is a bracing and clarifying goal that will reorder your finances and expose your idols faster than any sermon. For the person who has been giving faithfully for years, ten percent may be far too low, a comfortable plateau you have long since outgrown, and the honest question is not whether you are tithing but whether you are still being stretched.

The Guilt Question

What about the guilt? The chronic, low-grade shame that the word tithe produces in so many faithful people? I want to name it directly, because I do not think it comes from God. Guilt that drives you toward generosity as an escape from condemnation is not gospel motivation; it is precisely the compulsion Paul rejects. God does not want your ten percent extracted from you by fear. He wants your heart, and the giving is meant to follow the heart, not manufacture it.

If you are giving out of guilt, the problem is not that you are giving too little. The problem is that you have not yet believed the gospel deeply enough to give freely. The cure is not a larger check written in the same spirit. The cure is to sit long enough under the fact that Christ became poor for you, that everything you have is already grace, that you cannot buy God's approval because it has already been given, until the check stops being a payment and becomes a thank-you. A person who truly believes she has received everything does not tithe reluctantly. She gives, and gives past the tithe, and wonders why she waited so long, and cannot imagine going back.

The Malachi Problem

No conversation about tithing can avoid the one text that dominates every stewardship sermon: Malachi 3, where God says through the prophet, "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse. Test me in this, and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing that there will not be room enough to store it." This is the verse printed on the offering envelope, quoted from the platform, wielded as the clincher. And it is almost always misused.

Read in context, Malachi is addressing a specific covenant people under a specific covenant, accusing them of robbing God by withholding the tithes and offerings that supported the temple and the Levites. It is a national indictment of covenant unfaithfulness, not a universal formula for personal financial return. When it is ripped out of that context and turned into a promise that individual Christians who tithe will receive material blessing, it becomes a soft form of the prosperity gospel — give to get, tithe as investment strategy, God as the guarantor of your financial upside. That is not what Malachi teaches, and the preacher who uses it that way has traded the text's actual meaning for a fundraising slogan. God is not a vending machine, and the tithe is not a coin you insert to trigger a payout.

This does not empty Malachi of meaning. It genuinely does indict the withholding heart, the heart that clutches what belongs to God and calls it prudence. But the blessing Malachi promises is covenant faithfulness restored, not a guaranteed return on a religious investment. I have preached this verse badly, leaning on its promise of overflow because it moved people to give, and in doing so I taught them to give for the wrong reason and to expect the wrong reward. The honest use of Malachi confronts the robbery without promising the payout.

Giving as Warfare Against the Self

Underneath the whole tithing debate lies a truth that both sides tend to miss: the primary beneficiary of your giving is not the church. It is you. Giving is spiritual warfare against the most stubborn enemy you will ever face, which is your own grasping heart. Every time you release money that your instincts scream at you to keep, you strike a blow against the idol of mammon that wants to rule you. The tithe, whatever its precise status as command or principle, is training in that warfare — a disciplined, repeated act of loosening your grip on the thing you most want to hold.

This is why the question is finally not whether the ten percent is legally binding but whether you are being changed. A person can give the exact tithe for forty years and remain as tightfisted and anxious as the day they started, because the giving never touched the heart. And a person can give with such freedom and joy that the money means nothing next to the God who gave it all. The number is a starting place. The transformation is the point. Give, then — begin with the tithe if you have no better starting place — but give in order to be freed, and keep giving until the day comes when you cannot remember why you ever found it hard.

Where the Money Goes

A question that the tithing debate usually neglects is where the tithe should actually go, and it matters more than we admit. The default assumption in most churches is that the tithe belongs entirely to the local congregation — that giving to the church budget is what tithing means. But the Old Testament tithe supported not only the religious institution but the poor, the foreigner, the vulnerable. The third-year tithe was specifically for the destitute. To reduce the tithe to funding the local church's budget, much of which goes to buildings and staff, is to narrow something that Scripture kept broad.

This does not mean you should stop supporting your church, which needs resources to do its work. It means the biblical vision of proportional giving was always wider than the offering plate — encompassing the poor, the work of mission, the care of the vulnerable — and that a healthy giving life reflects that breadth. The person who gives faithfully to their church and never gives directly to the poor has captured only part of the picture. The tithe, in its fullest biblical sense, was always partly for the least of these, and our giving is impoverished when it forgets them.

Teaching Children to Give

One of the most lasting things a parent can do about money is to teach their children to give before the culture teaches them to accumulate, and this is where the practical wisdom of the tithe becomes a gift rather than a burden. A child who learns early to set aside a portion of every gift and every earning for God and for others is being formed in a habit that will guard them for life against the grasping that captures almost everyone else. The specific proportion matters less than the pattern: giving first, giving regularly, giving as a normal and joyful part of how one relates to money.

I have watched this formation take root, and I have watched its absence. The child raised to give grows into an adult for whom generosity is second nature, who does not have to overcome a lifetime of accumulation to open their hand. The child raised only to save and spend grows into an adult who finds giving painful and unnatural, who must fight against decades of formation every time they release a dollar. If the tithe is finally a trellis for growing generous people, there is no better time to set up the trellis than in childhood, when the vine is young and can be trained toward open hands from the start.
excerpt: The ten percent has become a Christian shibboleth few can defend from the New Testament and most give reluctantly. The truth is stranger and more demanding than the number.

title: Debt and the Christian
body:
The average American household carries thousands of dollars in credit card debt, tens of thousands in auto loans, and often hundreds of thousands in mortgage and student debt. We have built an entire economy on the assumption that you will buy things you cannot afford with money you do not have and pay for them slowly, with interest, over years. Debt is not a moral failing in this system. It is the system. And Christians have absorbed it as thoroughly as everyone else, which raises a question we rarely ask honestly: what does the Bible actually say about owing money, and does it have anything to say to a person drowning in it?

The answer is more nuanced than the two loud extremes suggest. There is a fringe teaching that all debt is sin, that a faithful Christian would never borrow, that a mortgage is a mark of unbelief. And there is the far more common practical assumption, held by most of us who would never say it aloud, that debt is simply a neutral financial tool with no spiritual dimension whatsoever. Both are wrong, and the space between them is where the biblical wisdom lives.

What the Bible Says and Does Not Say

The Bible never flatly prohibits borrowing. The law of Moses assumes that lending and borrowing will happen and regulates them rather than banning them. Deuteronomy anticipates that Israelites will lend to one another and legislates the sabbatical cancellation of those debts. Jesus assumes borrowing in his parables. So the position that all debt is sin cannot be sustained from the text. It reads a personal preference back into Scripture.

But the Bible is deeply wary of debt, and it says so plainly. Proverbs 22 states it as a proverb, which is to say as observed wisdom rather than absolute law: "The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender." That single sentence contains the whole biblical concern. Debt is not primarily a financial arrangement. It is a power relationship. It transfers a portion of your freedom to another party. The borrower is not the master of his own future; part of his future is already spoken for, already owed, already mortgaged to someone else's claim.

Debt does not merely cost you money. It costs you options. And the loss of options is the loss of a certain kind of freedom that the gospel means to give you.

This is why Paul, in Romans 13, writes "let no debt remain outstanding, except the continuing debt to love one another." He immediately spiritualizes the financial language — the one debt you should always carry is love — but the choice of metaphor is telling. He treats freedom from obligation as the normal Christian condition and love as the single exception, the one debt you can never fully pay off and should never want to.

The Interest Question

There is a long and largely forgotten Christian tradition on the subject of interest that would astonish most modern believers. For over a thousand years the church regarded charging interest on loans — usury — as a grave sin. The Old Testament forbade Israelites from charging interest to their poor countrymen. The church fathers thundered against it. Basil, Ambrose, and later Aquinas all condemned lending at interest as a way of profiting from another person's need, a way of selling time itself, which belongs to God.

We have quietly discarded this entire tradition, and mostly for good reasons — a modern productive economy genuinely depends on credit in ways an ancient agrarian one did not, and there is a real difference between lending capital to a business that will multiply it and lending bread to a starving neighbor at twenty percent. But we should not discard the tradition without noticing what it was protecting. The concern was always the exploitation of desperation. The predatory lender, the payday loan operation charging four hundred percent to people with no other options, the credit card company profiting most from the customers least able to pay — these are the direct descendants of the usury the church once condemned, and the church's silence about them is not neutrality. It is complicity.

The Two Kinds of Debt

It helps to distinguish, as the Bible implicitly does, between debt that funds consumption and debt that funds production. Borrowing to buy something that loses value and produces nothing — the vacation you cannot afford, the newer car to replace a working one, the lifestyle you finance because you cannot bear to wait — is the debt that most resembles the slavery Proverbs warns about. It mortgages your future to your present appetite. It is the financial expression of a heart that cannot delay gratification, and delayed gratification is very close to the center of what discipleship is.

Borrowing to acquire something that produces value or meets a genuine need — a home you will live in for decades, an education that will let you serve, tools for a trade — sits in a different category. It is not automatically righteous, but it is not obviously foolish either. Even here the biblical wariness applies: how much, at what risk, with what margin for the unexpected. But the distinction matters. Not all debt is equal, and a theology that treats the mortgage and the credit card binge identically is not being biblical. It is being lazy.

The Spiritual Weight of Debt

I want to speak now to the person actually carrying debt that is crushing them, because the theological discussion means nothing if it does not reach that person. Debt is not just a number on a statement. It is a weight you carry into every room. It changes your marriage, because money conflict is one of the great destroyers of marriages and debt is money conflict compounded. It changes your prayers, because it is very hard to trust God for your daily bread when you are already forty thousand dollars behind. It changes your capacity to be generous, to say yes to a calling, to take a risk for the kingdom, because your options are already spent.

And it produces shame — a private, isolating shame that keeps people from telling anyone, including their pastor, that they are in trouble. I have sat across from people who could confess an affair more easily than they could confess their debt, because the affair felt like a moral failure that grace could cover and the debt felt like proof of stupidity, of being a bad and foolish person, and they could not bear to say it out loud.

Hear this clearly: your debt is not your identity, and getting into it does not make you unlovable. Most people in debt got there through some combination of hard circumstance, cultural pressure, poor teaching, and ordinary human weakness, and God is not standing over your statement with a red pen. He knows the number. He knew it before you did. And he is not surprised, and he is not finished with you.

The Way Out

The path out of debt is not spiritual in the sense of mystical; it is spiritual in the sense of costly. It requires the two hardest disciplines in the Christian life applied to money: honesty and self-denial. Honesty means looking at the actual numbers, telling someone you trust the truth, ending the pretense. Self-denial means spending less than you make for long enough to reverse the direction, which will feel, in a culture built on consumption, like a kind of death. Because it is. It is a small daily death to the appetite that got you here, and the Christian life has always been about that particular death leading somewhere.

Do not do it alone. The isolation is part of the bondage, and confession is part of the freedom. Tell someone. Get help — from a counselor, a program, a wiser friend, a pastor who will not shame you. And do it not to earn God's love but because you already have it, and because the God who owns the cattle on a thousand hills does not want his children enslaved to the lender when he has already paid the only debt that could not be paid.

The Debt That Was Paid

There is a reason the New Testament reaches so instinctively for the language of debt when it describes what Christ accomplished, and it is worth dwelling on, because it changes how a Christian in financial debt understands their situation before God. Sin, in the Scriptures, is repeatedly figured as a debt — something owed that cannot be paid, an obligation that accumulates and enslaves. The Lord's Prayer itself, in its most literal rendering, asks God to forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. Paul writes that the record of debt that stood against us, with its legal demands, was nailed to the cross and cancelled. The cross is, among other things, the payment of an unpayable debt.

This means the Christian struggling under financial debt lives inside a gospel whose central image is precisely the cancellation of a debt they could never have cleared themselves. The One who forgave your infinite debt is not standing over your finite one with contempt. He knows what it is to see an obligation that cannot be met, and he knows the freedom of having it cancelled by another's payment. Your financial debt is real and must be dealt with, but it does not touch your standing before God, because the only debt that could have condemned you has already been paid in full. You can face the credit card statement as a forgiven person, and that changes everything about the shame.

The Discipline of Enough

The most effective long-term defense against debt is not a budgeting technique; it is a converted appetite. Most consumer debt is the financial residue of an inability to be content, a chronic reaching for more than we have because we have absorbed the culture's teaching that we are what we own and that more will finally be enough. The person who has learned the discipline of enough — who can look at what they have and say, this is sufficient, I do not need the newer thing to be whole — is largely immune to the trap that catches everyone else.

This is where the theology of contentment meets the practical problem of debt. Paul learned to be content in plenty and in want, and that contentment was a wall against the endless wanting that drives people into bondage. A Christian who is genuinely content is a Christian who is very hard to sell things to, and being hard to sell things to is, in a consumer economy built on debt, a form of freedom. The way out of debt is partly arithmetic and partly appetite. Fix the arithmetic, yes. But do not neglect the appetite, because if the appetite that created the debt is not converted, no amount of arithmetic will keep you free. The borrower is slave to the lender, and the deepest slavery is not to the bank but to the wanting that sent you to the bank in the first place.

When the Debt Is Not Your Fault

I have written so far as though debt were primarily a matter of appetite and choice, and for many people it is. But honesty requires acknowledging that a great deal of crushing debt is not the result of consumer weakness at all. Medical debt from an illness no one chose. Debt taken on to survive a job loss or a family crisis. The debt of the person who did everything right and was still caught by circumstances beyond their control — a collapsing economy, a betrayal, a catastrophe. To speak of all debt as though it were the fruit of undisciplined wanting is to add cruelty to injury for the many whose debt came upon them like a storm they did not summon.

For that person, the word is different, and it needs to be spoken clearly. Your debt is not evidence of your failure or your foolishness. It is evidence that you live in a fallen world where hard things happen to faithful people, and God does not read your balance sheet as a verdict on your character. The same wisdom about honesty, help, and steady steps toward freedom applies to you, but without the layer of shame that the appetite-driven debtor may need to face. You did not sin your way into this. You were caught by it. And the God who provides is no less committed to walking with you toward freedom because your debt arrived through circumstance rather than choice. Do not let anyone, including yourself, add false guilt to a burden that is already heavy enough.

Lending as the Church

There is one more dimension to the Christian and debt that we almost never consider, and it turns the whole question around: the church's role not as borrower but as a community that could keep its own people out of the hands of predatory lenders. The Old Testament envisioned a community that lent to its poor without interest, that cancelled debts, that would not let a brother or sister fall permanently into the debt-slavery the surrounding cultures accepted as normal. The early church shared so completely that there was no destitute person among them driven to borrow at ruinous rates.

What if the church recovered even a fraction of this? What if a congregation refused to let its own members fall into the clutches of the payday lender charging four hundred percent, and instead met the emergency need directly, generously, without interest, as an act of family? This is not fantasy; some churches do it. It requires seeing the debt of the person beside you not as their private problem but as a claim on the community, the way the biblical vision always did. The church cannot fix the whole debt economy. But it could ensure that no one within its own fellowship is handed over to the lender when the family of God has the resources to help. That would be a small jubilee, and it is entirely within reach.
excerpt: The Bible does not forbid debt outright, but it treats it with a wariness the modern economy has taught us to forget — because debt is not merely financial. It is a form of bondage that shapes the soul.

title: Generosity Beyond the Offering Plate
body:
Ask a churchgoing Christian whether they are generous and the mind goes immediately to the offering plate. Do I give to the church, and how much, and how consistently. That is the whole picture, more or less. Generosity has become, in the Christian imagination, a synonym for the weekly or monthly gift to the local congregation. And while that giving matters — it funds the ministry, it is a genuine act of worship, it is not to be minimized — the reduction of generosity to that single channel is one of the ways we have domesticated a wild biblical idea into a manageable line item.

The generosity the Bible describes is not a transaction. It is a temperament. It is not a category of spending but a way of holding everything you have — loosely, gratefully, ready to be spent on someone else. And when you recover that larger vision, the offering plate takes its proper place as one expression of a generous life rather than the entirety of it.

The Generous God

Christian generosity is not a strategy for self-improvement or a technique for church growth. It is imitation. The entire logic of New Testament giving flows from the character of a God who gives. "God so loved the world that he gave." "He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all — how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things." "Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights." The universe, in Christian understanding, is not a closed system of scarcity but the overflow of a giving God. Grace means gift. The gospel is the announcement that the most generous act in history has already occurred.

This means generosity is not fundamentally about what you do with your money. It is about whether you resemble your Father. A stingy Christian is a contradiction not because stinginess violates a rule but because it misrepresents the family. When you give freely, you are not earning anything. You are advertising something. You are showing the watching world what God is like.

Beyond the Financial

The New Testament vision of generosity extends well past money, and this is where the offering-plate reduction fails most obviously. The most generous people I have known were not always the wealthiest. They were the ones who gave things money cannot buy: time, attention, hospitality, presence, forgiveness. The single mother who has almost nothing to give financially may be more generous than the executive who tithes precisely because she gives her exhaustion away — sitting with the grieving neighbor when she herself is running on empty.

You can tithe your income and hoard your life. You can write a generous check and be miserly with your attention. God is after both, and the second is harder.

Hospitality is generosity of home — opening your table and your space to people who cannot repay you, which is precisely the kind of guest Jesus tells us to invite. Mercy is generosity of judgment — refusing to demand the last ounce of what someone owes you, forgiving the debt of the person who wronged you. Time is perhaps the scarcest currency of the modern professional, and the person who gives it away freely to those who need it is exercising a generosity more costly than most financial gifts. The offering plate never sees any of this, and yet it is the substance of a generous life.

The Danger of Efficient Giving

There is a temptation among thoughtful, high-capacity Christians toward a kind of optimized, arm's-length generosity — the giving that happens entirely through the well-run charity, the effective nonprofit, the tax-advantaged donor fund. And there is much good in this. Wise, effective, strategic giving does enormous good, and I would not discourage anyone from it.

But there is a spiritual danger in never touching the people you help. Jesus did not send money to the leper. He touched him. The whole scandal of the incarnation is that God did not help humanity from a safe distance through an efficient program; he came into the room, took on flesh, got dirty, and died. When all your generosity is mediated through institutions, you protect yourself from the mess and the inconvenience and the relationship — and you also protect yourself from being changed. The poor person you help through a check remains an abstraction. The poor person you sit with becomes a name, a face, a friend who will ask something of you that no charity ever will.

I say this to myself as much as to anyone. It is far easier for me to set up an automatic monthly gift than to notice the person in front of me and let their need interrupt my schedule. The automatic gift is good. But it must not become a way of buying my way out of the harder, closer, more human generosity that the gospel actually models.

Secret Generosity

Jesus said something about giving that we have almost entirely failed to obey: when you give, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing; give in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you. This is one of the most counter-cultural instructions in a thoroughly public age. We name buildings after donors. We publish giving levels. We recognize major contributors from the platform. And Jesus said the reward for public giving is the recognition itself — you got what you were buying, which was to be seen, and that is all you get.

Secret generosity is a discipline of the heart. It removes the return on investment. It gives you nothing back except the private knowledge that you served someone who cannot thank you and cannot repay you and will never know it was you. That kind of giving purifies the motive because it strips away every benefit except the act itself. I would gently suggest that the health of your generosity can be measured by how much of it no one knows about. If all your giving is visible, some of it is probably purchasing something other than the kingdom.

The Freedom of Open Hands

Underneath all of this is a promise, and it is the promise that makes generosity possible rather than merely obligatory. Jesus tells us not to store up treasures on earth where moth and rust destroy, but to store up treasures in heaven, and then he explains why: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The direction of causation is worth noticing. He does not say put your heart in the right place and your treasure will follow. He says move your treasure and your heart will follow it. Generosity is not just an expression of a changed heart. It is a means of changing the heart.

This is the freedom of open hands. The person who clings to everything is not free; they are guarded, anxious, forever calculating what they might lose. The person who holds everything loosely, ready to give it away, has already loosened the grip of the one master that competes most fiercely with God. Generosity is not primarily how you help others, though it helps them enormously. It is how you get free. And the offering plate, faithful as it is, was only ever meant to be the beginning.

The Cheerful Giver and the Reluctant One

Paul says that God loves a cheerful giver, and the phrase deserves more attention than it usually gets, because it locates the value of generosity not in the amount but in the disposition. The word translated cheerful is the root from which we get the word hilarious. God loves the hilarious giver, the one whose giving overflows from joy rather than obligation. This is a startling standard, because it means a large gift given grudgingly may please God less than a small gift given with delight. The heart is the currency God is actually watching.

This exposes the difference between two people who write identical checks. One gives because they must, calculating the minimum, resenting the loss, discharging a duty. The other gives because they cannot help it, because gratitude has made their hands loose, because giving has become one of the great pleasures of their life. The amounts are the same. The transactions could not be more different. And the difference is not something you can manufacture by trying harder to feel cheerful.
