That last phrase — the year of the Lord's favor — is jubilee language. Isaiah was drawing on the imagery of the jubilee year, and Jesus was applying it to himself. He was announcing that his ministry was the true jubilee, the great release, the year of the Lord's favor come in person.

What Jesus did with the jubilee is instructive. He did not enact it as national legislation; he was not a political reformer in that sense. But he took its meaning — release, freedom, good news to the poor, the reversal of the accumulated weight of debt and bondage — and made it the center of his mission. The kingdom he proclaimed was a jubilee kingdom, one in which debts are forgiven, the poor are lifted, the captives are freed, and the accumulated injustices of the world are being undone. The Lord's Prayer itself carries the jubilee impulse: forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. The jubilee did not disappear. It was transfigured and placed at the heart of the gospel.

What It Asks of Us Now

So what does jubilee economics ask of the church today? Not, I think, a legislative program that any congregation could adopt, and not a naive attempt to reimpose Mosaic land law on a modern nation. But it asks for something, and the something is real. It asks us to hold our own property as tenants rather than absolute owners, knowing that God owns it and has purposes for it beyond our comfort. It asks us to be a people of forgiveness in the economic sense — releasing what is owed to us, refusing to demand the last ounce, practicing in our own dealings the release the jubilee proclaimed. It asks us to care intensely about whether the poor in our reach are locked into permanent poverty, and to work against that entrenchment wherever we can.

And it asks the church, perhaps most pointedly, to be an outpost of jubilee in a world that runs on its opposite. Where the world accumulates, the church releases. Where the world lets inequality harden, the church works to reverse it. Where the world treats ownership as absolute, the church treats everything as held in trust from the God who owns it all. The church that forgives debts — literal and relational — that lifts the fallen, that refuses to let poverty become permanent among its people, that shares its resources so that no one among it is in serious need, is enacting the jubilee in miniature. This is not utopian. It is precisely what the early church in Acts did when they shared their possessions so that there was no needy person among them. That was jubilee, embodied in a community.

The Trumpet We Have Silenced

I suspect the reason we have dismissed the jubilee as impractical is not primarily that it is impractical. It is that it is inconvenient. Jubilee threatens the accumulation that most of us, myself included, are quietly organizing our lives around. It is easier to declare it a relic than to let it interrogate our own grip on what we hold. The trumpet that was meant to sound liberty across the land has been silenced, not because it could not be sounded, but because we would rather not hear what it says about our debts and our dispossessions and our absolute ownership of things that were never truly ours.

Why the First Sermon Was a Jubilee

It is worth pausing on the fact that Jesus chose the jubilee for his inaugural announcement, because the choice was not accidental and its implications are enormous. Of all the texts he could have read to launch his public ministry, of all the ways he could have summarized what he came to do, he selected the passage that proclaims the year of the Lord's favor — release for captives, sight for the blind, freedom for the oppressed, good news for the poor. He defined his entire mission in the vocabulary of the jubilee, and then he sat down and said, today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.

This means the gospel is, at its heart, a jubilee gospel. The salvation Jesus brings is release — release from the debt of sin, release from the bondage of the law of sin and death, release from every accumulated weight that the fall has piled on the human race. And it means the community that receives this gospel cannot be indifferent to the economic release the jubilee also proclaimed, because the spiritual release and the material release flow from the same heart of God and cannot finally be separated. A church that preaches release from spiritual debt while ignoring the economic bondage of the poor at its gate has torn apart what Jesus held together in a single sermon. The jubilee gospel liberates the whole person, and it forms a people who long to see liberation extend into every corner of a bound and burdened world.

The Practice of Release

How does a community actually live jubilee in an economy structured entirely against it? Not by waiting for the legislation that will never come, but by becoming, in its own life, a colony of the coming kingdom where the jubilee logic already operates. It begins small and concrete: forgiving actual debts owed to us when we are able, refusing to demand the last dollar from someone drowning, structuring our generosity so that the accumulated weight on the poor among us is genuinely lifted rather than merely acknowledged.

It extends to how we hold our own resources — as tenants rather than absolute owners, ready to release what God directs us to release, unwilling to let our wealth become the permanent fortress the jubilee was designed to prevent. And it extends to the character of our common life, a community where, as in Acts, the sharing is real enough that there is no destitute person left unhelped in the fellowship. None of this reforms the national economy. All of it makes the church a living sign of the jubilee it proclaims, a foretaste of the great release, a people who have heard the trumpet and begun, however imperfectly, to live as though the year of the Lord's favor had actually arrived.

The Objection of the Prudent

The immediate objection to jubilee economics comes from the prudent, and it deserves a hearing rather than a dismissal. If debts are cancelled every seven years and land returns every fifty, the objector asks, who would ever lend, and who would work hard to acquire what they cannot permanently keep? Does jubilee not punish diligence and reward improvidence, dissolving the incentives that make an economy function at all? It is a serious question, and the law itself anticipated it. Deuteronomy explicitly warns against the hard-hearted person who refuses to lend as the year of release approaches, calculating that the debt will soon be cancelled, and commands generosity anyway.

This is precisely the point at which jubilee economics confronts the logic of pure self-interest and refuses it. The law knew that jubilee cut against the grain of ordinary economic calculation, and it commanded the harder thing anyway, because the purpose of the economy in God's vision is not the maximization of individual acquisition but the flourishing of the whole community, especially its weakest members. Jubilee subordinates efficiency to justice, incentive to mercy, the accumulation of the strong to the protection of the vulnerable. It is not that jubilee ignores the concerns of the prudent; it is that it ranks them below the concern for the poor, and it asks the prudent to accept a less optimized economy in exchange for one that will not permanently dispossess anyone. That trade-off is the whole argument, and where you land on it reveals what you believe an economy is finally for.

The jubilee will not be legislated back into a modern economy, and I am not calling for that. But its trumpet can still sound in the life of the church and the conscience of the believer. It sounds every time a debt is forgiven, every time the accumulated weight on a poor family is lifted, every time a Christian holds their property as a tenant of God rather than a lord of their own domain, every time a community shares so that none among it is destitute. The year of the Lord's favor has been proclaimed. Jesus said it was fulfilled in the hearing of those who listened. The only question is whether the church that bears his name will let the jubilee it announced reach as far as our own bank accounts, or whether we will keep insisting, against our own Lord, that the land is finally ours.
excerpt: The ancient law of jubilee mandated a periodic reset of land, debt, and freedom. It has been dismissed as an impractical relic — but the impulse behind it may be the most urgent economic word the church has to offer.

title: The Church Budget as Theology
body:
There is a document in every church that reveals more about its true beliefs than any statement of faith, any mission statement, any carefully worded vision on the website. It is the budget. A church budget is a theological document — arguably the most honest theological document a congregation produces — because it records not what the church says it values but what it actually values, measured in the one currency that cannot lie: money spent. And most churches have never read their budget this way. They treat it as a mundane administrative necessity, a spreadsheet for the finance committee, when in fact it is a confession of faith written in dollars.

I want to argue that the way a church allocates its money is a direct expression of its theology, that the budget preaches a sermon every week whether anyone reads it or not, and that examining the budget honestly is one of the most spiritually revealing things a congregation can do. Because a budget cannot be spun. You can say anything you want in a sermon. The budget shows what you did.

What a Budget Confesses

Consider what a budget actually records. It records priorities in their most concrete form. A church may say it prioritizes reaching the lost, caring for the poor, and discipling its people. But when you look at where the money goes — how much to the building, how much to staff salaries, how much to the poor, how much to missions, how much to programs that serve the existing members versus outreach that serves those outside — a different and truer picture often emerges. The stated priorities and the funded priorities frequently diverge, and where they diverge, the funded priorities are the real ones. Money is a lie detector. It shows what a church is actually organized to do.

Jesus said it directly, and it applies to institutions as much as individuals: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. This is not merely a diagnostic — it is not only that the budget reveals the heart. It is also formative: the budget shapes the heart. A church that spends nearly everything on itself becomes a self-focused church, regardless of its outward-facing rhetoric. A church that gives generously to the poor and to mission becomes a generous church, and its people are formed by the pattern of its spending into generous people. The budget is both a mirror and a mold. It reflects what the church is and shapes what the church becomes.

You can preach any sermon you like. The budget preaches the sermon you actually believe. And the congregation is being discipled by the spreadsheet whether they ever see it or not.

The Building Problem

The single largest line in most church budgets, after staff, is the building — the mortgage, the maintenance, the utilities, the endless costs of keeping a physical facility running. And this deserves honest theological scrutiny, because the amount of kingdom resource poured into physical structures is enormous, and its justification is rarely examined. There is nothing inherently wrong with a building; the church needs space to gather. But when a congregation of modest size is spending the majority of its resources maintaining a facility used a few hours a week, while giving a fraction to the poor and to mission, the budget is confessing a theology that few would defend out loud.

The early church had no buildings. It met in homes, and it poured its resources into people — into the poor, into the spread of the gospel, into the care of widows and orphans and the sharing of possessions so that none among them was in need. Somewhere in the long history of Christianity, the resources shifted decisively from people to structures, and the shift was so gradual that we have never noticed it as a theological choice. But it was one. Every church that spends more on its building than on the poor has made a theological statement about the relative value of edifices and image-bearers, and it is not a statement the New Testament would endorse. I say this as a pastor whose own church carries the weight of a building, and the conviction is uncomfortable precisely because it lands close to home.

The Staff Question

After the building comes the staff, and this too is a theological matter deserving honesty. Pastoral and ministry staff are worthy of their wages; the laborer deserves to be paid, and Scripture affirms the support of those who labor in the word. There is no virtue in underpaying the people who serve the church, and much churches do it shamefully. But the professionalization of ministry carries a theological cost that the budget makes visible. When a large portion of the budget funds paid professionals to do the ministry, the budget is quietly confessing a theology in which ministry is done by experts on behalf of a paying congregation, rather than by the whole body of the priesthood of believers.

The budget, in other words, can either reinforce or resist the passivity of the laity. A staffing structure that hires professionals to do everything the members should be doing themselves is not neutral; it embodies a particular and questionable ecclesiology. A church that invests instead in equipping and releasing its members for ministry — that spends its resources multiplying ministers rather than employing them — embodies a different and more biblical vision. The staffing line is not just an administrative decision. It is a statement about who the church believes is called to do the work of the ministry.

The Missing Line

Perhaps the most theologically revealing thing about a church budget is not what is in it but what is missing or minimal. Look for the line for the poor. Look for the line for those outside the walls. Look for the percentage that leaves the congregation to serve people who will never attend, never give, never contribute to the institution's survival. In many church budgets, this line is small — a token, a rounding error compared to the vast sums spent on the church's own comfort and continuation. And that smallness is a confession. It confesses a church curved inward, spending its resources on its own life while the poor at its gate receive the leftovers.

The prophets measured the faithfulness of Israel's worship by its treatment of the poor, and they found the elaborate religious spending worthless when it coexisted with neglect of the vulnerable. The same measure applies to a church budget. A congregation can have beautiful facilities, excellent programs, well-paid staff, and a budget that testifies against it before God because it spends everything on itself and almost nothing on the least of these. The size of the mercy line relative to the comfort lines is one of the truest measures of a church's actual theology, and it is a measure most churches would rather not take.

Reading the Budget Rightly

What would it mean to treat the budget as the theological document it is? It would mean the leadership examining every line as a statement of belief and asking whether the spending matches the stated mission. It would mean the congregation being invited to see the budget not as a boring financial report but as a corporate confession of faith, open to examination and repentance. It would mean asking, honestly and painfully, whether the pattern of the church's spending would be recognizable to the church of Acts, or whether we have built something that spends on itself what the early church spent on the poor and the lost.

The Budget and the Watching World

There is an evangelistic dimension to the church budget that we rarely consider, and it emerges from the way the early church's economic life functioned as its most powerful witness. The pagan world around the first Christians was struck not primarily by their doctrines, which most outsiders found strange, but by their behavior — and specifically by how they used their money. They cared for their own poor and for the poor outside their community. They buried the destitute. They took in abandoned infants. During plagues, when others fled, they stayed and nursed the sick, often dying in the process. The Emperor Julian, who despised Christianity and tried to revive paganism, complained bitterly that the Christians cared not only for their own poor but for the pagan poor as well, and that this generosity was winning converts his own religion could not match.

The economic life of the church was its apologetic. A budget that pours out resources on the vulnerable, that visibly loves the poor and the stranger, preaches the gospel to a watching world in a way no advertising campaign can. And a budget that spends everything on the comfort of its own members preaches a different message entirely — that this church is a club for its own benefit, indistinguishable from any other organization that exists to serve its members. The world is watching what the church does with its money, whether the church realizes it or not, and the budget is a sermon addressed as much to the neighborhood as to the congregation.

Small Budgets, Faithful Churches

None of this should be heard as a rebuke reserved for large, wealthy churches. A small church with a modest budget faces exactly the same theological questions, and often answers them more faithfully than the megachurch with its enormous resources. The question is never the size of the budget but its proportions and its heart. A tiny congregation that gives sacrificially to the poor from its small offerings is preaching a truer sermon than a wealthy church that gives a token from its abundance. The widow's two coins, Jesus said, were worth more than all the large sums the rich threw into the treasury, because she gave out of her poverty everything she had, while they gave out of their wealth what they would not miss.

This is liberating for the small church, which often labors under a sense of inadequacy about its limited resources. Your budget is small, but it can be faithful, and faithfulness is what God measures. A small budget stewarded toward the poor, toward mission, toward the equipping of the saints, is a beautiful theological document, whatever its total. The question the budget poses is the same for the church of thirty and the church of three thousand: does the way we spend our money look like the heart of Jesus, or does it look like the heart of every other institution that exists to perpetuate and comfort itself?

The Congregation That Never Sees It

One reason the budget fails to function as the theological document it is comes down to a simple problem of access: most members of most churches never actually look at it. The budget is prepared by a committee, approved in a sparsely attended meeting, and filed away, and the average member has no idea how their church's money is actually spent. They give, and the giving disappears into a black box, and the theological confession the budget makes goes unread by the very people whose gifts compose it. This is a lost opportunity, and arguably a form of poor stewardship of the congregation's own discipleship.

Imagine instead a church that treated its budget as an instrument of formation — that walked its members through where the money goes, that explained the theological reasoning behind its priorities, that invited the congregation to see their collective giving as a corporate act of worship with a visible shape. Such transparency would do more than satisfy accountability; it would disciple. It would teach the congregation, concretely, what it means for a community to hold money faithfully, to prioritize the poor, to fund mission, to resist the gravitational pull toward self-comfort. The budget is a sermon, and a church that hides it from its own people has muted one of the clearest sermons it preaches. To bring the budget into the light is to let the congregation see, and be shaped by, the theology their giving actually expresses.

Repentance in Numbers

The most hopeful thing about seeing the budget as theology is that a budget can be changed, and changing it is one of the most concrete forms of corporate repentance a church can perform. Most repentance is invisible and internal; it happens in hearts and is known only to God. But budgetary repentance is visible, measurable, and real. When a church moves a significant portion of its spending from its own comfort to the service of the poor, from the maintenance of its building to the equipping of its people, from perpetuating the institution to reaching those outside it, something has genuinely changed, and it can be seen in black and white.

This is why the budget is such a searching test. Words are cheap; a church can confess any priority it likes in its mission statement. But to actually move the money is to actually repent, to align the treasure with the confessed heart, to make the sermon the budget preaches finally match the sermon the pulpit preaches. I say this to my own congregation and to myself, because it is far easier to preach about the poor than to move the line in the budget that would actually serve them. Show me your budget, and I will show you your theology. And if the two do not match, it is the budget, not the statement of faith, that tells the truth.
excerpt: Show me a church's budget and I will show you its actual theology — not the one on the website, but the one it truly believes. A budget is a moral document, and most churches have never read theirs that way.

title: Poverty Tourism vs. Partnership
body:
Every summer, hundreds of thousands of well-meaning Christians board planes for a week in a poor community somewhere — building a wall, painting a school, holding orphans, doing a Vacation Bible School — and return home moved, grateful, and convinced they have done something significant for the kingdom of God. The short-term mission trip has become a fixture of Western Christianity, a rite of passage for youth groups and a staple of the church calendar. And a growing body of honest reflection, some of it from missionaries and development workers who have watched the phenomenon up close, suggests that much of it does more harm than good, and helps the helper far more than the helped.

This is a hard thing to say, because the motives are so often genuine and the desire to help so real. I am not attacking the impulse to serve the poor. I am questioning whether the way we most commonly act on that impulse actually serves them, or whether it has become a form of consumption — poverty tourism dressed in the language of mission — that leaves the poor community much as it found them while transforming the visitors' Instagram feeds and self-image. There is a better way, and it is worth the discomfort of examining the current one to find it.

The Uncomfortable Arithmetic

Start with the arithmetic, because it is stubborn. A team of a dozen people spends thousands of dollars each on flights, lodging, and meals to travel to a poor community and perform a week of unskilled labor — building something local workers could have built better and faster, painting something that did not need painting, doing work that could have been done by local people who desperately need the wages. The money spent transporting the team would, in many cases, have accomplished far more if simply given to the local community to hire its own people and direct its own priorities. The visitors provide labor the community does not need at the cost of money the community could have used.

Worse, the presence of free foreign labor and free foreign goods can actively undermine the local economy. When a team builds a house for free, the local builder who could have built it does not get the work. When a team brings free goods, the local merchant who sells those goods loses the sale. Steve Corbett and Brian Fikkert, in When Helping Hurts, document how well-intentioned aid can foster dependency, erode local dignity, and displace the very local capacity that genuine development requires. The road to poverty is often paved with the good intentions of people who wanted to help and never asked whether their help was actually helpful.

We flew across the world to build a wall that a local man needed to build to feed his family, and we called it mission. We took his work, gave him our pity, and went home feeling generous.

The Dignity Problem

Beneath the economics lies a deeper problem, and it is a problem of dignity. The short-term mission model often positions the wealthy visitor as the one with something to give and the poor community as the one with only needs to be met. The visitors are the helpers, the doers, the ones with resources and competence; the poor are the recipients, the helped, the objects of the mission. And this dynamic, however unintended, is corrosive. It reinforces in the poor a sense of their own deficiency and in the wealthy a sense of their own superiority. It treats the poor as a problem to be solved rather than people to be known, as a mission field rather than brothers and sisters.

This inverts the gospel's own posture. When Jesus came among us, he did not arrive as the competent helper condescending to fix our problems from a position of superiority. He came as one of us, took on our flesh, entered our condition, and served from within it. The incarnation is the opposite of poverty tourism. It is not a week-long visit from a position of safety; it is a permanent entry into shared life. And any ministry to the poor that does not reflect this posture — that helps from above rather than accompanies from alongside — has departed from the pattern of the one it claims to serve.

What the Poor Actually Have

The poverty tourism model rests on a false assumption: that the poor are defined by what they lack and the wealthy by what they have. But this is not how Scripture sees it. The poor are frequently described in the Bible as rich in faith, as the ones to whom the kingdom belongs, as those whom God has chosen. The wealthy visitor who arrives assuming they are the ones with something to give and the poor are the ones with only needs has fundamentally misread the situation. Often it is the materially poor community that has the deeper faith, the richer relationships, the profounder dependence on God, and the wealthy visitor who is impoverished in exactly those things.

Genuine encounter with the global poor tends to disrupt this assumption for anyone who stays long enough to actually know people rather than serve them briefly and leave. The visitor who expected to give discovers they have received far more than they gave — that the poor believers they came to help possessed a wealth of faith and joy and community that put the visitor's own spiritual poverty to shame. This is not romanticizing poverty; material deprivation is real and painful and should be relieved. It is recognizing that the flow of blessing is not one-directional, that the poor are not merely recipients, and that a posture which treats them as such is both false and demeaning.

The Way of Partnership

So what is the alternative? Not, I think, the abandonment of cross-cultural mission, which is a genuine and biblical calling. The alternative is partnership rather than tourism — a fundamentally different posture and structure. Partnership means long-term relationship rather than a week-long visit. It means listening to the local community about its own priorities rather than arriving with a predetermined project. It means supporting and strengthening local leadership rather than displacing it with foreign competence. It means asking the people you want to help what would actually help, and then doing that, even when it is less photogenic than building a wall.

Partnership means that the resources flow in ways that build local capacity rather than dependency — funding local workers rather than importing foreign labor, strengthening local institutions rather than bypassing them, investing in relationships that last for years rather than experiences that last for a week. It means the wealthy and the poor come to know one another as equals before God, each bringing something, each receiving something, the wealth of faith flowing one way and the sharing of material resources flowing the other, in a mutual exchange that dignifies both. This is slower, costlier, and far less satisfying to the visitor's need to feel useful. It is also the only model that actually serves the poor rather than the helper.

The Cost of Real Love

The reason poverty tourism persists despite its documented harms is that partnership costs more than a plane ticket. A week-long trip is finite, controllable, and emotionally rewarding; you go, you serve, you feel the feelings, you come home, and your ordinary life is unchanged. Partnership demands the thing we are least willing to give: sustained relationship, ongoing commitment, the surrender of our need to be the competent helper, and the humility to let the poor lead. It asks us to keep showing up long after the emotional high has faded, to invest in people whose problems we cannot solve in a week, to love in a way that changes our own lives and not just our feelings.

The Difference Between Relief and Development

Part of what goes wrong in poverty tourism is a confusion of categories that any serious approach to helping the poor must untangle. There is a real difference between relief, rehabilitation, and development, and applying the wrong one does harm. Relief is the urgent, temporary provision that a genuine emergency requires — the food after the flood, the water after the earthquake, the immediate rescue of someone who cannot help themselves. Relief is right and necessary in a crisis. But most poverty is not a crisis; it is a chronic condition, and applying crisis relief to a chronic condition is precisely where the harm begins.

Development is the long, slow, relational work of helping a community build its own capacity to provide for itself — and it looks nothing like the emergency relief that short-term missions tend to imitate. When we airlift free goods and free labor into communities that are poor but not in acute crisis, we apply relief to a situation that needs development, and in doing so we undermine the very local capacity that development requires. The community learns to wait for the next team rather than to build its own future; the local economy is displaced rather than strengthened; dependency deepens rather than lifts. Knowing which kind of help a situation requires is not a technical detail. It is the difference between actually serving the poor and merely feeling that we have.

Reframing the Trip

I do not want to end on a note that discourages the young person longing to serve or the church wanting to engage the global poor, because that longing is good and it comes from God. The answer is not to stop going but to go differently, and to be honest about what the going is for. If a short-term trip is framed not as our heroic mission to fix the poor but as a chance to learn, to build long-term relationship, to be changed, to support and submit to local leadership rather than override it, then it can be part of something genuinely good.

The most honest framing of many short-term trips is that they are primarily for the formation of the ones who go — an exposure that, handled rightly, can produce a lifetime of humbler, wiser, more committed partnership. There is no shame in that, as long as we are honest about it and do not dress up our own formation as heroic service to people who did not need our week of unskilled labor. Go to learn. Go to build relationships that will last for years. Go under the leadership of the local church rather than in front of it. Go to have your assumptions dismantled and your comfort disturbed. And then come home and enter the long, costly, unglamorous work of real partnership, which is where the actual love happens.

The Photograph Problem

There is a small but telling symptom of the poverty tourism mindset, and it is the photograph. The image of the smiling Western visitor surrounded by poor children, posted to social media on return, has become so common that it barely registers as strange. But it is strange, and it reveals the underlying dynamic with uncomfortable clarity. Whose need does the photograph serve? Not the children's. It serves the visitor's need to display their compassion, to be seen as the kind of person who helps, to convert someone else's poverty into their own social currency. The poor become props in a narrative about the goodness of the person holding the camera.

This is worth naming not to shame anyone but to expose the reflex, because the reflex reveals the deeper posture. When our engagement with the poor is oriented, even unconsciously, toward how it makes us look and feel, we have made the poor into instruments of our own self-image. The dignity of the person in the photograph — who did not consent to becoming a symbol of another's virtue, whose poverty is now content for a feed — is quietly violated. Partnership, by contrast, does not need the photograph, because it is not seeking the return the photograph provides. It seeks the good of the other, and it is content for that good to go unwitnessed, because it was never about being seen. The presence or absence of the impulse to document our helping is a small but revealing test of whom the helping is actually for.

I have to confess that the tourism model appeals to something in me that partnership exposes and rebukes. I would rather help in a way that makes me feel generous and leaves me in control than in a way that requires me to be changed, to be dependent, to receive as much as I give. The poverty tourism industry exists because it serves the helper's needs so well — the need to feel useful, to feel generous, to have a story, to do something finite and satisfying. Partnership serves the poor's needs instead, and it costs the helper the very things the tourism model was designed to provide. That cost is exactly why partnership is the more Christlike way, and exactly why it is the road less traveled. The question is not whether we want to help the poor. Almost everyone does. The question is whether we love them enough to help in the way that actually serves them rather than ourselves.
excerpt: The short-term mission trip has become a Christian rite of passage, but much of what passes for helping the poor helps the helper more than the helped. There is a better way, and it costs more than a plane ticket.

title: Treasures in Heaven
body:
Jesus said something about money that we have almost entirely failed to take literally. "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moths and vermin destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moths and vermin do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." We treat this as beautiful poetry, a nice sentiment about not being too materialistic, a general encouragement toward spiritual-mindedness. And in treating it that way, we have missed that Jesus was giving concrete financial instruction. He was describing an actual investment strategy, and claiming it was the only one that ultimately made sense.

The passage is not vague spirituality. It is a comparison of two portfolios, and a recommendation to move your assets from one to the other. Jesus, the master teacher, was making an argument that any investor should recognize: one of these investments is guaranteed to be destroyed, and the other is guaranteed to last forever, so you would be a fool to keep your treasure in the perishable one. The strangeness is not that he used financial language. The strangeness is that we have refused to believe he meant it.

The Argument from Permanence

Follow the logic Jesus actually lays out, because it is more rigorous than we give it credit for. Earthly treasure, he says, is subject to three threats: moth, rust, and theft. In his agrarern context, wealth was stored as fine cloth that moths ate, as metal goods that corroded, as valuables that thieves stole. His point was that all earthly treasure is, by its nature, perishable and vulnerable. It decays, it corrodes, it can be taken, and even if none of these befall it in your lifetime, death will separate you from it completely. No earthly treasure survives your own death. Every dollar you accumulate, you will leave behind. The hearse does not pull a trailer.

Heavenly treasure, by contrast, is immune to all three threats. It does not decay, cannot be stolen, and is not lost at death — indeed, it is precisely what death delivers you into. Jesus is making an argument from permanence, and it is unanswerable on its own terms. If you have a choice between investing in something guaranteed to be destroyed and something guaranteed to last forever, and if you are going to exist forever, then the rational choice is obvious. To pour your life into accumulating what you cannot keep, while neglecting to accumulate what you cannot lose, is not merely unspiritual. It is, by Jesus' logic, foolish. It is bad investing.

Jesus was not being poetic. He was being practical. He looked at your portfolio and said: you are heavily invested in an asset guaranteed to be destroyed. Move your money.

What Heavenly Treasure Is

The natural question is what, exactly, treasure in heaven consists of, and how one actually stores it up. Jesus and the apostles give surprisingly concrete answers. In Luke, immediately after telling the parable of the rich fool, Jesus says: "Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide purses for yourselves that will not wear out, a treasure in heaven that will never fail." Storing treasure in heaven is directly linked to generosity toward the poor. The act of giving away earthly wealth is the mechanism by which heavenly wealth is accumulated. You transfer your treasure from the perishable account to the imperishable one by giving it away — a transaction that looks like loss to the world and is actually the shrewdest possible investment.

Paul makes the same connection explicit in his instructions to the rich, and it is one of the most remarkable passages in Scripture on this theme. Command those who are rich, he says, to be generous and willing to share, and in this way they will "lay up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life." The generous use of wealth is described as an investment that stores up treasure for the age to come. This is not metaphor stacked on metaphor. It is a claim about the actual mechanics of eternal reward: what you give away for the sake of Christ and his kingdom is not lost but transferred, laid up, stored where it cannot be destroyed, waiting for you.

The Heart Follows the Treasure

There is a further dimension to this teaching that is easy to miss, and it concerns the direction of causation between treasure and heart. "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." Notice that Jesus does not say where your heart is, there your treasure will be. He says the reverse. Your heart follows your treasure. This is a profound observation about human nature: we come to love what we invest in. The things we pour our resources into become the things we care about. If you invest heavily in earthly things, your heart will be bound to earth. If you invest in heavenly things, your heart will be drawn toward heaven.

This means that generosity is not only a way of storing up eternal reward; it is a way of reorienting your own heart. When you give to the kingdom, your heart follows the gift, and you find yourself caring more about the kingdom, more about the poor you have invested in, more about the eternal things your treasure is now accumulating. The person who wants to love God and the things of God more deeply has a concrete tool available: move your treasure there, and your heart will follow. Generosity is heart-surgery you perform on yourself, redirecting your affections by redirecting your investments. This is why the miser is trapped and the giver is free — the miser's heart is chained to what he clutches, while the giver's heart is drawn upward toward what he has sent ahead.

The Only Investment That Survives Death

What makes this teaching so urgent is the one fact we spend our whole lives avoiding: we are going to die, and death is the great liquidator of every earthly portfolio. The wealthiest person who ever lived left it all behind. The most successful career ends in a coffin. Every earthly treasure, no matter how carefully accumulated and guarded, is confiscated in full at the moment of death, and we take nothing with us. This is not morbid; it is simply true, and Jesus builds his entire argument on it. In light of certain death, an investment strategy that only pays off before death is a strategy with a guaranteed total loss at the end.

Treasure in heaven is the only investment that survives the one event that liquidates everything else. What you give away for Christ does not die when you die; it is waiting for you on the other side. This reframes the whole logic of accumulation. The person storing up earthly wealth is investing everything in an account that will be zeroed out at death. The person storing up heavenly treasure through generosity is investing in the only account that death cannot touch, that in fact matures at death. Seen clearly, generosity is not the sacrifice of wealth; it is the transfer of wealth from the account that dies to the account that lives forever. The giver is not the one losing money. The hoarder is.

Believing It Enough to Do It

The reason we do not live this way is not that we disagree with Jesus' argument; it is that we do not really believe it, not down in the places where our checkbooks are decided. We nod at the teaching on Sunday and invest in the perishable account on Monday, hedging our bets, treating the heavenly treasure as a nice hope while treating the earthly treasure as the real thing. Our spending reveals what we actually believe, and most of our spending confesses a functional unbelief in the very thing Jesus said was the only sound investment. I include myself in this indictment fully; my own account balances testify against my stated theology more days than not.

The Shrewd Manager

There is a parable of Jesus so strange that most preachers avoid it entirely, and it turns out to be one of the clearest illustrations of the treasures-in-heaven principle in all his teaching. In Luke 16, a dishonest manager, about to be fired, uses his last days of authority to slash the debts owed to his master, currying favor with the debtors so they will welcome him after he loses his job. And astonishingly, the master commends the dishonest manager for acting shrewdly. Jesus then draws the lesson: use worldly wealth to gain friends for yourselves, so that when it is gone, you will be welcomed into eternal dwellings.

The point is not that we should imitate the man's dishonesty but that we should imitate his shrewdness — his clear-eyed recognition that his current position was temporary and his use of present resources to secure a future beyond it. He understood that the wealth in his hands was about to be lost, and he leveraged it, while he still had it, to secure a welcome on the other side. This is exactly the treasures-in-heaven logic. Our earthly wealth is temporary; we are about to lose it all at death; and the shrewd thing to do is to use it now, while we have it, to secure friends and welcome and reward in the eternal home that awaits us. Jesus is calling us to be as shrewd about eternity as the dishonest manager was about his unemployment — to see clearly that the money will not last and to invest it accordingly.

What We Send Ahead

There is a moving way the older Christian tradition sometimes spoke about this, drawn from the missionary Jim Elliot and echoing ancient wisdom: the only things we truly keep are the things we give away, because what we hold we lose at death, and what we give for Christ we send ahead where it waits for us. This inverts the entire common-sense understanding of possession. We think we possess what we cling to and lose what we release. Jesus says the reverse: we lose what we cling to, because death confiscates it, and we keep what we release for his sake, because it is stored where death cannot reach.

This means the generous person is not depleting their estate but transferring it — moving their wealth, piece by piece, from the account that will be zeroed out to the account that will be waiting. Every gift to the poor, every resource poured into the kingdom, every dollar released for Christ is not gone but relocated, sent ahead to a home we have not yet reached but will not leave. The hoarder, who feels so secure behind their accumulated pile, is the one actually losing everything, because none of it will cross the threshold of death with them. The giver, who looks to the world like they are throwing wealth away, is the shrewdest investor of all, quietly building a treasure in the one place the universe cannot take it from them.

The Eye and the Heart

In the middle of the treasures passage, Jesus says something that seems, at first, like a strange non sequitur: "The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are healthy, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eyes are unhealthy, your whole body will be full of darkness." Placed between the teaching about treasure and the declaration that you cannot serve two masters, this saying is not a digression; it is the hinge. In the idiom of Jesus' day, a good eye meant a generous person and a bad eye meant a stingy, grasping one. He is saying that the way you see, your fundamental orientation toward money and possession, determines whether your whole life is filled with light or darkness.

This is a profound observation about how money shapes perception. The grasping person, the one with the bad eye, does not merely have a financial problem; their entire vision of the world is darkened by their greed. They see other people as threats or resources, they see their possessions as extensions of themselves, they see the future as something to be secured against rather than trusted to God. The generous person, the one with the good eye, sees differently — sees others as neighbors to love, possessions as tools to deploy, the future as held by a faithful Father. Your relationship to money is not one compartment of your life among others; it is the lens through which you see everything, and it fills your whole existence with either light or darkness. This is why Jesus takes it so seriously. It is never just about money. It is about whether you can see at all.

The Rich Man and the Regret

Jesus told a story about a rich man who died and found himself in torment, looking across an unbridgeable gulf at a poor man named Lazarus who had begged at his gate and was now comforted. The rich man's great desire, too late, was to warn his five brothers so they would not come to the same place. And the answer he received was that they had Moses and the prophets; if they would not listen to them, they would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead.

The story is a warning delivered from the far side of death, and its terror is precisely that the rich man cannot go back and reinvest. His portfolio is closed. The wealth he enjoyed in life, the fine clothes and sumptuous feasts, bought him nothing that lasted, and the poor man he ignored at his own gate turned out to be the one who mattered. The chance to store up treasure in heaven, to use his wealth to gain an eternal welcome, was available to him every single day, and he spent it all on himself, and now it is gone, and the regret is eternal. Jesus tells this story to the living, who still have time, whose portfolio is still open, who can still move their treasure while the market is open. The rich man cannot warn his brothers. But Jesus can, and does, and the warning is for us: the window in which you can send your treasure ahead is called your life, and it will not stay open forever.

To actually believe Jesus is to reorder the portfolio. It is to give generously not out of guilt or obligation but out of the shrewd recognition that this is the wisest possible use of resources that will otherwise be destroyed — to send treasure ahead where it cannot be lost, to store up what death cannot take, to invest in the age that does not end. Jesus was not asking us to be impractical for the sake of piety. He was inviting us to be more practical than the world, to see through the illusion that earthly treasure is the safe investment, and to put our money where it will still exist a thousand years from now. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. He told us where to send it. The only question is whether we believed him enough to do it.
excerpt: Jesus told us to store up treasures in heaven, and we have quietly filed this away as poetic and impractical. But he meant it as an actual investment strategy — the only one that survives death.

title: What Biblical Masculinity Actually Looks Like
body:
We need to say something uncomfortable at the outset, and it needs to land on both sides of the aisle. The secular critique of masculinity is not wrong about everything it names. Men do hurt people. Men do go silent and call it strength. Men do abandon their children and dress the abandonment in the language of freedom. I have counseled the wives and I have counseled the sons, and I have watched the damage that a certain kind of man leaves behind him like a wake behind a boat. So when the culture says something is broken in the way men are formed, I do not reach for defensiveness. I reach for the mirror.

But the church has its own version of the lie. We have taken the cultural anxiety about manhood and answered it with a mythology of our own making, and we have baptized that mythology and called it biblical. We have built conferences around it and sold books about it and preached sermons that were really just a Christian veneer over a very old set of tribal assumptions about what makes a man a man. And here is the trouble. Much of what we have called biblical masculinity is not biblical at all. It is American. It is Roman. It is the ambient masculinity of the culture with a few verses stapled to it.

The two counterfeits

Consider the two dominant pictures on offer. The first is the man as conqueror. He is decisive, dominant, unafraid, always in command. He does not weep. He does not ask for directions or for help. He leads because he is a man and leading is what men do, and the woman follows because she is a woman and following is what women do. This picture flatters something in us. It gives us a role we can perform. And it has left a trail of marriages where the wife feels like an employee and children who learned that their father's love was a thing to be earned through obedience.

The second counterfeit is the man as harmless. Sanded down, apologetic, permanently deferring, so terrified of being toxic that he has hollowed himself out into someone with no edges and no convictions and no willingness to bear weight. This man will not lead because leading feels like domination and he has been told domination is the sin. So he abdicates and calls it humility. He goes passive and calls it gentleness. And his family drifts because no one is watching the horizon.

Both of these are counterfeits. And both of them, notice, are about the man himself. His strength or his safety, his authority or his harmlessness. Both keep the man at the center of the story. The Scripture does something the culture never does. It moves the man off center.

The pattern is a person

When the New Testament wants to tell a man how to be a man, it does not give him a list of traits. It gives him a person. It says, in effect, look at Jesus. And the moment we look, every counterfeit collapses.

Here is a man with more power than any man in history, and the defining act of his life is that he laid it down. Here is a man who could summon legions of angels, and he let them drive nails through his hands. Here is a man whose strength was so total that he could kneel on a stone floor and wash the crusted dirt off the feet of the men who would abandon him within hours. We have been taught that strength is the capacity to make others serve you. Jesus reveals that strength is the capacity to serve others when you could have made them serve you. That is not the absence of power. That is power under perfect control, aimed entirely away from the self.

The world says a man's strength is measured by what he can take. The cross says a man's strength is measured by what he can lay down.

This is why the counterfeits fail. The conqueror uses his strength on other people. The harmless man has no strength to use. But the cruciform man has real strength and spends it entirely on the good of those he is responsible for. He is not passive. Watch Jesus in the temple with the whip, watch him name the religious leaders as whitewashed tombs to their faces. There is nothing soft here. But that same man wept at a grave and let children climb into his lap, and neither the whip nor the weeping embarrassed him, because both came from the same undivided heart.

What this looks like on a Tuesday

Let me bring this down from the mountain, because abstractions about cruciform manhood are cheap and I have traded in them myself. I have five sons. I know the temptation to preach a masculinity in the pulpit that I do not practice in the hallway.

Cruciform manhood on a Tuesday looks like a father who comes home carrying the day's frustration and does not unload it on the smallest people in the house. It looks like a husband who notices his wife is drowning and picks up the thing she has been carrying without being asked and without announcing that he did it. It looks like a man who apologizes to his children specifically, by name, for the specific thing he did, and does not soften it into a general acknowledgment that nobody in this family is perfect. That last move, the diffusion of guilt into everyone, is one of the great cowardices of fatherhood, and I have committed it more than once.

It looks like a man who bears anxiety so that his household does not have to. When money is tight, the family should be the last to feel the panic, not the first. That does not mean lying to them. It means the man metabolizes the fear before it reaches the table, the way a body absorbs a blow so the organs are protected. This is what headship actually is, and it is almost the exact opposite of what we have made it. Headship in Ephesians is defined by a husband who loves as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The head is the one who dies first.

The strength we are afraid of

I want to name a fear, because it sits underneath a lot of this. Many men are afraid that if they trade the conqueror for the cruciform, they will become the harmless man. That gentleness and leadership are on a single dial, and turning down the domination turns down the strength.

They are not on the same dial. This is the great confusion, and it has crippled a generation of Christian men who genuinely want to be good. Gentleness is not weakness. Gentleness is strength that has been trained to be safe. A war horse that has been broken is not less powerful than a wild one. It is more useful, because its power now answers to a rider. The Greek word we translate as gentleness was used for exactly this, for strength under command. The gentle man is not the man with no power. He is the man whose power has learned to obey.

A soft man cannot be gentle. He has nothing to restrain. Gentleness is only available to the strong.

So the invitation is not to become less. It is to become dangerous in the right direction. To develop real capacity, real conviction, real willingness to bear weight and take hits and stand in the gap, and then to aim all of it away from yourself and toward the people God has given you. That is harder than domination and harder than passivity, because both of those are ways of avoiding the actual cost. The conqueror avoids the cost by making others pay it. The harmless man avoids it by never being on the field. The cruciform man walks onto the field and pays.

The witness of the men who came before

It is worth remembering that the church did not always confuse manhood with the ambient masculinity of its culture. There is a long line of men who understood strength as something to be poured out, and their example rebukes the mythology we have built. Consider the martyrs, who had every ordinary marker of male dominance stripped from them, no army, no throne, no ability to make anyone do anything, and who nonetheless demonstrated a strength that outlasted the empires that killed them. Their strength was not the capacity to overpower. It was the capacity to remain faithful when overpowering was no longer possible, and it changed the world in a way no conqueror ever has.

Or consider the fathers of the faith who wrote from prison cells, who fed the poor when it cost them their reputations, who stayed in plague cities when the powerful fled. Their manhood was a manhood of laying down, and history remembers them not for what they seized but for what they surrendered. The point is not nostalgia for a golden age that never quite existed. The point is that the cruciform pattern is not a modern softening of an older, harder Christian manhood. It is the oldest thing we have. The harder, more dominant version is the newer arrival, the intruder, the thing we absorbed from outside and mistook for the tradition.

And so when a man today feels that following Christ into servanthood is somehow a betrayal of a more robust masculinity, he has the history exactly backward. The robust masculinity was always the servant one. The domination was always the counterfeit. He is not being asked to trade a strong Christian manhood for a weak one. He is being asked to trade a borrowed pagan strength for the far more demanding strength his own tradition has held out to him for two thousand years.

Where this leaves us

I have preached versions of this sermon and watched men nod, and then I have watched those same men go home and do exactly what their fathers did to them. The nodding is easy. The pattern is not changed by agreement. It is changed by repentance, which means actually stopping, actually turning, actually letting the Spirit reach into the reflexes we inherited and rewire them.

Most of us are carrying a picture of manhood we never chose. We absorbed it from a father, or from the absence of a father, or from a locker room, or from a movie, and it runs underneath our conscious life like plumbing in a wall. We do not decide to become our fathers. We become them by default, in the moments when we are too tired to choose. The only way out is to put a different pattern in front of us so often, so deliberately, that it begins to run underneath our life instead.

The question underneath the anxiety

I want to name what I think is really driving the modern anxiety about masculinity, on all sides, because I think it explains why the counterfeits are so seductive. Underneath all of it is a man asking whether he is any good. Whether he matters. Whether his particular life, with its particular failures, adds up to anything worth respecting. That question is old and it is human, and every man carries it, and the counterfeits succeed precisely because each of them offers a fast answer to it. The conqueror answers it with dominance. The harmless man answers it by at least never being the villain. Both are trying to quiet the same fear.

The cross answers the question differently, and more deeply, and it is the only answer that finally holds. It says that a man's worth is not established by his performance at all, not by his dominance and not by his harmlessness, but by the fact that God considered him worth dying for. This is the ground a man's manhood can finally rest on, not the shifting sand of whether he measured up today, but the settled fact of a love that came for him before he had done anything to earn it. A man secure in that love no longer needs to conquer to prove himself, and no longer needs to disappear to avoid being the problem. He is free, for the first time, to simply serve.

A man who has to prove he is worth something will spend his strength on himself. A man who already knows he is loved can finally spend it on others.

This is why biblical masculinity cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, a checklist a man works through to certify himself as a real man. It flows from a heart that has been secured by grace, and it cannot be manufactured from the outside by willpower and rules. The rules produce Pharisees, men who perform the marks of godly manhood while their hearts remain as anxious and self serving as ever. The grace produces sons, men whose worth is settled and who can therefore stop performing and start giving. The difference between the two is invisible from a distance and total up close, and it is the difference between a man who is exhausting to live with and a man who is a shelter.

The pattern is a man on a cross who could have come down and chose not to, for the sake of people who did not deserve it and had not asked. Everything I know about being a man that is worth passing to my sons, I know from looking at him. And everything in me that still needs to die, I know is exposed by the same light. That is the honest position. Not a man who has arrived at biblical masculinity and now dispenses it. A man still being remade by it, one Tuesday at a time.
excerpt: Neither the cultural left nor the evangelical right has given us a faithful picture of manhood. The Bible offers not a checklist but a cruciform pattern that dismantles every comfortable mythology.

title: Fatherhood: The Most Overlooked Ministry
body:
There is a strange silence in the church about the most consequential thing most men will ever do. We will spend a Sunday celebrating the missionary who spent two years in a difficult country. We will honor the man who left his career to plant a church. We will build entire services around vocational calling and radical obedience. And we will say almost nothing, from any pulpit, to the man sitting in the fourth row who is shaping five human souls at his kitchen table every single morning and has no idea that he is doing ministry at all.

I want to argue that fatherhood is not a lesser calling that some men happen to have alongside their real work. For most of the men reading this, fatherhood is the real work. It is the most sustained, most intimate, most eternally significant ministry they will ever be given, and the church has largely failed to tell them so.

The ministry no one applauds

Part of the reason we overlook it is that fatherhood produces no measurable numbers. A pastor can report baptisms. A missionary can report converts. A conference speaker can report attendance. But what does a father report. That he was patient at dinner. That he did not lose his temper in the car. That he prayed with a frightened child at two in the morning and forgot it by breakfast. None of this shows up on a spreadsheet. None of it will be mentioned from a stage. And so the man begins to believe, without anyone ever saying it directly, that this part of his life is not really the important part. The important part is out there, where the applause is.

This is a lie, and it is a lie with a very long tail. Because the father who believes it will pour himself into the arenas that reward him and give his children the exhausted remnant. He will be present at the church and absent at home. He will disciple other people's teenagers and be a stranger to his own. And he will do all of it with a clear conscience, because everyone around him is telling him that his kingdom work is what happens under a steeple, not what happens under his own roof.

A man will be tempted to give his best hours to the place that applauds him and his leftover hours to the people who need him most.

What a father actually transmits

Consider what is really being handed down at that breakfast table. A child does not learn who God is primarily from a sermon. A child learns who God is from a father, long before the child has language for it. Every time a father is faithful, the child's imagination of a faithful God is quietly built. Every time a father is absent, or cruel, or distracted, or unpredictable, that too is being written into the child's picture of the divine, in a place too deep for later argument to reach.

This is a terrifying thing to say out loud, and I say it as a man who has failed at it. My children's earliest and most durable sense of what a father is, they got from me, not from a book. When they hear that God is a Father, they will not run that word through a dictionary. They will run it through me. If I was harsh, God will feel harsh until grace does surgery on the memory. If I was distant, God will feel distant. If I was safe, they will have a head start on trusting a God they cannot see.

No missionary carries a weight like this. The missionary influences strangers for a season. The father shapes the deepest instincts of a soul that will exist forever, in the years when the clay is softest and the hands leave the deepest prints. If we understood this, we would treat the ordinary father with the reverence we reserve for the ordained.

The ministry of showing up

Let me be concrete, because I distrust sermons on fatherhood that stay in the clouds. The ministry of a father is not mostly made of the big moments. It is not the annual trip or the perfect Christmas or the one profound conversation. Those are real, but they are the exceptions, and children know it. What forms them is the accumulation, the ten thousand small hours.

It is the fact that you were there at pickup. That you knew the name of the friend and the name of the teacher and the name of the thing they were afraid of. That you noticed when they came home different and asked about it instead of turning on the television. That you were, above all, predictable, in the good sense, so that a child could build a life on the assumption that Dad would be where Dad said he would be. Presence is not glamorous. It cannot be photographed. But it is the raw material of everything.

Children do not remember the days you gave them. They remember that you were the kind of man who gave them the days.

I have watched men grasp this too late. Men whose children are grown and gone, who suddenly realize that the years they thought were preliminary were in fact the whole thing. That the career they were building toward some future season of presence was the very thing that stole the season from them. The season never comes later. There is no later. The children get older on schedule whether the father is watching or not.

The father as pastor of a small church

The most useful reframe I can offer a father is this. You are the pastor of a very small church. Your household is a congregation of a few souls, and you have been given spiritual authority over them, and you will give an account for how you shepherded them. This is not a metaphor to inflate the ordinary. It is a description of the actual structure the Scriptures assume. When Paul lists the qualifications for an elder, he asks whether the man manages his own household well, because the home is the training ground and the test of every other kind of leadership.

So think of your family as a flock. What does the pastor of a small church do. He teaches. He prays for his people by name. He knows their struggles. He is present in their crises. He models repentance when he fails them. He does not pretend to a perfection they can see through. He points them, again and again, past himself to the God he serves. Every one of these is available to you at your own table, tonight, without a title or a seminary degree or anyone's permission.

And here is the sobering symmetry. A man can be a competent pastor of a large church and a negligent pastor of the small one at home, and the Scripture is clear about which failure disqualifies him. We have it backward. We honor the man who succeeds publicly and shrug at his private neglect. God asks about the household first.

The discipleship that happens in the ordinary

Let me press further on what this ministry actually consists of, because I fear that even calling fatherhood a ministry can inflate it into something ceremonial, something a man does at set times with a Bible open. That is a small part of it, and not the largest. The formation of a child happens mostly in the unscheduled hours, in the car and at the sink and in the moments of interruption that a busy man is tempted to treat as obstacles to his real work. Those interruptions are the real work.

A father disciples his children not primarily through the family devotional, valuable as that may be, but through ten thousand ordinary responses to ordinary situations. How he reacts when the milk is spilled. Whether he tells the truth when a small lie would be easier. How he speaks about the neighbor he dislikes, the boss who treated him unfairly, the driver who cut him off. His children are watching all of it, absorbing a theology of daily life that no formal lesson could ever install, learning what it looks like to be a person who believes what this family claims to believe. The catechism is real, but the deeper catechism is the father's character under pressure, observed daily, unedited.

This is why fatherhood is such a searching ministry. It cannot be performed. A man can prepare a sermon and deliver a version of himself for forty minutes. He cannot prepare his whole life, and his children see the whole life, the unprepared parts most of all. They see him tired, they see him frightened about money, they see him at his least impressive, and they are forming their picture of God out of exactly those moments. The ministry of fatherhood is the ministry of being watched at your worst by the people whose souls you most want to protect, which is why it drives a man to grace faster than almost anything else. He cannot fake his way through it. He can only be honest, repent when he fails, and trust that God works even through a flawed father who is trying.

A word to the men who feel too late

Some men reading this are already grieving. The children are older, the pattern is set, the distance is real, and the temptation is to conclude that the ministry was missed and cannot be recovered. I want to speak against that despair, gently and firmly.

The ministry of fatherhood does not end when the children grow up. It changes shape. An adult child can still receive a father's repentance. A father can still, at sixty, go to a thirty year old son and name specifically the ways he failed him and ask his forgiveness, and something can be healed that no amount of earlier presence would have healed as deeply. It is never too late to become the father God is calling you to be, because the God who calls is a Father who restores the years the locusts have eaten.

The long view of a father's work

There is a temptation, in the middle of the exhausting years, to measure fatherhood by the day and to despair. A father comes to the end of a long day, having lost his patience twice and connected meaningfully with no one, and he concludes he is failing. But fatherhood is not measured by the day. It is measured by the decade, and by the direction of a life, and by the accumulation of ordinary faithfulness across years that no single day can reveal. The father who shows up, again and again, imperfectly, is building something that will not be visible for a very long time.

I have found it steadying to remember that God himself works this way with us, as a Father whose formation of his children unfolds across a whole life and is rarely visible in any given season. He is patient with the slow work, unbothered by the days that seem to accomplish nothing, faithful across the long arc when the results cannot yet be seen. A human father is invited into that same patience with his own children, released from the tyranny of measuring today and freed to trust the long work of a lifetime of presence. The seeds a father plants in a small child may not visibly grow for twenty years, and some of the most important ones will only bear their fruit after the father is gone.

Fatherhood is not measured by any single day. It is measured by the direction of a life, and most of its fruit ripens after the father can no longer see it.

It also helps to remember that our children do not need a perfect father, and in fact would not know what to do with one. A flawless father would give a child no template for grace, no picture of failure and repair, no model of how a good man handles his own wrongdoing. What our children need is a present father who is honest about his failures and faithful across the long arc, and that kind of father, imperfect and repentant and there, is available to any man willing to keep showing up. The pursuit of the perfect fatherhood is itself a trap, because it can drive a man to despair over the failures that were always going to happen, when what his children actually needed was not his perfection but his presence and his honesty about its absence.

So the father who feels he is failing on a particular Tuesday should take heart. The ministry is not the flawless day. The ministry is the faithful direction, held across years, through the failures and the repentances and the ordinary unremarkable presence that a child absorbs without either of them noticing. That is a ministry no applause will ever reach, and it is among the most important work being done anywhere on earth, and the God who assigned it is watching it with a father's own attention, and he does not overlook what the church so often does.

But do not use grace as an excuse to keep waiting. If your children are still in the house, the hour is now, and it is short, and it is holy. Put down the thing that has your best hours. Look at the small congregation God has entrusted to you. Learn their names again. This is not a distraction from your ministry. For most of you, this is your ministry, and it always was, and heaven has been watching it all along even when the church was looking somewhere else.
excerpt: We celebrate the men who plant churches and cross oceans, and we say almost nothing to the man who is quietly shaping eternal souls at his own breakfast table.

title: The Father Wound and the God Question
body:
I came to faith out of atheism, and I was raised without a father, and I have come to believe those two facts are not unrelated. For years I would not have connected them. I thought my unbelief was a matter of argument, a conclusion I had reached by reason, a position I could defend. It took me a long time to see that underneath the arguments was a wound, and that the wound was shaped exactly like a father, and that a great deal of what I called thinking was actually grieving in disguise.

This is dangerous territory, and I want to walk it carefully, because there is a cheap version of what I am about to say. The cheap version claims that all atheism is just father issues, that no one really disbelieves for honest reasons, that every skeptic is simply a hurt child throwing a tantrum at the sky. That is false, and it is insulting, and it lets believers dodge the actual questions. So let me say clearly, the arguments matter, the questions are real, and a wound does not make an objection wrong. But a wound does shape the ground the arguments grow in. And most of us never examine the ground.

The picture underneath the thought

Here is what I have come to understand. No one meets the concept of God as a blank slate. By the time a person is old enough to consider whether there is a Father in heaven, that person has already spent years with a father, or with the absence of one, on earth. And that earthly experience has already laid down a picture, a felt sense, an emotional template of what the word father means. When the theological word arrives, it does not land on clean ground. It lands on top of the picture that is already there.

So the man whose father was a tyrant hears that God is a Father, and something in him flinches before he has thought a single thought, because in his body father means the one who is never satisfied, the one whose approval could not be earned, the one whose mood set the weather of the whole house. He may go on to construct sophisticated reasons for rejecting God. But the flinch came first, and the reasons came to justify the flinch.

We think we are reasoning about God. Often we are only defending ourselves against a father who is no longer in the room.

The man whose father was absent hears that God is a Father, and the word lands on emptiness. Not on tyranny, on absence, which is its own kind of wound and in some ways a deeper one. A tyrant at least proves that the father exists and that you matter enough to be controlled. Absence proves nothing except that you were not worth staying for. That was my inheritance. And so when I heard, as a young man, that there was a Father in heaven who saw me and knew me and would not leave, the honest response of my heart was not argument. It was a bitter laugh. Fathers leave. That was the one thing I knew for certain. That was the truest fact of my life.

How the wound disguises itself as reason

The most important thing I can tell a skeptic, and I say it as a former one, is not that your arguments are bad. Some of them are quite good, and Christians should stop pretending otherwise. The most important thing I can tell you is that you may not know what you are actually arguing with. You think you are examining a proposition. You may be defending yourself against a memory.

I know this because I did it. I built a case against God that was intellectually respectable, and I believed the case was the reason. It was only years later, well after I had come to faith, that I could look back and see the machinery underneath. The passion in my atheism, the heat of it, the way it mattered so much more than a mere metaphysical conclusion should matter, that heat did not come from logic. Logic is cool. My unbelief was hot. And the heat came from the wound. I was not calmly concluding there was no God. I was angrily insisting there had better not be, because if there were a Father, then the Father had watched my father leave and had done nothing.

That is the real objection underneath many objections. Not is there a God, but if there is a God, where was he. And that question does not yield to argument, because it is not fundamentally a question of the mind. It is a wound in the shape of a question. You cannot reason someone out of a grief they have mistaken for a conclusion.

The two roads out

So what happens to the wound. In my experience there are two roads, and most men take the first without noticing.
